Mr. Hornsby to Mr. Redington.

I AM directed to forward you, for tlie information of his Excellency the 
Lord Lieutenant, the enclosed copy of report from the Board's officer, tot-ether 
with copy of certificate from the foreman of the jury assembled at the coroner's 
inquest, held at Castletown Roche, on the body of Patrick Daly, who was em- 
ployed on the Public Works at Ballyadeen, and alleged to have died from

Enclosure. 

Mr. Wilson to Mr. Patterson. 

Castletown Roche, December 23, 1846. 

A report of the particulars connected with the employment of the late Patrick Dab- 
on the. Ballyadeen Public Works may be acceptable, and the move particularly as the facts 
detailed occurred immediately under my observation. 

Deceased immediately after quitting his employment on the Coni ngberry grand jury pre- 
sentment road where he was engaged during the past summer, applied to me for employment 
on the Public Works on the 9th November last, and not conceiving myself warranted in com- 
plying with his application, independently of the sanction of the "engineer in charge 1 con- 
sequently refused, having at the same time the number of persons, as appointed for employment 
on the works, completed, as also a very disproportionate supply of implements to keep those 
iairly engaged; at about 11 o’clock on the same day, Mr. Moore, who has entitled himself to 
the gratitude of the labouring classes of this district, arrived, and immediately, on deceased’s 
application to him for employment, ordered him to be enrolled. He, the deceased, procured a 
spade and shovel, with which he employed himself until the evening of that day, and had been 
allowed a full day s pay. Deceased absented himself the following day until the 11th and 
then remained at work until Saturday the 14th, on which day he again disappeared he never 
at anytime assigning a reason to me why he, for twice during that week, deserted his employ- 
ment, out of which he remained till he died, which, I believe, occurred on or about the 22nd. 
of the same month. I must observe, that his second return to his employment was attributable 
to my sending a messenger for him. 

Deceased had been several times requested by Mr. Smith, of Renny, on whose property he 
lived, to become an inmate of the Fermoy Union workhouse, which he as often indignantly 
refused and objected to ; and also his- (Mr. Smith’s) steward, Russell, assured me that a few 
days previous to the interment of deceased, he, the deceased, had the sum of two pounds in’er- 
sown between the lapelle of his body coat. r 

Surgeon Tuckey (the dispensarian of this district) who attended, and operated at the post 
mortem examination of deceased, discovered in (lie stomach the presence of mixed portions of 
animal and vegetable composition, which he considered would be sufficient to sustain existence, 
had not sufferings arising from manifold privations, to which deceased had been exposed 
existed at the then particularly inclement season. I herewith transmit you, enclosed, a certifi- 
cate signed by the foreman who attended the inquest, which, coupled with the foregoing facts 
renders apparent any attempt to account for deceased’s death, otherwise than herein represented’ 
both ungenerous and unfounded. 1 ’ 



I certify as foreman juror at a coroner’s inquest held at Castlefown Roche on the 
body of Patrick Daly, deceased, who was alleged came by his death from starvation, that after 
a close examination of several witnesses, amongst whom was Surgeon Tuckey, I, in con- 
junction with my brother jurors, were unanimous in our verdict that deceased came by his 
death induced by numerous privations, particularly the want of day and night covering - and 
that, m our opinion, the wretched and filthy hovel in which he lived, having its roof opened to 
the elements of the heavens, and having no other bed than a litter of dung to lie on was the 
principal cause of death, which I certify this 23rd day of December, 1846. 

(Signed) Henry B. Goold, Foreman.

Extract from the Clare Journal of Thursday, January 7, 1847. 

Public Distress. “ 

“ We fiad our space utterly insufficient for placing before our readers 
“ the heart-rending and constantly increasing statements on this subject. 
“ Throughout the entire extent of this county destitution prevails to a frightful 
“ ^nt, but perhaps in no part of it is the condition of the people more pain- 
“ fully distressing than in Kilkee and the surrounding country. We learn from 
“ the ‘ Limerick Reporter,’ that on Friday last a deputation from that district 
“ °* °ur county waited upon Mr. Labouchere, to represent to him the present 
“ condition of the people, and to solicit the Government for further relief. The 
“ deputation consisted of Henry Stewart Burton, Esq., D.L., Carrigaholt Castle; 
“ the Rev. James Martin, Protestant Rector; and the Rev. Messrs. Comynand 
“ Duggan, parish priests. These gentlemen represented to the Chief Secretary 
“ that the people at present employed on the public works in the district do not 
“ amount to more than 1 in 7k of the destitute ; that the men are actually seen 
“ to stagger on the works, and the stewards state that hundreds of them are 
“ never seen to taste food from the time they come upon the works in the 
“ morning until they depart at nightfall; and it was confidently stated by the 
“ deputation, and offered to be sustained by proof, that 200 persons and upwards 
“ had fallen victims to the destitution in the parishes of Kilfeera and Killard ; 
“ that on the Saturday previous oatmeal sold at Kilkee at the rate of 5s. per 
“ stone, and that to afford one meal in the day to the destitute people of that 
“ district would require 1500/. per w r eek ! The people have pledged their day- 
f< clothes and night covering, and they have, after a hard day’s work, to lie down 
“ at night on a bed of straw, without a blanket or coverlet of any kind. The 
“ horses in the district are so ill-fed, that it is supposed impossible they can be 
“equal to the spring work, or the people either. It was represented* that in 
*' th e district of Kilfeera and Killard there are 20,000 acres of bog, which have 
“ a fall at either side to the Shannon and the sea, and it is estimated that 11. per 
“ acre would suffice for its reclamation, for sea sand is to be had at each side; 
“ and it was urged upon the Government that the people should be located on 
“ the waste lands, in preference to the colonial lands. The deputation were 
“kindly received by the Under Secretary, and were also promised assistance 
(i both by the Commissary- General and the Commissioners of Public Works. 
“ Sir Randolph Routh advised that local subscriptions should be forthwith col- 
" lec.ted, which was met by the deputation reminding him that in a district of 
“ 26 miles long by 7 wide there was only one resident landlord, Mr. Burton, 
“ whose benevolence it was impossible to surpass, upon which he stated that 
“ ^ey ought to make trial, and he would promise on the part of the Govern- 
“ ment that a grant equal in amount would be given.” 

Great destitution undoubtedly exists in the district referred to, but certainly 
not from “ insufficient employment .” The proportion at present employed is 
one in five of the whole, and about one in four of the destitute population, 
according to the census of 1841. Increased employment ■will no doubt benefit 
individuals who can afford to keep the money expended in their locality, but 
where the scarcity of the commodity causes the remnant to run up to the un- 
precedented price of 5s. per stone for oatmeal,* I cannot see how advanced 
wages or increased employment can remedy the evil, which arises not from 
want of means to purchase food, but from the absence or scarcity of that food. 

F ood, or our worst anticipations, I fear, will be realized, and that ere long. 

Edmund Wynne.

I wish it were possible to get possession of the Stationery Office apartments. 
In this building we are dreadfully pinched for accommodation ; I have been 
obliged to give up our Board-room to clerks, as well as our waiting room. This 
puts us all to great inconvenience, for the consequence is everybody is incom- 
moded, and our corridors are filled with strangers waiting for interviews, and 
many seize us when passing from one office to another. 

Our country accounts continue much the same, complaining of a scarcity of 
food in the country, and the absence of tillage, and high prices ; there have hem 
large quantities of grain imported. The demand for farinaceous food is very 
general, and not confined to those who generally live upon and depend upon the 
potato, but the upper classes who made use of that vegetable now use bread 
stuff to replace it. I understand that the deposits in the branches of the Bank 
of Ireland are increasing very much, and this, coupled with what was contained 
in a paper I sent lately respecting the withdrawal by the National Bank in 
Wicklow of their advances to farmers, See., is by many considered indicative of 
some commotion being likely to take place. I merely mention this that you 
may be aware of what is passing in the minds of the people, and those of a 
superior class. 

I am very glad Parliament is so soon to meet, for our system could not con- 
tinue under such a regular increase, and we may hope some beneficial change 
will be made. The bow may be kept bent too long. I must do all my people 
the justice to say that they have done their work well, but at the same time 
none of us are the better for it; there is no excitement in it — mere drudgery.

Mr. Lowe to Lieut.-Colonel Jones. 

Sir, limoleague, January 8, 1847- 

In accordance with your instructions I again address you. 

I regret to say that since I last had this pleasure a change for the worse has taken place 
throughout this neighbourhood. Although works are in operation in almost every locality, 
the relief afforded is unable to keep pace with the increasing destitution, and it is only partial 
in its effects, taking into consideration the numbers who get employment, or the wages earned, 
compared with the price of provisions. Indian and wheaten meal are both selling at 2s. 6 d. 
per 14 lbs. ; at this rate a family consisting of five persons cannot, out of the wages of one 
person, say 6s. per week, have even two meals per diem for more than four days in the week. 
I fear that prices must range still higher, as the quantity of home-grown corn is now reduced 
to a small compass, and that principally in the possession of persons who will keep it for their 
own consumption, and the late importations from abroad seem to have had no effect on the 
markets. The prospects for next year are even more gloomy than the present, as farming ope- 
rations are at a complete stand-still, no preparation being made for green crops, and ground fit 
to receive seed for a crop of corn not sown in many places. 

It may seem irrelevant in my expressing an opinion on political economy, still I cannot avoid 
saying that emigration offers one of the best modes of enabling us to get through "the crisis,” 
and it has one material point to recommend it, namely, that it coincides, as I have reason to 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 



6 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



believe, with the wishes of the people themselves. I have no doubt that it will bo carried out 
to some extent by one class of the community without the aid of legislative interference. I mean 
by those farmers who have made the present calamity a pretext for not paying either their rents 
or other claims upon them, and having sold their stock and corn are preparing with the proceeds 
thereof to remove themselves out of the country. We have, however, the “ labouring poor” to 
provide for, who have not the means to purchase even a change of raiment, much Jess pay 
passage money and procure provisions for a voyage; the expense of their trausit must therefore 
be defrayed out of some public fund. The plan I would adopt for their conveyance would be 
to make our vessels used as transports for troops available for the purpose of carrying them to 
whatever colony they are disposed to go to, and the sum that, would be paid for passage-money 
to a merchant vessel, say 21. to 31. per head, would be a great assistance either to procure outfit 
here or to support them till they could get employment, in their adopted country. As, however, 
the offer of a “ free passage” would hold out inducements to imposition by making persons who 
could afford to pay for their removal feign inability to do so, a certificate furnished by some 
controlling body, similar to the present Relief Committees, should be made the condition on 
which any person would be taken on board, due regard being bad that only a proportion of the 
population (the per centage to be fixed by law) be allowed to leave any townlancl. 

I observe that the Board are earning a revision to bo made of the check clerks employed on 
Relief Works. If I might take the liberty of offering a suggestion, it would be that persons of 
known integrity , above suspicion, and having a knowledge of the people in their neighbourhood, 
be appointed. My reason for this remark is, that I believe persons arc at work who have no 
right (o be so, owing partly to the check clerk’s being a stranger in the locality, and there- 
fore ignorant of the people. It would also be advisable to have an inspector of check olorks, 
whose duty would be to be constantly passing through the. works in his district, and see that 
the check clerk is in regular attendance , and keeping a proper account of the men and the work 
executed. I believe in many cases this is taken from the gangsman’s account, and not from 
their own personal inspection. The check clerk should be prepared at all times to hand to the 
inspector the relief lists, or a copy thereof, to enable him to check the numbers at work. 



Captain Froode to Mr. Walker. 

Swineford, January 8, 1847. 

After minute enquiry, and personal observation, so far as I have travelled through my 
districts, I think it right to bring to your notice the frightful prospects for this country. Desti- 
tution is greater than can well be described, even at present.; but what it. will be in the course 
of two or three months no one can foretell. The price of food is enormous ; and even wore 
the markets down to the usual rate, unless an abundant supply of foreign provisions shortly 
comes into the country, the consequences must be most disastrous. Next year will be much 
worse than this, as beyond a dispute there is nothing like a sufficiency of grain in the country 
to crop the land, not taking inlo consideration the numbers of acres formerly planted with 
potatoes, as well as the fact that whatever quantity of land may be seeded, owing to the want 
of manure, no great return can be expected. Altogether it is a very disheartening slate of 
affairs, at. least it strikes me as such, being a stranger to the scenes I witness, and the back- 
ward state of cultivation. I was present yesterday at the meeting of the Guardians for the 
Swineford Poor Law Union, and positively had not Mr. Jackson and two other gentleman come 
forward and entered into personal security for the payment of provisions for one week, 050 
paupers must have been turned out of the poor house and taken to begging, by which they 
° 0l » d ’ as things are at present, get nothing, and could only add to the list of claimants for the 
Relief VV orks, which are already overburthened. My life is u constant worry ; from morning 
until night, my house is beset with men, women and children, all crying together, and say in" 
I can save them by giving them an order to work; they have an idea that" my power is un- 
limited, and that I can authorize the expenditure of any sum of money. 



Captain Wynne to Mr. Walker. 

Miltown Malbay , January 12, 1847. 

I have the honour to enclose you a letter which was handed me in the 
Court-house at Ennistimon during the sessions yesterday. 

In passing through the crowd about 60 letters were given me, which I had 
not time to open till I got to the jury room, where I found the enclosed amongst 
them. ° 

R was handed to the bench of magistrates by Captain Macnamara, and 
elicited their strong reprobation expressed in a resolution, accompanied by a sub- 
scription and reward for the discovery of the writer. 

I am bound to add that the magistrates and other gentlemen present availed 
themselves ot the opportunity of expressing themselves most strongly in appro- 
bation oi my conduct since my arrival in this country.

BOARD OF WORKS: 



7 



I can scarcely lie surprised at any insult or violence that may he offered to 
me, when I am constantly held up as standing between the people and employ- 
ment for daring to reject some of the recommendations of the Committees. 

I do not, however, anticipate any violence ; I feel assured that there is not a 
man in Clare will attempt it, prepared as they know I am on all occasions. 

The pressure for increased employment is almost irresistible ; from some 
quarters there is a demand for double the number at present employed. 

I scarcely know what course to. take ; the people are starving notwithstanding- 
the enormous extent of employment, which it is scarcely possible to increase 
without producing disorder and confusion. I must declare my inability to feed 
the people on employment or money. I have stated this frequently, but 
consider it my duty to repeat it again and again ; the supplies of food obtainable 
from day to day do not give the people a meal a-day.

Lieut.-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works , Dublin, January 13, 1847. 

I have just completed the perusal of the weekly reports from our In- 
specting Officers, and the impression they have made upon my mind is anything 
but cheering ; many of the Relief Committees are very troublesome, forgetful 
of the object for which they were constituted, and apparently have only one 
end in view, which is to get as many persons employed as possible, instead of 
anxiously endeavouring to keep the numbers as low as the existing calamity 
will permit. The pressure upon some of our officers is so great that they 
have felt themselves forced to yield, or else to refuse all, and by so doing 
to draw down upon themselves and the Board all the odium and vindictive 
feelings of the poorer classes. I believe we have reached the utmost point to 
which we can find work, that is, road making. It may be a very consolatory 
reflection for gentlemen to know that they have voted thousands and thousands 
of pounds for work, without considering how it is to be expended, and very 
probably at the moment they did so, they were well aware that neither the 
Board nor its officers could find roads to make or improve which would afford 
employment. They cry out that the great communications of the country are 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




8 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



destroyed, and I have no doubt that for this season they arc all more or less 
severely injured and many nearly impassable, but whose fault is that ? not ours. 

You will observe with regret, the serious apprehensions which many of the 
officers entertain of the mortality which will occur from the want of provisions, 
and that within a very short period. I allude to Leitrim, Roscommon, Galway, 
Mayo, Clare, Kerry, Cork, and Tipperary as well as Wicklow. I am well 
aware that the tillage of the land and seed has occupied and still occupies the 
attention of Government. 

It is really provoking to hear the calmness with which people talk. 
They say the period has not arrived. All the great farming operations 
are regulated by particular days in the calendar and not by the season ; 
and it is generally admitted that the cropping of land is performed too 
late, and such would appear likely to take place this year. I cannot help 
thinking that the Agricultural Society has not put forth all its energies or 
turned its attention to questions of vital importance by pointing out through 
their agents what was proper to be done with the land, so {is to ensure early 
crops; here we are in the middle of January, the land unfilled and choked 
with weeds, and no preparation in the way of seed. It has been suggested to 
us by several individuals, that in order to force the tillage, all the Public 
Works should be stopped for a fortnight or three weeks. I do not think, con- 
sidering the numbers looking to us for their daily support, that such could now 
be done; but it only shows what opinions there are upon the subject, and the 
conviction that nothing but some very decisive steps on the part of Government 
will accomplish it, is beginning to force itself apon men’s minds. There is a great 
delusion about emigration. It is generally supposed that all the small farmers 
are hoarding all the money they can procure in order to make a stock for the 
spring, when they intend to bolt, leaving their landlords in the lurch. 



Enclosure. 

Mr. Gamble lo Mr. Radcliff. 

Ennis, January 9, 1847. 

It was ray intention long since to have written to you relative to my district, as 1 have 
good reason to know you are not indifferent as to how I am getting on. 

I delayed writing in the hope of being able in some time to give you a satisfactory account 
of the state of things here ; but that time appears to be now receding instead of approaching, 
and my chief hope now is, that a termination will soon be put to a system of relief altogether 
unsmted to the emergency. 

In my seven baronies I have 33,000 individuals employed, and yet there remains much un- 
relieved destitution, and the poorest class of the people can only be saved from starvation by 
the introduction of large quantities of food, and by gratuitous relief in some instances. 

Modes of relief suited to more favoured localities, are altogether unsuited to this ovor-popu- 
lated poor district, which now possesses scarcely any provisions; the introduction oi' large 
quantities of which by Government, be the consequences what they may, is the only way of 
mitigating the sufferings of the people. 

Notwithstanding the vast numbers now employed, there are hourly applications for further 
employment which cannot be attended to. Give us food or wo perish. Already there have been 
many deaths, and our only chance is to have food introduced, and given directly or indirectly in 
exchange for labour to those able to work; and gratuitously to the inlirm, whoso removal from 
the Public Works would facilitate their execution. 

There is no hope of any effort, being made by the landed proprietors to meet the emergency 
by undertaking reproductive works, nor will subscriptions to any amount be entered into. 

One great objection to undertaking reproductive works is, that, the landlords do not believe 
that they will be called upon to pay the present expenditure, and they think the hull- starved 
labourers would give but little value for their wages, so that if so dosirablo an object, as the 
general adoption of reproductive works is to be calculated upon, the non-oxoculion of them must 
be made in some degree penal. 

I am astonished at the Board being able to bear up against the immense mass of business 
pressing on them ; but where is this to end! I cannot see the termination. Captain Wynne, I 
need not say, is a most valuable officer; he and I work together most cordially, and will 
struggle to the last. 

Captain Wynne to Captain Wynne, R. E. 

Ennis, January 9, 1847. 

I received a very kind and encouraging letter from Larcom to-day, which is some 
corsolation under the frightful pressure upon me this moment, from the. unprincipled conduct of 
the Committees; they are sending in upon me lists containing thousands of names, which it is

9 



quite impossible to employ, even if they required employment. I have come to a stand still ; 
shut shop. They refuse no applicant, and throw the entire odium of refusal on me. You may 
imagine whal the consequence is the last two days ; I am hunted by thousands accusing me of 
refusing them relief, and intending to starve them. I am puzzled how to meet this move of 
the Committees. I am afraid they will checkmate me ; however I shall persevere to the end, 
only taking a little additional care and precaution, which will be now indispensable, as I fear 
my popularity, even amongst the very poor class, is at an end for a while. From my know- 
ledge of the people, and from various inquiries I have made amongst them, I am clearly of 
opinion that the plan of paying which I send you, would knock a third of the people off the 
Public Works, viz., to pay in food instead of cash. The Committees, who at present receive a 
portion of the cash payment in the shape of rent, dues, §c., would no longer have this induce- 
ment to be dishonest, and few men would work for food who had it of their own ; many would 
be ashamed to work for meal who would not scruple to grasp at cash under any circumstances ; 
the circulation of food would insure us against starvation ; whilst the circulation of money is a 
strong temptation to dishonesty. 

I have no doubt of this plan having the effect of sending thousands to till their farms, and 
thereby saving the country. 

I start on a tour of the district to morrow, and shall not return till this day week. I am not 
sorry to get away for some time from my people here, but fear they will be as bad everywhere 
else. I go on Monday to Ennistimon, to the Extraordinary Presentment Sessions.

Mr. M'Elligott to Captain Hill. 

January 10, 1847. 

I am just going to Glenpatrick Road, No. 71, as I am just informed by the overseer 
that the people employed, upwards of 240, broke out from his charge yesterday, and wan- 
tonly undertook to ruin the line of road by levelling fences, and all before them for upwards of 
two miles through the country, far beyond where the road was to terminate, and in a contrary 
direction to where we intended running it, and I understand they have done considerable injury 
to the farmers in the neighbourhood. There was no necessity whatever for this sort of conduct, 
as the people had plenty of employment on the part of the road in progress for six weeks, and 
were regularly paid ; but I am informed that the people were directed to do it by some persons 
concerned, who wished to have the road run in a contrary direction to that approved of by the 
county surveyor. 

T have written to Captain B. Mayne on the matter, and I think it right to apprise you as the 
inspecting officer. 

In my visit to Glenpatrick yesterday, I only escaped these foolish people with my life, having 
been pulled off my horse in order to force me to turn the line of road in a contrary direction, . 
encouraged as I could see, bv a farmer named Inply, who lives in the locality, and who boldly 
told me that it should not go on otherwise but as he wished, and I fear it was he encouraged 
the people employed to act as they did. Upwards of 200 of them collected around me, and in 
fact would not let me look in the direction the road should properly be laid out. 



Captain Hart to the Military Secretary. 

Dundalk, January 12, 1847. 

I beg leave to enclose a copy of a letter from the resident engineer of the barony of 
Ardee, county of Louth. 

This county has been very peaceable and quiet hitherto ; but the high prices of provisions 
are creating very great discontent. The people are beginning to evince a turbulent spirit. I 
am no alarmist ; but it is my decided opinion that if provisions do not very soon fall in price, 
the peace of the county will be broken, unless another detachment or two of troops be stationed 
in it. The localities I would suggest would be Ardee and Carlingford ; and if a small detach- 
ment could be at once sent to Ardee, I think it would have the very best effect, as well to curb 
a turbulent spirit among a number of discontented people, as to reassure the peaceably disposed, 
many of whom feel in considerable alarm. Every exertion has been and is still making to 
put every destitute person into employment on the Relief Works ; but the evil-disposed, owing

Enclosure. 

Mr. Browne to Mr. Smith. 

Ballingarry, January 23, 1847. 

I have to report that about 4 o’clock p.m. on the 22nd inst., eight men, two of them 
armed with blunderbusses, five with guns, and the other with a bayonet fixed on a stick, and 
having their faces blackened, came on the old road leading from Kilmihill to Ballyscanlon, 
where a number of men are employed improving and lowering hills under the Board of Works, 
and asked for the steward, William Hederman, as they passed along the works, and went into 
the houses of Tobias Roche and John Harrington of Ballyclan to search for him ; and as they 
went on they met him, and asked was he steward ; and on his answering in the affirmative, 
one of them struck him on the head with a gun, which cut him ; they then placed him on his 
knees, and gave him another blow on the head and one on the side. Hederman asked them 
why they beat him? and they said because he rated some men on the works higher than others. 

Three brothers, named John, Patrick, and Michael Reidy, and a man named James 
Hanrahan of Ballyclan, convenient to the works in question, seeing the armed party running 
along the road, followed them and came up to them while Hederman was on his knees, and 
said they would not permit him to be beaten, and to desist from doing so at once ; and as they 
were closing upon them, one of the party turned round and missed fire at Michael Reidy. 
Hanrahan was also closing on them, and another of them made a blow at him. On the fellows 
seeing that it was likely resistance would be made, and the men engaged on the works being 
collecting, they made off through the fields in the direction of Ballyvelogue ; they were followed 
some short distance by the above named, with several others who were striking off work. 

On hearing of the outrage I proceeded with five men in the direction, but got no clue to the 
parties. Hederman and several others who saw them deny any knowledge of them, nor can 
they give a description of their persons. 

Received from Mr. Smith this report at 12 o'clock, 23rd inst. 

(Signed) T. Fitzroy De Courcy, 

Lieut. 47th Regiment. 



Lieut. De Courcy to Mr. Walker. 

Rathkeale, County Limerick , 
January 24, 1847. 

With reference to my communication of yesterday’s date concerning the 
attack made by an armed party on the steward of the “ Kilmihill and Bally- 
scanlon” Public Work, barony Connelloe Upper, I proceeded to Ballingarry for 
the purpose of making the necessary inquiries. 

I found, on reaching that town, the steward and a number of men who had 
been employed on the Public Work above mentioned, aided by the constabulary 
officer, Mr. Smith, and others. I found no difficulty in commencing at once an 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 11 

investigation ; from which it appeared that the steward had not by any miscon- 
duct, but, on the contrary, probably, by a faithful discharge of his duties, given 
cause to the cruel and cowardly attack upon him. 

With respect to the conduct of the labourers on the road at the time of the 
attack, I am of opinion that had they so wished it, they might easily have pre- 
vented the attack, and perhaps have apprehended some o£ if not all, the parties 
concerned in the attack. 

I examined and questioned most carefully four men, who were mentioned as 
having attempted to prevent the attack; and, failing in this, afterwards pursued 
the armed party. 

The result of this investigation leads to form this opinion, that they were not 
over zealous in their endeavours to prevent the attack, however active they 
might have been afterwards in pursuing the armed party. 

But on this point I was only able to procure their own evidence as to their 
own exploits. In fact, I feel sure that these men were not over anxious to come 
up with those they were pursuing. The steward was severely cut on the back 
of the head ; and if he did not make any resistance, it was not, I think, from a 
want of will, but power on his part to deal alone with so strong a party. 

The armed party were for some time on the work, during which they were 
seen by several of the men employed thereon, and from one or two of them they 
asked for an answer to the repeated question put as to “ where the steward was.” 

These are, Sir, the best features of the case, and as yet the principal ones. 

To morrow another investigation will take place, I hope, under the stipendiary 
magistrate, Mr. Goold, who will, I am sure, do everything in his power that 
may tend to the apprehension and conviction of the parties implicated in this 
outrage. 

I need hardly say that this will be very difficult; but I can assure you that 
no exertions will be found wanting which may bring about so desirable an object, 
and one so beneficial as an example of this kind would be. 

I mentioned in my letter of 23rd inst that the Kilmihill and Ballyscanlon 
Public Work had been stopped by order of the engineer in charge. 

Should I receive any further information on this subject I shall lose no time 
in communicating it

Capt. Carey to Mr. Walker. 

Westport, January 12, 1847. 

I have to report that this morning I was obliged to order the work 
No. 361, Burrishoole-road, from Westport to Castlebar, in the barony of Burris- 
hoole, to be suspended, under the following circumstances : — 

It was reported to me, some days ago, by the engineer in charge of the district 
(Mr. Roberts), that it was desirable the two check clerks on the above line 
should be removed as soon as possible. I, consequently, sent a Mr. Flinn, to 
whom, however, the check clerks would not give up their books, &c., as they 
had been appointed by another person, nor would the labourers allow Mr. Flinn 
to perform his duty. I then had the appointments of the check clerks cancelled 
by Mr. Roberts, who had put them on. 

This day I found Mr. Flinn had been again prevented from checking the men. 
I went to the line with him and told the labourers that as he had been appointed 
by me, they must permit him to do his duty. They were very angry, and 
declared they would keep their old check clerks till they were paid everything. 
I explained, as well as I could to an angry mob, that the change of check 
clerks would not interfere with their being paid their balances, but that if they 
wished to continue working on that road, it must be under such persons as I 
thought fit to appoint. I moved on to see which gangs would allow Mr. Flinn 
to check them ; but the men collected and followed in such an angry manner 
that I was unable to do so ; and whilst crossing a drain I was suddenly pushed 
from behind, and one or two sods were thrown. As soon as I could get my face 
round towards them they declared it was accident, but as I could get no answer 
to my question who had done it, I desired the work to be suspended, and left 
them. Three gangs allowed Mr. Flinn to check them properly in the morn- 
ing, and were not present where I was in the afternoon ; these will, therefore, 
be allowed to continue working : one of the dismissed check clerks was on the 
line to-day, and was, no doubt, in part instigator of this conduct. 

I report this at length, in consequence of there being several hundred men 
on this line of the most discontented parts of my district. A cart was plun- 
dered this morning within a mile of this road, and I know some of the labourers 
were present. I explained the Board’s orders on this subject, but for want of 
available proof did not suspend the work on that account. 

I also this day had to dismiss four gangs, No. 29, Murrisk, who told an 
assistant engineer, yesterday evening, when setting the task, that if he came 
again he might as well bring his coffin with him. 



Mr. Frazer to Mr. Walker. 

Borris-in-Ossory, January 13, 1847. 

I have to report that for some time past a factious spirit has been 
evidenced amongst some of the labourers engaged upon the Shim-one district. 

They were dissatisfied at not getting high wages without working for them. 
They earned about ll^c?. per day. 

One or two of the gangers have used violent language and threats to the 
overseer whom I believe to be a very trustworthy person ; and on the night 
of the 8th instant four or five men attacked Daniel O’Brien, one of our own 
gangers, and would have beaten him severely, but that some persons came to 
his assistance; the object of the attack was clearly to intimidate O’Brien, and 
prevent him doing his duty. 

My assistant at Shihrone consulted the resident magistrate, Captain Kelly, 
and certain steps were taken which brought the case and the offenders yester- 
day before the magistrates. Several witnesses were examined, and the delin- 
quents were all convicted and bound over to keep the peace, severally giving 
security for 10/. and two sureties of 51. each. 

This summary justice has proved most satisfactory to all the other work- 
men, who feel indignant at the conduct of those who disturbed the peace. 

I trust the manner in which this affair has been dealt with will meet with 
the approbation of the Commissioners. 

My assistant states that many circumstances connected with the working of 
our system were examined in Court, and the result has been to increase their 
confidence in our operations.

I Have to report, that on Tuesday the labourers on the works at Moyout were hunted 
off the works by a party of disturbers who turned out against task work. I did my utmost to 
keep the men in tile work, but they were panic stricken, and I had to give in. I then 
lodged informations before the stipendiary magistrate, Mr. Barrow, who gave me summonses to 
have served on the ringleaders. On Wednesday I took the sessions bailiff, and when these

named Golden, when the fellows commenced throwing stones. As the quarrymen showed a 
determination to stick to their work, this being a partial outbreak, headed by persons from the 
Relief Works, I thought, it my duty to stand by the labourers iu preference to stopping the 
work. 

I succeeded in preserving order, and on Thursday had the fellow fined 51. ; and [a warrant 
has been issued against his goods, &c. 

The bench of magistrates expressed much pleasure at the steps I had taken, and declared in 
open Court their fixed determination to uphold our work and give us every support. I hope I 
may also have your approval. 



Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, January 16, 1847. 

It is, I am afraid, but too true that we have arrived at a very important 
crisis in our operations, and it has been so strongly forced upon us during the 
last few days, that we considered it to be our duty to bring the subject under the 
notice of the Lord Lieutenant ; and I now enclose a copy of the letter written to 
him upon the subject -of the overpowering demands made upon us for employment, 
and I may add our inability to meet them. The want of food drives everybody to 
the works ; we have neither staff, nor work upon which we can employ them, and 
if prompt measures are not taken, I do not know what will be the result. The 
accompanying copy of a letter this instant received from Lord Glengall, conveys a 
fair idea of the state of many parts of the country. As during the present week 
numerous additional works have been ordered, I have little doubt that the num- 
bers employed, amount to half a million; the weekly expenditure, calculated at Is. 
per head, would give a larger number.

The Commissioners of Public Works to the Lord Lieutenant. 

Office of Public Works, 
January 17, 1847. 

We beg to draw your Excellency’s attention to the numerous deputations which have 
recently come to Dublin for the purpose of waiting on your Excellency, who hare afterwards 
called on this Board, to represent the rapid increase of destitution in their several districts. 
Want of work and want of food have been the subject of their representations, and they work only 
as a means of obtaining food. All our reports codcut in stating that from want of food the men 
are becoming so weak as to be wholly unable to perform a fair day’s work. This has led ns 
seriously to consider the means of providing work to such an extent as must be necessary so 
long as it is the only means by which food can be obtained by numbers who are rapidly in- 
creasing.

During the week ending this day, judging by the money which has been issued on demand, 
it cannot be much less than 470,000, and we have reason to believe that even this number does 
not contain more than two-thirds of those who are already returned to us as destitute, although 
there are few cases in which more than one is taken from each family. 

It is therefore obvious that the works are insufficient, and it must be inferred that the point is 
passed at which it is possible to provide for the destitution by Public Works of the ordinary 
character, which alone are suitable to unskilled labour, and that other modes of relief are become 
indispensable. 

When the Act 9 Vic., ch. 1, and its sequel, 9 and 10 Vic., ch. 107, passed the Legislature, 
this extent of distress was not anticipated, and it might reasonably have been expected that the 
spare labour of 40 or 50 or even 100,000 men might have beeiv profitably employed on Public 
Works, but it. must be presumed that the employment of the whole labouring population of the 
country on Public Works was not expected. 

Public Works, indeed, properly so called, are in their nature the reverse of local works, and 
are therefore not suited for providing labour at every man’s door. It was only by a strained 
construction they could ever have been made so. Yet for a time they to some extent answered 
the purpose, but the degree to which they have been strained for this purpose produces in itself 
a great evil in the idle habits they engender, and the interference with more useful employments. 

As soon as it became apparent that the work was provided for the people and not the people 
for the work, the necessity for exertion was diminished. A labour ticket became as it were a 
bill at sight for 8 d. or 10J. a day, and where the increased price of provisions rendered these 
wages too small, great efforts were made to enforce task-work, by which higher wages could be 
obtained, and it was hoped industrious habits restored and maintained. But while the expen- 
diture was thus increased, the work was consumed more rapidly, and new works became sooner 
necessary, which became more and more difficult to provide from the impossibility of finding 
overseers qualified to estimate and measure tasks for 10,000 separate working parties. The 
task-works became paid for by subsistence, leaving the balance till the work could be measured, 
while the unequal strength of the men composing the gang so soon led to uncertainty as to the 
quota of work and profit to be performed or received by each, as gradually to leave the task- 
work only in reality a higher rate of daily pay, and at this moment the rate of pay which beo-an 
at 8rf. and KM. over the whole country, varies from 8 d. to Is. 4 d., averaging about Is. a day. 

This is a higher average rate than the farmers can afford to pay, even those who can pay, or 
have been accustomed to pay in money wages ; and payment in food, as in former years, there 
is now none : so that the Public Works offer a direct premium to labourers to quit their 
natural and useful occupation. They in fact afford subsistence to the agricultural labourer on 
condition that he leaves his work. 

Far better than such a result no doubt it would be, to give him the same rate of pay, on the 
certificate of a proper officer that he had worked on some farm, even if no security could be had 

of repayment from the crop, as from whatever source repayment may be assessed food for another 
year would result to the country. 

In viewing the class of works applied for and then granted, we find first, that many works in 
themselves useful have been of necessity rejected, as buildings, piers, and works of masonry or 
carpentry, generally because the work they provided was not suited for the class who required 
labour ; others, as arterial drainages through several lands, involved conflicting rights of pro- 
perties, and required the special provision of the Drainage Acts; others, of deepening beds of, 
or straightening considerable rivers, could nqf; be executed at this season. Thorough drainage 
remained, and this was promptly provided for by your Excellency’s letter of the 5th October, 
and was coming into operation, when it was to a great extent checked by the more favourable 
terms of the Treasury Minute of the 1st December, which has induced many proprietors to 
apply to withdraw their undertakings, and stopped any more from undertaking. These suc- 
cessive steps, however, leave no doubt that the Legislature will, at no distant period, provide 
suitable employment, so far as the evil can he met by employmunt, and the experience of the 
last four months will not be thrown away. 

It is to that experience we now appeal, whence we beg respectfully to represent, that to what- 
ever extent employment may he provided, first, by enabling proprietors to create a large mass 
of local employment, and second, by enabling us to devise and carry out Public Works, pro- 
perly so called, of a really useful and creditable character, by which we shall, in our legitimate 
capacity, minister to relief as employers of labour, there will yet remain a great number of 
unemployed, infirm, and destitute families, for whom relief must be sought from some more 
direct source than labour. We would submit that real labour ought not to be stigmatised as, 
if DC * - f ^ at not t° k e called labour when labour cannot be exacted in return, 

mid when, m demanding it, charity loses even its character of benevolence, as the idleness of the 
idle cannot be distinguished from the feebleness of the weak and infirm. 

To this great amount of unemployed people we would especially solicit the attention of your 
Excellency. The number employed is nearly 500,000, and 300,000 or 400,000 in addition 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



15 



will shortly require it. It will not be possible much longer to find work of the nature now pro- 
vided even for those who are employed, and of course still less for the large remainder. In 
ordinary times the ordinary distress of the country is provided for by the Poor Laws ; at present, 
in Ireland, the Commissariat is added for the emergency. The question of supplying food 
gratuitously, or in any way, by the agency of Government, is one on which we need not enter. 
Our object is to point out, that no labour at present within our control can meet for more than 
a month or two, if so long, the wants even of our present labour roll ; but if to drainage can be 
added tillage and reclamation, or the general control of road^, under Acts to be prepared for 
the purpose, a great addition will be made to our powers, provided steps can be taken to sup- 
port the people in the interval which, must elapse before they can be brought into operation. 

Lord Glengaxl to Colonel J ones. 

Iffa and Offa West, Tipperary , 

Cahir, January 15, 1847. 

I am reluctantly obliged by the Relief Committee of this district to inform you, that 
the numbers requiring employment are increasing hourly upon them ; our works are inadequate 
to furnish employment. 

The people, in consequence, have openly told the Committee that they must now commence 
robbing, and go to jail, for starve they must, if they do not. Meal and soup are given out 
daily to many hundreds, but the numbers increase upon us awfully. 

We, therefore, urgently request that orders be sent down to Mr. Jones, the county surveyor, 
to place more people on the present works, and we request the Board to sanction the present- 
ments made at the late sessions held on the 5th of this month, as soon as possible. 

We have endeavoured to keep back the Public Works as much as possible in this barony, 
expecting the railway to be in operation, but as that now appears to be almost hopeless, we 
must begin cutting up the roads in the barony to prevent plunder and starvation. 



Captain Wynne to Mr. Walker. 

Ennis, January 17, 1847. 

I have just returned, from my week’s excursion, a most eventful one 

indeed. 

The amount of destitution is very alarming, and although the present 
amount of employment, if fairly and honestly distributed, is fully sufficient 
to meet it, still in some localities it is not met, in consequence of the Com- 
mittees filling up the lists (to the number they conceive themselves entitled to) 
with those persons in whose welfare they have most interest, and leaving to 
the last and supplementary lists those whose claims are strongest upon the 
Inspecting Officer, and will afford them the strongest grounds of complaint 
should additional employment he refused. My Committees are in tolerably 
good order, with the exception of two, which ought not to exist, being slices 
from the legally constructed ones, at Miltown Malvay, and Kilrush. The 
former has been sanctioned by the lieutenant of the county, without any 
notification to me ; and in neither case have pains been taken to acquaint me 
with their separate existence •, they have been formed only a short time. 

I shall just mention a very shameful case that came under my observation at 
the Killan Committee, the latter of those alluded to above. 

On leaving the Committee room, a man half starved, and considerably more 
than half naked, bare head, bare legs and arms, nothing to cover him but the 
skeletons of an old pair of breeches and waistcoat, which upon enqniry appeared 
to be all he was possessed of, seized me by my coat with the grasp of death, 
and insisted upon being heard, when I found an interpretation of his tale was 
simply this : — None of the Committee had any interest in his life, and he was- 
therefore left to die. I brought him into the Committee, and exhibited him 
before them. It was a picture well calculated, as I thought, to bring the colour 
to their cheeks, but I cannot compliment myself on my success. It is hard to 
deal with such heartless men. Under such circumstances, the Relief Works 
must fail to keep the people from starvation. I met with many similar cases, 
and immediately redressed them; but I cannot discover 1 in 50. I stated my 
intention of calling upon the Lieutenant of the county to abolish these Com- 
mittees, if within one week these abuses were not corrected. 

There are, at present, employed in my district one in four' of the population, 
according to the census of 1841 ; allowing one-fifth increase since then, it leaves, 
at present, one in five, which at the present average of wages and price of food, 
would give nineteen-twentieths of a pound of Indian com per day to each mouth, 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




16 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



which would be ample, and more than the present prospects of supplies would 
afford. It is therefore obvious that, if the people starve, it is not from insufficient 
employment. It must be from its improper distribution, or the impossibility of 
procuring food for wages. 

I visited Ruan, where our works have been suspended ; distress exists there 
to a frightful extent, and strong symptoms of riot. I should not, however, 
recommend the resumption of the works ; an example must be made. It is a 
fact worthy of notice, agricultural works have made considerable progress there 
since the suspension of the works. I have failed in discovering the offenders, 
though they are well known to many. 



Mr. Brett, C.E., to Mr. Walker. 

Castlebar , January 17, 1847. 

The pressure for employment has now arrived at such a height, that 
nothing short of universal lists for the entire population will suffice, the blame 
and odium of refusing to put on more than one-fifth of the destitute being heaped 
on me. 

The sessions fix an amount of destitution at one in three, to one in four of the 
population ; the maximum of one to each family is looked upon as useless ; and 
certainly the extraordinary high price of provisions gives strong grounds for 
additional demands. 

The alarm and excitement consequent on the late quarter sessions are almost 
indescribable (6,000 civil bills at BaUina) ; several villages are being deserted, 
and vast numbers proceeding to Liverpool on their route to America. 

It would be most essential to issue some further instructions as to the extent 
of relief to be afforded ; the notion exists among the Committees and others, that 
it rests with us here to put on what numbers we please, and this would be most 
important to have explicitly understood, so as (if possible) to allay the feeling at 
present excited against us. 



Mr. King to Mr. Walker. 

Cork, January 17, 1827. 

I HAVE to report that, on yesterday, I found it indispensable to the proper 
influence of the Board’s officers on the Clonakilty Slob district to suspend 
temporarily, the works. r 

I have observed a growing spirit of discontent among the labourers employed 
within the last fortnight r J 

I attribute this, in a great degree, to the intervention of the Christmas 
holidays, when the men absented themselves, and consequently reduced their 
weekly payments for works executed, and the facility of getting employment 
on the Relief Works, where, I am informed, they can make (or, which is the 
same to them, can get) better wages. 

Yesterday, a large mob of fellows swept round the works, and forced off 
those that were better disposed, and anxious to have the opportunity of earning 
the support of their families. I remonstrated to what extent I could and many 
stated that they would return to their work again; but I said that those who 
were disposed to return should prove their disposition to be quiet and steady 
by identifying the party or parties who intimidated and forced them off and 
therefore, previous to my coming away, I stopped the works altogether 

The men earn good wages for the time they work ; many of them live a good 
distance lrom the works, and, consequently, don’t stick constantly to their 

Many have stated positively that they cannot make wages, whereas in every 
instance of such assertion that I took the party to see the account of his time, and 
thernoney he got for that time, it was shewn that the wages were from 14 d to 
16a. per day. 

I regret that this should occur, as hitherto all went on well. I regret it the 
more s° as the present is a crisis in our operations, having a great length of 
wall built and not backed up, as well as considerable stretches of embankment 
partially formed, and more or less subject to demolition by every successive 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 17 

tide ; in fact, it is difficult to conjecture what the result of a stoppage in the 
•works just now may entail in the way of additional cost ; yet on yesterday 
there was no alternative but to stop the works, or submit to he mastered by the 
misguided creatures we are all endeavouring to benefit. 

Distress prevails to a fearful extent in and around this district, yet such is the 
infatuation of the labourers, that for the last four or five payments, I had 
repeatedly to hunt away from the works women who come round on such days to 
sell whiskey to the men, and it is, (in spite of my instructions to have those 
whiskey vendors removed) sold to numbers on such days. Now, this would be 
considered evidence of any thing but distress ; I can only term it infatuation, lor 
want, to the greatest imaginable extent, is nevertheless every where perceptible.

Lieutenant-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public TForA-s, January 18, 1847. 

I regret much to repeat that our accounts from the country are most 
gloomy, as regards the amount of food in the country, and the melancholy and 
deplorable state of the population. In some districts, the men who come to the 
works are so reduced in their physical powers, as to be unable to earn above 4 d. 
or 5d. per diem. This is evidently too little, and with the present high price 
of provisions precludes the possibility of purchasing sufficient food to support 
life. The state of destitution of the people about Skibbereen, and the increasing 
mortality, renders it imperative to send in supplies. The position of this district, 
in a distant corner of the country, without any great lines of communication 
and removed from any large town from whence provisions could be obtained, 
is peculiar and different from most other distressed districts.. 



Major Townsend to Mr. Walker. 

Cavan, January 19, 1847. 

I beg to report, that between 8 and 9 o’clock in the morning of 16th 
instant, two men, armed with pistols, came on the work S 70, Upper Loughton, 
and served a threatening notice on the overseer, Thomas Morris. Having done 
this, they discharged their pistols in the air. 

This outrage was perpetrated openly, and in the presence of the workmen, 
none of whom interfered either to protect the overseer, or to capture the two 
men. 

At my request Captain Battersby, County Inspector of Constabulary, has 
furnished me with copies of the notice, and of the report of Mr. Lock, Sub- 
Inspector, both of which are inclosed. 

I proceeded to the spot this morning, accompanied by Captain Battersby, and 
assembled the workmen. They fully admitted their cowardice. I told them 
that unless by this day week, Tuesday 26th instant, the criminals were in the 
hand of justice, I should suspend the work, dismiss them all, and replace them 
by another set of workmen.

Lieutenant-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin, 
January 19, 1847. 

Each day brings us more distressing accounts from the country, 
particularly from the inland districts of Mayo, where it will he necessary to 
send food. You will perceive by the accompanying notes from Mr. Brett, our 
engineer in Mayo, the pressure which is put upon him for employment; in 
fact, every man, woman, and child is put forward for relief from the works. 
Captain Wynne, in Clare, states that he has one-fifth of the population 
employed. We are pressed for instructions by our officers to know how they 
are to act. Those which now regulate their actions are no longer applicable 
to the altered state of affairs. If they refuse employment, they are held up to 
the poor as the stumbling-block between them and the means of obtaining 
food. I am of opinion, that it would he better, in many cases, to give food, 
than to be paying money away, as we are now obliged to do. At the same time, 
the people are discontented at the small sums they are entitled to. The fact is, 
that the system of task-work is no longer beneficial employment to many, their 
bodily strength being gone, and spirits depressed : they have not power to exert 
themselves sufficiently to earn the ordinary day’s wages. This necessary outlay 
will be stigmatised as a wasteful expenditure, and the works will be left incom- 
plete. Mr. Barry, our Fishery Inspector, has just returned from Glandore, near 
Clonakilty. The accompanying is a short statement of affairs in that district. 
You will perceive the great benefits derived from the soup establishments, and 
how very cheap is the preparation. The small amount of nourishment has a very 
great effect upon the famished individuals, whose stamina is thus partially 
revived. So far as we are concerned, I believe our powers have attained the 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



19 



utmost. We have, I trust, made a good staud; but the numbers which are 
now forcing themselves upon us will incapacitate our officers from affording 
employment, and all our efforts, hitherto so successful, will be paralyzed.

Mr. Barry to Lieut.- Colonel Jones. 

Fishery Office, Tuesday , January 19, 1847. 

I have just returned from the south, the vicinity of unhappy Skibbereen. Things are 
surely bad enough, but not so bad as they are likely to be, food becoming daily more scarce. 

Over 100 vessels in the harbour of Cork, but not destined for that market ; all touching for 
orders. Some few arrivals into the western ports, Castletown and Baltimore, taken by the 
millers. When I left the prices were, 

Indian corn, 2.v. 6 d. 

Indian meal, 2 s. 10 d. 

Wheaten meal, 3s. 

Beans meal, 14s. per cwt. 

Rice had risen from 23s. to 30s. 

Soup is keeping thousands alive. It was a blessed plan. 

In a village near my residence they gave out daily 700 quarts, at jd. per quart, at a loss 
under 10s. per day. It is an amazing relief to the creatures on the roads. They take a 
pint in the morning going to work, and the second pint on their return. It is composed of 
poor beef in the proportion of 141bs. to 80 gallons, boiled down in a digester, and thickened 
with about equal proportions ol peas, or beans, meal, rice, and barley meal, toell peppered. 

I fancied that the aspect of the people had greatly improved since its introduction. It is capital 
stuff, and decidedly the most effectual mode of affording relief. Tickets are sold to all who 
wish to buy, and by that means only is gratuitous relief afforded. These boilers for soup 
are becoming very general. Assistant Commissary- General Bishop has been through the 
whole West Riding of Cork, encouragiug these establishments. He offers from the Govern- 
ment a contribution equal to local subscriptions, which has been a great stimulus. 

The sowing of wheat has not been as much neglected as we feared. In Kinalmeaky, east of 
East Carberry, and Ibane, and Barryroe, there has been merely the usual quantity sown ; 
in the west of East Carbery they are at work ; but in the whole of West Carbery there is 
a most deplorable prostration, they have no seed of any kind. The same, I am told, is the 
case in Bere and Bantry, and West Muskerry. 

There was a great influx of sea manure lately at Glandore ; and I was delighted to find 
that all who could leave the roads, even for a day, availed themselves of the opportunity of 
covering some small portions of land for potatoes, to which they still cling as to fife, and well 
they may. It induced me to make close inquiry about seed, and I find that creatures who 
have been existing on a scanty meal a day have reserved some little stock of potatoes, such as 
they are ; but I am sadly fearful, that never having come to maturity, their growth is very 
doubtful. Some small importations have come into Cork, chiefly from Jersey. They look 
well : the price asked is about 20 d. per stone.

Mr. Deering to Mr. Walker. 

Cashel , January 21, 1847. 

I have this moment.. heard a report that Mr. E. H. Wayland, pay-clerk 
of Kilnemanagh Lower, was attacked this morning in. the neighbourhood of 
Dundrum, whilst proceeding on a car with two policemen, to pay labourers. 

I deeply regret to have to state, that although Mr. E. H. Wayland escaped 
with a slight, gun-shot wound, one of the policemen was shot dead beside him 
on the car. 

The second policeman made his way to a house with the money, which he 
succeeded in defending. 

Mr. Wayland fired three shots at the assailants, who were five in number. 
It is said that one is wounded. 

I hear the country people proceeded in pursuit. 

I am now about to proceed to Mr. Wayland, about five miles distant. 

The labourers shall not want a pay-clerk to give them their money, if Mr. 
Wayland is unable to act. 

As I have no assistant to spare in whom to place confidence, if required, I 
shall pay them myself. 

Note. — Mr. Wayland appears to have acted very gallantly, and is not wounded. — 
H. D. J.— Jan. 22, 1S47-

Mr. Deering to Mr. Walker. 

Cashel, January 21, 1847. 

I have the honour to inform you that at a quarter to two o’clock, p.m., 
this day, a gentleman rode in express, to inform me that an occurrence of a 
most melancholy character had taken place this morning in the Canpawhite 
district of Kilnemanagh Lower, in fact, another fearful tragedy to add to the 
long catalogue of offences committed in this county. 

Mr. Edward H. Wayland, a most zealous and humane pay clerk, proceeded 
on a car attended by two armed policemen, to pay the labourers in his district 
from the village of Dundrum. 

Whilst approaching the works in progress at Glenpadden and Cartron, seven 
men with their faces blackened, all armed with flint guns, rushed out from 
between two gate piers. 

Three of the men levelled their guns at Mr. Wayland and the policeman, 
who sat side by side on the left seat of the car. They fired, instantly the 
policeman fell dead on the car shot through the head. 

Mr. Wayland thrust one of the guns aside when the assailants were in the act 
of firing ; the shots happily took no effect on him. 

Mr. W. stood up on the car, prepared to leap off with a cocked pistol in his 
hand, and fired at the two men next him; he is uncertain with what effect. 

Mr. Wayland then jumped off the car, seized a second pistol, looked round 
for the second policeman and driver ; neither were to be seen. He then ran 
after the car to endeavour to get the policemen’s carabine; it was not to 
be found. 

Four men advanced upon him. Mr. Wayland advanced some paces ; one or 
two of the men fired at him without effect; he discharged his pistol with a 
similar result. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



21 



The circumstances detailed did not occupy a period of above two minutes. 

Mr. Way land then hastened to the car under a volley of stones, jumped on it, 
and gallopped up the hill to the house of overseer Ryan. 

He then placed the money, amounting to about 50/., in a room in the house, 
locked the door, and placed a number of men of Glenpadden and Glencarberry 
Works as a guard over the house. 

Mr. Wayland then proceeded to the place where this sanguinary occurrence 
took place, found the policeman lying dead, his carabine and cartouche box had 
been carried off, his side arms being left untouched. 

He obtained a horse, galloped to the police station of Annacarty, also 
despatching messengers to Hollyford and Dundrum police barracks. 

The labourers of Glencarberry and Carhow went in pursuit of the murderers. 

I need scarcely observe, that the perpetrators of this barbarous murder com- 
mitted in open day remain undiscovered. 

On after inquiry, it appears that the carabine of the murdered policeman was 
loaded, whilst that of the policeman who disappeared with the driver during 
the conflict, was unloaded. 

I beg to observe that, on my arrival in this district, I gave positive orders to 
the pay-clerks not to travel with funds of the Board in their possession without a 
police escort, and to state, as the result of my experience, that unless a mounted 
escort is, in future, sent along with each car, the pay-clerks cannot, 'with 
any certainty of safety, pay the labourers except in the towns, and I decidedly 
object to large bodies of impatient men being brought into towns under existing 
circumstances. 

Mr. Cooper, the engineer, was near the spot, having proceeded in the morning 
to that district to set on works. I hastened thither as rapidly as possible, and 
had the gratification of finding Mr. Wayland unhurt, although the contrary 
had been previously reported. 

I beg to recommend Mr. Wayland specially to the consideration of the 
Board. To his dauntless gallantry and coolness, his own safety, and what 
appeared dearer to him than that, the safety of the funds of the Board are alone 
to be attributed. Time will not permit of my doing justice to his self-devotion, 
but he is a gentleman from whom I could have anticipated as much. I under- 
stand that the poor fellow who has been so barbarously murdered was a brave 
and well-conducted man. I have directed Mr. Wayland to take an extra escort 
to-morrow, and shall attend myself at Dundrum. 



Lieut. Inglis to Mr. Walker. 

Annacotty, January 22, 1847. 

I have to report, for the immediate information of the Board, the fol- 
lowing particulars of an attack made upon Mr. Hanrahan, pay-clerk under the 
Board, this day. 

Mr. Hanrahan left Limerick this day, at about the hour of 12 at noon, having 
with him about 320/. for payment in the Castle Connell district ; and when 
about half way between Annacotty and Castle Connell, lie was stopped 
by three men (two of whom were armed, one with a blunderbuss, the other 
with a pistol) ; his horse was immediately shot, and the men decamped with 
the money over a demesne wall. Search has since been made, and one bag of 
silver was found by Private Herring, Royal Sappers and Miners, hid in a 
plantation. 

A policeman has captured a man under suspicious circumstances, and Mr. 
Hanrahan identified him, selecting him from amongst a number collected 
together; and Mr. Hanrahan’s depositions are now being taken before the 
stipendiary magistrate. 

Up to the present moment nothing further has been heard of the other 
offenders. 

From all the circumstances of the case, it does not appear that the labourers 
of any Public Works in the district are in a body implicated in the transaction.

Mr. Carrol to Mr. Walker 

Limericfc, January 22, 1847 

I feel it my duty to state, with the least possible delay, that Mr. John 
Hanrahan, pay-clerk for the barony of Clanwilliam, has just now (6 o’clock) 
called on me to report that he was attacked to-day, about 1 o’clock p.m., by an 
armed party, who stopped him on the road leading from Limerick to Castle 
Connell, and robbed him of a sum of 320 1. with which he was proceeding to 
pay labourers in his district. 

Mr. Hanrahan at once proceeded to Castle Connell, and reported the robbery 
to the stipendiary magistrate there, who caused an immediate search to be 
made by the police, and one man has been arrested and fully committed for 
trial, on Mr. Hanrahan’s positive identification, who is also prepared to identify 
another of the party whom he has described to the police. 

On making search at the place where the robbers climbed over a wall at the 
side of the road, Mr. Hanrahan found 251. of the money of which he had been 
robbed, which he left in the hands of the engineer, Mr. Whyte. 

I have taken measures to send an assistant pay-clerk to make the payments in 
Mr. Hanrahan’s district to-morrow, and provided that both shall be escorted by 
police. 

As I am informed that Lieutenant Inglis, inspecting-officer, has fully 
reported all the circumstances of this case to the Board, I deem it unnecessary 
to trouble you with further observations. From all I have heard of this matter, 
it will appear that no blame can attach to the pay-clerk •, but, on the contrary, 
his presence of mind appears to have been laudable. 



Captain Gordon to Mr. Walker 

January 23, 184/. 

I have to report that, during my journey from Dublin to Cork, I 
observed that, throughout the part of Queen’s Comity I passed through, a fair 
quantity of wheat had been sown, and a certain quantity of tillage going on. 

Between Cork and Macroom, I was also glad to observe a great change, and

I did not observe much going on between Mill-street and Charleville ; but 
in Limerick, especially about BrufF, a much larger quantity of wheat is sown 
than in former years, and a great breadth of oats will be sown throughout the 
district. 

I regret to say, however, that the seed will be very high priced. Oats are 
now Is. 7 \d. a stone, and by all accounts, in Limerick, will rise to 2s. 7 cl. 

Turnip and carrot seed have increased in price two hundred per cent., in 
Cork ! 

About BrufF, land lets as high as from 3 1. to 3/. 10 s. per acre*, and for 
conacre paid in advance, not less than from 10/. to 12/. an acre. 

In Cork, this year, by retail, turnips met with ready sale at 20s. a ton *, and 
at Limerick, no less a sum than 30s.

Lieut. Milward to Mr. Walker. 

Glenties, January 25, 1847. 

I have the honour to report that a disturbance took place this morning, on my leaving 
Donegal. 1 had issued a list of 200 persons to be employed on the road from Donegal to 
Barnesmore ; a crowd assembled in the town, and declared their intention not of allowing me to 
leave it. On leaving the hotel, I found them assembled round my car, and when I appeared, 
they cried out they would have my life or employment, and seized the horse’s head, determined 
not to let me leave the town. 

I, after much fighting, succeeded in seizing the ringleader, who had hold of my horse by the 
head, and held him for some time, until obliged to let go by a severe blow on the arm, 
the priests and others who were present pulling me back while the crowd removed the fellow. 
In the mean time I received several blows, and, had it not been for the priests, who were for- 
tunately present, I should not have escaped so easily. The police were all absent at a fair. 

I was obliged literally afterwards to fight my way out of the town, and had much difficulty 
in doing so, and fully expect to be attacked on my return. 

I am convinced that the principal persons concerned are not those who require work, and 
I took care to tell them, as clearly as I could, that I would give no further employment after 
what had happened. 

I immediately communicated with a magistrate, and hope to be able to arrest the man who 
appeared the ringleader, and whom I can easily identify. 



Lieut.-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, January 28, 1847. 

Mr. Ginger has just left me. He has, in concert with Mr. Kennedy, 
taken a house, which, he says, is suited for the business of the Stationery Office. 
Some trifling work is required, and, acting upon the applications I have received, 
instructions have been issued accordingly. I presume an authority will be given 
to take charge of it as a public building, and to perform all necessary repairs, 
after which we shall have the rooms at present occupied by the Stationery Office 
in the Custom House. 

I was obliged, this day, to brine under his Excellency’s notice the very great in- 
convenience and suffering that will be experienced where works are stopped in con- 
sequence of the amount presented having been expended, and no sessions held to 
provide for the additional sums. We ought to have authority to proceed in 
anticipation of the several presentments. His Excellency fully agrees in the

necessity for continuing the works in such cases, and, I believe, will issue direc-

Col. Archer goes over by this night's mail. From him you will learn the

their husbands or sons had earned upon the works.

Major Parker to Colonel Joxes. 

Skibbereen, January 26, 1847. 

The weather has now been very tempestuous for so long a time, that I fear the distress 
will be very great indeed. As the labourers cannot earn full wages, generally speaking not 
more than Ad. or 6 d. a-day, upon which, with food at the present extremely high price, namely, 
Indian meal, 2s. Sd. to 2s. lOd. a stone, and bread at 3 \d, a lb., it is impossible to live and 
maintain families. 

I venture to write to ask if under these extreme circumstances some special relief may be 
afforded by allowing something more than the half-pay ? If something is not done, I am sure 
next week matters will be worse here than ever, the weather having been so unusually severe 
and tempestuous that it has been impossible, to work. 



Mr. Mulvany to Mr. Walker. 

Drainage Office, Richmond llarhour, 
January 29, 1847. 

I beg to report that on Wednesday night last the dams in the Buskin 
division of the Dungolman District were malicious] y broken, and much injury 
caused to the works. By the watchman’s report, the outrage was committed by 
a body of 20 or 25 men, some of whom were armed, and tired a shot or shots 
when they saw him. 

Last night the dams in the lower portion of the Rath or Cloneen District 
were also cut, and some injury caused to the works. 

Under these circumstances, I have ordered the suspension of the works in both 
districts for the present, and intend to proceed to visit the works, and make detailed 
inquiries into the outrage to-morrow morning. 

The only reason that can be at present assigned for the occurrence is, that the 
labourers in parts of the works got bad pay on Wednesday, which was attributable 
to the bad way in which they had worked during the preceding fortnight. 



Captain O’Neill to Mr. Walker. 

Letterkenny, January 5, 1847. 

I have the honour to state, for the information of the Board, that the Hon. 
Charles Clements, Chairman of the Kilmacrenan and Mevagh Relief Committee, 
and myself, went this morning from Milford to Carrigort to issue labour lists, and 
after issuing about 130 names, the people crowded round the door of the school- 
house in a dense mass, and would not permit us to go out Mr. Clements 
and myself went to the door to reason with them, hut they still kept closely 
packed together, and were very clamorous for more lists, although I had given 
as many as I had on my lists furnished to me by Mr. Clements. 

It appears that some persons who had been looking on, and who heard the 
people say that they would not let us out of the school-house until we issued 
more lists, went to the officer of the revenue police, who ordered down his men* 
when the mob gave way, and scattered all about, the police following them in 
the same irregular manner for a few yards. One of the police, who happened 
to he a short way in advance, was attacked by four of the country people, when 
some of his comrades coming up drove them away. The mob then commenced 
throwing stones of from one to three pounds weight, and I am sorry to say that 
one of the country people, a man of the name of James Lynagh, was severely 
hurt by a blow of a musket on the head from one of the police. 

The mob shortly after dispersed, and some of them threatened to break the 
wheelbarrows and other tools on the works that are already in progress, if they 
were not employed.

May I request to be informed by the Board whether I am to commence the 
work for which these lists were made out, or am I to stop for a time all the
