I should have acted at once on the latter, but it would have been punishing 
the poor people who are already employed, and who were not within three 
miles of where the disturbance took place. 

I have, therefore, to request you will let me know what the wishes of the 
Board may be on the subject, when I shall carry them out to the best of my 
ability. I beg further to add that, from the excited state of the people in that 
part of the country, and the great poverty, wretchedness, and destitution that 
exist, it would not be advisable to stop any of the works now in progress, as it 
might drive the people to desperation. 



Document forwarded to Mr. Trevelyan by Lieut.-Colonel Jones, 
February 24, 1847. 

Now, Armstrong, you put me to the necessity of writing to you again 
uppon an emportant affair, I mean the new line of road leading from Bally- 
hilland to Ballydouglass Bridge. 

I sent two of my men there some few days ago to give them and you warning of 
your doom,- but I understand that you made very little of it. You also encou- 
raged the check clerk, that is Christy, to work on and not fear, but as sure as I 
have the pen in my hand he will repent of his presumption. It is my opinion 
that you can hardly save him. 

But it is useless for me to talk of him here ; I will meet him on another 
day. As for you, I suppose you think yourself to great a man to be conquered ; 
but you may know that I never took any thing in my head but I performed one 
time or other, but always as soon as opportunity served. It is not this way I 
should talk but that I would like you to understand the danger that you are 
instinctively running into now. Why I wonder how I have the patience to talk 
tliis way to you, the greatest of all robbers. Now, by the powers of the Most 
High, in less than — I wont mention the time, but be sure sooner than you are 
aware of— thou shalt die. Remember, you are as sure of it, one time or other, 
as hell is waiting for you ; and that other impudent scab of a ringsend, or 
townsend, or whatever the devil you call him, if he has not better manners than 
to come out and say that he would drive the road through hell if he was to put 
soldiers ou every yard of it ; but let him take care and warning by this, or if I 
do not mistake he will be in hell before it is finished. Now remember you are 
warned, and we are freed of your murder by giving you timely notice, and if you 
do not stop going on with said road you will meet with the same death that 
others of greater authority, for their villainous deeds, were punished with. 
Remember, you are as sure of it as I send you word, and if you had the Queen’s 
armey round you, by all that is sacred and just, die you must, was 3 to perish 
in the attempt. 

Given under my hand, 

(Signed) Mary Maguire, 

Greene Grove Island.

Lieut Milward to Mr. Walker. 

Donegal, January 26, 1S4/. 

I have the honour to lay before you, for the information of the Board, 
the position of affairs in my district as regards the demand for employment. 

In some districts the demands are now, if possible, more pressing than they 
were some time ago but arising from a different cause. At that time the distress 
was really very great, but it is now to a very great extent relieved, and the 
present applicants for relief are, for the most part, those who do not require it, 
but are anxious to be employed on the Public Works to get, as they say, then- 
share of the money, and, in the mean time, the land is quite neglected. These 
people are more pressing in their demands than the really destitute, and so im- 
portunate, and make out such pitiful stories, that they impose on the Relief 
Committees, and almost compel them to return them as destitute, and the 
Committees are doubly pressing on me, in order to save themselves, and from 
my determination to resist their demands, I am subjected to much annoyance 
and even threats. 

There are some localities in which distress still prevails to a great extent, and 
in these places every exertion is being made to forward the works, hut the outcry 
is greater from places, in my opinion, well provided for the present. There is 
no doubt that destitution is increasing, and that from the high price of pro- 
visions, persons who would be otherwise well off, are approaching a state of 
destitution, but not nearly to so great an extent as the Relief Committees would 
make it appear. 

In one locality (Pettigo), the demand for labour arises from the desire of the 
Relief Committee to have their share of the assessment spent in their distict 
although the destitution does not nearly require it.

Barony of Bunratty Lower,

I regret having to inform the Board of the following outrage having-

On the night of the 17th instant, two men entered the house where an

the house ; there are informations sworn against the parties, and a warrant in the

ployed. 

On the 25th instant, the labourers on the work No. 142, at Knockaxn, 
threatened a steward named M‘Namara with death, and obliged him to leave 
the work. I have directed it to he stopped. 

On the night of the 25th, a watchman on No. 95, Lisduff hill-cutting, was 
beaten ; this work is also suspended. 

I have directed that the proper notice should be given to the relief officer 
and a list of the men employed on the day of the occurrence should be forwarded 
to him.

Mr. IIotham to Mr. Walker. 

Barony of Upper St. Mullins, 
Carlow, January 28, 1847. 

I visited the works in the above-named barony yesterday, and found 
the cultivation of the soil wholly neglected. 

The Committee in this barony are composed of clergymen only, of both 
persuasions, and have compelled me, by repeated remonstrances, to put a 
number on the works, quite out of proportion to the labouring population as 
given in the census of 1841. 

The result I have shown; and in this county it is the only case which lias come 
before me. 

I have given directions that 40 labourers shall be dismissed from the works 
immediately, and when I have ascertained that they have got private employ- 
ment, I propose to dismiss 30 more. 

We find, from experience, that where works are carried on in too great pro- 
fuseness, agriculture is neglected ; for the higher price they are earning from 
the works makes them unwilling to serve with the farmers, and even if the 
farmer, according to the orders of the Board, obtains a labourer from the works, 
the man will seldom or never do anything for him. 

These are the real difficulties which we have to contend with, and as in this 
case I feel sure the Committee will lay their complaint before the Board, with 
the usual statement of starvation, I have written beforehand to put the Board in 
possession of the facts.

Mr. Forsyth to Mr. Walker. 

District Office, Belturlet, 

January 29, 1847. 

I have to report, for the information of the Commissioners, that on the 
26th instant, about 4 o’clock in the afternoon, Mr. Andrew Hanlon, paymaster 
of this district, was attacked on the public road between Bawnboy and Ballina- 
more, in the townland of Garadice, by a gang of six men, who succeeded in 
taking from him a box containing the pay sheets of the district, and nearly 16 1. 
in silver. 

He was proceeding to Ballinamore in the discharge of his duties, and had 
about 300/. in his possession •, fortunately it was in bank notes, and concealed 
about his person, except the sum above stated. The gang were armed, three 
with pistols and three with bludgeons ; two of them seized the horse, two of 
them the box, and the others presented their pistols at Mr. Hanlon and the 
carman. It appears some reluctance to fire was manifested, the carman en- 
deavoured to free the horse and escape, and a desperate struggle ensued between 
Mr. Hanlon and those who were endeavouring to possess themselves of the 
box, but being overpowered, the gang succeeded in making their escape with 
it into the plantations. The occurrence took place about 300 or 400 yards in a 
straight line from the police barracks at Corduff. Mr. Hanlon has not received 
much personal injury. The box and pay-sheets were found yesterday in the 
plantation at Garradice, and are in the possession of Captain Kelly, magis- 
trate. 

I was most anxious to have forwarded the particulars of this unpleasant 
affair by yesterday’s post, but having heard nothing but vague and contradictory 
reports, and Mr. Hanlon being detained by the magistrate to identify, if possible, 
the parties who committed the robbery, as a strong suspicion is entertained that 
they are persons employed on the works, he did not reach Belturbet until 
three hours after post time. 

The magistrate objected to Mr. Hanlon proceeding to make the payment 
then, as such a strong feeling exists, that the workmen were aware that an 
attack on him was contemplated. I may, however, remark, that neither of us 
had heretofore the least suspicion of violence being intended, no symptom of 
such an intention having been manifested, but kindness and goodwill throughout 
the district generally. 



Captain Farren to Mr. Walker. 

Castlebar , January 30, 1847, 

I beg to state, for the information of the Commissioners, that on Satur- 
day last, the 23rd instant, a cart of whole flour, proceeding from Westport to 
Partry, was robbed at a place called Monalumin near Killawalla, by some of the 
labourers employed on the Public Works on the line of road from Clonee to 
Killawalla, No. 154, barony of Carra. 

James Feeny, the driver of the cart, detailed the circumstances of the case to 
me on the evening of the 25th instant, in presence of one of the magistrates of 
the county, at whose request I deferred taking any steps in the matter until the 
parties could be arrested. 

It appears from Feeny ’s statement that on the day in question, when about a 
mile on the Ballinrobe side of Killawalla, he overtook one of the gangsmen 
[b. w. 2.] F 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




30 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



named Tom Gibbons, who asked him. for a bag of meal, and said that if he 
would not give it to him, he would rob the cart when he got help ; accordingly, 
when they came up with the rest of the gang. Gibbons seized the bag and a 
struggle ensued ; three or four of the gang came up to help Gibbons, and the 
bags were taken away; two men, Charles M'Gweely and Pat Kelly, saved the 
remainder of the meal. A gangsman named Michael Gibbons, whom Feeny 
called upon to assist him, refused to do so, and said he was afraid they would 
kill him at night if he did. Several were looking on, who did not assist in the 
robbery, but made no attempt to prevent it. 

One of the parties, Thomas Gibbons, has been brought before the magis- 
trates at petty sessions, and the witnesses bound over to prosecute at the next 
assizes. I proceeded this morning to the spot where the robbery was com- 
mitted, and found that it occurred at a turn of the road near a hill where three 
gangs were working ; and having satisfied myself that these gangs could, if so 
disposed, have prevented the. robbery, (they admitted that the carman had 
asked for help and they refused it through fear,) I conceived it my duty, in 
compliance with the Board’s Circular upon the subject, to direct these three 
gangs to be at once suspended from work. 

It appears that when the police went to arrest Gibbons there were evidences 
of great destitution in his cabin ; no food of any description could be found ; he 
has eight in family, and, as I before remarked, was employed on the Public 
Works. 

As very great distress prevails in this district, I purpose, with the permission 
of the Board, to continue the suspension of the gangs for a limited period only, 
(one of the parties who committed the robbery having been brought to justice,) 
and to remove from the labour list the names of those who took an active part, 
upon proof being obtained to that effect. 

The locality in which the affair occurred: is a wild district, situate in the 
south-western part of the barony of Carra. The lawless character of the 
people renders it extremely difficult to carry on the Public Works in a satis- 
factory manner ; the people are united by secret societies, and they endeavour 
to coerce the overseers and check clerks to their purposes by co min g to their 
lodgings at night, in large numbers, and administering illegal oaths to rate them 
at higher wages whether they work or not, to rate all gangs alike, no half- 
day’s pay, & c. So perfect is the combination that it is quite impossible to obtain 
proof against any ; nobody can be induced to afford information. 

The high roads from Westport to Claremorris and Ballinrobe run through 
this district. The character of the people, coupled -with the robberies which 
have been committed here and in the adjoining barony of Burrishoole, have 
been the means of aggravating the distress in other localities, as well as dis- 
turbing the peace, as carriers from the remote parts are apprehensive of going 
singly to Westport, and wait for an escort, or until a number of other carmen 
can accompany them. The nearest police station is Ballyhean, on the road 
from Castlebar to Ballinrobe, between which and Trurmakeady, on the western 
shore of Lough Mask, there is a wide interval. Another station on the road 
between Westport and Ballinrobe, at Killawalla or another point of the line, 
would be of great service as a preservative of the public peace and a support to 
the under officials engaged on the Public Works in this neighbourhood. 



Lieut.-Col. Jones to Mr. Trevelvan. 

January 30, 1847. 

The accounts from the country continue much the same ; in some parts 
great destitution and distress. I was sorry to learn by a private letter from the 
county of Leitrim that four men died on a road near Mohill yesterday, and the 
writer stated that, on his road to Rooshey, he passed six cabins with a dead 
person m each. Our works are inundated with men y and the Relief Committees 
appear to be powerless as a check upon improper applications. In many places 
they are afraid to refuse them. The Lord Lieutenant has sanctioned our pro- 
ceeding with roads on which the amounts presented have been expended. In

short, every man, woman, and child who mn once get employment, consider 
they have a right to continue. The idea or report of the intention of the Board 
to stop ia work creates a feeling of alarm throughout the entire district, and we

Mr. Griffith toLieut*-Col. Jones. 

New Ross, County Wexford, January 29, 1847. 

I have little to say except in regard to the farm work of the country. My route has 
been from Dublin to Kildare and thence by Poftarlington to Tullamore. Between Kildare and 
Tullamore'I did not see a single plough at work or a labourer in the field, but in the neigh- 
bourhood of Gensehill wheat has been sown in the potato land ; in other places, except in the 
lands .held by large farmers, nothing has been done; the potato and oat fields of last year 
are untouched. Yesterday I returned to Kildare, and proceeded from thence by Carlow and 
Bagnalstown to this place (New Ross). In this line, a distance of nearly 60 English miles, 
agricult ure is in full progress, all the potato lands have been sown with wheat, and, for the 
most part, the oat stubbs have been or are being ploughed ; this comprehends the entire valley 
of the river Banow, in no part of which, excepting on the iron granite soil in the neighbour- 
hood of Graig-na-managh, is the country populous, whence the farms as well as the fields are 
large. In the poor district of Graig-na-managh, both on the north and south sides of the 
river Banow, in the counties of Carlow and Kilkenny, the land is bad aud the people poor and 
numerous; here distress prevails and road works, or rather road idleness, and labourers 
may be seen crowded together in each other’s way. I was ashamed of it, and the sooner it is 
over the better ; on my return I must ascertain the names of the works in order to inquire 
why the men were not employed by task in making a new road; crowded as they were men 
•could not earn wages. I dare say we shall be told they are working by task ; as I travelled 
by a public conveyance I could -not stop to inquire. 



Captain Walker to Mr. Walker. 

County of. Longford, Barony of Longford, 
January 30, 1847. 

I regret to be obliged so soon to report a similar outrage to that stated 
in my letter of the 29th December. 

In consequence of great irregularities on project 28, Schedule A, barony 
Longford, Bernard Reily was dismissed by the assistant engineer and W. Dun- 
leary appointed. The enclosed notice was served on Dunloary, and this day- 
given me by the check clerk, to whom he gave them. 

This work is in one of the worst neighbourhoods in this county, and I con- 
sidered it absolutely necessary to suspend the work for the purpose of showing 
them I have the. power. I find two other notices were served in the course of 
this month in the same vicinity ; one the overseer destroyed, and did not report 
until found out by other. means. The other was not reported to me until long 
after it occurred, and as the labourers showed no disposition to annoy the over- 
seer, I did not report it. 

As this project employs above 100 men, it would occasion great distress to 
prolong the suspension beyond a few days; if it meets the approbation of the 
Board I shall put them to work on Thursday, the commencement of the labour 
week. 

P.S. I suspended this work with the concurrence of the engineer in charge. 
Pray return the notices.

Mr. T. Mulvany to Mr. Walker. 

Drainage Office, Richmond Harbour, 
January 31, 1847. 

Is consequence of the outrages which were committed on the works in 
the Dungolman and Rath or Clooneen district, as reported in my letter of the 
29th, I proceeded to Ballymelin early yesterday morning to examine the works 
and inquire into the matter. 

At Buskin, in the Dungolman district, the principal injuries were committed. 
On Wednesday night the watchman was alarmed by hearing a sudden rush 
of water down a portion of the new cut, which had been laid quite dry some 
time ago by me an s of a dam across the upper end, in order to enable the men to 
finish off the sloping, and, on going up near the dam, he saw a party of about 10 
men employed cutting it; and there were two men in advance, armed, with 
guns, who fired towards him, but he does not think with the intention of injuring 
him, as he judges from the nature of the report. The party then proceeded to 
the head dam, about a quarter of a mile higher up, which was a large one, and 
the principal means of enabling us to work at Buskin during the winter ; this 
they cut in several places. The watchman immediately gave information to the 
overseer and ganger, who live at Buskin Bridge, and they proceeded at once to 
the police barrack at Collinghstown, and brought some policemen with them to 
the works, but the party of men had, of course, gone away immediately after 
doing the mischief. There was a very heavy flood at the time in the extensive 
flat reach between Dungolman Hill and Ummera, which was poured down with 
such rapidity and violence after the cutting of the dams as to occasion much 
injury to the slopes of the work, which had just been finished at considerable 
expense; any plank and tools that happened to be lying on the banks were 
either thrown into the cut, or swept away by the first rush of the flood, but have 
all been secured. 

From all I can learn on the subject, and from the workmanlike way in which 
the flams were cut, I have no doubt the mischief was done by some men 
connected with the works. There are some very bad characters in the neigh- 
bourhood, and I believe the intention of the men to be to bully and frighten our 
people into employing them by day at high wages. The men have worked 
exceedingly badly for the last four or five weeks, and have, consequently, made 
very poor wages, although getting fair prices for their work. They appear to 
be acting thus purposely, indeed there can be no doubt about it, and as it will be 
more economical to complete the works in the Buskin division at a later period 
of the year, it will answer our purposes better in every way to discontinue the 
works in this division for the present. I have accordingly had all the tools 
collected and stored. 

The facts of the case were deposed to by the watchman on Thursday morning 
before Mr. St. George Grey, the nearest magistrate. 

The works in the lower division of the Dungolman district are proceeding 
satisfactorily. 

At Rath Bridge, near Newcastle, in the Rath or Clooneen district, attempts 
were made to destroy some of the dams on Thursday night, and all the planks, 
wheelbarrows, and other tools, were thrown into the cut, some of them broken, 
and others carried down the river to the quarry. These tools have all been since 
collected. . The works at Rath had been partially discontinued for some days 
in consequence of the flood, but arrangements had been made for resuming 
work but for this occurrence. I have directed the suspension of all work in 
that division of the Rath or Clooneen district for the present, as there is some 
reason to expect that we shall be able to ascertain who were the perpetrators of 
the outrage in the latter case.

Mr. Murray, Manager of the Provincial Bank of Ireland, to Mr. Stickney. 

Dublin, February 1, 1847. 

Silver continues to accumulate rapidly at some places— Cork, Skibbereen,

Mr. Hill to Mr. Walker. 

Ennis, February 1, 1847. 

With reference to Sir Lucius O’Brien’s letter, I have to report that there 
must be very little inconvenience felt in the way mentioned, as up to this time 
I got but two complaints of the nature. I visited some of the lines lately, and 
on eight miles of roads I observed but one field which could be fairly com- 
plained of. I have also to observe, that the fields the new roads run through 
form a very small portion of the farms of the country, and the inconvenience 
alluded to does not extend beyond the land intersected, yet, not a man is to be 
seen tilling through the whole country, except a few extensive farmers. 

I have also to observe, that I gave early notice to the landholders that no 
damage would be allowed where heaps of broken stones would be laid. In 
several cases these heaps are prepared so badly that in justice they cannot be 
paid for nor drawn. It is their own act to allow them on their land and they 
cannot now in justice complain. 

I have given directions to the assistants that where the formations are not 
forward to admit of permanent fences being made, you will have temporary 
fences made, enclosing all fields from the road necessary to have tilled, and 
remove all heaps of stones that are properly prepared from the fields where 
they are injurious.

Sir Lucius O’Brien to Lieut.-Colonel Jones. 

Dromoland, January 28, 1847. 

I wish to call your attention to the state of many of the new roads in this county, and 
request you will send an order to have the fences put up, and such other changes made 
respecting passages to the work, and placing the heaps of broken stones in such positions as 
shall allow of the tenantry cultivating their fields ancl gardens, which in many places have been 
laid open and are subject to so much trespass, that to attempt to do so, under present 
circumstances, would be ruin. 



Lieut-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, February 1, 1847. 

I send you an extract from the successor to Captain Wynne, in Clare, 
and as far as zeal, intelligence, and firmness go, I have no doubt of Captain 
Gordon being able to preserve the good order of the district placed under his 
surveillance. I have brought the subject of doing away with task-work under 
the notice of the Lord Lieutenant, who has desired me to wait a few days before 
any change shall be made. I shall not lose sight of it, for the abuses and evils 
are too great to be allowed to continue. Wherever works have been stopped, in 
consequence of misconduct, good has resulted, for the people have taken to farm 
labour. While the price of provisions was high, and the days short, task-work 
was desirable, but the sooner we train off the better.

Ennis, January 30, 1847. 

I must revise the lists for the entire district from end to end, and make the Committees 
revise theirs. In fact, I will have them very nicely made out, provided you think it will (at 
this period) be worth while to make the Committees work properly, and if I commence 
I should like to finish. 

The great disadvantage of these high wages is, that not a farmer can get a man, and they 
are afraid to ask for them. 

I would strongly call your attention to the expediency of issuing a circular, stating that 
where task-work cannot be regularly set and measured it is not to he attempted, and that the 
men must be paid according to the Treasury Minute. If this is not done, I am afraid the 
farmers will not get men. 

I am quite disgusted with the Committees, and there is an air of intimidation through the 
country ; however, be assured I will not give in to one of them. 

Pray look at my journal. I understand in the next, district the men receive as high as Is.

employment which confined them to their fields and farms, and banded toge- 
ther instead into regular squads of fifties and twenties, placed in a position of 
all others perhaps the most dangerous to society, and the most liable to be 
tampered with. 

We will not further allude to this subject, being aware that it engages the 
serious attention of those best able to judge of and meet the difficulty. But 
this much was due, in justice to the directing and superintending staff, the 
magnitude of which has been so much commented upon, without, we submit, a 
due consideration of the numbers they control, the haste with which they have 
been brought together, and the circumstances in which they are placed. 

The duties performed by each class, with their relative positions, and the 
connecting links between them, have been from time to time described in our 
monthly reports. 

The. inefficient are gradually replaced by better, but as long as the labour 
roll increases, the directing power must increase with it. 

The 74 inspecting officers have on an average 13 Relief Committees to attend, 
to, and 8000 labourers to distribute among the engineers, with whom they 
communicate. 

The 72 engineers and county surveyors have each 140 working, parties, with, 
on an average, only five assistant engineers: 

The 6894 overseers are distributed among not less than 10,000 working 
parties. 

The 2832 check clerks, under the inspecting officers, move from work to 
work during the day to see that the men are present, and that there are no 
others than those furnished by the Inspecting Officer from the lists of the 
Relief Committees. 

The anxiety and labour increases as it ascends, and in many branches there 
is considerable personal danger. One Inspecting Officer, Lieut. Millward, 
R.A., was openly attacked, and dragged from his car in the streets of Donegal, 
on the 25th of January, while proceeding to his duty, and the most continuous 
daily and nightly toil is too little to accomplish the intense duty required in 
the higher branches. In the Appendix to our several Reports ample proof 
will be found of this, and we are satisfied that if the staff be compared with the 
officers and sub-officers of any organised body, civil or military, its small 
number and inconsiderable expense will be at once apparent. 

Taken in gross there is one director of labour to 80 labourers, and the cost 
of superintendence, from the highest to the lowest, is only 7 per cent. 

In regard to the appointments and the patronage, as it has been called, we 
can only say it has been one of the most difficult part of our duties. Every 
complaint has usually wound up with an application for employment. But the 
appointments have developed much useful ability, which will be required 
under any system of relief, and in the humbler classes of officers- have them- 
selves furnished considerable relief to deserving and suffering individuals. 

During the month of January little has occurred of an unusual character. 
The Relief Committees, pressed themselves by increasing numbers, have pressed 
on us, and we have met their demands to the utmost of our means 

In some places, as in Clare for example, they appear to have thrown up all 
control, and to have placed nearly the whole population on their lists without 
discrimination. 

When works have, from; the increased numbers, fallen out before others 
could be provided, new sessions have been called, and his Excellency the Lord 
Lieutenant has in such cases allowed the works to be continued in anticipation' 
of the-presentments. 

The character of these works will be found to vary Very much in different 
counties'; many new roads of much utility have been, constructed;, and such- 
works are ultimately reproductive,, and will be highly beneficial, not only to 
the districts themselves, but to the public generally. In the better cultivated' 
and more populous parts of the country the communications have- been, for the 
present injured/and many roads rendered nearly impassable, while, from the 
crowded and confused nature of the labour, the original estimates have been 
expended without proportionate results. The completion of. these works, 
however, will still furnish useful employment for a considerable number of 
labourers.

The attacks on pay clerks have continued, but we have, as far as possible, 
persevered in the effort to carry the money to the men, as a less evil than 
bringing the men to the money ; the congregation of large numbers in towns 
being fraught with danger. Indeed, when the amount paid daily is considered, 
when every day nearly 50,000/. is actually on the roads, in process of transport 
from party to party, it must be rather matter of surprise that so few robberies 
have taken place, and so little loss has occurred. Our payments are now 
become regular, and are seldom in arrear, which is highly creditable to the 
vigilance of the inspectors and to the activity of the pay clerks. To the credit 
of the latter, it is gratifying to record, that there has been as yet no single 
instance of malversation or defalcation. 

In consequence of the attacks, it has been found necessary to provide escorts. 
We have on every occasion experienced the most cordial assistance from the 
constabulary, and we have authorised the attendance of an armed civilian when 
escorts could not be procured ; indeed, from all the public departments we 
have met the fullest support and co-operation. 

The want of tillage, and cessation of farm labour, are still dwelt on, in many 
of the reports from our Inspecting Officers. This evil will probably be, to 
some extent, inseparable from any system of relief ; at present it is no doubt 
due to the temptation of money wages, and it is worthy of notice that, while 
one deputation comes to us to complain of the low rate of wages, scarcely, as 
they say, above the level of starvation, another follows perhaps the same day 
to represent the ruin which is brought on agriculture by the temptation of the 
Public Works. 

In regard to the Drainage Presentments under Mr. Labouchere’s letter, we 
have to report that, during the month of January, presentments for repro- 
ductive works have been made in 54- baronies, which, in addition to the 68 
mentioned in our last report, makes a total of 122 baronies in which drainage 
presentments have been, or will be immediately commenced.

It is our anxious wish that the Drainage Presentments, being works to be 
paid for by the voluntary undertaking of individuals, should be carried out in 
an economical manner, and we are happy to say, excepting in a few cases, that 
our object has been attained, and the work has been executed at a fair rate. 

In some localities, particularly at Patrick’s Well, in the county of Limerick, 
a number of men having been forced upon the drainage works, owing to defi- 
ciency of employment on the roads, some irregularity took place, and fair value 
was not given for the sum expended. And in others the labourers, anxious for 
day s work, neglected their tasks, but, on the whole, the drainage task works 
have been well executed, at prices which enabled the willing labourer to earn 
from 1.9. to Is. 3d. per day. It is to be observed that the drainage presentment 
works have been carried out by an establishment newly created, and, as few 
professional drainage engineers could be obtained, the conductors of the works 
have been selected from among a class of young gentlemen, who within the 
last few yearn have studied farming as a profession, and who have been pupils 
m several of the principal farming establishments of Scotland and England, 
and who, among other branches, have studied and practised scientific draining 
according to the modern system; and we are happy in being able to state that 
a sufficient number of persons, duly qualified, have offered their services, and, 
m consequence, we found no difficulty in forming our establishment, which, on 
tne whole, is working m a satisfactory manner.

The recent decision of your Lordships on the Waterford and Limerick 
Railway, will enable us to proceed with the earth-works of that line, as soon as 
we receive from the secretary and solicitor of the company, with whom we are 
in communication for the purpose, the detailed map and the schedules of 
assents from the proprietors, lessees, and occupiers. 

We append to this Report an abstract of the principal outrages which have F., P so. 
occurred, and we think they will be considered very few indeed, when all the 
circumstances and temptations are considered ; this is highly creditable to the 
people, to whose exemplary patience, fortitude and resignation we have before 
borne testimony. But we cannot close our Report without also adverting to the 
conduct of our Inspecting Officers, indeed officers of every grade, who, from 
the highest to the lowest, have exerted themselves in their respective capacities 
to maintain subordination. They have felt the pressure, and suffered from the 
distressing nature of their tasks ; but they have also felt that the public eye was 
upon them, that they were armed with powers, and entrusted with discretion, 
which demanded moderation and temper. Outrage or intimidation was 
promptly followed by suspension or stoppage of the works, till the people saw 
the injury fell upon themselves in the long run. 

This power, to possess its full effect, required to be exercised promptly, and 
it was necessary to devolve it on the local officers. It has had the fullest effect, 
and has no where been exercised without full occasion. 

And, among the various classes of our assistants, we would especially mention 
the small party of Royal Sappers and Miners. They have been distributed in 
the counties of Roscommon, Mayo, and Limerick, from the officers in each of 
which, we have received the most gratifying reports of their efficiency and 
ability. 

They were accustomed to obey, and they have made themselves obeyed. 

Frequently, in circumstances of much delicacy and difficulty, they have 
shown a readiness of resource highly to their credit, and when they shortly 
return to their corps we shall request from your Lordships a commendatory 
testimony to their conduct for the Master-General of the Ordnance. 

In Dublin, also, the labour has been of no ordinary character, but the divi- 
sion of our duties into departments, prescribed by your Lordships, has been 
highly beneficial. The magnitude of the relief operations in the country 
required of course an equally sudden and extensive augmentation at Head 
Quarters. The rapid examination of the numerous schedules from Presentment 
Sessions, each of the projects having to be considered ; first, as to its relative 
necessity for relief, with other projects ; then as to its engineering advantages or 
disadvantages ; the investigation of the conflicting individual interests benefited 
or injured, of which every one acquainted with Ireland will appreciate the 
difficulty. The engineers, surveyors, overseers, and a due supply of tools to be 
provided as rapidly as possible, frequently with every exertion very ill pro- 
vided. 

The correspondence alone growing out of this single branch of the Relief 
Works, viz., that relating to schedules, is of immense magnitude. 

Finally, the furnishing of funds, arrangements with banks, supply of silver, 
organization, and inspection of pay clerks and payments, with the preparation 
and examination of vouchers and pay sheets, for the mixed task and daily 
labour of half a million of men, paid ■weekly. Those who have paid working 
parties of hundreds, or of thousands, on ordinary service, will feel the magni- 
tude of this task, on which it is not necessary to dilate; the statement of 
numbers is sufficient. These unusual and uncertain labours have, of course, set 
all regular hours at defiance ; the night, as well as the day, has been cheerfully 
given by all.

Some of the parties applying for thorough drainage have expressed their 
desire to have their applications postponed until the details of the new law 
shall be known. The examinations and reports, however, are being made, so 
that no delay may arise under whatever form it may determine to proceed with 
the works.

Whenever the weather permitted the number of men employed have been 
increased, but the frequent interruptions caused by floods occasionally dimi- 
nished the number, and compelled many to seek employment on the Relief 
Works; and though the disposition manifested by the labourers has been good 
in general, yet the frequent interruption by floods has been injurious to their 
steady perseverance in the execution of task-work, which, by diminishing their 
earnings and, as a consequence, reducing their physical powers to a considerable 
extent, disqualified them for the effective execution of the work.

Fisheries. 

It was hoped that ere this some addition might have been made to the scanty 
means of subsistence of the inhabitants of. the coasts, by the operation of the 
three fish-curing stations established in the west of Ireland. From reports 
made to us, however, it appears that several reasons have combined to retard 
this result. The weather has been unfavourable, whilst the fishermen them- 
selves, weakened in body from want of food, are still more reluctant from 
this cause to undergo the increased exertion which severe weather unavoid- 
ably requires ; and which, from the wretched nature of their equipments, is 
inevitable. 

Reports, however, which will be found in our Appendix, have commenced 
to hold out some prospects of success. The Board’s Inspector, Mr. Ffennell, 
speaks most favourably of the fishermen at Belmullet, who are making pre- 
parations and anxious to begin. At Killybegs, another station, some fish have 
been taken, which were sold from the boat at fair prices ; and a further report 
states, that the agent there had purchased one lot, upon which he had com- 
menced the operation of curing. 

In conclusion, we can only say that we shall hail with joy any change in the 
system of relief which may prove satisfactory to the country, and restore us to 
our legitimate capacity, as Commissioners of Public Works, and therefore large 
employers of labour, in which we shall endeavour to devise and create as many 
really useful works as can be found to afford occupation, till the people can 
again be absorbed into their natural channels, but unembarrassed by the necessity 
of employing the weak and infirm, and destitute, merely for employment sake, 
with very little reference to the work they do.

APPENDIX. 

(A.) 

Sir, Wexford, February 1 , 1847. 

I beg to state for the information of the Commissioners that, in obedience to their 
orders, conveyed in your letter of the 27th ult., requiring me to proceed to this place for the 
purpose of inquiring into and reporting certain allegations, to the effect that great irregularities 
had taken place in the Public Works in the neighbourhood of Enniscorthy, in respect of 
labourers not commencing work until a late hour, and working only four hours and a-half in 
the day ; of farmers holding 20 acres of land being, with their horses, employed on the Relief 
"Works, all of which appeared in the “ Times” newspaper of the 23rd ult., I arrived here on 
the 28th, and put myself in communication with Mr. Farrell, the county surveyor. 

Captain Dyer, the inspecting officer, was then absent on duty in the northern part of the 
county ; I therefore was without the advantage of seeing him until to-day. 

The work alluded to in the anonymous letter in the “ Times ” is not particularized ; but in 
the opinion of Mr. Farrell and others acquainted with the locality, it was the new line of road 
from Enniscorthy to Kiltealy now in process of formation. Accordingly I visited this road on 
the 29th, accompanied by Mr. Farrell. 

I made particular inquiries as to the allegations contained in the following paragraph : — 
“ They (the labourers) commence work at 9 a. m., give up for dinner at 11 a. m., resume at 
1 p. m., and are dismissed at half-past 3 P. M., thus working but four hours and a-half per 
day.” And so far as this work is concerned the statement is untrue. Instead of there being 
anything to censure there was much to praise. I ascertained from the labourers, overseers, and 
assistant engineers, whose statements entirely agreed, that the men came to work at daylight, 
had but one hour during the day for their single meal, and only remitted their labours when it 
was too dark to carry them on. 

Reference to the accompanying document will show the rate of wages and other particulars 
relating to this work, marked No. I on Schedule, as well as to Nos. 5, 28, 29, 30, and 32. 

The wages on this work, ranging from Is. 2d. to Is. Id., are certainly above the general 
average throughout the country ; but, on the other hand, they have been honestly earned. 
The principle of task-work has been acted upon, and the labourers have given a fair day’s 
work for a fair day’s wages. 

I am happy to add that the road in question will be highly useful, as it will open out a con- 
siderable mountain district, and afford a direct communication to the lime districts of the county 
Carlow. There is no lime found in the neighbourhood of Enniscorthy, where it is much re- 
quired for agricultural purposes. This line of road will supply what has hitherto been a great 
deficiency. 

With respect to the allegation in the paragraph, “ The employment may be called a family 
affair, as the 100 people do not belong to more than 30 families, and of these many are of 
farmers holding 20 acres of land, &c.,” I have this day questioned Captain Dyer, the 
inspecting officer. He stated distinctly that he believes such to be untrue. From the inquiries 
he is in the habit of making, he is quite sure that if such abuses existed he could not but be 
aware of them. 

But though the allegations referred to are not at all applicable to the Enniscorthy and 
Kiltealy road, which, as I have already stated, is the road supposed to be alluded to, I regret 
to state that so much as relates to irregularities respecting hours of attendance was applicable 
to another work, called the Neville Hill cutting, No. 32 on the Schedule, 
in y i f i,e , d P^ ace on 30th; it was noon; all the men were off work, having left it at 
10 o clock to go into Enniscorthy to receive their pay. I inquired why they were not paid on 

. ff 011 . ‘ .7 was tcdd ^hat such had been the custom ; the labourers were permitted by a 
neighbouring farmer to go into one of his meadows by the road-side for that purpose, but they 
stole his fowls, and he would no longer allow them on the premises. Afterwards they were 
permitted to go into the town at their dinner hour, when the pay-clerk usually met them. But 
on the day I was there they had all gone at 10 o’clock ; and at half-past 12, when I quitted 
the work, but few of them had returned. It appeared that the pay-clerk could not settle with 
afternoon 6 m ° rmUg ’ the pay sheets not having been completed; but they were all paid in the 

I found that these labourers were by far the most unruly and irregular in the county. They 
consisted chiefly, if not entirely, of destitute artisans from the town, wholly unaccustomed to 
field labour, and fully impressed with the notion that they were to be paid in ratio to their 
wants, and not in ratio to their labour. They were for the most part thrust upon the work at 
its commencement, the 11th of January, by the Relief Committee of Enniscorthy, without 

, . ,\ in most lrre o u ^ ar manner. The work was overcrowded with men ; insubordination 
and idleness was the natural result; and Mr. Hill, the assistant engineer, though anxious to 
per orm his duties, was quite unequal to the emergency. He was incapable of controlling 

em. In these circumstances which continued through a week, Mr. Farrell found it neces- 
Sar i\'r t °A UperSe ^ e ^ r * and sencl another assistant to the work. 

Mr. Cowman chosen for this purpose, fully justified the confidence placed in him. He took 
charge on the loth, and explained to the labourers the principle of task-work, from which 
nothing wouM induce him to deviate. This was repugnant to them ; a riot was on the point 
™ \ Mr ' Co ' v T n WaS firm ’ They threatened to take his life if ho attempted to 
m k ‘ mP® took . one « nd of the measuring tape himself, and ordered the overseer 

to take me other 1 hey continued -their threats and imprecations, but Mr. Cowman completed 

his measurements, and returned them for the small sum of Id. per day. 1

BOARD OF WORKS. 



41 



I beg to draw the attention of the Commissioners to Mr. Cowman’s conduct on this occa- 
sion ; they will remember the historical character of an Enniscorthy mob, and they will appre- 
ciate the determination of an individual who knew them, defied them, and, single handed, 
controlled them. The ensuing week the labourers worked better. 

I beg most respectfully to recommend this valuable and assiduous officer to the favourable 
consideration of the Board. 

On the whole, therefore, I have to report that the allegations contained in the "Times” 
are untrue, inasmuch as where the labourers were well paid they earned their wages fairly ; 
and where irregularities took place they earned but little money. 

I have alluded to the. Enniscorthy Relief Committee having sent a number pf persons to the 
Neville Hill road, and the .sub-engineer, Mr. Hill, having employed them, without having 
received the sanction of the inspecting officer. I have reason to believe .that the inspecting 
officer, Captain Dyer, has not succeeded in disabusing their minds in this respect; I, therefore, 
beg to suggest that a public letter be written to Captain Dyer, desiring him on no account to 
permit a recurrence of such irregularity, and also to make this Committee comprehend that 
their powers do not extend to controlling or interfering with the progress of the Public Works, 
or the persons employed thereon in any way. 

I have, &c., 

J. C. Walker, Esq., D. O’Brien. 

£ c - i* c - 

Sir, Wexford, February 1, 1847. 

In compliance with the request contained in your letter of the 29th ult., I have had 
the accompanying table drawn gut, which sets forth all you require, with the exception of the 
“ hour at which, the people come and leave the works.” On this point I beg to inform you 
that with reference to one work only, “ Cutting at Neville’s Hill,” have I been able to dis- 
cover irregularity, and here there may be some reason for the complaint, the investigation of 
which is your object. I shall not enter into details further than to say, that except on this 
work the labour has been from day-light to dark, with one hour allowed for meals. 

As you will have every evidence afforded you that you may require, it is unnecessary to occupy 
you further. 

The irregularities complained of I had remedied as soon as discovered, and you will find 
that now and for some time past there have been grounds for satisfaction rather than for 
censure. 

I have, &c. 

Capt, O'Brien, General Inspector, (Signed) James R. Farrell.

Labourers working willingly at low rate of 
wages (8 d.) were forced off the works by a

a meeting for the demand of a higher Tate of 
wages (lOd.) ; inciting addresses were de- 
livered by several of the speakers.

The labourers on works “ strike,” because of a

they enter the town to the number of 300, 
and on being remonstrated with by Captain 
Hawkins (who considered his life in danger), 
and Mr. Kelly, county surveyor, they threat- 
ened to plunder the town unless their wages 
was again settled at lOd. a-day.

Mr. Kearney, county surveyor, on leaving 
Court-house, after having attended present- 
ment sessions, was hunted, hooted, abused, 
and pelted with stones, and would have been 
murdered by an enraged mob but lor the 
interference of the police, and the “ extra- 
ordinary exertions” of a Roman Catholic 
priest, who accompanied him in his escape 
for several miles out of town ; the people’s 
excitement and cause of vengeance against 
Mr. Kearney attributable to the inciting lan- 
guage used in Court, in his address To the 
people, by a magistrate.

[Poor Relief Department.] (G.) 

Barony of Famey , County Monaghan. 

Works under Mr. Labouchere’s Letter. 

I cannot describe the poverty and destitution among the people in this barony ; unfor- 
tunalely the works in aid of relief were not commenced until the people were almost starving. 
Hundreds of them came to work without having tasted food for days before ; the result was, 
they were unable to earn wages capable of supporting themselves, and numbers of them left 
the employment, in despair to go to the poor-house. 

Throughout the whole barony I. witnessed the same painful distress. 

I found that they were unable to earn wages exceeding 8 d. a day (see Schedule annexed) at 
the ordinary and customary prices for task-work in the country ; every effort was made to 
induce them to exert themselves, and rouse their energies, but to no effect. I placed over them 
the host and most experienced overseers I could obtain, those who had aided in establishing 
with success tile system of task-work in other parts of the country, but their efforts have failed; 
the men were unable to do more, and after every exertion had been made I found myself 
obliged to raise the scale of prices, so as to enable them, weak, infirm, and badly fed as they 
were, to earn wages that would save them and their families from actual starvation. Since 
then, everything has gone on well ; the number of hands has increased to about 4500, and the 
people are, generally speaking, industrious. 

At the sessions at which these works were presented for, it was thought it would not be 
necessary to employ more than 3000 people. 

The people are peaceable and quiet, no riot or disturbance of any kind has taken place. 

The works are progressing satisfactorily and well, though we have not experienced that aid 
or assistance from the proprietors or their agents that might have been expected, and which 
would have helped us through our difficulties. The class of people employed as stewards or 
gangers, and recommended by the proprietors, have been found most inefficient, and their 
inefficiency has of course increased largely the difficulty of controlling so large a work. 

Works are now open in upwards of 50 different localities in the barony, so that employmen 
may be said to bo at the door of every labourer. Men, infirm and able-bodied, women, and 
children, have been employed, and I do not think relief in the shape of employment could be 
more effectually afforded. The annexed is an abstract of the number of men employed in the 
barony since the works were commenced, the average rate of wages made, and the total amount 
expended for labour up to the 30lh January last. 

Payments are made once a week. I have divided the barony into four divisions, the pay 
returns of which terminate on different days; by this means all men are paid a day or two 
after the week’s earnings arc due. 

* S. W. Roberts. 

Drainage Commission Office, Castlchellingham,

BOARD OF WORKS. 
(H.) 



Sir, 



Fishery Station , Killybegs, 
February 3, 1847. 



Enclosed I beg to hand monthly account current, which I hope may be found correct ; 
the vouchers have already been forwarded, the form for the monthly account not having been 
received at this time. u 

I beg to report that I have purchased a small lot of fish, being the first one offered ; though 
ready to purchase some time ago, as advised, such is the destitution of the people in regard to 
food, that the fishermen are selling their fish at higher prices from their boat (say 7s. or 7s. 6 d. 
for cod, and 8s. for ling) than I can give laid down here, and as I do not like to interfere with 
the local demand, the quantity brought to me has been small. 

At St. John’s Point I saw, myself, ling and cod sold all round at 6s. Qd. per dozen from the 
boat. The printed notices were all posted at Julan, Kilcar, Cargy, Killybegs, St. John’s Point, 
Killighter, and Duncansby, within 24 hours after their receipt, and I informed the people 
myself what prices would be given, so that they were fully aware , on every particular, of the 
objects and intentions of the Board. 

I am in hopes, now that the weather is fair, that the take of fish will be more abundant, and 
consequently produce a surplus over the present demand, so that the station may be supplied 
with a larger quantity and in a regular manner. 

The agent has not spared, and will not, either his time or energies in the promotion of the 
views of the Board ; at the same time he would remark, that it is impossible at a fixed price to 
force a market, though he certainly would make no alterations in the prices as they stand ; a 
market will surely be made, and a ready one, so soon as the fish are more plentiful. 

You will please excuse any informalities in the accounts rendered already, the agent not 
having bad die forms, or knowing the exact manner in which they were to be kept. I will thank 
you to inform me in what manner the receipts for fish bought are to be taken, on the pay lists, 
or otherwise. 



Jos. C. Walker, Esq., 

Secretary. 



I am, &c. 

(Signed) J. C. Kennan. 



Extract from a Letter of Mr. W. T. Ffennell, one of the Board’s Inspectors of Fisheries, 
dated from Belmullet, February 2, 1847. 

I arrived in Belmullet on the 31st, and found at the curing station that everything 
was in readiness to purchase and cure. No fish had been offered for sale, the weather for the 
preceding week being so severe that no boat could attempt to venture out. This day the weather 
appears to have settled, and I have no doubt that the fishermen here will avail themselves of it. 
Several this day, for the first time, have purchased hooks from the agent, and I find by con- 
versing with them that they are very anxious to avail themselves of the advantages which the 
purchase of their fish will afford. The people here appear to appreciate it highly, and they 
express themselves in terms much to be commended. They appear very anxious to be instructed 
in the modes of fishing, and it has been very gratifying to me to experience the attention with 
which they listened to many little matters of detail which I conveyed to them with regard to 
tackle, bait, &c. ; the anxious manner in which some of them put queries to me evinced a desire 
to be instructed not often found to exist among fishermen, who, generally speaking, are more, 
perhaps, as a class, wrapped up in a belief of self excellence than any other body of persons. I 
feel it only just to make this comment on the Belmullet fishermen, and I feel great confidence 
of success at this station in particular. I hope in my next report to be able to state some sub- 
stantial evidence to justify my anticipations.

As it is often difficult to know whether Minutes, &c., on original letters sent from this

Circular, No. 50. 

[Relief Department.] 

Office of Public Works, 
January 12, 1847. 

Frequent representationshaving been received of accidents, from the unguarded state 
in which roads in progress have been left at night, the Commissioners desire to call the attention 
of the engineers to the circumstance, and desire that proper watchmen and lanterns be always 
placed on the dangerous parts. 

The Commissioners also desire that when works are left incomplete, from the deficiency of 
funds, especial care may be taken to leave them as safe and passable as possible until additional 
funds are provided. 

. By order, 

Jos. C. Walker, Secretary. 



Reproductive Works. 

Board of Public Works, 
January 12, 1847. 

Reply to Applications as to how far Electoral Divisions become practically responsible for 
their own poor only, and for those in their immediate neighbourhood, as long as the Works 
presented for within them remain unexecuted, no Relief Lists being supplied from any 
place within distance of them by reason of private employment. 

All the destitute labourers of a barony are eligible for employment in any electoral division 
or part of any electoral division within it, but practically only those who reside within a conve- 
nient distance of any such division are able to avail themselves of its labour. 

The works under the 9 and 10 Vic., cap. 107, are sanctioned solely for the relief of destitu- 
tion, and the lists of Relief Committees are the official test of destitution. 

So long, therefore, as no Relief lists exist within convenient distance of the works in any electoral 
division, those works will not be sanctioned, and as no levy can be made for works not executed, 
the electoral division in which, from the non-existence of such lists, there have been no works, 
will be exempted from taxation. 

By order, 

Jos. C. Walker, Secretary. 



[Relief Department.] 

Instructions for Engineers and Assistant Engineers in charge of Operations for Relief 
under the Authority of the Board of Works. 

N.B.— The perch in these Instructions is the statute perch of 5 J yards. 

Sir, 

You have been already informed that it is the desire of the Commissioners that all the 
works under the Relief Act shall be executed by task. 

In addition to the personal communications you have had with the district engineer, your 
attention is directed to the following instructions. 

It is difficult to give general directions for work at once sufficiently comprehensive and specific ; 
a great deal must depend upon the judgment and practical knowledge of the executive officer; 
so that any rules that may be laid down must be modified by circumstances. They are merely 
intended to supply in some measure the place of practical knowledge when that cannot be com- 
manded. 

Presentment Works. — New Roads. 

' Before lockspitting, the intended line of road should be walked over and carefully examined. 
The best direction and inclines that the nature of the ground will admit of should be ascer- 
tained, adhering, as nearly as circumstances will permit, to the points described in the present- 
ment. 

The theodolite will be a good instrument to determine the slopes, and fix the main points at 
which the gradients vary, (an accurate section can afterwards be taken with the spint level). 
The laying out of the line between these fixed points may be entrusted to the men who under- 
stand the Devonshire level and boning rods. These men will be able to put in the curves and 
distinctly mark the line of road by a loekspit, and also the cutting and filling along it, by 
making excavations to the depth of the cuttings, and by raising mounds of earth to the height 
of the fillings (at short intervals) ; this done, the overseer can, with great facility, determine on 
the proper division of the line into lots of, say, 15 to 40 perches; he will be guided chiefly by 
the equalization of the cutting and filling within the boundary of each lot, as it will not answer 
to have stuff to shift from one lot into another. 

At the end of each lot, the transverse section of the roadway should be made by a narrow 
formation, which will serve to define the extent of the lot, and guide the men as to the proper 
shape of the roadway. This may be contracted for with a party of handy men. 

The overseer in charge will examine and number the several lots, enter in his book the 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




72 BOARD OF WORKS. 

length, average cutting and filling, quality of the. soil, whether of sand, peat, clay, gravel, or 

The engineer in charge will examine the work, and determine with the overseer on the 
value to be affixed to each lot for formation, in proportion to the quantity of cutting and other 
circumstances, fencing and draining by the lineal perch of 5J yards, having reference to the 
scale of prices and instructions herewith sent. 

A short table can be readily drawn up, by which the number of cubic yards for the various 
widths and depths of cutting will appear on inspection, and may save some trouble and time 
in calculation. 

It is essential that the water tables should be gradually opened with the least possible delay 
in all flat and marshy lands, to admit of the bed of the roadway drying quickly, so as to com- 
plete the work in those places with as little delay as possible. 

In passing through cropped lands every exertion should be made to complete the forming of 
fences, that no unnecessary damage may arise. 

Care should be taken to leave a sufficient vent for draining off the surface waters from the 
road, by small pipes constructed with stones 6 inches in width, under the fences and footpaths, 
at 20 perches or 110 yards apart, on each side of the road. 

No time must be lost in the construction of cross pipes under the roads, to be let by con- 
tract to a mason, who will be attached to each overseer’s party for this puipose, as soon as the 
necessary materials are provided, at the places where such pipes are required. 

In constructing roads over bog soils, the best preparation for forming and soling is to strip 
off the surface sod, shape the ground underneath according to the section directed, lay on a bed 
of heath, when it can be procured, and lay down the sod afterwards, putting on a second or 
third coat of such sods before laying on the soling. 

Before constructing the fences, the base on which they are to stand should be levelled 
uniformly with the roadway, and not, as is generally the case, constructed on the natural sur- 
face of the ground, without regard to its inequality and undulations. The sod fences should 
be in general 5 feet at base, 3 feet 6 inches in height, and finished to 1 foot in width at top, 
with an offset of 6 inches betwixt the base of the fence and the drain ; a facing of stones, of 
15 inches in height, will be an improvement. The outer drains may be excavated 5 feet in 
width at top, 3 feet 6 inches in depth, and 1 foot in width at bottom. Single gullets from 
IS inches to 2 feet 6 inches in width, paved at bottom and flagged at top ; side walls 18 inches 
in width, with good quoins. 

The side slopes of earth-cutting and embankments should not be less than one to one, and 
in all cases where embankments exceed 5 feet in height, one and a half to one. An allowance 
should be made for subsidence ; this will be proportioned to the height and description of filling, 
whether of bog, clay, gravel, or sand. 

No. 1 may be considered the section of a 24-foot road, with footpath. 



24 feet 




No. 2 is to be the section of the 21-foot roads.

The economy of labour is of much consequence ; it will therefore be necessary to see that the 
men employed keep correctly to their sections in cutting and filling, and that they are properly 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 





BOARD OF WORKS. 73 

apportioned on the several parts of the work, and that the excavators, fillers, and wheelers are 
in due proportion. 

The number of men to be employed in excavating will depend on the kind of stuff, whether 
of sand, clay, or gravel, and the length of the runs for the barrow-men will define the number 
of fillers. 

Take, for example, a hill to be excavated consisting chiefly of a stiff clay, and the lead as 
two stages of 24 yards each. To work this with a double run would require the following 
men : — 

Finders . . . . 6 to 8 

Fillers .... 4 
Wheelers. . . . 4— 14 to 16. 

A man can probably be spared from the finders, occasionally, to clear the way before the 
barrows at the tip ; the regulation of the roadway and of the slopes of the banks should after- 
wards be contracted for. If the material to be excavated be loose, a smaller number of finders 
may answer, and if it be compact a greater number will be required. If the stages be made 
too long the fillers will not be constantly employed, if too short the wheelers must wait till the 
barrows are filled. There may be cases in which, from want of space, or want of barrows, it 
may be necessary to employ three fillers for two barrows, and make the stage longer. 

Ihese are matters, however, which will right themselves. If the men are disposed to work, 
and earn good wages, they will soon discover the most economical mode of working. At the 
commencement, however, the overseer employed by the Board should be able to place the men 
and put in the runs in the best manner. 

Models for fences should be made of laths, and kept on the works. 

Stewards, to be paid by the Board, must be appointed to take charge of the several gangs as 
usual, and see that the work is properly executed. 

The check clerks are to keep their check accounts of each gang as usual. 

It is of the utmost importance that the ordinary labour of the country should not be inter- 
fered with by the Public Works, and overseers must recollect that these works have been insti- 
tuted for the sole object of employing poor labourers who cannot by possibility find employment 
elsewhere from private persons. The overseers are, therefore, strictly required to strike off their 
lists any number of men who may be required by any farmer or other employer who may have 
occasion for labourers. 

Measurement and Valuation. 

It is of importance that the work be measured before being commenced, and be divided into 
lots, the dimensions of which should be carefully preserved for future reference if any question 
should arise. 

The value must also be determined beforehand, and the work may be let either by the lot 
or by measurement ; but in all cases the quantity must be stated as near as may be in the 
periodical returns made to the engineer’s office. The determination of the value of a piece of 
work, either by lot or by measurement, must be in a great measure a practical question, but, as 
some guide, from 2>\d. to 4 id. per yard may be stated as a high but not an unreasonable price 
for finding and filling stiff clay, and from \d. to id. per cubic yard per stage of 24 yards as the 
price for wheeling. From id. to 2d. per yard would be a high price for finding and filling 
bog stuff, and \d. per stage for wheeling. If any stones occur in the excavation, and are pre- 
served and wheeled into heaps, about 5 d. per cubic yard may be allowed for them in addition 
to the value entered for the measurement of the cutting. When the old metalling is taken 
off existing roads, the same principle of valuation may be applied. The price allowed for 
breaking stones should vary from 6 d. to lOd. for limestone, according to quality ; and from 
lOd. to Is. 2d. for compact sandstone, or harder rocks. 

For rock cutting, it is impossible to fix a price which would approach even to an approxi- 
mation, as it may vary from 6 d. to 2s. 6 d. per cubic yard, according to circumstances. 

The value of quarrying stones for metalling or walling differs widely from rock cutting, and 
may be stated at from 4 d. to 8 d. per cubic yard. 

The price of a well-made sod fence, 5 feet to 6 feet wide at base, and 3 feet 6 inches high, 
may be taken at from 3s. to 6s. per lineal chain of 22 yards. If stones are used in the inuer 
face for one foot high, the style of the fence will be much improved thereby, and 6s. per chain 
will not be an unreasonable price. These prices take for granted that the fences should be 
constructed with much care, and in most cases the outer drain will be made at the same time, 
without further cost. Light formations of the roadway under one foot cutting may be valued 
by tbe lineal chain of 22 yards at from 6s. to 8s. Gullets to be priced at so much each ; a 
good 2-foot gullet is worth from 20s. to 30s. when well built and paved. 

There are many parts of the work the value of which it will be difficult to determine, espe- 
cially in the case of half-finished works, such as fences, formations, &c. But such difficulty 
should not prevent the engineer from setting the work by contract; let sufficient allowance be 
made, and if a doubt exists the labourers should have the advantage of it. Under present cir- 
cumstances, it will be generally found that, even at very high rates, work will be executed 
cheaper by task than by the day’s work. 

It is the desire of the Commissioners that such prices be allowed that a man working mode- 
rately may earn from lOd. to 12 d. per day, and that any man who can and will work hard 
may earn from 15 d. to 18c?. per day. 

It is of importance to explain to the labourers that the introduction of taskwork has not been 
adopted for the purpose of reducing their earnings, but as a great boon to them, inasmuch as 
it will enable them to earn, if they wish, in the broken weather of winter, more than they could 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




74 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



by day’s work in summer. In short, by task work alone can the labourers hope to'earn suffi- 
cient to supply their families during winter ; and it is expected that every exertion will be made 
to introduce the system generally. 

The labourers are to be employed on a list having been made out and signed by the inspect- 
ing officer of the district, to whom you will send a requisition for whatever number of men you 
are prepared to employ, distinguishing the number in each relief district. 

In commencing any work care should be taken to divide it into small lots, each of which is 
to be let by task or measurement to a gang of men, to be composed, as the case may be, of 
from 10 to 12, to be headed by a working ganger, who is to receive one shilling in the pound 
in addition to his portion of the earning of the gang ; but payment in the way of subsistence 
must be made at the end of each week. 

The men may choose their own ganger, whose duty it will be to take directions from the over- 
seers, settle with his gang for the task work, when measured and valued by the engineer, and 
take charge of the implements supplied to his gang. 

The subsistence to be paid weekly ; and on the completion of each lot of work it will be 
measured and valued according to the following scale of prices, made out in accordance with 
the Board’s directions.

Where stones or rock occur in excavations care should be taken to preserve the stones, to be 
piled in convenient heaps, measured and paid for at the rate of 4 d. to 6 d. per cubic yard, in 
addition to the value allowed by the measurement of the excavation ; the same principle of 
valuation to be applied to removing and piling into heaps the old metalling of roads. 

When wheelbarrows are used for shifting the material, the stages are to be from 20 to 30 
yards, according to circumstances ; but for valuation a stage is to be considered 25 yards, and 
an allowance of |d. per stage is to be made. 

When the lead is more than 100 yards it will be necessary to employ horses, and the price 
for cartage to be from 3d. to 6 d. per cubic yard, for distances from 20 to 120 perches. 

Where there is less than 1 foot cutting or filling, the formation is to be valued at from Is. 6 d. 
to 4s. per perch. 

Fencing . — Sod fences on embankments are to be 4 feet 6 inches wide at base, 3 feet high, 
and may be valued at from Is. to Is. 4 d. per perch ; on level ground they are to be 5 feet wide 
at base, 3 feet 6 inches high, and the price per perch will be Is. 6 d. The fences will be im- 
proved by a facing of stones, 15 inches in height, along the road side, and the price may be 
increased to 2s. per perch. The prices for sod fences include the value of side drains. 

Stone Walls to be 3 feet high, 2 feet wide at base, and 1 foot 6 inches at top, and will cost 
from 3s. to 4s. per perch, according to circumstances. 

Retaining Walls, of dry masonry, to be paid for at from Is. 6 d. to 2s. 6 d. per cubic yard, 
according to the situation and convenience of materials. 

Drains. — Catch-water drains to be 4 feet wide at top, 2 feet 6 inches deep, may be valued 
at from 3d. to 5d. per perch. Bog-drains, 6 feet wide at top, 3 feet 6 inches deep, will cost 3d. 
to 5d. per perch. 

Rubile Drains, 3 feet deep, filled 1 foot high with small stones, will cost from 6d. to lOd. 
per perch ; they are to be carefully excavated and covered in. 

Gullets . — Single gullets to be from 10s. to 1Z. 10s. each, and double gullets from 21. to 3 1. 
each ; they are to be in every case covered with strong flags, and securely paved, well built, 
and the ends carefully squared, to consist of well-bedded large stones. 

Soling is to be of either clay or sand, free from stones and vegetable earth, and to be paid 
for at same prices as excavations, according to the length of lead. 

Stones, whether quarried or gathered, are for all purposes to be measured and paid for at 
from 3d. to 7 d. per cubic yard, and for carriage at the same rate as excavations, that is, where 
the length of lead varies from 20 to 120 perches, 3d. to 6d. per cubic yard ; and where the 
lead is greater, the price to be regulated so that a horse may earn 3s. per day, to be valued 
according to the quantity. The price for breaking stones to be from lOd. to Is. 2d. per cubic 
yard, according to quantity ; the stones are to be broken so as to be no more than 2 inches in 
their greatest dimensions ; from 2d. to 4 d. per perch to be paid for spreading, according to 
quantity of material, and for blinding from 6 d. to 8<f. per perch. 

The foregoing prices have reference chiefly to new works and to hill-cutting. Where the 
surfaces of old roads are to be reconstructed, the price for picking up the surface, forming, 
levelling, and raking out large stones, may be from Is. to Is. 6 d. per perch; the large stones 
should be collected, piled in heaps, and paid for at 2d. to 4 d. per cubic yard in addition. For 
breaking these the usual price allowed for breaking stones may be given, and for spreading 
them and maintaining the road an agreement should be made by the perch. 

Where hills are cut, or embankments made on these, works, they are to be paid for same as 
other earth-work, or by the perch. 

It is hoped the practical knowledge and due examination and deliberation of the local 
engineers will supply the deficiency of these directions, as the valuation of a piece of work is 
a difficult professional question. In making the valuations the engineer will give the workmen 
the benefit of every doubtful case, and we are confident that they will be acting best for the

Memorandum, No. 53. 

[Relief Department.] 

Office of Public Works, January 26, 1847. 

The attention of the Commissioners has been directed to the class of persons employed 
as overseers on the Relief Works, and the importance of those officers being competent to 
discharge the duties required of them. On the overseer devolves the measurement and letting 
of the tasks, the proper distribution of the labourers on the works, and the due performance 
of the labour. They are also charged with the care of the tools and implements. They ought 
to be able to read and write, and keep accounts, and be examined and instructed in making 
measurements. Those who are most expert should be recommended for a higher rate of pay, 
and every exertion made to create emulation among them. Overseers of parties working by 
task should always be paid more than when the parties are on day-work. 

By order, 

J os. C. Walker, Secretary.
