Circular, No. 55. 

[Relief Department.] 

Office of Public Works, January 25, 1847. 

The Commissioners of Public Works have heard, with much regret, that the destitute 
labourers employed by task to execute certain drainage presentments, have shown great indis- 
position to work, and in consequence the sums earned have not been in proportion to their 
necessities.- 

According to the prices allowed, a willing labourer can earn from one shilling to fifteen pence 
per day; but if he determines not to use any exertion, and in consequence his earning does not 
exceed sixpence or eightpence per day, the fault lies with himself, and not with the contract 
price. 

It is necessary that both the overseers and labourers should understand that the Drainage 
Presentment Works, under Mr. Labouchere’s Letter, are to be paid for by the landed pro- 
prietors who undertake them, and that the work must be considered to be a private one, com- 
menced by an individual for the purpose of employing the people. Hence it becomes the duty 
of the overseer, as well as of the labourer, to do justice to the proprietor who undertakes, at has 
own cost, to employ the destitute on reproductive works, and thus prevent an unnecessary expen- 
diture on road works, which would have been defrayed by a general assessment. 

If the drainage be not executed at a reasonable cost, the works commenced will not be com- 
pleted for the amount of the estimate which corresponds with that that of the presentment. In 
this view the inspecting officers of the Board are requested to remove from the relief list any 
labourer who, through laziness or design, will not exert himself to execute his task, as it would 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




76 BOARD OF WORKS. 

be most unjust that the proprietors, who through benevolence have undertaken the works, should 
be injured by the combination or indolence of the labourers. 

By order, 

Jos. C. Walker, Secretary. 



[Relief Department.] 

Instructions to the Inspectors of Drainage, Stc. 

Sir, Office of Public Works, January 22, 1 847. 

The Board of Public Works have appointed you to examine and report on the several 
drainage presentments, in the baronies of in the county of 

The maps of the several districts will be forwarded to you at by 

and the Board wish that no time may be lost in commencing your inspection. 

You will see by the documents which accompany the maps what your duties are. 

In making your estimates, you will take care always to retain at least 10 per cent, out of the 
presentment, to cover contingencies. 

The works should be so laid out and estimated that no part be left unfinished, consequently ' 
it will be always desirable to keep within the amount of the presentment., and if, in the progress 
of the work, it becomes evident that there will be an overplus, then the draining of an additional 
portion of land may be commenced, for the purpose of expending the balance. 

The cost to be charged to the presentment will, in each case, include a portion of the pay 
clerk’s salary, a portion also of that of the check clerk, the local overseer, and all tools supplied, 
and it is to cover such contingencies that 10 per cent., on the original estimate should be re- 
tained ; but allowance should also be made for casualties, such as the tailing in of drains, 
difficulty of procuring stones, tiles, &c. 

Where necessary, you can have the assistance of a surveyor to measure and take sections for 
the main drains. On this subject you will communicate with who 

will render you every assistance in his power. You will probably require the assistance of one 
or more sub -inspectors to carry into effect the works recommended by you in each of the 
baronies; such persons are usually paid about 1/. 10s. per week, according to ability. You 
will recommend to the Board such persons to fill this office as you may think suitable, naming 
the pay you would recommend for each. 

The local overseers of each for the principal Presentment Works will be recommended by 
the undertakers, and you may appoint such of them as appear to you to be suitable. Such 
overseers are, in each case, to be paid out of the presentment, consequently it is desirable that 
the salary should not exceed 2s. per day, but the usual price will be Is. 6 d. per day. 

The prices for the different portions of the work, originally determined by you, should be 
entered in a leaf of the field book, a copy of which, in each case, you will hand to the sub- 
inspector of drainage for his guidance, and he will communicate the detail of the prices to be 
paid for each portion of the work to the local overseer of the presentment. 

It is most important that the laying the sod and the filling of the earth over the broken stone 
should be postponed in every case until the sub-inspector of drainage shall have seen and 
approved of the work. 

To insure regularity, the Commissioners require that the inspector of drainage, and likewise 
the sub-inspector, should keep diaries, according to the form sent, staling how and where they 
were employed on each day. 

The sub-inspector is to forward to this office a weekly return of the number of labourers 
employed on each of the works, according to the form which will be supplied, and care should 
be taken that it be posted so as to reach this Office on the following Monday. 

The payment of the tasks earned by the labourers will be made once in each week. 

To effect this object, it will be necessary that the overseer of each presentment should notify 
to the sub-inspector of drainage the sum that will probably be required to pay the people, 
taking care that the estimate may not be under the sum required ; such estimate to be posted 
so as to reach this office in sufficient time to enable the pay-clerk to be funded previous to the 
appointed pay day. 

At the end of the week the overseer of the work is to measure the work done by each con- 
tractor, and make out a return of the amount due on each contract, according to the prices 
fixed on, whether for cutting drains, collecting and breaking stones, quarrying, or drawing 
stones for the drains, filling the drains, See., and this pay-list or return must be certified by the 
sub-inspector, and handed to the pay clerk when he arrives to pay the labourers. 

This return should also be certified by the check clerk, should such have been appointed to 
visit the work. 

Instructions as to -proceeding when Works have been sanctioned. 

You are to place yourself in communication with the inspecting officer in charge of the dis- 
trict, who will supply each Drainage Work with labourers selected from the relief lists, on your 
requisition, stating the number you require and the day on which it is to be commenced. 

The check clerks employed under the inspecting officer on the said works will, when required 
to do so, take an account of the men’s time, and having certified the returns for payment, will 
forward them to the sub-inspector for his certificate as to their correctness, who is to affix the 
prices to the names. 

The inspector of drainage in each district is to put himself in communication with the 
inspector of accounts for the district, for the purpose of making precise arrangements relative to 
the payment of the people. The inspector will also give the names and addresses of the sub- 
inspectors of drainage, who are to certify to the accuracy of the weekly returns. 

By order, 

To Jos. C. Walker, Secretary .

Extract from a Report of Captain J. Airey. 

Royal Barracks, January IT, 184/. 

From my own observation and inquiry I am sorry to report that, 
although just at present it is the slack period of the year, the usual farm opera- 
tions are not generally carried on. The large farmers indeed are tilling their 
ground to a certain degree, but not to the same extent as in former years. In 
the same month of 1846 there was not so much tillage as in the previous year, 
but now there is still less among the large and scarcely any among the smnll 
farmers. This arises, as far as I can ascertain, from various causes, viz., the 
inability of dieting the labourers, which has hitherto been the custom, and either 
not haying the money to pay their wages, or having an aversion to part with it. 
The high price of grain greatly affects the farmer, as, from a want of proper 
food or a sufficiency of it, not only the labourer but even the horses are unable 
to perform the amount of labour required of them. 

The small farmer, I hear, does not generally do much at tliis season from the 
shortness of the day, and consequently the few hours that the labourer can 
work ; but this year, from want of seed, want of food to diet the men, want of 
ready money to pay wages, and,. I fear, dislike to take the labourer from the 
Public Works, from the dread of creating a bad feeling in the country against 
themselves, they are doing scarcely anything. Farmers holding even a hundred 
acres are, from this latter cause, deterred from employing many people as they 
have done. The only methods I can propose of preventing tliis evil is to insist 
on task-work, or very considerably decrease the wages on the Public Works. 



Lieutenant Miller to Mr. Walker. 

Nenagh, February 3, 1S47. 

I have to report that as William Kennedy, overseer on the Bally annee 
road, parish of Kuigli, barony of Lower Ormond, was going to the work tliis 
morning he was met at a distance of about half a mile from the work, by two 
armed men who beat him severely about the head, and one of them snapped a 
pistol three times at him, and the other fired at him with another pistol, but 
without effect. 

This is the third outrage committed on overseers in this district within the 
last few months, and I therefore beg to recommend that all the works in the 
Monsea Relief District, which comprises the five parishes of Monsea, Dormi- 
neer, ICuigh, Killodiernau, and Cloghprior be suspended for a short time. 

As a temporary measure I have stopped five works in the immediate neigh- 
bourhood, having issued a notice, of 'which the enclosed is a copy.

Notice. 

In consequence of the attack made this morning upon William Kennedy, overseer of 
Ballyannee road, the following works will be stopped until the Lord Lieutenant’s pleasure is 
known : —

Lieut-Col. Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 



February 4, 1847. 

As the roads in many parts of the country will he found, when the new 
machinery comes into play, in a very unfinished state, I have endeavoured to 
press upon his Excellency’s attention how very desirable it will be to put all 
the roads under the Board of Works, with power to complete such as they may 
consider useful to the country, and make it imperative on the counties to present 
for the amounts expended; we should then have power to exercise our judg- 
ment and discretion in the - selection of the works as well as the time for 
executing them. 

For the coming assizes we are preparing certificates for the grand juries, for 
part of the advances under the Act Viet., c. 1. You are well aware that 
we have not yet been able to ascertain the exact amount expended under that 
Act, the sums recommended in many cases not having been issued until the 
second season; however, we shall be prepared with certificates for every 
county, but not to the full amount to which they will be liable. We do not 
propose sending any certificates at the coming assizes for monies advanced 
under the Act, c. 107, inasmuch as the accounts are not yet closed.

Lieut.-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

February 6, 1847. 

I suggested to the Lord Lieutenant^ a few days ago, the expediency of 
immediately placing all the labourers on the Relief Works on the reduced rates 
of farming wages, or say 10c?. per diem, in order to do away with the premium 
held out by our supposed system of task-work, on which a large proportion of 
those employed are receiving much higher rates of pay. Without somet hing of 
the sort is done, it can scarcely be expected that the labourer will leave the 
Public Works. 



Captain Butler to Mr. Walker. 

Newcastle, February 7, 1847. 

I sent out Mr. Thompson on Friday, according to the Board’s instruc- 
tions, to supersede Mr. Keating at Shanagolden in charge of the barony of Shanid. 
Mr. Thompson was accompanied by Mr. Buck, engineer, who had directions to 
assist him in taking over his charge. 

Mr. Keating refused to surrender the charge and papers connected with his 
office, upon the pretence that my authority was insufficient, and that he knew of 
no such person as “ E. Hornsby,”* a copy of whose letter was shown to him. 

Mr. Buck, after a fruitless application to the magistrates, who declared that 
they apprehended a riot, and had no force to keep it down, left Mr. Thompson, 
and returned to Newcastle to consult with me. 

Mr. Keating told Mr. Thompson, when he was left alone, that he had no 
grudge against him, but that “ he had better not meddle •” and at night a mob 
assembled, and began to shout out for Mr. Thompson and Malony, a clerk 
whose dismissal Mr. Keating had been endeavouring to procure. The mob 
became violent, and Messrs. Thompson and Malony were with difficulty ex- 
tricated by the police, and escorted to Newcastle, which they reached at three 
in the morning. 

Having consulted with Captain Kennedy, one of my predecessors, the next 
morning I employed a Mr. Dowling, an attorney, to prepare a notice of “ filing 
a bill in equity ” against Mr. Keating, if he failed to surrender the papers ; but 
I also instructed him to see Mr. Keating, and induce him, by showing him the 
expense and penalties that he would incur, to make a prompt surrender. I 
directed Mr. Buck to accompany the attorney for the purpose of pointing out 
the several papers and documents ; and I procured an escort of police on cars, 
with their officer, to accompany Mr. Buck to ensure his personal safety. 

Unfortunately one of the cars broke down, and five policemen were 
left behind on the road ; and Mr. Buck, seeing no appearance of a mob, 
imprudently separated from the police, instead of remaining at the barrack. A 
mob shortly after assembled, broke into the house where Mr. Buck was, beat 
him in a furious manner, and he with difficulty escaped to the barracks in dis- 
guise, whence, being confused by a blow on the head, he returned across the 
comity to Newcastle on foot, instead of waiting for the police. The mob then 
searched for the attorney, who, however, succeeded in making his escape to the 
barrack, and returned with the police. 

He sent this message to me by the attorney, “ that he begged to assure 
“ Captain Butler that he was offering no factious opposition *, and that as soon 



* Assistant Secretary to the Board.

The Mayor of Cork to Lord John Russell. 

Mayor s Office, Cork, February 1, 1847. 

In compliance with a resolution at a special general meeting of the 
trustees and managers of the Cork Savings’ Bank, I beg to address your Lord- 
ship on a subject of no small importance to this country at the present awful 
crisis. 

F rom the terms of the enclosed resolution your Lordship will perceive that, 
at the various savings’ banks in Ireland, in addition to the separate surplus fund 
of 11,000/. of realized profits, there is at the end of each year a large amount 
of unfunded profits over and above all engagements and debts due to the 
depositors, the disposal of which is now by law confined strictly to the expenses 
of the management of these concerns, for which it is more than sufficient. 

Deeply sensible of the appalling nature of the calamity with which Provi- 
dence has been pleased to visit this afflicted land, arid convinced of the necessity 
of the most strenuous efforts on the part of all public bodies for the preservation 
of human life, the trustees of this institution believe that in no manner onn the 
surplus funds and unfunded profits of those institutions, or at least a portion of 
them, be better employed than in the relief of the poor of this country. 

It may be urged that such a disposal of those funds is contrary to the 
fundamental laws regulating such institutions ; but, my Lord, if ever there was 
a time when objections of such a nature ought to be disregarded it is surely 
now, when so many human beings are daffy perishing for the want of the means 
ol subsistence. A strong reason for sanctioning the appropriation of the funds 
in question is the consideration that it can be done without the slightest viola- 
tion of vested interests, or in any manner limiting the usefulness or security of 
those most valuable institutions. 

Most earnestly, then, my Lord, do I press this matter upon your attention, 
and 1 hope that your Lordship will see the propriety of enabling the trustees of 
savings banks in Ireland to apply a portion of such surplus funds as aforesaid 
in the manner they may deem best calculated to relieve the distressed, by 
mtioducmg an Act, or inserting a clause into some Act now before Parliament, 
containing such permissory power, with such limitations and provisoes as to 
your Lordship shall seem necessary.

Mr. Higham to Mr. Arbuthnot. 

National Debt Office, February 8, 1 847. 

Every year the several savings’ hanks render to the Commissioners a 
statement of their debt, and the means they possess of meeting the same ; and 
whenever a surplus appears on the face of such statement, the 23rd section of 
the 9th Geo. IV., c. 92, directs that it shall be paid over to a separate account 
to he kept by the Commissioners. The same section provides that the trustees 
may claim, for the purposes of the institution , the whole or any part of the said 
surplus ; and it has been generally applied for by the trustees for the purpose 
of building a house or office for the carrying on the business of the institution. 
An application was made a short time since from the savings’ hank at Parsons- 
town for a similar purpose to that now received from Cork, and the trustees 
were informed that the Commissioners had no power under the before-men- 
tioned Act to sanction the appropriation of any part of the surplus to the object 
in question. 



Treasury Minute on the above. 

February 9, 1847. 

Write to party in the terms of Mr. Higham’s note that the proposition is one 
which the law does not sanction.

Extract from Letter of Mr. Prendergast, Inspector of Drainage in Carrigallen, 
Co. Leitrim, Ballinamore, February 7, 1847. 

I wish to report to you, as succinctly as possible, the state of things here, and may 
begin by telling you that the distress is such as no newspaper stories can exaggerate. Famine 
actually prevans, and the deaths are frightfully numerous from want and disease caused by 
insufficient food and clothing. Some poor women were in this town before daylight last 
market day to conceal their bedding and a few articles of furniture that were to be sold for a 
few days' food . A man was in the town carrying a dead child on his back, himself half 
stupified by want, and wandering in and out of doorways without asking aid. A woman lately 
mentioned the excellent soup she had made after killing her cow, there being no other resource. 
Now this speaks volumes, for the pigs being already gone and the poultiy too, there will 
remain absolutely nothing but the meal in the market for all provisions. Pale sickly faces 
surround me when I am in the fields; and I assure you the country presents a picture like the 
storied famines of old; under all this the poor people are wonderfully patient. Outrages 
there are certainly, but they are comparatively rare ; and although provisions are stolen and 
cattle are occasionally killed, yet the wonder is that any are left when the people are thus 
famished. A bullock of Archdeacon Agars was taken last night; but there are sheep and

letter to a gentleman, such statements usually convey more correct impressions than mere 
official reports.

Mr. Parker to Lieut.-Colonel Jones. 

Armagh , February 6, 1847. 

Captain Glascock, R.N., who has arrived here, holding the appointment of Inspector 
of Relief Committees, proposes that spinning-wheels should be supplied to the females, and 
flax to be gratuitously given the children to be kept to knitting and sewing ; and although 
at first he met with opposition, the better thinking gentlemen, and especially the clergy of all 
religious creeds, seem now to come into his views; and it is the general opinion, if habits of 
industry could be established, that sanguine hopes might be entertained of seeing peace, con- 
tentment, and plenty once more in this unfortunate country. In some localities where my 
duties call upon me to visit there is no resident landlord, nor even an agent ; and were it not 
for the admirable exertions of the clergy — Protestant and Roman Catholic — the poor would 
be left to starve. Armagh city is highly favoured, his Grace tire Primate setting the noble 
example of benevolence. His charity and munificence are unbounded. Even in localities 

Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 







BOARD OF WORKS.

that might he considered as haring no claim on him, his donations are the theme of general 
admiration, ihe soup-kitchen under the superintendence of his Grace's agent is suonorted 
and conducted in a praiseworthy mamer Long may his Grace be sparedto preside ov£ the 
established Church, for it would bo difficult to {nd his equal either as a minister or a guardian 
of the poor. ° 

I h a ve been exceedingly gratified, in my tours through this country, to witness the patience 
with which the peasants bear up against the present calamity, and their exemplary conduct 
but one instance of serious theft having been committed in the barony of Upper Fews where 
the greater portion of the peasantry are paupers, and not one-half of the population employed 
on the Relief works and very few resident gentry. Captain Glascock is a practical man of 
business, and bids fair to create a great moral improvement in the counties of Armagh and 
Tyrone, over which he is inspector. 6 



Captain Broughton to Captain Larcom.' 

Cork, February 7, 1847. 

I HAVE just got home, after a very fatiguing week in Duhallow, and am almost knocked 
up. Still, as there are sessions to be held in Middleton to-morrow, at which I must attend 
and which will occupy me, in all probability, the entire day, I must make out a line to you 
now or it will be delayed. Things, I regret to say, are in a most deplorable state, the poor 
people dying by half dozens at a time, and I do not know how to meet the wants and 
exigencies ot the case. There were six coroner’s inquests held there on Friday : the verdicts 
for each were starvation. The works, which were presented for three months, and which have 
been extended over 15 weeks, are either completed or run out ; and unless fresh works are sanc- 
tioned, both here and elsewhere, during the next three weeks, one-half the population must 
inevitably starve. r 1 

The works, as fax- as the character of them is concerned, are beautifully executed, and reflect 
credit on us all, and this, too, in the remotest and most neglected districts. The roads I visited 
are all of the greatest importance to the country as reproductive works, and I do not hesitate to 
say will advance the civilization of those parts at least 30 years; by which I mean that under 
ordinary circumstances, being a district in which no grand juror resides, these works would 
not have been executed for that period, whilst by opening some thousand acres of remarkably 
fine mountain, the future means of subsistence to a large extent will be increased, which must 
become a very important object consequent on the potato failure. There is as large a breadth 
of wheat sown and up as usual, and I should not consider the farming operations behind. I 
observed in one or two places they were digging over the ridges of last year’s potatoes (which 
had not been dug out), and were making them up with the hopes of their succeeding for the 
ensuing crop a fatal delusion, I am convinced, and one I do not wish to see successful. 
Ultimately, as an accessory and food for cattle, it might be again desirable to use them ; but 
the love and prejudice for them must be got rid of first, or they will inevitably fall into the old 
system, so beneficial to the landlords and so destructive to themselves and their industry. 



Mr. Denver to Captain Larcom. 

Ballyquirk Castle, Burrischane, 
February 5, 1847. 

The parish priest here, at our last Relief Committee, Lorha and Dorha, represented 
to me that the pressure on the works was gone too far, and that the sooner we could stop cash 
payments the better. There were over 100 persons pressing to have their names put down. 
He told of one, a widow’s son, who was employed to enable him to support his mother and 
iamily, who bought a gun instead of taking home his earnings, which gun was taken from him 
again. The lads, who never touched a shilling in their lives, are now, since the potatoes’ 
departure, wild, past the control of their clergy, gambling, dissipating, or buying arms or 
ammunition. Such was the parish priest’s report to me. We talked over a plan, a'sketch of 
which is enclosed, which, though not perfect, for still they might gamble for the tickets, or the 
shopkeepers might buy up the tickets at half value for cadi, yet still these are comparatively small 
evils to the present, and, with the present scarcity, would not be so likely to be abused. Pray 
give it your consideration, and bring it to notice if it appears likely to prove generally useful. 



There is a depot for the Lorha aud Dorha Relief Committee at Munster Harbour 
near Portumna Bridge. 

There are 13 shops, which sell meal, &c., under the rules of the Committee, difiused through 
the district. ° 

The shopkeepers now lodge the cash in the bank at Birr to the credit of the Committee ; on 
producing the deposit receipt, the Committee give each his order on the depot for provisions. V* 
2 r j P ro P ose d that, the pay-clerks should pay for labour only in tickets, representing L., 2*., 
ba., or 5s ; these tickets to be received by the shopkeepers as cash in return for food, and 
to be negotiable in no other manner. The pay-clerks to visit the shops, and take up the

tickets from the shopkeepers, paying for them by checks on the bank, which the Committee 
would receive as cash. Such a plan might have a good effect : — 

1st. Save robberies of pay-clerks. 

2nd. Reduce pressure for work on roads. 

3rd. Avoid bad characters, who work only for cash, to be used in purchasing arms, powder 
and shot, or in gambling. 



Mr. Nicol to Mr. Lbifevre. 

5, Hyde Par/c-terrace, February 9, 1847. 

I have a small property in Scotland, in the county of Kincardine, which 
I have for some years past been improving, by draining and by bringing into 
cultivation moorland ; but my operations were last autumn nearly brought to 
a stand by the scarcity of labourers, owing to the increased demand for them in 
similar operations on other estates in the neighbourhood, as well as from the 
Aberdeen Railway, now in course of formation. 

The rate of wages to an able-bodied man I have been paying is about 2s. per 
day, and board and lodging were afforded on the property at Is. per day, until 
the late enhanced price of provisions, when Is. 2d. or Is. 3 d. would now be 
required. 

In my anxiety to get on with my works I have had some communications 
with Irish gentlemen, who were in hopes of supplying me with their unemployed 
countrymen; and the result, so far, is given in the enclosed extract of a letter 
received this morning from my agent. 

I am willing to expend, in the course of this year, some 4000/. on my pro- 
perty, and you will observe that my agent says that it cannot be done from want 
of labourers ; and when the amount applied for under the Drainage Act comes 
to be expended, in addition to the numerous railways and other works in con- 
templation in Scotland, the difficulty must, of course, be greatly increased, and 
it is, I hope, a subject worthy of the consideration of Government. 



Enclosure. 

Stonehaven, February 6, 1847. 

h ave some trenching still going on, but we cannot get labourers, and we shall be 
able to do little until the railway is nearly done. 

Last week an Irish labourer from Limerick came here with a note from Mr. Stephen Spring 
Rice, m order to get employment on your property ; he was an able-bodied young man, and 
we sent him to James Hutt, with instructions to employ him in trenchino- or other Work. 
James says, ‘‘ I showed him the work (trenching) ; but he declared he could not do it, nor 
would he begin. I wished him to try the drains ; but he would not stop.” 

James adds, “ There were some Irishmen came here a few weeks ago, but they would not 
take any contract work ; they had letters mehtioniug the prices of the contract, aud I said, 
how could they expect, to be employed otherwise than was done by our own people 1" There 
are at present upwards of 2000 labourers employed on the railway in this neighbourhood, and 
so eager are they to get on with the work, that, every labourer is laid hold of ; and throughout 
this year, at all events, wages will remain very high. 

Several of the tenants are desirous to make further improvements by means of draining and 
otherwise ; but little can be done from this scarchy of labour.

Extract from Journal of Major Stoneafund, Inspecting Officer, County Cavan, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

Agriculture is progressing very slowly, and I hear complaints of die unwillingness of the 
men on the Public Works to enter into the service of the farmers. 

The peasantry are stated to have formed a notion that, whether they choose to work or not, 
Government will not permit them to starve, and it has been said that they suppose that Govern- 
ment will sow the crops for them, without their working ou the land. 

The works are in general progress through the country, hut the workmen are often found 
not to labour so much as is desirable, and endeavours are making to bring on the system of 
task-work. 

Extract from Report of Major Townsend, Inspecting Officer, County Cavan, for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

The neglect of agriculture still continues, and some alarm prevails as to the consequences 
of the future harvest. 



Extract from Journal of Captain O’Neill, Inspecting Officer, County Donegal, for week DONEGAL, 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

Barony of Kilmacrenan. 

Issued lists for labour this week to the amount of 882. The lists sent in from the Com-

Extract from Journal of Lieut. Milward, R.E., Inspecting Officer, County Donegal, for 
week ending 2nd January, 1847. 

Baronies of Banagh and Boylogh. 

The people in the poorest parts of the barony of Boylogh have eaten all their com, and as 
they cannot procure any for seed they are neglecting the land and not preparing for any crops 
at all, and the reason they assign for not working is, that a man working requires two meals 
a-day, and he can do with one when idle. The Board’s officers are making every exertion to 
get on the works as fast as possible. We do not rest day and night, and still cannot get on 
fast enough to meet the destitution. 

Baronies of Killybegs and Killater. 

The lists were made out well and in good time. The parishes of Killybegs and Killoghtee 
are partially employed. Provisions are plenty, and the people, although very poor, are quietly 
disposed, but easily led. At the time the Committee were writing to the Government and 
the Board to press on the works they were not prepared with any lists of destitution. 

The Relief Committee in the parish of Templecarn never ceased writing to the Government, 
to the Board, and myself, to press the works, to save the population from starvation, and all 
the time only 58 names appear on the lists for employment, who might all have been very 
easily employed by the gentlemen in the neighbourhood. They are all now employed. 

The parishes of Killea, Clonleigh, Toughboyne, and others in the north of this barony, are 
the best in the county. They are principally on the Marquis of Abercorn’s estate, and there is 
very little destitution among them. I find generally that the people on the Marquis of 
Conyngham’s estate are the poorest This property is much neglected; it comprises an 
immense tract of land, principally waste, but a large proportion of it could be easily reclaimed, 
however not a shilling has been spent on it. 

The other great estates in my districts are Lady Anne Murray s, which is under Chancery, 
and so situated that nothing can be done with it; Lord Abercom’s, which is very rich; and 
Colonel Conelly’s, which comprises a large tract of waste land, and some very good. Colonel 
Conelly is very averse to drainage under the Board, and as the baronies of Banagh, Boylogh, 
and Turugh belong principally to him. Lady Anne Murray, and the Marquis of Conyngham, 
it is not likely that any drainage will be adopted in those baronies.

DONEGAL. Extract from Journal of Captain O’Neill, Inspecting Officer, County Donegal, for the 

week ending 9th January, 1847. 

Barony of Kilmacrenan. 

On Tuesday, the 5th instant, at Carrigort, the Hon. C. Clements, Chairman of the Com- 
mittee of Kilmacrenan and Meragh Relief Committee, went to issue tickets or labour lists 
when the mob attempted to force me to issue more lists than the Chairman had given me lists 
for, and on my peremptorily refusing to do so the people assembled round the door, and would 
not allow us to pass out, and the revenue police came down and forced the mob off. One of 
the country people received a severe cut on the head from the blow of a musket., but four of the 
peasants attacked one of the police, and on his comrades coming up to his rescue one of the 
four was knocked down by a policeman. Afterwards they went on to some of the works about 
three miles from Carrigort, to break the barrows, but did not attempt any violence, nor did 
they attempt to destroy any of the tools belonging to the work. 1 have, in consequence, 
stopped the work that I issued tickets for on that day at Carrigort, until I hear from the 
Board. 

A full report of the above transaction has been sent by me to the Board, on the evening- of 
the 5th January, 1847. 

The Relief Committees generally send in very imperfect lists, inasmuch that in many cases 
there are individuals returned as being in a destitute state that are by no means so, and I am 
obliged to reject many of such people, and have been obliged to issue a circular to the Relief 
Committees to revise their lists. The increase of labourers put on this work amounts to 1205, 
making a total in the baronies of Kilmacrenan, East and West Ennishowin, and part of Raphoe, 
of 4688 employed up to this date. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Milward, R.A., Inspecting Officer, County Donegal, for 
week ending 9th January, 1847. 

Complaints are general that labourers will not work in the farms. I refuse them work on 
the roads, but they prefer starving, with the prospect of getting on the works, to goin» to the 
farmers, for they think they then lose all chance of getting on the works. ° 

I wish an order was given that no man having land who could dispose of it should get em- 
ployment. The tenant-right in some parts of this country amounts to 25 years’ purchase, and 
in some cases even to 30. 

Notwithstanding all my exertions, I find that several persons get on the works who should 
not get there. For instance, at Glenties, one of the poor-law guardians, and at Dunkinely 
the clerk of the church. I have refused to give any more employment until their Committees 
revise their lists.

There have been about 2100 additional names on labour lists issued during the week, and

In the neighbourhood of Corndonagh the people are in a great state of want, and generally 
in the mountain districts, some distance from the sea, the destitution is the greatest. An outrage 
took place on Thursday night at Mr. John Chourluseers, of Vauxhall, Glenswerly, about four 
■miles from this town. It appears that a number of people assembled at night, and carried off 
a stack of corn, and thrashed it, leaving the straw behind. No trace, as yet, of the people 
who committed this outrage. I only heard this last night, on my return from Rathmullin, 
where I had been issuing labour lists. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Milward, R.A., Inspecting Officer, County Donegal, for 
week ending 30th January, 1847. 

The conduct of the people in this district is, in general, very good, and I do not apprehend 
any disturbance whatever. I was attacked in Donegal on Monday last, but I do not regard it 
as anything serious. The feeling of regard for the Board’s officers is very general amongst the 
lower orders. The people who stopped me belong to a particular district in the mountains 
near Donegal celebrated for lawlessness. The distress in some one or two places, where it has 
been impossible yet to get on much work, is very great ; but, in general, the destitution is very 
much relieved, although the demands of the Relief Committees are not at all lessened. The 
want of a sufficient staff is still very seriously felt. 

On Friday, the 29th instant, I attended a special meeting of the Ballyshannon Relief Com- 
mittee. Complaints most numerous, and charges without number, made against all parties, 
but I could not get any of them put in writing. The accounts of the destitution here are very 
distressing, and the Committee declare it is not relieved, although upwards of 1000 people are 
employed in the neighbourhood. This Committee is most exorbitant in its demands ; they say, 
<( Put all on the works, and let the money go as far as it will.” They are most unreasonable, 
and complain greatly of neglect, whereas they have double as many persons employed as any 
■other district in the barony.

Extract from Journal of Captain Brereton, Inspecting Officer, County Down, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

The people employed on the Public Works in the barony of Mome are generally well 
behaved, although lately they have evinced much dissatisfaction, owing to a great number on 
the lists of the Relief Committee being without employment. The Public Works at present 
in operation only giving employment to 400, which scarcely amounts to half the number of 
the destitute in the barony on the Relief lists. There is one Public Work in the barony which, 
when the engineer has orders to commence, will give work to the greater number of the 
unemployed population. At the extraordinary Presentment Sessions held at Castlewuliam on 
Friday last, the people assembled, to ihe amount of 5000 or 6000, evinced a very angry 

feeling, it having been circulated among them that no money would be passed at the sessions 
for their relief, owing, I believe, to a letter of the Marquis of Downshire, published in some 
of the newspapers, calling on the rate-payers of the barony to be present and resist, as far as 
possible, any money from being passed at the sessions, and had it not been for the large force 
of military' and police serious consequences might have arisen. From my very recent arrival 
in the proclaimed barony it is difficult for me to discover the exact amount of destitution, but 
from my inquiries I found it to amount to upwards of 2000 families ; this destitution 1 was 
enabled to lay before the sessions, and I am sorry to say there was a great desire evinced by 
the landed proprietors to hide the poverty of the people. 1 was, therefore, most urgently 
attacked by many of them for performing my duty in bringing the destitution of the baronv 
before their notice. When the famishing people found there was a sum of money presented o- 
their relief they departed quietly to their homes.

DOWN. Extract from Journal of Captain Brf, reton. Inspecting Officer, County Down, for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

In most parts of this county the farmers are occupied at their usual farm operations for this 
season, and the greater number of them have a supply (though not to any great amount) of 
com in their stack-yards. The very small farmers, 1 am sorry to say, are now compelled to 
commence consuming the small stock of corn they had intended for seed for this year’s crop 
and, in most instances, their stack-yards will be completely empty in a month hence. 

I attended the Relief Committee at Kilkeele on the 11th instant, and selected 30 additional 
men for employment. I am sorry to say there were 300 destitute, whose names were on the lists 
of the Relief Committee, anxiously awaiting outside for relief by being permitted to be placed 
upon the Public Works. They were in a very excited state, and on learning that, there was no 
employment for them, they sent a written statement, into the Committee " that they were 
starving, and if they were not relieved they would find some other means of supplying themselves 
with food.” I told them that such threats could only tend to prolong their hardships, inasmuch 
that should they commit a breach of the peace their names would be immediately struck off the 
lists of the Relief Committee ; to bear their privations for a little while longer and I would 
ensure them relief in a few days by getting some new work commenced. This promise had 
the effect of appeasing them, and they separated quietly t.o their homes. I would again beg 
respectfully to remind you that it is absolutely necessary that some, further Public Work 
should be opened at or near Kilkeele, in the barony of Morne. The people hitherto, by 
promises of relief, have been kept orderly, but now their destitution is such that nothing but 
instant relief, by employment, can keep them from committing some flagrant outrage. 



Extract from Report of Captain Brereton, Inspecting Officer, County Down, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The Public Works in the barony of Morne are mostly in an advanced state, the labourers 
are generally very well behaved, employed principally by task-work, earning on an average 
Is. per diem. Owing to the severity of the weather on Wednesday last it. was impossible for 
the men to continue on the works, and those who were present at the roll-call of the check 
clerks in the morning were allowed for one half day’s pay. The extraordinary Presentment 
Sessions which were held at Newry on the 15th instant, and at which I informed the meeting 
there were between 700 and 800 families in a state of destitution in the barony, presented for 
their relief for two months the sum of 2400/. The amount of misery in the town portion of 
the barony particularly, arising from scarcity of food and want of employment, is now perfectly 
frightful, and were it not from the exertions of the Relief Committee formed some length of 
time previous to the calling of the extraordinary Presentment Sessions, the funds of which, 
from private subscriptions, amount nearly to 1000/., relieving from their soup kitcheu daily 
1100 individuals, I have no doubt the destitution in the town would be far greater than at pre- 
sent. I would therefore beg respectfully to urge, that orders be forwarded to the engineer, as 
soon as possible, for the commencement of works, passed for at the extraordinary Presentment 
Sessions for the above barony of Newry.

Extract from Report of Captain Handcock, Inspecting Officer, County Fermanagh, for 
week ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The distress throughout this county, I regret to say, seems daily to increase, soup shops 
have been established in several parts of the county with good effect, but provisions are 
increasing in price every market day, and the farmers do not seem inclined to take any labourers 
into their employment. Several men have left the Public Works from sickness. The county 
remains quiet, but in the neighbourhood of Belleck I understand several robberies have 
taken place lately. 

Extract from Report of Captain Handcock, Inspecting Officer, County Fermanagh, for 
week ending 31st January, 1847. 

The hill cutting at Ballinaleek, in the barony of Glenawley, has just commenced again, and 
the men returned from employment on it are so weak and infirm that they could not do a day’s 
work so must be put to breakstones; in this barony there is a great deal of illness, men 
leave their work daily, more particularly on the bog roads, and numbers of deaths, I under- 
stand, occur amongst them. I write this from my bed, but hope to be all right to-morrow. 

The poor-houses in parts of this county are full. I should like therefore to have some 
instructions how to act, as I fear that, many feeble persons will now be returned for employ- 
ment who would be better away, and it will be only a dead loss of money putting them to such 
work as road making ; and the general cry when they are put to stone breaking is, that the 
cold of sitting on stones kills them.

Extract from Journal of Captain Dill, Inspecting Officer, County Londonderry, for week 
ending 31st January, 1847. 

The usual farming operations of this county can scarcely be said to have commenced with 
vigour. In almost every instance the farmers are having the people to work on the Public 
Works. These Public Works have in almost every district of the county become now almost 
exhausted. 

Unless, therefore, the Board can forthwith commence drainage by presentment, a vast 
multitude of starving people must, be turned out of employment to endanger the peace of the 
county. I have this morning received a great number of letters complaining of this matter. 
From my own knowledge also I am aware that these complaints are just.

Extract from Journal of Captain Flude, Inspecting Officer, County Monaghan, for week 
ending 9th Jan., 1847. 

The people are very peaceable, although suffering dreadfully from want of employment and 
the high price of every description of food ; the farmers give no employment whatever, although 
the land is lying idle ; in very few instances is there any attempt made to prepare it for crops. 
The appearance of everything is most melancholy, and much land, I fear, will remain uncropped, 
unless a great change takes place ; neither does it appear to me that the landlords are doing 
anything to meet the evil consequences of such neglect.

Extract from Report of Captain Wynne, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week ending CLAKE. 
2nd January, 1847. 

Saturday, visited the works at Clare Abbey ; did not see such good work in County Clare, 
the men exert themselves to the utmost, and seemed to have profited by the lesson they have 
had. Works in the parish of Ruan have been suspended in consequence of the outrage on Mr. 

Harrington ; the district generally quiet, but symptoms of insubordination among the labourers. 

The pay clerks and other officers of the Board are greatly alarmed, and are afraid to discharge 
their duty efficiently. Symptoms of riot at Clare ; the offenders in custody, and to be brought 
to justice. A fair prospect of discovering the perpetrators of the outrage on Harrington. 

Relief Committees most clamorous for an extension of employment, and numbers on the lists. 

The district not more disturbed than hitherto ; the works going on far better ; a sufficient 
number employed for purposes of relief at present. 



Extract from Report of Captain Wynne, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week ending 
9th January, 1847. 

Our prospects with respect to a supply of food are alarming in the highest degree; we know 
not where to turn to seek it. In many localities this week the supplies completely ran out, and 
a single meal of food could not be got for one and two days. It is in vain to think of getting 
on much longer without food; we want, nothing else, but without this, we must give up all hope 
of being able to hold our ground much longer. In the immediate neighbourhood of this town 
Colonel Wyndham’s depdt has kept the people alive; they come eight and ten miles for a few 
pounds of meal, and often return without it. 

Monday, visited Corofin with Captain Mann; found the men working quietly, but very idly. 
Very great distress prevails there. 

Saturday, attended Relief Committee of Clencabby. Found the labourers most orderly and 
industrious, working as well as could be desired bond fide task-work, and I don’t think rioters 
would be well received in that locality at present. The district is tranquil at present. No 
outrage.

The engineers have lately commenced a system of measuring the work every week, and paying

The people, seeing immediate advantage to be derived, are becoming very industrious. 

The sowing of wheat continues, but in smaller quantities than is usual at this season.

Extract from Report of Lieut. Swinburne, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week ending 
17th January, 1847. 6 

No outrage or disturbance has occurred in my district during the past week. There is a 
gang of Terry Alts in the immediate neighbourhood of this place; they have been seen lately, 
and followed by the police, but I have not heard of their doing any mishief. The land through- 
out this part of the country remains unfilled, and I see no effort made anywhere to cultivate it. 
The scarcity of seed is generally given as an excuse for their neglecting the land. The Relief 
Committees generally are exerting themselves to relieve the people. Owing to the poor-house 
of this Union being full, and closed against further admission, great demands are made on the 
Relief Committees for gratuitous relief. The conduct of the men on the works is orderly and 
good, but they are very idle. 

There are persons also seeking employment now, that have hitherto been able to support 
their families without relief from the Public Works, and who have, up to the present time, been 
refused employment upon the grounds of their having corn or other provisions. These provi- 
sions are in most cases exhausted, and the persons who possessed them are now as great, or 
perhaps greater objects for relief, than those who never had provisions, and have been trusting 
from the first to the Public Works for their support. From these causes I fear there will be a 
considerable increase during the next fortnight to the number employed in my district.

Extract from Report of Lieut. Swinburne, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

The labourers, in very many instances, would rather have their subsistence and be idle, tliau 
draw good wages by industry. I regret to say some of the Relief Committees do not give me 
any assistance, in keeping the comfortable farmers and those that could get employment else- 
where off the works. In consequence of this, I believe gross abuses existed in some places, but 
I trust, I have, in a great measure, succeeded in correcting them. The country in the vicinity 
of this post, is tranquil ; no outrage or disturbance has occurred in this neighbourhood during 
the past week. The land remains untilled, and, except by the most comfortable farmers, I see 
no attempt made to cultivate it. The scarcity of seed is the general excuse made for allowing 
the land to remain untilled. The prices paid for provisions in some parts of this district are 
enormous, owing to many of the Relief Committees not selling meal, and the immense profits 
demanded by retail dealers.

East Muskerry. 

I have visited the electoral divisions of Aghinah and Aghaballoge this week, I find that 
certainly the same quantity of wheat is in the ground as is usually the case, and perhaps more, 
as there is never much grown, hut the country is mountainous at parts, and the roads going on,

Although many deny it, yet I am quite certain a fair quantity of potato seed for this year 
remains and will be planted, although, at present, there are no labourers employed on the land, 
the farmers having discharged them all, and endeavouring themselves to obtain situations as 
stewards, overseers, &c. 

West Muskerry. 

Some of the Committees return the head of the family first, and some distance down one 
of the sons, and after a few more names another son and so on. This renders it impossible to 
check the lists. I fortunately have a good power over them from their first lists, and I now 
require a certificate from the Chairman, stating, that in an additional list, none of the family 
are previously employed unless it is o stated. 

I am confirmed in my opinion that the potato disease is not going on at present, and those 
that remain are quite sound. 

A few potatoes were brought into town for sale a few days ago.

Extract from Report of Captain Huband, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
9th January, 1847. 

I am happy to be enabled to report, that a greater degree of activity appears am one the 
farming classes generally than heretofore. The gentry of the country are now doing their 
utmost to get the workmen to return to their usual employments, and Relief Committees are 
resisting the placing persons upon the works who can get employment from the farmers ; the 
wages offered by farmers are Is. per week and diet. The Dunmanway Committee have ex- 
tensively placarded their district with notices to farmers to induce them to get labourers. 

Petty robberies are on the increase, from the impunity now existing for these offences. The 
deaths among the poor are still increasing, as also severe sickness; the late heavy rains will, 
I fear, yet further cause disease. The country is flooded. 

I had. the whole of the lists of my district revised within these last few days, and find it yet 
most difficult to get Relief Committees to make any inquiry as to the persons whom they place 
ou the relief lists. It is a remarkable fact, that where the Relief Committees are negligent, 
destitution prevails there to the greatest extent. They place every one that asks them on 
their lists and induce the people to desert their ordinary occupations in hopes of soon getting 
upon the Public Works, consequently, if they do not get on immediately their destitution is 
extreme. Had they not been placed upon the lists they would have remained at t he ir usual 
occupations. 



Extract from Report of Captain Carev, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending

The people about Kanturk are in a wretched state of destitution, there are at least 300 at

52. This road, I opened on Thursday, near Kilbrin, the distress is very great about there also;

Baronies of East and West Muskerrx/, Bear, and Bantry.

blight, is perceptible ; however a great quantity of sound seed remains.

Extract from Report of Sir T. Deane, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, Tor week ending CORK. 

23rd January, 1847. 

The last week has been one of great anxiety to me in consequeuce of the great pressure for 
employment. In the early part of it (at least) 600 persons crowded round the office for work. 

Though my preparations were not as perfect as I could wish, I put into immediate motion 
the works on the navigation wall and at the north side of the city, so that I rejoice to say, that 
I have 900 men at work, and am making arrangements, thaL towards the end of the week, will 
enable me to increase the number to 1200. 

My expectation of relief from the large number of men I have employed, I regret to say, 
has not been realised, as importunities are increasing and great wretchedness evident, did I 
want 1000 men more, a day would produce them. 

It is with great pain I make this communication, a result so contrary to my forethouoht. 

The indefatigable Captain Broughton aids me in every way, by exertion and advice. 



Extract from Report of Captain Hobaud, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
24th January, 1847- 

There has been a very large addition made to the numbers on the relief lists this week, by 
all the Committees simultaneously. I think that an impression has gone abroad that the 
Government are not going to levy the expenses of the Labour Act, and that is the cause of this 
simultaneous and sudden increase of the lists, the number of aged and infirm persons, women, 
and children, are considerably increased. 

I have heard of several outrages upon property and persons this week, stopping people upon 
the roads after dark to rob them, hut they are not the acts of destitute persons. 

The wheat-crop is looking well where it is up. 

Several experiments in potato culture in the locality have failed. The plants, upon digging 
up, having been found rotten, these were planted last autumn, notwithstanding which, several 
gentlemen are preparing to plant potatoes on an extensive scale in the north of my district. 

Amongst the smaller farmers there is no attempt at cultivation. The roads absorbing all 
labour. 



Extract from Report of Captain Brooke, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
24th January, 1847. 

There appears to be a very fair portion of wheat sown by the large farmers through the 
country, and many have still a quantity of potatoes in the ground intended for seed, but as yet 
there seems to be no preparation making for sowing any or the spring crops; however, March 
is the month they usually sow their oats, which is the chief crop in this part of the country, and 
many of the larger farmers still have seed in store. From the number of small farmers, hold- 
ing from two to ten acres, who have applied to be taken upon the relief works, it is evident 
there will be a great portion of land unsown this year. The people seem perfectly tranquil. 
Very great destitution prevails. Provisions are exceedingly clear. Meal 2s. 6 d. per stone. 
Bread is completely out. of the reach of the poor, and no vegetables excepting turnips which are 
also dear. The Relief Committees seem anxious for more works to be opened, but the press 
of business is so great in the engineers’ department that they cannot be opened as speedily as 
could be wished. The landlords generally seem averse t to drainage under the present Act, 
having to pay their share of the other works as well as the drainage. The engineer has no 
complaint against the overseers. 

Extract from Report of Captain Brooke. Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
30th January, 1847. 

The Relief Committees, with a few exceptions, are very careless in making out their lists. 
A general complaint is the great distance that many people have to go to their work, hut I see 
no way of obviating this unless than by erecting temporary sheds along the extensive works, and 
providing straw in them for these people who have to come a distance to sleep there during the 
week. Many have to go six or seven miles, and it is impossible to have works convenient to 
all parties. The people are very quiet here, but clamorous for work. The preparations for 
sowing oats, &c., are going on very slowly about here, very few are getting employment from 
the farmers ; some are preparing for setting potatoes, and many farmers have still a good 
quantity of grain unthrashed. The Indian meal is 2s. 8 d. per stone, and oatmeal 3s. 1 Jd. per 
stone ; bread is 2 \d. per lb.

KERRY Extract from Journal of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week 

ending 2nd January, 1847. 

The barony of Corkaguiney is in a fearfully destitute state, the peasantry appear to have 
resigned themselves to their fate, and, never energetic, seem now to have lost all self reliance. 

The Dino-le Committee has not obeyed the Government instructions so accurately as might 
have been expected, their books being very incomplete, and the classification very imperfectly 
made. Farm operations in this district were never vigorously carried on at this period of the 
year, and there is certainly no disposition shown by any one to alter the system now that so 
great a change has taken place ; the resident gentlemen, with one exception, do not appear to 
differ in any way from their poor neighbours. I can hear of no measures being taken by them 
to provide their tenants with rye, barley, or other grain ; in fact, those persons are left to their 
own resources, and I understand that they are very generally selling their cattle and other 
moveable property, paying no rent, and keeping the money with the intention of emigrating at 
the proper season to America. 



Extract from Report of Captain Laualmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for 
week endiug 9th January, 1847. 

I am afraid things will not go on peaceably much longer at Killorglin ; in fact, there have 
been already there very frequent ,s turns out,” and the language and threats used towards the 
engineers are very violeut The people are discontented ; there are literally no resident gentry. 

The poor-houses are quite full, and more than full, and the number of sick in them very 
large. 

There appears to be quite sufficient work going on in North Dunkerron to relieve the pre- 
sent distress there, at least in the Knockbane Relief district. There does not appear much 
prospect of anything being done in the fields till about the beginning of March. 

There is an indisposition in three of the four baronies in my district to attempt the drainage 
under Mr. Labouchere’s letter, in the idea that more favourable terms for the landlords will 
he obtained by the expected Bill in Parliament. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

The chief portion of the land in the barony of Corkaguiney is held in common by several 
tenants on the different townlands, and the distress in some districts where squatting has been 
carried on for years, and the population has increased beyond the powers of the soil to supply 
its wants, is peculiarly great. The better class of farmers are, I am credibly informed, selling 
their stock and making preparations for emigration during the next two months ; their land is 
untilled ; the collection of sea-weed, formerly so much attended to at this season of the year, 
is now apparently forgotten ; nothing has yet been done, and inclination is shown by none to 
provide for the wants of the coming year. 

In fact, everything foreshadows the certainty of an impending calamity by far more dreadful 
than the present. 

Particular attention should be directed to Corkaguiney, the soil in every direction is capable 
of great improvement, and if properly cultivated equal to the support of its present large popu- 
lation ; and that population, though ignorant and indolent, are yet intelligent and peaceable, 
and appear only to require instruction and a proper guide to their labours, to bring forth the 
resources of the land they live in. That instruction and aid cannot, or will not, be given by 
the present owners of the soil ; and, therefore, without the powerful intervention of the Govern- 
ment, the lives of the people and the hidden capabilities of the soil will be lost for ever. 

The business of the Dingle Relief Committee is very unsatisfactorily carried on ; farmers 
have been recommended, and the really destitute not attended to ; their work is neither correctly 
nor fully filled up, and there is always a difficulty in getting lists of labourers. 

In the Ahanascaul district, owing to the Continual squabbles of the clergymen, it is quite 
impossible to obtain correct lists. All farm operations are suspended. 



Extract from Report of Captain Labalmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for 
week ending 16th January, 1847. 

I find no where the works progressing so regularly, and with such satisfaction to both 
labourers and the gentry of the district, as in the barony of Magunihy, where the Board’s 
officer, Mr. Robinson, cannot be too highly praised ; where 40 or 50 per cent, has been required 
in other localities on the original estimates to complete works, not more than 20 per cent, was 
requisite in Magunihy. It is certainly (now that task-work is more general in it) the pattern 
barony of this county. I find everything in the works in the neighbourhood of Tralee (barony 
Trughanacney) is in the greatest disorder ; there crowding in on the works in all directions, and 
if any attempts are made to quit them engineers are threatened ; and no doubt exists that if 
they were turned ofF a popular emeute in Tralee would-be the result. I shall remain here 
until I have introduced some kind of order and system. Now that our districts are more 
limited we may hope to effect something ; heretofore, before we could accomplish anythingi 
we were obliged to remove to another part of the country ; very little appearance of agricul- 
ture anywhere.

Extract from Report of Captain Forbes, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week ending

Mr. Thomas Fuller, pay-clerk, wrote me a letter to-day, stating the impossibility of his pro-

Extract from Report of Captain Labalmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for

Extract from Report of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week

Extract from Report of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

It is almost impossible to come to any arrangement with some of the Committees in Clan- 
maurice, nearly all the members being farmers, or persons having but a slight concern about 
the immense sums of money now being expended, and desirous of providing in any way for 
their own or their friends’ support, quite regardless of the claims of those really destitute. 

The gentry are very few in number, and with one or two exceptions quiet, indolent persons, 
unwilling to act in any way likely to draw down on themselves the ill-will of the people. 

It is not to be expected that any great assistance will be given by Relief Committees towards 
scrutinising the lists, and otherwise decreasing the number of labourers now employed on 
Public Works. As the members generally are too much wanting in moral courage to stand 
firm against the entreaties or threats of an excited people, and many also are so ignorant as but 
slightly to understand the great importance of weaning the people trom their present unprofit- 
able and demoralising work.

LIMERICK. Extract from Report of Lieut. Inglis, Inspecting Officer, County Limerick, for week ending 

2nd January, 1847. 

The neglect of the usual farm operations is still very remarkable, but I think it may now be 
said to be confined to the land of small farmers. 

A farmer of the name of Lynch behaved in a very violent and offensive manner towards me 
when visiting this work, complaining of not having received compensation for the land occupied 
by the road : and the labourers are dissatisfied by prices given by task. 

The stone-breakers have struck to work with the prices allowed, viz., Is. 2 d. per cubic yard, 
and have left the work ; and, further, have refused a higher rate of Is. 4 d. per cubic yard. 
The stone is of a peculiarly hard description ; but I think the latter price would be amply 
remunerative, and, with a skilled person, the former sufficient. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Telfeu, Inspecting Officer, County Limerick, for week 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

When in the barony of Coonagh last Tuesday and Wednesday, I ascertained 10 individuals 
had been sent on the Public Works with tickets from various members of the Doon Relief

Extract from Report of Captain Watson, Inspecting Officer, County Limerick, for week

employed there is generally good. There are some people on the works who are not in desti-

days since : informations have been sworn against the party, and the case is not yet disposed of.

operation. Task-work is now general on all the roads, and they are going on very fast. The 
Relief Committees continue to exert themselves, but some of them have but little, if any, system 
of working, and a few are intimidated. 

Extract from Journal of Captain Norris, Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, for week TIPPERARY, 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

Some of the Relief Committees cause me a great deal of unnecessary trouble by the incor- 
rect way their lists are made out, and by their attempts to interfere with the stewards on the 
different works. 

If it were possible for the pay-clerks to have sufficient silver to pay each man individually, 
instead of being obliged to give a pound to four men to divide, it would be of great advantage, 
as several instances have come before me in which, by the latter mode, some poor fellows have 
been done out of their pay altogether. I am aware that the men acknowledge this receipt by 
their work, but this I imagine is done before the pound is divided, and does not insure the 
money being justly divided. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Miller, Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, N. R., 
for week ending 9th January, 1847. 

The labourers are fast sinking into open idleness, not earning inmany places above one-third 
of what they receive for subsistence. This state of affairs is, I regret to say, attributable to the 
rate of subsistence having been lately raised from 8 d. to 1(M. wherever the men were clearing 
the latter sum. It was a measure to which Mr. Crawford and I reluctantly gave in, owing to 
the urgent representations made from all quarters as to the impossibility of the people being 
able to exist on the lower rate. Under ordinary circumstances, a suspension of the works for 
a few days would, I have no doubt, remedy the evil ; but, with the existing destitution, I con- 
ceive it to be a step which could not be safely adopted.

Extract from Report of Captain Ogle, Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, S. R., for 
week ending 23rd January, 1847. 

Monday and Tuesday 1 8th and 19 th January, 1847. — Engaged, in conjunction with members 
of the Tubbria Relief Committee, revising the list of labourers employed on the new line of 
road from Clogheen to Cahir. 

Many cases were discovered of three persons out of the same family being employed, which 
were, consequently, obtaining more relief than was actually necessary for their subsistence, 
leaving other families in the district without any employment whatever : 65 persons were 
dismissed. 

Extract from Report of Captain Norris, Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

I was yesterday (30th) called upon by Mr. Ryan, J. P., and chairman of the Committee, to 
say that the Inch men would not allow the Drum men to work in their parish, and that, unless 
I sent the Drum men away, he feared bloodshed would be the consequence : this I declined to 
do, as giving way to intimidation is too much the order of the day in Tipperary; but I imme- 
diately started to Ballypatrick, where the disturbance took place. On my arrival I found the 
Drum men had been driven away, but without bloodshed. After remaining with the Inch men, 
I soon brought them to their- senses by letting them know that I would not only suspend the 
work if anything of the sort took place again, but that I would strike their names off the relief 
lists: this had the desired effect, and they promised to let the Drum men return quietly. 



Extract from Report of Captain Ogle, Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, for week- 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

From my own observation whilst travelling, and from inquiry, the lands of small farmers 
remain neglected in the baronies of Iffa and Offa East and West. 

No employment visible in the fields. 



RFORD Extract from Report of Captain Sir Thomas Ross, Inspecting Officer, County Waterford, 
for week ending 2nd January, 1847. 

With reference to last paragraph of directions at foot, I have to observe that farm operations 
are almost at a stand-still, and will continue so until some bold and decided step be taken to 
remove all farmers from the Public Works. Such is their love of participating the Government 
money, as they call it, that farming is a minor consideration as compared with it. What 
I would suggest is, that all farmers be removed from the works (except those known to be 
destitute) during alternate weeks until the middle of February, and altogether from that period 
until the loth ot May, when the crops are supposed to be in ground. 

An assistant of Mr. Owen had been placed as overseer in Kilrosenfy district. I had occasion 
to reprimand him for disobedience of orders, and for admitting persons on the Common Road 
without authority. The workmen, with whom he is a great favourite, having heard me 
(although 1 moved off from them), swore that, if they thought they could overtake me, 
1 should not reach Dungarvan alive. I have insisted on this person’s dismissal from the 
service, and 1 do not value threats.

Extracts from Journals of Inspecting Officers, County of Waterford, for week ending 
9th January, 1847. 

Farming operations going on very slowly, in some instances the farmers are trying to sell 
their manure. Overseers and stewards improving, but still very remiss iu their duties; great 
difficulty in finding efficient persons to fill these situations. 

A few robberies of trifling nature going on in Coshmore and Coshbride, on the borders of 
County Tipperary ; several soup kitchens established throughout the country, which give great 
relief, and ought to be encouraged as much as possible. 

Dungarvan Committee carrying on business most irregularly, refusing to pay a secretary ; 
the consequence is no books are kept, and they cannot tell what number of a family are 
employed. This is the case with several of the Committees. The priests are doing all they can to 
crowd the works ; with a few exceptions, and in most of the Committees, the priest is the 
leading person. The landlords are afraid of rejecting applicants for employment on the Public 
Works. The priests force them on them.

Extract from Journal of Captain Way, Inspecting Officer, County Waterford, for 
week ending 23rd January,- 1847. 

Baronies of Middletlrird, Gannetin, Upperthird, and Borough. 

The Relief Committees are everywhere besieged with applications for employment on the 
Relief Works. The great majority of the people employed are wholly dependent on the 
wages paid them, and their food is most scanty, owing to the high price of meal. Many 
instances occur of labourers being unable to accomplish a day’s work from want of sustenance ; 
they are quiet and well-disposed, and the works are very fairly executed. Farm operations 
are scarcely perceptible in any direction. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Downman, Inspecting Officer, County Waterford, for 
week ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The works in general going on well; the stewards in many instances very bad, but impos- 
sible to find better, check-clerks the same. No farming operations, with the exception of 
sowing a little wheat. The people very peaceable, and beginning to be quite reconciled to 
task, but in many instances it is very unfairly set. The Relief Committees improving, with 
the exception of three in this immediate neighbourhood, which are getting worse and worse 
every day. 

The farmers have dismissed all their servants. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hill, Inspecting Officer^ County Waterford, for week 
ending 24th January, 1847. 

The farming operations of the season are increasing, but very moderately, in consequence of 
the want of seed, which the farmers affirm they cannot purchase ; and many use all the influ- 
ence they can to obtain work on the roads. 

Seed has been procured for some on the estate of Mr. Osborne, M.P., by the proprietor, 
but I have heard of no other instance of the kind. 

The people are generally tranquil considering the privations they have to endure. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Downman, Inspecting Officer, County Waterford, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

A plough is now occasionally seen on the farms, but instead of labourers being employed, 
the farmers’ sons guide the plough. The farmers can scarcely be blamed for dismissing new 
servants, having so little food for themselves in very many instances. 

Soup kitchens doing a great deal of good in the towns, but the country derives no benefit 
from them. No good would be done by giving clothing, as every article would be pawned for 
food. 

Witnessed an horrible case of an unfortunate creature who died near Ring from want, not 
actual starvation, as there was a very small quantity of meal in the cabin. One old sheet was 
her only covering for the family, five in number. The father, (whose death I witnessed, a 
few moments after,) had been employed on ttie Public Works about three weeks previous, but 
was unable to work in consequence of ill health ; the rest of the family, all females, had not 
applied for work, thinking they would not get it. This is the only case of the kind I have met 
with, but I fear there are many similar ones. The cabin is on a property of Lord Stuart 
De Decies, the poorest district in the country — Sieve Grind.
