Extract from Journal of Lieut. Hotham, Inspecting Officer, County Carlow, for week CABLOW. 
ending 2nd January, 1847. j 

I do not think in this county that agriculture is being neglected. It may be rather late, 
but it is certainly in progress. I think that the Relief Committees are doing their duty very 
well and firmly. The number employed on the works is under one to every three labouring 
families ; and as spring advances I hope that we shall reduce it lower. 

The great difficulty which exists about the works arises from the incompetency of the 
stewards. I think we shall get a very good staff of check-clerks, but it is very hard to hear of 
good stewards. 

Frequently it turns out that the money voted at sessions for a work is utterly inadequate, 
under favourable circumstances, to complete it. * 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Hotham, Inspecting Officer, County^ Carlow, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

The distress is increasing. Our numbers employed do not increase as fast as one might 
imagine, because the wages are kept strictly to what the farmers can afford to pay, and because 
the Relief Committees are doing their duty firmly. I am not of opinion, in this county, that 
agriculture will not be neglected ; in some districts it may be backward, but that is, I think, 
owing to the late severe frosts. Ploughing is going on in all directions. 

I think that the works are, generally speaking, progressing satisfactorily. There have been 
three or four attempts on the part of the labourers to strike for an advance of wages, conse- 
quent on the high price of provisions, but we have uniformly resisted, and the Committees 
are assisting us in selling meal to them at a cheaper rate. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Hotham, Inspecting Officer, County Carlow, for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

A movement is going forward in the county to stop the Public Works, and all to unite in 
employing the poor in agriculture. There is to be a meeting to-morrow in Carlow about it. 
The small farmers, under 10 acres, are much behind in agriculture, and there seems some 
doubt if they have seed to sow. The large farmers are not. 

I have remarked several pasture fields ploughed up this season. 

Mr. Burtchaell complains of the general inefficiency of his stewards, and the impossibility 
of getting good ones ; also of the expensive nature of pauper labour. One woman has died of 
starvation, which is the first authenticated case in the county. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Hotham, Inspecting Officer, County Carlow, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

With the exception of 2500 people being employed on Public Works, I do not think any 
person travelling through the county would perceive the slightest difference from ordinary 
years ; agriculture is not behind, the people orderly and quiet ; the farmers are inclined to 
have fewer labourers under their employ, but the high price of meal, and the cash payments 
account for that very naturally.

KILKENNY. Extract from Journal of Lieut. Gallway, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, for week

The people are very generally employed on Public Works, but a great many are still apply-

Extract from Report of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, for week 
ending 9ih January, 1847. 

I find the destitution is very great, but there is not sufficient care taken by the Committees 
in selecting the proper objects. Sir Richard Languish, the chairman of the Knockropher 
Committee, is wishing to defer the Presentment Sessions till the meeting of Parliament, 
whereas, in his own immediate district there is not urgent necessity, there is very great in others 
adjoining. Attended relief meeting at Newmarket ; found great necessity for more persons 
being upon the works, from the number of applications. The works in this district will not 
afford employment much longer. I find that many persons are registered, and put to work, 
who have no right to be, having means for present support at least. I endeavoured to point 
this out, but with the exception of the chairman and secretary, the rest are all farmers, who 
look to getting their own people employed. 

Attended Relief Committee, at Dungarran, with Captain Stopford, the inspector. Found 
that many persons had been admitted on the works, who had other means of support, and too 
many in one family. I had struck out a great many from the lists of applications, but in dif- 
ferent lists, the number previously employed of that family was not stated. 

I find that great abuses have been going on in the ticket system, that names are scratched 
out. and others substituted. I am endeavouring to take up all the tickets and refer all irregu- 
lar ones to the Committees, though I cannot get them to strike of all where there has been de- 
ception practised, though I do now', till properly registered and returned to me.

KILKENNY. Extract from Journal of Lieut. Gallway, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, for week 

ending 25th January, 1847. 

I am glad to observe that task-work is being introduced gradually, and the people much 
more contented to work by measurement, than by the day, with one or two exceptions. There 
is a great decrease in the nightly robberies of sheep, and the county is very quiet. 

There is very little doing by the farmers. 

With reference to the stoppage of the work at Rathmoyle (visited by me on Wednesday 
last), I must observe that- it was no fault of the people, but of the Relief Commitlee of Tul- 
larm, who told the men, that, other men were earning their money, and that they ought not to 
allow it. 



KING’S COUNTY. Extract from Report of Lieut. Hamilton, Inspecting Officer, Southern Division of King’s 
County, for week ending 2nd January, 1847. 

I do not perceive any change, since my former reports, in the state of this county, as regards 
the arming of the peasantry, which is going on ; the existence of great distress, and the neglect 
of making preparations for next year’s crops. 

There is a slight change as regards the quality of crime, though not the quantity ; on an aver- 
age eight robberies a day being the number reported to the Lieutenant of this county by the 
police. 



Extract from Report of 'Lieut. Hamilton, Inspecting Officer, King’s County, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

I have made inquiries from persons I consider most qualified to give a correct and unbiassed 
opinion on the subject, and I find that from six to eight weeks supply of provision, is about the 
period that the home produce is likely to last. 

Applications for employment on the Public Works, are now made by persons holding up- 
wards of 10 acres of land, and in one instance a farmer holding 21 acres, was returned to me for 
work. I have struck out several such persons from the Relief Committees list; but they 
assure me that these persons are starving, and it is sometimes difficult to know how to act.. 

Complaints have, I understand, been lately made by farmers, of a difficulty in procuring 
labourers. With the exception of the state of the country, I cannot see the objection they have 
to apply for them from the Public Works. 

I have frequently written, and expressed my desire to assist them, but I have never received 
one application ; taking into consideration the large number of labourers who are still unem- 
ployed in every locality, I can scarcely attribute the great neglect, of making preparations for 
next year’s crops to this cause. Every person employed by Mr. Mason, is working by task at 
a very liberal allowance, but in a great measure from idleness, and in some instances from 
inability, their earnings are occasionally very small. Now some of these farmers are the very 
loudest in demanding increased allowances for the men at one time, and at another I have no 
doubt equally loud in complaining that their labourers leave them to idle on die Public 
Works. 

I do not think that either the landlords or the labourers have much to thank the farmers for. 

The patience and endurance of the really destitute is almost incredible. I am happy to 
say that soup kitchens have been established by most of the Relief Committees, and that they 
are affording a great deal of relief. 



Extract from Journal of Major Bennett, Inspecting Officer, King’s County, for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

Farming operations among small holders much neglected, asses being employed. Manure 
not as usual collected. If seed is distributed gratis, it is used for food.

Extract from Report of Captain Watker, Inspecting Officer, County Longford, for week 
ending 2nd January, 1817. 

I regret to say bad outrages in the shape of robberies of property and arms, all by armed 
parties, still continue. Threatening notices on various subjects are also served. 

Little or no improvement in agricultural operations, and nearly all that is being done is 
horse-work. The whole labouring population are seeking for employment at the public expense, 
and thev cannot avoid it, as too many of the wealthiest gentry of the county have turned off 
their labourers, and the better class of farmers have, almost to a man, followed the example.

HEATH. Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for rvrek 

eliding 2nd January, 1847. 

Many tenants of 10 or 12 acres have no seed nor the means of buying it. Unless some means 
be devised of supplying this class with seed, their farms will be idle : a serious consideration. 
Many proprietors would give extensive employment, were they exempt from baronial taxation. 
At present they add to their burthen by giving employment. The destitution in many localities 
very great. 1 have seen turnips of poor quality sold at 2 \d. per stone, — there the sole food of 
many. The farm operations (with the exception of small holdings) by no means backward. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847-. 

The holders of small farms (10 acres and under) are in most instances destitute, and will not 
be able to crop their lands without speedy assistance. 

It is a serious consideration, and the consequences cannot, in my opinion, he overrated. Most 
of the Relief Committees act independently and conscientiously ; but I regret to say there are 
exceptions. 

All the works are necessarily crowded. The people, in general, are well behaved, but indo- 
lent and tardy ; their wretched feeding indisposes them to exert themselves. I have scru- 
tinized the lists in several localities, and very successfully have turned off many. The ganger 
and overseer classes are in very many instances improper persons, as well as check clerks. 
Mr. Lindsay co-operates with me in weeding them. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for wed 
ending 16th Januaiy, 1847. 

The state of the county is peaceable, though some outrages and robberies have occurred 
during the week, but I think quite unconnected with the general state of the comity, and com- 
mitted by ruffians residing out of the county. The increase which has taken place in the police 
force of the county will check this. Very great destitution exists, and the people are very 
patient under extraordinary privations and sufferings. I am fortunate in the zealous co-opera- 
tions of all classes. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

I am satisfied, from observation and experience, that there are paid emissaries employed for 
the purpose of counselling the labourers against working by task, though in all task work through 
the county they have, on the average, earned above a shilling per diem. The small farmers in 
this county are in a very destitute state, few of them having the means of buying seed. Unless 
they are speedily assisted, their land will remain untilled and uncropped. One of this class, to 
whom I was speaking a few days since, observed, in reply to a question, “ The short and the 
long of it is, if the graziers do not break up some of their farms to allow employment, the 
labourers will eat the farmers, and the farmers will eat the landlords.” 

Those works being executed by task are progressing favourably, and men earning well; those 
at day’s wages going on unsatisfactorily. I am introducing task- work as much and quickly as 
I prudently can ; but such is the objection and resistance to it, that I am obl'ged to go on all 
occasions to enforce it in person. I have, however, succeeded in every instance I have under- 
taken throughout the county.

Extract from Report of Major M'Kee, Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, for week 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

There is a general opinion prevailing that Her Majesty’s Government will never call upon 
the baronies to pay the amount advanced for unproductive works. This idea has an evil ten- 
dency, and the Relief Committees think it. of no moment how much is expended, and take no 
pains to ascertain that applicants for relief are really in need of assistance ; in consequence their 
lists are crowded. It would be, in my humble opinion, of much advantage to convince the cess- 
payers of their error.

Extract of Journal of Major M‘Kee, Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, for week ending QUEEN’S 
9th January, 1847. COUNTY. 

The distress is on the increase, the price of provisions being so high that the money earned 
by the labourer is quite insufficient for the support of any one but himself, and in many instances 
not enough to support his own existence. Instances are frequent where gangs earn less than 6 d. 
per day per man ; the labourers complain loudly. I have had another petition fromBallicolla, 
forwarded by Mr. R. W. Fitzpatrick, and I am most anxious this case should be investigated. 

The engineers say the labourers are idle, and there is no doubt this is generally the case. I had a 
remonstrance yesterday from some men, because the engineers had objected to their going to their 
meals twice a-day, that is, at 9 a.m. and again at noon. Yesterday a case came uuder my own 
observation. Three gangs complained they had earned but 6^d. per day for the last week. 

They were only returning to their work at half-past one o’clock, when I first visited them, and 
on mv return, at a quarter past four o’clock, they had all left the work. I regret to say the 
Relief Committees do not in most instances attend to their duty, or to the instructions they have 
received. They complain loudly of the delay in sanctioning the works which have been pre- 
sented ; they complain of the delay of sending these lists to the inspecting officers, instead of 
furnishing them direct to the engineer. Notwithstanding these complaints, the Committees, 
when required to send in a list of labourers, delay doing so for several days. The Ballicolla 
Committee have been loud in their complaints, and yet have only this morning returned me a 
list I left with them 011 the 6th. The reason is obvious. Their registers are not correctly kept, 
and when a list is required, they have to meet and determine on each case de now, -unless, as 
I am persuaded is the case in some instances, they allow the chairman or secretary to take the 
trouble off their hands. A member of the Ballicolla Committee informed me that at their last 
meeting a member had objected to an applicant’s name as not requiring relief, and that this 
member, on his way home, had been upbraided for so doing. Of course some member of the 
Committee had told the man, and by these means are honest members prevented from doing 
their duty conscientiously. The Cooham Committee, after urging strongly the necessity of 
putting on more work on account of the number of destitute, passed a resolution on the 
4th instant that they would not fill up the lists I had sent them, as t hey wished the drainage to 
be commenced. This resolution was passed after I had left, and believed the meeting to have 
closed its proceedings. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Baillie, Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, for week 
ending 10th January, 1847. 

The whole time of the meeting of the Relief Committee at Maryborough was consumed in 
going over all the minutes of their proceedings since I had last attended, reading their numerous 
resolutions, and making speeches. Near the close of the meeting all those waiting to have 
their names registered were admitted, when Dr. Jacob, who takes the lead, addressed them at 
considerable length, urging them to adopt some means of letling the Government know their 
condition ; for his part he was satisfied they were dying slowly of starvation. A most ineffectual 
attempt was made to show that many of them then admitted had been returned to me, but were 
still unemployed. 

I then showed that whatever number still remained unemployed, no statement whatever on 
this subject had ever been made to me ; that the Relief Committee was the proper channel 
through which to make their case known, and that the Committee were then to report it to me. 
This had never been done. 



Extract from Journal of Major M'Kee, Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The destitution is still very great, and the price of food has not yet fallen. Considering the 
distress which prevails, the people have been generally very well behaved. In Maryborough 
West, which I visited on Friday and Saturday, I found the labourers seeking employment 
more orderly and civil than they were before the dissolution of the Relief Committee, some of 
the members of which had too much encouraged unfounded complaints. The new Committee 
has been formed. There is every prospect of having all the destitute in employment within a 
week. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Batllie, Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The road works in Stradbally are also drawing to a close. The people are enduring their 
privations and sufferings with great patience. I have not heard lately of any outrages. A 
clergyman, a member of the Relief Committee of Luggacurren, writes to me to say the people 
on the works in that district are getting weaker every day, owing to the insufficiency and 
inferior quality of the food which they are able to obtain with their earnings, which are again 
diminished from their increased inability to perform a good day’s work, and urging me to use 
my influence to have higher rates allowed for the tasks. Such a system it would, of course, be 
impossible to carry out, and it would be better to permit day-work than to attempt to execute

Extract from Journal of Captain Hart, Inspecting Officer, County Louth, for week ending 
-9th January, 1847. 

I have been very much pressed during the past week to find employment for the destitute 
but the prompt compliance of the Commissioners to my application for increased means has 
relieved me from what was a very painful and ciitical position. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hart, Inspecting Officer, County Louth, for week ending 
16th January, 1847. 

I have had a very anxious time of it during the past week, and but for the moans so promptly 
placed at my disposal by the Board, by which I have been enabled to put several hundred 
persons into immediate employment, I do firmly believe that the peace would have been 
broken in several parts of this county. All is now comparatively quiet, although much desti- 
tution still remains unrelieved. With 19 Relief Committees to visit and regulate, it has not 
been possible for me to visit the works throughout the county, but those I pass by daily appear 
to be judiciously managed. Farm operations are progressing, and I am doing all in my power 
to induce the small farmers, holders of one, two, and three acres, to cultivate their land, by 
making it generally 'known that I shall dismiss from the Public Works every person holding 
land who neglects it. An announcement of this kind may have the desired effect. There is 
still a large quantity of unthrashed corn throughout the country. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hart, Inspecting Officer, County Louth, for week ending 
23rd January, 1847. 

The destitution in every section of the country is rapidly increasing, owing to the high prices 
of provisions. At the same time, there is a very large quantity of unthrashed corn everywhere 
in the country, a larger quantity, I am credibly informed, than has ever been known at this 
season in any former year. The destitute people have been enduring great suffering, owing to 
the want of employment on the Relief Works, but the Board having now issued prompt and 
specific orders to immediately remedy this, I hope to have it in my power to make a more 
favourable report next week. 



Extract from Report of Captain Telford, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, N. D., 
for week ending 9th January, 1847. 

Barony of Moycashel. 8fc. 

From the hurried and slovenly manner some lists are prepared I am obliged to return them, 
and state that it is time enough to let me have them on obtaining the engineer’s requisition, 
when I shall call for the number to be employed on some specific work. This has given 
umbrage in some quarters, but were I to comply with the whims of Relief Committees my 
services would be of little avail. 

W here proprietors who have undertaken drainage have appointed a superior class of persons 
as stewards to look after the labourers, and keep them regularly to their work, I find fair hire 
has been earned, and no dissatisfaction expressed ; but some of the gentry have men as over- 
seers little or nothing removed as to condition in life or intelligence from those they are placed 
over, and, consequently, without frequent measurement and great firmness on the part of the 
engineer, little value can be obtained. This is a point I have been impressing and insisting 
on, and shall see carried out. 

Men in the barony of Cockaree, whose weekly subsistence was cut down one week, more 
than made up the deficiency of what they had expected, and a fair rate of hire the week 
following. I was obliged to give instructions to check clerks not to enter men for work em- 
ployed for drainage who did not. use the tools supplied for that purpose, many objecting from 
not being accustomed to them. 

Extract from Report of Mr. Maxwell, Inspecting Officer, County W 7 estmeath, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

In some instances the people employed on the Public Works in my district have worked 
hard and constantly, and have earned excellent wages, but the majority are very indolent, and 
in some cases their day’s pay has been reduced in consequence. 

I have had to complain of two or three instances of individuals of Relief Committees sending 
men to the Public Works without any authority whatever. Of course they were not checked 
for payment or acknowledged by the check clerks, .and when they applied to me I referred 
them to the individuals who sent them to the work.

Extract from Journal of Captain .Telford, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, N. D., 
for week ending 16th January, 1847- 

I found at Killnean, barony of Farbile, that the Committee had made excellent arrange- 
ments for the supply of food which is the most important duty they have to perform at this 
calamitous period. The registry of applicants for employment so carefully and scrupulously 
kept that. I had not to strike out a single name. 

I begin to see the plough going in a variety of places, but the small farmer is doing nothing. 

Owing to the drainage works being now in operation in the barony of Demifore, ample em- 
ployment for those requiring it is afforded; but previously not within 500 of those in the 
utmost distress were provided for, and had it not been for ihe munificence of the Earl of 
Longford and Mr. Pollard, of Kantuck House, great difficulties must have ensued. I feel 
myself greatly relieved by the miserable beings in this district having now some means to keep 
body and soul together; and I must sav,. to their credit, that, they submitted to their hard 
trials with the utmost fortitude, and were determined, if compelled to supply their wants by 
taking provisions from the more comfortable class, they would do so openly in the day-time. 

Wednesday . — Engaged all day at Castlepollard, preparing lists for Mr. George Duffers, 
appointed to superintend drainage in the barony of Demifore, who undertook, on his own resr 
ponsibility, to give employment on works not yet sanctioned ; but being perfectly satisfied, from 
his report, that they must, I; thought he used a wise discretion, under all the circumstances, 
starvation being depicted in the faces of a numerous pauper population, for whom no other 
means of relief were open. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Maxwell, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

Baronies of Brawney, Clonlonen, Kilkenough , Moycashel, Rathconrath, and Fartullagh. 

The conduct of the people on the works is quiet and orderly, hut in general they are very 
indolent. Seven sheep and one cow have been stolen at night this week, and a barn was 
broken into close to the town of Kilbeggan. The assistant engineer in Moycashel has been 
introducing much more extensively the task-work system, and, in consequence, many of the 
gangs were only paid 8iZ. per day. I am in hopes this will cause greater exertion next week. 
The farm operations have been much neglected as yet. I have had a few of the labourers on 
the works applied for by the farmers. I have given them every encouragement to go to the 
farm work, by promising to readmit them on the works if they should be without employment. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Telford, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, N. D., 
for week, endipg 23rcl, January,. 1847. 

The farmers of a better class are beginning to use the plough freely, but the small holders 
of land are quite at a stand still ; however, the usual season for their operations in this part of 
the country has not arrived, and when it does, I greatly fear they will not have seed to put in 
the ground. 



Extract from Report of Captain Teleord, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, N. D., • 
, for week ending 2nd- January, 1847. 

Wherever Relief Committees have come forward in good earnest, and made it their business 
to provide lists of the really destitute only for the Public Works, I have found the pressure for 
employment met at once, and farm operations not generally neglected, as in the case of the 
Ballinacargy district, barony of Moygoish, where every arrangement from the onset was made 
for the supply of good sound articles' of food at fair prices; thereby effectually checking all 
attempts at extortion on the part of small dealers in meal, and whatever else is now a substitute 
for the potato.

Extract from Journal of Lieut. Anderson, Inspecting Officer, County Wicklow, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

f Barony of North Ballinacor. 

The prices of provisions are, I regret to say, increasing. One poor object came to me on 
the works yesterday and said, “ I got 5s. last week, but all I could get for it at Dunlavin was 
a stone and a half of meal, and how. Sir, will that support a small but helpless family of four 
beside myself.” 

On Monday, the 4th, I attended a meeting of the Anamon Relief Committee, and ordered 
31 more men to be employed, and ordered 10 to be struck off the lists, as I had received 
information that they were not destitute. On Tuesday, the 5th, I attended a meeting of the 
Sheanna Relief Committee and struck off 25 names, and gave employment to 10 more men. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Anderson, Inspecting Officer, County Wicklow, for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

Sheep stealing is daily becoming more frequent. Several outrages of a more serious nature 
have occurred in this neighbourhood. About 20 barrels of corn, the property of the Rev. W. 
West, of Arramoe, were burnt. I would suggest that a supply of Circular No. 47, be sent down 
to me, that I may have them posted in different parts of the county. Persons to whom- 1 have 
hitherto refused employment I have found it necessary at last to admit ; a panic has seized the 
small farmer, and one and all have ceased to cultivate their lands. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Anderson, Inspecting Officer, County Wicklow, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

This morning I received the following communication from one of my check clerks in South 
Ballinacor. 

“ I have also to inform you, that the men employed on the Killadoren, part of the same road, 
were on the eve of turning out this day at dinner time, partly on account of not having been 
paid, and partly for an increase of wages, as they all told me they were starving. I was also 
informed by the stewards along the entire line that about one-third of the men under their charge 
had not eaten anything for the last 36 hours. I should mention that I met the pay-clerk as I 
left Tinnahely in the evening, and that he reported all were paid. I met many on my journey 
here, and all were thankful, as they had got their pay. I have selected considerably upwards 
of 8000 men for employment on the Public Works, and I am sure they only require food to 
remain peaceable.” 



Extract from Report of Major Ainslie, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

Barony of Clonmacnoon. 

The most prominent event is the robbery of Mr. F. Coffey, pay-clerk, barony of Longford, 
of about 670/., on 28th December, near Flower Hill, between 12 and 1 o’clock mid-day. 
About 1 50/. has been found when searching for arms in the barony of Longford, at the house 
of a notorious offender, called Steel Madden, by an active sub -inspector, Mr. Abbott, who has 
taken the notes to Mr. Coffey, at Loughrea, to identify them, and Mr. Hall, the Board’s 
auditor, accompanied him, and thence they go to Portumna, where two more men are in 
custody on suspicion of being accessories. 

I found that cultivation around the districts in Ballymoe, Tyaquin, and Killian baronies 
suspended, and I admonished the workmen, that if the spare hands did not work and prepare 
their fields it was practicable to suspend the works to give time for tillage, but this duty, which 
is not done in many parts of the county till the eleventh hour, has yet I hope some chance of 
performance. 

Agricultural operations in the north of my district appear to be suspended. I admonished 
the labourers about this neglect. 



Extract from Report of Major Clerke, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

Destitution and starvation still increasing, and every one looking forward with earnest 
anxiety to the arrival of the time when it may be deemed expedient by the Government to 
check the inordinate extortion of the provision merchants, on which subject I am daily fearing 
some popular outbreak. 

In the course of my inquiries, in this district, in which from former residence and con- 
nexions I have the best sources of information, I ascertain that there is a good deal of corn still 
extant. It is not to be seen stacked, as in other times, but I know that it is kept threshed and 
stored by the middle class of farmers, evidently with a wish to escape public observation.

Extract from Report of Major Burns, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week ending 
9th January, 1847. 

The state of the country is lamentable. There have been many outrages during the past 
week. Bands of armed men have been robbing houses of arms, money, and provisions. 
Alarm appears to pervade the minds of all classes, and destitution is said to be attended with 
fatal effects in an awfully great degree, and yet the people will tamely see their neighbours on 
the Public Works, who have the means of supporting themselves, without pointing them out. 
Some of the poor people have recently given me private information, which has enabled me to 
remove nearly a hundred men of that description alluded to, and in their place, destitute people 
employed. 

The labourers, such as have families, cannot, from the high price of provisions, provide for 
them on the daily wages of 8 d. Men who labour by task do not complain. Several labourers 
came to me yesterday, but in a peaceable and orderly manner, and stated what I have just 
reported. On the Shanaglish line, on Friday, the labourers insisted on the check clerk 
returning them for 1 j. a-day, and threatened violence if he refused. 

I assembled the people and explained to them the fearful results that would attend refractory 
conduct on their part. I dismissed four of the ringleaders off the works, two of whom I after- 
wards discovered had ample means of supporting themselves. 



Extract from Report of Captain Hutchison, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, W. D., 
for week ending 9th January, 1847. 

I beg leave to call the particular attention of the Board to the state of the county town. 
The works in progress nearly finished, and the state of the fishermen of the Claddagh is a 
prospect far from cheering. There are very few boats employed now. The tackle of the others 
either pledged for their support or worn out, and they without the means of replacing them. 
An attempt, I hear, was made to stop grain on Loch Corrib, but the police fired, and the 
country boats dispersed. 



Extract from Report of Major Clerke, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

Sixteen cars, laden with meal and flour, were plundered near this, on Thursday. 

Distress and applicants at the poor- house much augmented. Indian corn and meal reduced 
in price, in Galway, owing to extensive importations, while home produce is dearer from want 
of enterprise and importations of wheat. Bread sold, this day, at Is. OJd. the 41b. loaf; 
although the weather has been fair the corn market has been miserably supplied, and at 
exorbitant prices. 



Extract from Retort of Major Ainslie, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week

I regret to say that agricultural operations are generally neglected, and where the least 
employment was given there the seed was put in. The conduct of the people around Athenry

they have yet found their way there. 

The principal part of the gang who robbed Mr. Coffey have been committed for trial. 

Engaged in an interview with the members of the Ey recourt Relief Committee respecting

Extract from Report of Major Atnslik, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, E. D„

The state of the country is still tranquil, but apprehension increases on the minds of many 
gentlemen. I have heard of arms being in possession of many around Portumna on the

Extract from Rkport of Captain Hutchison, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The works I have visited this week are going on as well as the state of the weather (which 
has been very severe) will admit of. 

The state of the country is remarkably quiet, considering the very great distress the popu- 
lation are now labouring under. The deaths are, I hear, numerous, chiefly among the 
aged. 

The high prices of food and:the distances they have to bring it,, chiefly done by the women 
on their backs, in many cases from 20 to 30 miles, add much to their privations, yet I have not 
heard of a single outrage on person or property in this remote part of the country. I am sorry 
to say there is an apathy, and no desire for cordial co-operation in the Rounclstone Committee, . 
their days of meeting a scene of quarrelling amongst themselves. There are the clergymen 
of the Established, Presbyterian, and Roman Catholic churches, but no gentleman of note as 
chairman ; this will, I fear, lead to lamentable results. I observed some of the usual farming 
operations in progress while travelling through the country. 



Extract from Report of Major Clerke, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week ending 
23rd January, 1847. 

The preparatory farming operations usual at this season in other years appear suspended in 
this district, except where the people have some peculiarly favourable tenure of their ground. 
I never make a tour of inspection without wishing that the poor labourers were paid in food 
instead of money, and that small depdts of provisions were established wherever there was a. 
military or constabulary station. Amongst other advantages it would diminish the risk of pay- 
clerks travelling about with large sums of money. 

The labourers being supplied with a ticket for meal in lieu of money would keep off from 
Public Works all but those actually in want of food. 



Extract from Report of Major Ainslie, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

The district is still tranquil, but the representations at present of well-informed persons are 
more and more pressing and energetic for employment. 

The conduct of the labourers is- good, but. I am everywhere asked for further employment; 
what has been done appears like -a small reply to urgent exclamations of distress and demands 
on all sides. The markets are rising still. 



Extract from Report of Major Clerke, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

I regret that I experience much difficulty in encouraging soup establishments amongst the 
rural Relief Committees of the baronies in my charge, principally from the number of non- 
resident proprietors, who will not subscribe, and from the natural repugnance of the residents 
to have the whole onus thrown on them. 

I find throughout the same pervading system of jobbing” amongst the Committees. 

One chairman, a man of large fortune, had to resign his seat, on discovery that he caused 
to be put first on the relief lists those of his own tenants who had paid him their rent. 

I sincerely hope that the method I suggested to the Committees, as to admission of appli - 
cants’ names on their relief books, will obviate much abuse and monopoly, of patronage.

'Extract from Report of Captain Layaud, 'Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week LEITRIM, 
ending 2nd January, 1847. 

I am still of opinion that,. in many instances, -the valuations for labour are too low, as proved 
by the fact that now the measurements are made -some gangs only get from L. lid. to 
2s. 10d. for the week on No. 13 work ; an enormous quantity of arms are coming into the 
country daily, and many pistols. 

The men on No. 31 were very much inclined to become mutinous, and abused the check- 
clerk simply because the measurements having been made they had not earned what they 
expected. I at once proceeded to the spot, and told them that, unless they returned to work 
at once and undertook not again to abuse the check-clerk, I would stop the works in that 
locality ; and, as for getting day’s wages it was contrary to the regulations, and unless they 
choose to work by task everything must cease. 

The country is at present quiet, but the anxiety evinced by all the lower orders to purchase 
arms is so great and so many have done so that any moment might see an outbreak. The 
market still continues high ; sickness is very prevalent. I am of opinion that a letter should 
be sent to the Relief Committees to discourage the practice of giving out meal with an under- 
standing that. the same should be stopped out of the wages at pay-day, as it leaves open a wide 
door for abuse. For example, one poor woman has informed me she got an order for two 
stone of meal, and that the price of two was stopped from her, though only one stone of meal 
was given her husband. 



Extract from Report of Captain Ball, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week ending 
.2nd January, 1847. 

On Wednesday I attended the Committee at Kirlough, and on Friday at Drorahair, at all 
these Committees the business of the day wa3 transacted and the lists investigated, but I am 
'sorry to say that each succeeding day the difficulty increases as to removing from. the lists those 
who have been improperly placed there at first. A few individuals who came forward to give 
information have been.ill-treated or driven from the country ; those who ought to do.it did not, 
from the reason that, in having removed those who -are not indigent, they lose their dues or 
rents, and the employment of the really destitute seems to be set aside. It is on this point 
that unpleasant differences arise between the Inspecting Officer, and the Committees, and the 
total impossibility of arriving at truth almost sets aside the earnest endeavours of myself (and 
I suppose others) to relieve the lists of the comparatively independent. Much distress exists 
throughout these two baronies, and the heavy press and demand for employment prevents the 
.possibility of giving second tickets to large families, who find it almost impracticable to feed 
themselves, at the present enormous price, upon meal and provisions. 

Tiie poor people have been generally peaceably disposed, with the' exception of pilfering 
poultry, &c.

Extract from Journal of Captain J. Bull, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

My time this week has been devoted as much as possible (but four days attending the 
Committees, and Saturday occupied in making out reports, &c., leaves little time for other 
duties) in attempting to suppress the frauds that now exist with regard to the tickets. Every 
possible invention of imposition, forgery, and tampering with the check-clerks have brought 
this evil to such a pitch it is almost impossible to check it, and quite impossible to correct it 
without crreat assistance. I have none. Many persons of the Committees are the very persons 
implicated, and the Committees are so divided among themselves, and their time taken up 
with violent personal altercations, that it is impracticable to get through business or obtain any 
assistance from them. There appears no inclination on the part of the people to cultivate 
their lands. The invariable answer is, ,f they have nothing to put into it,” and a very great 
portion of this mountainous district will not ®row grain. If the Public Works are not 
stopped shortly the land will be left untouched. There is a great preference shown for working 
on roads. 



Extract from Report of Captain Layard, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

I attended the Carregallen Relief Committee on Thursday the 14th, but was obliged to 
leave early in consequence of illness. The registry of this Committee is also uncompleted. 
They have done a great deal during the season in the way of providing meal for the poor. 

Arms have been sold to a great extent in this locality, and the land appears to be neglected. 

I attended the Mohill Relief Committee on Wednesday, 13th instant, and I beg to bring to 
the notice of the Board the fact, that the registry for this Committee is not completed, and I 
cannot succeed in getting it done, I have therefore determined to grant no more issue tickets 
until every man’s name is registered, there were strong representations made at this meeting by 
the landed proprietors and farmers, as to the difficulty of obtaining labourers to till the land. 

I consider in the Relief Committee of Mohill, that the preponderance of the clergymen and 
priests in proportion to other members, is far too great, as, having no stake in the country, they 
are regardless as to the numbers they recommend for employment. The country is quiet. As 
I drove through the country, I observed three or four instances where the lands were being dug 
for cultivation, but it was very partial, I consider it most desirable that a Government Depot 
for corn meal and other provisions should be established in the town of Mohill for the benefit 
of South Leitrim. Arms have been purchased to a great extent by the peasantry in this 
barony, especially on the borders of Longford. 

I beg to state that illness obliges me to have this report written by my clerk. 

The works in this barony are conducted with great regularity, and few, if any, complaints 
ever reach me. Mr. Gisborne informs me that some of the labourers employed on the works 
bordering on the county of Longford, are striving hard to get day’s wages. There are loud 
complaints that improper persons are put upon the works in this barony, but the greatest diffi- 
culty is experienced by myself and the Committee in finding out the improper parties, and I 
cannot but feel that much blame is attributable to some members of this Committee for the 
injudicious and inconsiderate manner in which they bring forward the names of parties for employ- 
ment. The Rev. Mr. Evers, P. P., and Mr. Fanning, P. P., are the parties I allude to. 

I am of opinion that the land which ought to be dug at this time for the oat crop, is being 
very much neglected, and the farmers experience so much difficulty and unwillingness on the 
part of the labourer to go to farm work, that I have thought it expedient to print off 100 of th-‘ 
Board’s Circular, dated 29th October, 1846, for the purpose of distributing them more gene- 
rally through the country.

Extract from Report of Captain Layard. Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, For week

Mr. Famer, P. P. for the parish of Cloone, submitted lists at the commencement of this 
month for the employment of 80 persons on the Auskeet line, 3l of whom were struck off by

A soup shop has been established in this town by private subscription, and the shopkeepers 
and tradesmen of the place have come forward handsomely to support it, and I consider it 
would be a desirable thing that a moiety of the Relief Committee funds should be given in aid 
of it, but the members of tne Relief Committee seem to fear, that by so doing, the Government 
would curtail their donation to the relief funds. As far as my own observations go, the famine 
operations in this barony are not meeting with that attention that they ought. The people in 
the country are most tranquil and patient ; arms are still being sold. 

A soup shop has been established at Ballinamore, but it does not appear to be well conducted. 
Great exertions have been made throughout the season by the Carrigallen Relief Committee, 
in the way of keeping up a constant supply of meal in this locality, and much credit is due to 
the Rev. Mr. H. O’Brien, for the personal risk he has subjected himself to, in obtaining this 
most desirable object by advancing money for the purpose. 



Extract from Report of Captain Bull, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week ending 
23rd January, 1847. 

As I am about to leave this county (according to orders received), I wish to show to the 
Board, what exertions have been made to rouse the Committees to exertions, but without any 
avail. I have taken the liberty of enclosing a circular, I addressed them on two important 
points, they have, however, given no proof of attending to either. 

The price of provisions daily increases, and meal is selling in some of the districts at the high 
price of 3s. 9 d. per stone. 

It is melancholy to observe the declining and haggard appearance of the town class, few of 
them being enabled to afford themselves more than one wretched meal a-day. Their general 
conduct is peaceable. 

However, it is satisfactory to believe, that although great, distress prevails, much sickness, and 
occasional deaths, there have not been instances that could be proved to be caused by actual 
starvation. 

The preference shown for working on the roads, to that oflabouring in the fields, has caused 
me to exert myself much in endeavouring to counteract that, which must bring great ulterior 
injury upon the country. I have not yet seen an instance of a man working upon his own 
land, and I heard it to be a fact, that the people are now consuming for food what they had re- 
served for seed. 

Unless some steps are taken to force the labourers from the works, the consequences must be 
most serious. 

Sir, Manorhamilton, January, 1847- 

In consequence of the pressing demands for additional employment for the poor, upon 
the Public Works, and at the same time, the decreasing state of the monies allowed on the 
different projects, I beg to call the attention of the Committees to the serious consequences 
that are likely to occur, unless some steps are taken to remedy the coming evil, and which must 
affect the community at large. 

1st. I would suggest, that every member of the Committee should exert himself to ascertain 
the circumstances of their tenantry and parishioners, in order that those who are enabled to 
support themselves without assistance from the Relief Works, should be at once removed from 
the lists. 

2nd. That the Committee make it their duty to inquire among their tenants and parishioners, 
whether the aid of labourers is required to cultivate their lands, receiving fair wages, and if so, 
to apply to the Inspecting Officer, who will select the required number from the Works adja- 
cent to their properties or lands ; persons refusing to accept of this employment, will be struck 
off the lists. 

The vast numbers now employed upon the Public Works, are such (and the known fact of 
many being in tolerable and better circumstances) that unless the Inspecting Officer receives

Extract from Report of Captain Layard, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

Deaths from want are in my opinion of daily occurrence in this barony ; the works are near 
finished, and something must be done to find employment. A murder was committed on the 
side of Cloone parish, near Ballinamuck, on Wednesday night, by a party in search of arms. 
The country from this to Carregallen, is in a slight measure presenting patches here and there 
ready for seed. Soup shops have been established at Mohill and Streamstown. The neigh- 
bourhood of Dromod is in a deplorable state, no resident gentry, or clergy, also few, if any, 
Public Works in that locality. Deaths to a fearful extent are daily occurring, and I am of 
opinion that Government should establish a soup shop itself at Dromod, as I see no other way of 
getting one up. 

A pay-clerk of the drainage was robbed miles distant from Ballinamore, on Wednesday, 
at 4 p.m. It would appear that some of the labourers were going home about this time, but I 
cannot find out that they could have prevented it. The soup kitchen which was established 
here proved a failure, and gratuitous issues of bread and meal are given out weekly. Deaths 
are of daily occurrence to a fearful extent, and 1 fear much greater distress will prevail in the hill 
country to the north of Ballinamore. The land is neglected, and some immediate steps should 
be taken to get it under tillage. On the Carrigallen side, especially Aughavass, there is much 
requiring to be done to the land, but in consequence of the number of absentees, there is no 
one of any substance to employ the people. 

. In conjunction with Captain Dent I attended the Carrick-on-Shannon Relief Committee 
and revised lists, but was unable to put more men on ; a resolution was entered into request- 
ing Government to establish a provision depot for South Leitrim, al°o for the sale of seed. It 
is absolutely necessary, but the Government must hold in their own hands the power of selling 
to every one who applies, or else the locality alone in which it is placed will benefit, and not 
the other baronies, all of which I conceive ought to be equally benefited by it. 

The land is very much neglected in this barony ; the people are quiet, but the sale of fire- 
arms is as constant as ever. Distress is on the increase. Soup kitchens have been established 
at Carrick-on-Shannon, but as yet every thing is given out.

Extract from Journal of Captain Farren, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for 
week ending 2nd January, 1847. 

An impression is abroad amongst the people that fair value is not expected for fair wages ; 
it is most difficult to remove this, and I regret to say that remarks made (perhaps with a dif- 
ferent motive) at the presentment sessions this day are, in my opinion, calculated to deepen this 
impression on the minds of the labourers ; when an idle gang is returned for trifling wages, 
though proportionate to the work performed, the engineer is assailed with a torrent of com- 
plaints, and memorials immediately forwarded to the Government. 

On Saturday (this day) I attended the extraordinary presentment sessions for barony of 
Carra, held at Castlebar ; the meeting, after a long discussion, decided upon acting under Mr. 
Labouchere’s letter, and agreed that a sum' equal to the whole poor-law valuation, 56,000/., 
for the employment of the people for three months, should be presented for. After presenting 
sums in each electoral division sufficient for the completion of the unfinished works, the meeting 
adjourned until Monday next, to give the proprietors an opportunity of bringing forward pre" 
sentments for drainage and reproductive works. 

Little signs of agricultural industry can be oberved.

Extract from Report of Lieut. Primrose, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 9th January, 1847. 

On Monday I attended the adjourned extraordinary presentment sessions for the barony of 
Carra, at Castlebar ; 56,000/. the whole poor-law valuation of the barony had been at the pre- 
vious meeting determined on for the relief for the next three months ; very small sums were taken 
for drainage, and the greater part of the remainder for the completion of the roads now in 
progress. 

The works on two roads in the barony of Claremorris, as I reported, were obliged to be sus- 
pended, in consequence of the insubordination of the labourers, who would, on no consideration, 
allow the measurement to proceed, and threatened the overseers in a manner most violent; the 
same thing occurred with two gangs on the road from Clare to Mayo, but of which I made no 
special report. The engineer suspended the work most justly, but in consequence of the distress 
the work is resumed, and the names of the ringleaders cancelled. I have no doubt that a 
memorial relative to this particular case will be forwarded to the Commissioners by a Mr. 
Hughes, the Catholic clergyman of this parish, who disapproves much of the proceeding, 
however little right he may have to interfere ; such an example is absolutely necessary, and 
unless measures of this sort are resorted to, no order or regularity can be observed. 

The country is quiet in this particular part of the district. 

The price of provisions raising daily.

MAYO. As the men, I understood, were in an excited state, I directed the overseer not to accompany

Extract from Journal of Lieut. Primrose, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for the week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

No less than eight different works in the barony of ICilmaine were stopped at the end of this 
week, the money having been expended; in consequence of which about 800 persons have been 
thrown suddenly out of employment. 

No arrangements can be made for a few days to have these persons transferred to other 
works, and consequently great excitement prevails in their localities. 

Notwithstanding the orders of the Board, men seldom if ever commence working till after 
ten a.m., and cease about half past three, aud even during these hours do not accomplish one 
half what might be done. 

Want of energy prevents any exertion, and the feeling seems to have gone abroad they must 
be supported whether they work or not. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Cox, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for the week ending 
16th January, 1847. 

The people here are much excited by the number of processes for rent. There are at present 
between five and six thousand of them brought before the quarter sessions now sitting at 
Ballina. 

In Erris the people appear to be quite dependent on the Government supplies, which are now 
opened at Belmullet. 

I am afraid that destitution is very much on the increase in this part of the county. There 
are a great number of deaths, and the coroner’s inquests are numerous. I think that many, if 
not caused by actual starvation, are the result of diseases produced or hastened by an insuffi- 
cient supply of food, but the people are too much inclined to attribute more deaths to this cause 
than is really the case.

Extract from Report of Captain Stirling, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, [for week 
ending 16th January, 1847. 

Observed on the different main roads during the past week considerable numbers of people, 
men, women, and children, proceeding to the coast for the purpose of going to England and

Extract from Report of Captain Farr.en, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week ending 
16th January, 1847. 

With regard to agricultural operations I have observed a few labourers in the fields, but 
little preparation, however, appears to be making for the future; all throw themselves upon the 
Public Works. 

The disinclination to work still exists, inability from an insufficiency of food being given by 
them as an excuse ; in some instances the labourers imagine they will not be paid according 
to their exertions, and complain of a want of tools ; there is however no doubt that making 
every allowance for the former and latter causes, a far greater quantity of work could be per- 
formed than has hitherto been done. Threats relative to the weekly ratings have been made 
to the overseers and check-clerks, and secret intimidation resorted to.

Extract from Report of Lieut. Primrose, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

Under existing circumstances, and taking iuto consideration the great want of tools in every 
part of the district under my charge, the works are progressing as well as can be expected; 
and on some roads much more than the average rate of wages has been earned. In one part 
of the barony Is. 4 d. per diem seemed a common sum, and on one road the last payment 
amounted to Is. 7d., of course adding one-fourth stopped as a clearance. 

Great discontent exists amongst the labourers as to their mode of payment, that is in the 
disparity in amount for some weeks some gangs being retained for much more than others • 
and it is much to be feared the class of men employed as overseers, although in most cases quite 
competent, are not entirely above bribery, and will show favour to particular parties, and yet 
it is impossible to accuse any of them directly of such a proceeding, however much inclined we 
may be to stop such an abuse. 

The country is quiet. The example made by the suspension of some of the roads for insub- 
ordination has had a wonderfully good effect. 

A little is going on in the farming operations, but most of the small holders are nevlectin» 
everything, and eating the seed which should be saved for the next year. 



Extract from Report of Captain Farren, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 23rd January, 1847. 

It has been stated to me that gentlemen and farmers requiring men to work on their lands, 
(although aware that if required the labourers must go to them and will be struck off the list 
if they refuse,) will not employ them, knowing their preference for the Public Works, and that 
they will not give fair value. 

I have not remarked any increased signs of agricultural industry, little if any preparation 
appears to be making for the ensuing season, the lands are almost neglected. 

The state of the district generally is peaceable, an inclination to plunder meal carts in one 
portion of it excepted. 



Extract from Report of Captain Carey, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week ending 
23rd January, 1847. 

An occasional woman or child is all that is to be seen at work in the fields, yet on every visit 
to a district I see fresh earth turned up, and, I believe, as much preparation for the coming 
crops to have been made as is usual in this county. The disposition to outrage, interference 
with traffic, prevalent a short time ago, seems to have passed away for the present, and escorts 
are certainly not required now, where a fortnight ago they would have been indispensable; 
there is but little difference in some of the Relief Committees since the first commencement, 
the lists of applicants being still brought forward by individuals not taken from any scrutinized 
registers.

I have succeeded in striking off this week the names of improper persons who were employed 
on the works. 

I do not think any vessel is safe at anchor in the bay. The people are afraid to move meal

Extract from Report of Captain Carey, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week ending 
30th January, 1847. 

General misconduct on the part of the labourers in the parish of Kilgane has been reported 
to me this afternoon ; to stop all the roads on which complaints are made would throw an un- 
precedently large number of persons idle, in a district where there are but few police, and no 
other restraint of any sort. 

It appears that the men on one particular road were offensive this day to the assistant 
engineer on his way into this town to report to me. I have, therefore, suspended this till 
further inquiries can be made. This will be known generally to-morrow (Sunday), and will, I 
hope, be sufficient. 

The men in this district are in large numbers on the same road, and appear to have deter- 
mined not to work by task, which wiu, of course, be enforced. This district is most unfortu- 
nate, it has no resident gentry whatever, and its Committee does not deserve the name; it is 
said that a report, that they are to be fed for nothing, has been circulated amongst them with 
injurious effect during the last few days. 

The proportion of able-bodied men employed on the works seems to get smaller and smaller 
every day. Husbands and fathers go constantly to England and Scotland, leaving their fami- 
lies behind them. The great mass of persons labouring consists, therefore, of old men, women, 
and children ; they nevertheless receive on an average, including the balances, about 1 lcf. 
when tasks are regularly carried out. I find the wages run rather nigh.

Extract from Report of Captain Farren, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

Since the letting of tasks by the assistant engineer the quantity of work done on the different 
roads has increased, though in many cases it does not equal the amount which with ordinarv 
exertion might be performed, making every allowance for insufficiency of food, &c.; one great 
cause is the short period the labourers remain on the works; it is most difficult, from the great 
number of overseers and check-clerks required for the works, to obtain persons for these situa- 
tions who will do their duty and check the men when absent or late. Intimidation and it 
is not improbable, bribery, and every other means except the legitimate one (individual exer- 
tion at the task itself) are resorted to by the labourers to obtain their end — high wages, which 
as their distress is great, they undoubtedly require, and could obtain, as the contract prices' 
are all framed on the most liberal scale. 

Some of the labourers on another line, Clooner to Killavalla, were engaged in the robbery 
of a meal-cart ; three gangs have been suspended in consequence of this affair, a special report 
of which will be forwarded by this post for the 'information of the Commissioners. 

Farm operations are iu progress to a very limited extent; great apathy prevails in this 
respect, coupled, however, with an impression that Government will employ the people on their 
own lands, and pay them for it. 



Extract from a Report of Lieut. Cox, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week ending 
30th January, 1847- 

There is still no appearance of any farming operations. Wheat has not been produced in 
this part of the country at any time, and, of course, none could be expected to be sown this 
year; but, I regret to say, the usual crops are also neglected. I think there is more oats in 
the haggards than I was at first led to suppose ; though very many are without any at all, still 
there are a number of persons who have much more than they could possibly require for seed, 
and who have been keeping it back up to the present period, in the hope that prices would still 
continue to rise. 

The destitution is very great, and as employment increases the demand for it appears to 
increase also. 



Extract from Report of Captain Burmester, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, fcr 
week ending 2nd January, 1847. 

There have been several instances of sheep and cattle stealing in various places. The pay- 
ments of the men are becoming more regular ; with regard to farming operations little or 
nothing is doing on my road from Roscommon to Frenchpark ; on the 30th, a distance of nearly 
-0 miles I saw but one man at work in the fields. The whole of the labouring population is 
pressing on the works. I have reason to believe that a very considerable quantity of potatoes 
still remains in this country,, having been preserved for seed. I have heard of several persons 
who have saved some, and instances of their being seen in the markets are not unfrequent. I 
saw four men digging a field of them near Knockview Bridge on the morning of the 2nd; some 
of them were of fair size, and the whole perfectly sound. 

Extract from Report of Major Donald Stewart, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, 
for week ending 2nd January, 1847. 

Much inconvenience arises from the practice pursued by some Committees of sending to the 
inspecting officer long lists of people requiring relief, without waiting for the intimation of the 
number of people required for the particular works, who are consequently liable to be put on 
works at a distance from their abodes. The same result is occasioned by the drafting of men 
from one work to another by the engineers. 

Extract from Report of Captain Burmester, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for

Extract from Retort of Lieut. Wethered, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for

The state of this district is tranquil, no outrage of a serious nature having come to my know- 
ledge beyond robberies of sheep. The sale of arms is very extensive, several walking-stick 
guns have been sold in this town. The description of persons who principally purchase them 
are small farmers, though I have known them purchased by men whose families were starving 
The labourers on the Relief Works conduct themselves orderly. The Committees, generally 
speaking, transact their business very indifferently ; they generally depend on oue working 
member; where they are deficient of a person, which is the case in the Strokestown and Clon- 
furlough Committees, no business is transacted. All the Committees are now occupied 
revising their lists. 

At the extraordinary sessions held for the barony of Roscommon at Strokestown, which 
lasted four days, there was much argument, which is universally the case at all meetings held 
in that town. 

The distress of the people is on the increase, provision having reached such a fearful price, 
meal selling in Roscommon market this day at 1Z. 7 s. 6 d. per cwt., and from 3s. 6tZ. to 3s. 7 d. 
per stone ; numbers are dying daily from want. A soup shop has been established in this 
town, which has given great relief.

Baronies of Tirerill, Coolevin, Corran, and Carlury.

the labourers. Provisions are rising in price daily. 



Extract from Report of Captain Gilbert, Inspecting Officer, County Sligo, for week 
ending 30th January, 1847. 

Great complaints from the labourers on all the roads of the high price of provisions, and that 
their daily earnings, even by measurement or task-work, are not sufficient to support themselves 
or families. In general, the people are so reduced and weak that they cannot perform a good 
day’s work. The works progress as well as can be expected. 

Very great distress in the town and immediate neighbourhood of Sligo. Fever very prevalent, 
and many deaths daily, particularly in the Union, and 400 are now ill in fever.

ments, so that the loan shall be paid off within the period originally specified. 



Commissioners of Public Works to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works , Dublin, 

January 21, 1847. 

We beg to state, for the information of the Lords Commissioners of Her 
Majesty’s Treasury, that owing to the great increase of applications for main 
drainage of districts and thorough drainage of the properties of individuals under 
the General Drainage and Loan Acts, it becomes absolutely necessary to have 
increased assistance in Dublin to manage the engineering and valuation details. 

It was at first thought that the services of Mr. Smith of Deanston, or some 
other agricultural engineer, could have been obtained on reasonable terms for 
this purpose ; but upon consideration of the whole matter, we find that tliis 
arrangement, even if effected, would not suffice for the objects required, now 
that the mass of this class of business is greatly increased and likely to increase 
to a still greater extent. 

For this service we require the whole time of an able assistant, well acquainted 
with drainage operations, the whole details of the law in relation thereto, and 
such a general knowledge of Ireland, and the relations of landlord and tenant 
therein, as will facilitate his operations and prevent the numerous errors which 
a person wanting this knowledge would be almost certain to fall into, if suddenly 
called upon to enter into the details of such a mass of business. 

In addition to those important and more immediately pressing duties, we 
require that such assistant should be at the head of the department of valua- 
tions connected with the drainage of lands, to examine and revise the reports of 
the local valuators (upon which depends the security for monies advanced), and 
the assessment for the expenditure. His aid ■will be constantly required in the 
purchase of lands and premises, the adjustment of questions of compensation, in 
[b. w. 2.] T 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




130 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



the preparation of the engineering and valuation details of the numerous awards 
under these Acts, and in the still more difficult and delicate duty of assisting us 
in fixing the amount of increased rents to he paid by the tenants of the drained 
lands. 

Considering the duties of such an officer, the fact that they may be expected 
to extend over many years, the necessity that his whole time should be devoted 
to the service, and that, to be perfectly impartial, he should hold an independent 
position as an officer of this Board, without being allowed to take private busi- 
ness, we recommend that he should be paid by the Government at the rate of 
800/. per annum. 

All the officers of every class, locally comiected with the Drainage Works, 
either as regards their execution, payment, or supervision, are paid out of the 
funds provided for the works, and we do not propose in any way to trench on 
this wholesome arrangement ; but for the duties herein referred to, so variable 
in their nature and having reference to numerous Acts of Parliament, we feel it 
would be impracticable to attempt any apportionment of the salary of such an 
officer over the various measures, and are, therefore, led to submit the propo- 
sition that he should be paid as an officer of the establishment. 

For this service we recommend to their Lordships Mr. Robert Harding, who 
has, after many years’ experience in the valuation of Ireland, been now, for more 
than six years, connected with the Shamion Navigation and Drainage Depart- 
ments of the Board, in both of which he has most ably and zealously discharged 
precisely similar duties to those we now require. 

In these capacities and in the making of valuations for the Board by contracts 
in various parts of Ireland, he has been, and, if not appointed to the office now 
proposed, will probably continue to be in the receipt of a much larger income ; 
and we conceive his professional knowledge as an engineer and valuator entitles 
him to our recommendation of this amount of salary. 

This officer will require a suitable office, and, during the present emergency, 
several clerks having a knowledge of plans and calculations, under him. 

We look to the immediate establishment of a suitable system and arrangement 
of this heavy and important business as indispensable to the success of our pro- 
ceedings and those contemplated by their Lordships, as to advances for perma- 
nent improvement of land. 

We have evidence that the Irish landlords are prepared to avail themselves of 
the facilities offered for drainage, and deem it essential to meet the pressure that 
our arrangements be completed without delay. 



Treasury Minute on the above. 

February 9, 1847. 

Write to the Commissioners of Public Works that their Lordships are pleased, 
in compliance with their recommendation, to appoint Mr. Robert Harding to be 
their assistant for the execution of the duties adverted to in their letter, and of 
any others which they may think proper from time to time to assign to him. 

Mr. Harding’s salary will be at the rate of 800/. a year, to commence from the 
present date, and it will be provided for and paid in the same manner as the 
salaries of the other officers on the fixed establishment of the Board of Works. 

Their Lordships desire that written instructions may be furnished to Mr. 
Harding for his guidance in the several duties entrusted to him, and especially 
in respect to preliminary proceedings comiected with the adjustment of questions 
between landlords and tenants, and that copies of these instructions may be 
submitted to this Board.
