Mr. Redington to the Commissioners of Public Works. 

Dublin Castle, January 14, 1847. 

Adverting to your minute of the 8th instant on the report of the inspecting officer at 
Ennis, I am directed by the Lord Lieutenant to acquaint you that his Excellency considers it 
to have been a judicious course, under the circumstances, to have given to Mr. Petty the pro- 
tection referred to. 

It is not, however, possible to give constabulary protection to every officer engaged on Public 
Works, however anxious and desirous his Excellency may be to afford it to them in an ample 
manner, and his Excellency, therefore, considers the course adopted on this occasion by the 
inspecting officer to have been necessarily required. 



Captain Wynne to Mr. Walker. 

Emis, January 3, 1847. 

I have the honour to state, for the information of the Board, that in consequence of the 
extent to which intimidation is at present carried in the barony of Inchequin, in this district, 
Mr. Petty, local engineer, waited on me this day to state his inability to exercise any super- 
vision over the Public Works, unless under the protection of a police force. 

I immediately waited on Captain Leyne, R.M., and was informed by him that in the parish 
of Kilkeedy, where protection is most required, there is not a slated house to be had for the 
accommodation of police, and that Government require such in all cases. 

At present the overseers and stewards are quite at the mercy (both day and night) of the 
workmen, having neither arms nor other means of protection ; and as it is well known that the 
outrage on Harrington was not committed on him in consequence of any part of his conduct 
(which has been uniformly considerate and humane), but merely as a warning to others in his 
situation not in any way to interfere with the labourers, they (one and all) expect the same fate, 
if not protected. 

I should say that Mr. Petty is not a man easily intimidated. He is a most resolute voung 
man, and determined to discharge his duty under any circumstances ; but considering it unfair 
to expose him to almost certain destruction, Mr. Gamble and I think it our duly to allow him 
the protection of a person chosen by himself till such time as some other arrangement be 
made. 

With regard to the outrage on Mr. Harrington, I have no doubt of our being able to discover 
the perpetrators, provided we receive the zealous co-operation of the magistracy; and I would 
strongly recommend that the works in the locality remain suspended till such time as this most 
desirable object be attained. The consequences may be trying ; but we should be prepared to 
meet them. The offenders are well known, and we are not far from the knowledge of them. 



Treasury Minute on the above. 

January 26, 1847. 

Write to the Commissioners of Public Works that their Lordships entirely 
approve of the course adopted by Captain Wynne under the circumstances stated, 
and it is their wish that in cases in which escorts cannot be furnished by the 
constabulary, the Commissioners should take such other steps as may be neces- 
sary for the safety of the persons employed under them. 



To the Right Honourable the Lords of the Treasury. 

The Memorial of the Kinsale Relief Committee, 

Sheweth, 

That at the Special Sessions held in this town under the Labour Rate 
Act, the assembled rate-payers agreed to tax themselves to the amount of 7,000?., 
in order to afford employment to the starving labourers of the barony, there 
being nearly 1300 applicants for relief within its compass. 

That the Board of Works ordered roads to the amount of 2,800?. of the sum 
presented to be forthwith commenced, thereby affording employment to about 
700 persons, and leaving nearly 600, with their families, totally destitute. 

That this small sum is now nearly exhausted, and that memorialists look 
forward with horror to the consequences likely to ensue, so soon as the small 
balance of money remaining in the engineer’s hands shall have been disposed of. 

That to obviate this state of things, memorialists have repeatedly urged on 
the Board the propriety of forthwith commencing certain reproductive works, 
calculated to be of immense utility to this locality, and that hitherto all their 
remonstrances have been neglected and their applications treated with the most 
marked indifference. 

T 2 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




132 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



That the works so applied for consist of the approach and earthworks of a 
bridge, which it is intended to erect across the Bandon river, to facilitate the 
intercourse of a large and important agricultural district with the town of 
Kinsale. 

A presentment to fill certain docks in the town of Kinsale, thereby very much 
improving the town, and having a tendency to promote the health and well-being 
of the inhabitants. 

A presentment for two piers, in dangerous and exposed situations, two-thirds 
of the expense to be borne by the Fishery Board, works likely to confer great 
advantages on those engaged in the sea fisheries, at a comparatively small expense 
to the rate-payers, Kinsale being one of the most important fishing stations in 
Ireland, the great mass of the population depending for sustenance on the produce 
of the sea. 

That under these circumstances memorialists see that they have no resource 
left but in appealing to your Lordships, with the hope that you may direct the 
Board in Dublin forthwith to order these works to be commenced, and save 
memorialists from the necessity of calling a second special sessions, and raising 
money to construct roads through a barony already intersected by them in every 
direction. 

That the workhouse of this Union is now occupied by nearly double the 
number of paupers which it was originally built to accommodate, notwithstanding 
which the streets and public roads are crowded with a squalid and hungry popu- 
lation, miserable, dejected, and scarcely able to crawl along for want of food. 

That memorialists earnestly appeal to your Lordships to take these premises, 
without delay, into your most serious consideration, thereby mitigating the 
almost intolerable miseries of the naked and starving poor, and preventing them 
from being driven by dire necessity, into acts of violence and insubordination. 

And memorialists will pray. 

J. T. Heard, Chairman. 

Kinsale , January 22, 1847.

to be required, and report their proceedings to this Board. 

Acquaint Mr. Heard. 



Mr. Redington to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Dublin Castle , January 22, 1847. 

With reference to the last paragraph of the letter to the Treasury of 
the 24th ultimo, forwarding the miscellaneous estimates for the year ending 
the 31st March, 1848, I am directed by the Lord Lieutenant to transmit, for 
the information of the Lords of the Treasury, the enclosed ^statement of the 
Managing Committee of the Cork Street Fever Hospital, with the report 
thereon of the General Board of Health, dated the 15th instant. Looking to 
the last paragraph of this report, his Excellency considers that a due regard to 
public health, imperatively requires that this institution should be provided 
with the means of meeting promptly (as in former instances has been the 
case) the calls that must inevitably be made upon it, should the apprehended 
infliction of epidemic disease fall on this city. 

Their Lordships are aware, that on the recommendation of the Managing 
Committee, the vote for the Cork Street Fever Hospital was, in 1843 — 44, re- 
duced from 3,800Z. to 3,000Z. The experience of the last four years has shown 
that the reduced votes since the above date, have not furnished sufficient funds 
to meet what may almost be considered the ordinary calls upon the institution. 
His Excellency, therefore, has no hesitation in recommending that the vote 
should be 3,800Z., the amount previous to its reduction, and that to the vote 
for the year ending the 31st March, 1848, there should be a further addition 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



133 

of 1,200/. to make up" the amount short issued since 1844, as shown in the 
accompanying memorandum. 

As by the issue of the 600/. applied for to their Lordships on the 16 th 
instant, the vote for the current year will have been exhausted, his Excellency 
proposes that to meet the expenses to the 31st March next, (which have been 
estimated at 1,300/.), 1,200/. on account of the vote for the ensuing year, should 
he advanced from civil contingencies, to he repaid on the passing of the vote. 

Their Lordships will perceive that the foregoing proposition provides only 
for freeing the institution from the difficulty in which it is now placed from 
want of funds, that it may thereby he prepared to meet the calls upon it, in 
the event of epidemic disease. 

His Excellency is unwilling to propose any addition to what has been the 
usual amount of the Parliamentary grant, considering that, as heretofore, funds 
should be specially provided to meet the apprehended contingency, should it 
unfortunately arise. 



Enclosure. 

Report. 

The explanation of the Managing Committee of the Fever Hospital in Cork Street 
having been fully inquired into, it is submitted for his Excellency’s information, that the state- 
ments therein contained are in every respect correct. 

There, is a considerable increase in the number of patients received into that hospital. Their 
diseases are generally of a very debilitating description, either more, fatal than is usual, or pro- 
ducing tedious convalesance, during which a diet comparatively expensive is indispensable to 
promote recovery, and prevent relapse. 

The accounts of the hospital are kept with great exactness, under the superintendence of ex- 
perienced and judicious managers, well acquainted with the details of business, who devote their 
time, at regular weekly or even more frequent intervals, to the inspection of the concerns of this 
establishment, and to controlling the expenditure. 

At no period of time did this institution manifest a stronger claim to public support than at 
present, when the country is threatened with the invasion of epidemic disease, and is suffering 
from a scarcity of food, nearly, if not altogether without precedent. 

General Board of Health, Fras. Barker, M. D., Secretary. 

15 th January, 1847. 

Fever Hospital, Cork Street, 

Sir, 31rf December, 1846. 

I am directed by the Managing Committee of this Institution, to acknowledge the 
receipt of your letter of the 22nd instant, requesting that his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant 
may be furnished with a full statement of the causes of the expenditure of the current year 
being so much in excess, and also stating that similar information will be necessary in regard to 
the contemplated expenditure for the ensuing year. 

In reply, the Managing Committee beg to submit for the information of his Excellency, the 
following statement of the numbers in the hospital for the preceding three years, as contrasted 
with those for the current year, and particularly to draw his Excellency’s attention to the in- 
creased pressure upon the hospital for the last three months, which they see no reason to expect 
will relax for the ensuing year. 

The high prices of provisions will also increase very materially the expenses of the hospital, 
to which the Committee may add, that from a communication lately received from their physi- 
cians, it appears that " the fever of the present year, complicated as it often is with dysentery 
and heavy chest affections, beiug altogether of a lower character, requires a longer period of 
sojourn in the convalescent department, and a more supporting diet,” a fact which will render 
the maintenance of patients in the hospital more than usually expensive. With respect to the 
grant of 99 5 Z. alluded to in your letter, the Committee direct me to observe that this sum was 
to clear off a debt incurred by the previous deficiency of income, and that the additional sum of 
1,300Z. now required to carry on the institution till the 31st of March, has been calculated on 
the experience of the last three months. 

I am further directed to state, that on this day there being 27 applicants for admission, and 
only four vacant beds ill the fever department, the Committee have desired four tents to be 
erected for the accommodation of patients, as has been usual in similar cases. 

I have, &c., 

James Montgomery, Registrar.

Treasury Minute on the above. 

February 9, 1847. 

Write to the Paymaster of Civil Services in Ireland, desiring that he will take 
the necessary steps for the recovery of the sums advanced under the Act of 
9 Vic., c. 2, in the manner directed in each letter authorising these advances, 
respectively, namely, the sum advanced in each case to be repaid by the number 
of instalments specified in each letter, the first instalment to be presented for at 
the Spring Assizes, 1847, and so continued half yearly till the whole advance, 
with interest on the sum outstanding is repaid ; but my Lords desire that the 
interest claimed on the sum outstanding shall be calculated at the rate of 4 per 
cent, per annum, instead of 5 per cent., as directed in the letters. 

With respect to the balance of 4,309/. 9s. 7d., which remains in his hands of 
the sum advanced under the Acts of 9 Vic., c. 2 and 78, desire that unless he 
should be aware of any further demands upon the same, he will transfer the 
sum to the account of the Consolidated Fund.

January 26, 1847 

Write to the Secretary for Ireland, and, referring to the intention of 
Her Majesty’s Government to propose to Parliament that a sum of 50,000/. 
should he appropriated for making loans, repayable after next harvest, to landed 
proprietors in Ireland, for the purpose of assisting them to furnish necessary

Commissioners of Public Works to the Lords of the Treasury. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin, 
January 28, 1847. 

We have had under consideration an application from H. Courtenay, Esq., 
for a loan, under the Act of 9th and 10th Viet., c. 101, of 550/., to enable him 
to thorough drain 115 acres of land, his property, in the barony of Upper 
Iveagh, county of Down. 

An examination has been made of the lands by an experienced surveyor, com- 
missioned for that purpose, who has reported favourably on the proposed 
improvements. 

We are satisfied, after having duly considered the report of the surveyor, that 
the benefits to be derived from the projected works of drainage, on the lands to 
be charged, will enable the proprietor to repay the instalment of 6^ per cent, 
per annum, pursuant to the Act, for a period of- 22 years, as well as the cost for 
inspections durmg the progress of the work. 

We, therefore, in accordance with the terms of the 17-th section of the Act 
before mentioned, request your Lordships’ sanction to our issuing a provisional 
certificate to Mr. Courtenay when the time prescribed by the Act for so doing 
shall have arrived •, the loan to be issued in three instalments of amounts pro- 
portioned to the extent of work that shall have been executed ; and the cost of 
inspection, during the progress of the work, to be added to the amoutit of the 
loan, instead of being immediately paid by the proprietor. 



Treasury Minute on the above. 

• February 2, 1847. 

Authorise the Commissioners of Drainage to issue a provisional certificate, 
approving of this work in the form required by 17th section of the Act 9th and 
10th Viet., c. 101. 



Mr. Walker to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin , 
January 20, 1847- 

I am directed by the Commissioners to request you will bring under the 
notice of the Lords Commissioners of Her Majesty’s Treasury the present state 
of the negotiation lor executing the earth-works of the Limerick and Waterford 
Railway, in several baronies which have presented for the same as a Relief 
Work at extraordinary presentment sessions. 

The baronies in question are Iffa and Offa East, and Iffa and Offa West ; 
and Clanwilliam, in the county of Tipperary ; and Iverk, in the county of 
Kilkenny.

Previous to recommending the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury to 
sanction the above works, the Board, in the exercise of their prescribed duty, 
proceeded to ascertain whether and to what extent the Commissioners’ printed 
memorandum, which was circulated for the consideration, of presentment 
sessions in baronies desirous of presenting for the construction of railways, for 
which Acts of Parliament have been obtained, under the 9 and 10 Vic., cap. 
107, had been complied with, viz. — 



1st. That the Company be actually in possession of the land through 
which the railway is to pass, or that security for their becoming so 
be given before the works begin, so that no after payment or debt 
whatever for purchase, compensation, or damages may remain charge- 
able on the barony beyond the amount of their presentment. 

2nd. That the Company give or undertake to give security to the barony 
for the due half-yearly repayment of the advances with interest. 

3rd. That the barony should not present for any work which cannot be 
completed by August next. 



For this purpose the Commissioners directed a general inspector of works, 
Captain D. O’Brien, to visit the district, and to report fully on these points. 

Subjoined are that officer’s report and correspondence. 

From these it will be seen that the formal consents of the proprietors, lessees, 
and occupiers of the land to the Railway Company taking possession, have only 
been obtained in the barony of Iffa and Offa West, and these consents but in 
respect of two portions or blocks, so to speak, of the line, of inconsiderable 
lengths divided from each other by an extensive deviation for which as yet no 
Act of Parliament has been obtained, though the Company are now before 
Parliament for that purpose. 

Their Lordships will observe that the Commissioners directed inquiry to be 
made as to lock-spitting the line, and will perceive that this operation has been 
but partially performed. 

If the line actually to be constructed by the Company had been continuous 
through the barony of Iffa and Offa West, without any important deviation 
from that which had been sanctioned by the Legislature, the Commissioners 
were prepared to waive the question of lock-spitting beyond the central line of 
general direction; but inasmuch as the portions of the railway about to be con- 
structed in this barony, according to the Parliamentary plan, are inconsiderable 
and detached from each other, the Commissioners have reluctantly delayed 
requesting their Lordships’ sanction to the earth-work to be done by relief labour 
being commenced until the further proceedings now in progress of the Company 
in the adjacent baronies should permit of a greater extent of line being made 
available for the purpose. . . 

Their Lordships’ instructions having precluded the Commissioners Irom 
taking into consideration the deviated part of the line, it was not in their power 
to treat the intended railway through the barony as a whole, though pressed to 
do so by the Vice Lieutenant of the county and the Railway Company, ana. 
consequently they have been obliged to regard the portions of the line in. Iffa 
and Offa West, in reference to the portions in Iffa and Offa East, and m Clan- 
william. . , , 

With respect to the second condition, touching the security to the barony by 
the Railway Company, a deed has been prepared, and a draft thereof submitted 
to the Attorney-General, who appears to have perused and amended it ; so that 
the Commissioners conclude he was satisfied it was sufficient, when executed by 
the Company, to indemnify the baronies from the payment of the instalments m 



the presentments. . 

As regards the 3rd condition, the arrangements made by the 
[b. w. 2.] 



Commissioners 

U 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




138 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



would, in their opinion, prevent the earth-works being carried on by relief labour 
beyond the month of August next, should it be found necessary to stop them at 
that period. . 

At the present moment, therefore, the full sanction of the Commissioners only 
awaits proof on the part of the Company that they are in possession of the land 
in the baronies through which the line passed, bordering on Iffa and Offa West, 
or at least of such unbroken lengths as would justify the Commissioners’ sanc- 
tion. They are in correspondence with the Company on this point, and they 
are informed that very shortly the required proofs will be adduced. 

Before concluding, however, the Commissioners desire to bring under their 
Lordships’ notice the question as relates to the deviated line, for which the 
Company are now before Parliament ; and this opens the important general 
question, whether their Lordships would empower the Commissioners gene- 
rally, or in part, according to their discretion, to sanction presentments for earth- 
work where — 

] st. The line is inconsiderably deviated, and still runs in the general direc- 
tion of the original line, without partaking in any way of the character 
of a branch or extension line, and commencing and terminating at 
points of junction with the Parliamentary line, intended bond jide to 
be constructed by the Company ; and 

2nd. Where the Company are either in possession of the land required for 
the deviated line by purchase, or have entered into arrangements with 
the landowners, lessees, and occupiers for that purpose, which arrange- 
ments may, in the opinion of the Commissioners, be considered equiva- 
lent to having obtained possession. 

The Commissioners have this question now practically before them for the 
first time. 

Under their present instruction they believe that they are bound to exclude 
such a case from their consideration, but if their Lordships should be of opinion 
that a difference may be made between an original line, or a branch line, or ex- 
tension, for which no Act has been obtained, and a line only deviated in small 
degree as before described, they pray their Lordships may be pleased to give 
them definite instructions for their future guidance.

Waterford , January 2, 1847. 

I beg to report, for the information of the Commissioners, that in pursuance of their 
instructions, under date 30th ult., I arrived last night in this place, and placed myself in com- 
munication with the chairman, directors, and secretary of the Waterford and Limerick Railway 
Company this morning. After discussing the subject matter of my mission, I placed in their 
hands a letter (a copy of which I herewith transmit), which embodied the inquiries I am en-

I am about to proceed in the course of the afternoon to Carrick-on-Suir, and from thence to 
Cahir. 

I will again communicate with the Commissioners from Cahir or from Clonmel. 



Captain O’Brien to Mr. Saunders. 

Waterford, January 2, 1847 . 

I beg to enclose for your information a copy of a letter of instructions, addressed to me 
by the Commissioners of Public Works in Ireland. 

You will perceive that my attention is solely directed to the land which you are empowered 
to take, compulsory under your Act of Incorporation. 

With respect to the agreements which have been entered into between the Railway Company 
and the owners, lessees, and occupiers being duly completed in the baronies alluded to, viz., 
Iverk, Iffa and Offa East, Iffa and Offa West, and Clanwilliam, I beg to be informed, — - 

1st. If agreements have Oeen entered into with all the owners, lessees, and occupiers, as above 
stated, in each of the baronies respectively ? 

2nd. If agreements have not been entered into with all the owners, lessees, and ocoupiers in

each of the baronies referred to ; then, I desire to be informed as to how many of the owners’ 
lessees, and occupiers in each barony have agreed to give possession of their land to the Com- 
pany, and how many have up to this date not done so? At the same time I should be glad to

Mr. Saundehs to Captain O’Brien. 

Waterford, January 2, 1847. 

I have the pleasure to acknowledge your favour of this date, enclosing copy of a letter 
of instructions addressed to you by the Board of Works, in which you request information on 
certain points to which your attention has been called respecting the presentments for the earth- 
works of this railway in the baronies of Iverk, Iffa and Offa East, Iffa and Offa West, and 
Clanwilliam, and will proceed to reply to each interrogatory in order. 

First, with respect to the agreements. I am informed by the solicitors employed for the 
purpose of obtaining the consents of parties interested in the lands, that in Iffa and Offa West 
all the consents have been obtained, both for the Parliamentary line and' deviation ; but as you 
inform me you are precluded from inquiry as to the deviation, it will be confined only to a very 
small proportion of the whole, about two miles. In Offa and Offa East, I am also informed that 
all the consents on the Parliamentary line, with one exception (Mr. Power, occupier of Ballydine), 
have also been given. In Iverk 1 am not prepared to state how many have consented, but I 
believe a very large majority ; and in Clanwilliam there are one or two dissentients, whose con- 
sents, however, we have the hope of obtaining in a few days. 

I propose, however, accompanying you to the engineer’s offices at Carrick and Caher, where 
we can obtain the maps of the line as it is correctly laid out, and then, by comparing it with the 
Book of Reference, it will be easy to ascertain the exact particulars you require. 

I will prepare immediately lists of all the parties interested in the land, in compliance with 
the terms of your request, and forward them to you as soon as completed. 

With respect to the lock-spitting of the line, I beg to inform you that, in consequence of a 
former communication from the Board of Works, I have already given instructions to the engi- 
neers to proceed as rapidly as possible to do so ; but I may be allowed to observe, that it is a 
matter which requires to be done with great care and exactitude, inasmuch as the outside lock- 
spitting indicates the quantities of land we propose taking ; and any slight error exposes the 
Company to great expense and interminable disputes with the occupiers and owners, particularly 
if too little be taken in the first instance. I would also take the liberty of suggesting that the 
lock-spitting of the line is not generally considered a proof of possession, as it is always done 
before we even treat with the owners ; and I humbly submit that the consents, when authenti- 
cated by your inquiry, will be best proof of the transfer of interest to the Company. 

The centre line has been lock-spitted throughout, with a slight exception.

Mr. Redington to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Dublin Castle , February 6, 1847. 

I am directed by the Lord Lieutenant to transmit, for the consideration 
of the Lords of the Treasury, the enclosed memorial of the magistrates and cess- 
payers of the barony of Bere, county of Cork, on the subject of the advancement 
of county cess. 



Enclosure. 

To His Excellency the Earl of Bessborough, Lord Lieutenant General and General Governor 
of Ireland. 

The Memorial of the Magistrates and Cess-payers of the Barony of Bere, assembled at 
JNeenmeen (Glengamff), in said Barony, on the 8th January, 1847, 

Respectfully sheweth. 

That memorialists beg respectfully to state to your Excellency, that from the great 
distress which prevails in this barony, where the landholders and occupiers are obliged to turn 
to the purposes of procuring food not only their earnings on the Public Works, but such of their 
ettects m cattle, &c., as they can get sale for, the subject of the collection of the county rates 
has occupied the serious attention of memorialists ; and from a communication had from the 
treasurer of this county,, it appears that the difficulty, if not the impossibility, of collecting the 
county rates for next assizes has also engaged his serious consideration. 

From what memorialists know of the state of destitution to which the occupiers of the land 
m this remote and densely populated barony are reduced, they give it as their conviction that 
the difficulty of collecting the levy of last assizes will be extreme, and they believe it will he 
impossible to collect those rates not only in this barony but in the western part of the county; 
your memorialists, therefore, respectfully suggest to your Excellency to order that the amount 
ot the levy oflast. summer assizes should be advanced by the Lords of the Treasury. It was 
so done in the year 1822; but your memorialists do not give this precedent with a view of 
impressing on your Excellency the act of the then Government at a period of scarcity, as they 
are tully satisfied that your Excellency has at heart every thing tending to meet the wishes and 
wants ot your countrymen in these awful times of destitution and famine.

grant the indulgence contained in this their respectful petition ; for which, as in duty bound thev

Captain O’Brien to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Dublin, February 9, 1847. 

On the 28th I was again en route, having received instructions from 
the Board of Works to proceed into Wexford, and afterwards into Waterford 
counties, in the execution of certain duties which were entrusted to me. 

My observations and enquiries were directed to the cultivation of the land 
through which I passed ; and again I find myself differing in opinion with 
many of the inspecting officers as to the extent of land under cultivation. 

In spade-husbandry nothing appears to be doing ; but so far as I saw in the 
general tillage of the ground, so as to supply food for the future, by sowing wheat, 
and preparing for oats, barley, and rye, much more is being done by ploughing 
now than in previous years. 

Between Carlow and Tullow, about eight miles, I counted eight ploughs at 
work. In the next eight miles I saw only four •, but the land was not only poor, 
but in want of general care and proper culture. Between Newtown Bay and 
Enniscorthy I saw no evidence of neglect, and from Enniscorthy to the town of 
Wexford the cultivation was apparently good. Between Wexford and Water- 
ford I had no opportunity of observing the country, as I made this portion of my 
journey in a snow storm. 

In this county wheat has been extensively sown. Mr. Farrell, the county 
surveyor of Wexford, whose intelligence and means of information cannot be 
questioned, stated to me that he regards the quantity of wheat sown this winter 
in his county to be to the quantity sown in other years in the ratio of five to three. 
On the other hand, however, ditching and digging in the fields had ceased. In 
fact, all that the farmers, who were above destitution, could accomplish with 
horses of their own or that they could hire, by their own labour and that of their 
families, had been performed ; but they employed no hired labourers. The 
small farmers being reduced to destitution, — falling back, indeed, into their 
natural position as labourers, — flock to the Public Works, and their land remained 
untilled. 

Wexford, however, is a peculiar county. The peasantry have not hitherto- 
subsisted entirely on the potato, but oatmeal has formed a large ingredient in 
their food. The failure of the potato here could not, therefore, have caused so- 
much destitution as elsewhere. Unfortunately, the oat crop failed also. Hence- 
a great extent of destitution, but not so overwhelming as in other southern, 
counties. 

From the city of Waterford, proceeding westward, the land is cruelly neglected 
as far as the bounds of the Marquis of Waterford’s estate of Curraghmore. 
Here a different aspect presents itself. The farms are large, being from 30 acres 
upwards to 200. Draining is going on extensively ; the cottages have a com- 
fortable look in comparison with those off* the estate, and the farmers have corn- 
stacks near their dwellings. Hence onwards to Lismore there was nothing 
particular to notice. A few ploughs were in the fields, but no labourers were to 
be seen. 

At Lismore I was fortunate in meeting Mr. Curry, agent to the Duke of 
Devonshire. He stated positively that on the Duke’s estates there was a decided 
increase in the sowing of wheat, and that, as yet, it remains to be seen whether 
there will be enough oats, rye, and barley, sown to meet the deficiency caused 
by the failure of the potatoes. On the mountainous grounds nothing is being 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




144 BOARD OF WORKS. 

done, because the cultivation is by spade-labour, and there, as in other places, 
spade-labour has ceased. 

I crossed the mountains from the valley of Blackwater to the valley of the 
Suir, and afterwards came from Clonmel to Carlow, a distance of 40 miles. In 
this latter distance the cultivation of the land was proceeding rapidly, so far 
as it could be done with horse labour. I was seated next to Mr. Chaytor, agent 
to Lord Glengall. We carefully observed the fields we passed, and nothing 
was wanting to convince us that tillage was not being neglected. Mr. Chaytor 
(whom I had before known), like myself, was under the impression that much 
misconception existed on this point, and his opportunity of knowing the state 
of agriculture was considerable. He said that not only had the wheat sowing 
gone on to a greater extent than usual, but that, in his opinion, preparations 
were making earlier than usual for sowing oats, rye, and barley. He also 
mentioned a curious and important fact, viz., that in the last three weeks 11 or 
12 small farmers under Lord Glengall came to him to request his sanction to 
their giving up their land to their neighbours with large farms, who were 
willing to take them. He gladly acceded, and the land has been given up 
accordingly. Moreover, he said he expected that before Easter a great portion 
of Lord GlengaU’s small farmers would do the same. 

This fact is important. It is a step in the right direction, and all the better, 
as being taken by the small farmers themselves. 

But notwithstanding all which has as yet been done, the prospect of food for 
the end of the year 1847 and the year 1848, in this country, mainly depends 
upon what may be done between the 20th of this month and the 1st of May in 
respect of manure, seed, and labour. 

Previous to this last journey I had not seen any manure being put out on the 
fields, and I believe generally, as yet, but little has been spread. Still there is 
something doing in this respect, and between Clonmel and Carlow I saw pre- 
parations being made to lay manure on the fields. Indeed the time is hardly 
arrived for spreading stable or yard manure. 

With the cultivation of the potato, spade husbandry has disappeared. Beyond 
fencing, draining, and turf-cutting, I do not see what is to employ manual 
labour in this country for nine months in the year, and in winter there will be 
very little, indeed, to give the spade man work. I asked Mr. Chaytor what 
would be the effect of introducing green crops. His answer was, none at all 
upon the daily labourers, because the green crops will be set in drills by the 
plough. 



Lieut.-Colonel Fitzmaurice to Lieut.-Colonel Jones. 

February 10, 1847. 

Having terminated the inquiry you directed me to make at Strokestown 
and reported thereon, I proceeded to visit all the towns and districts of Ros- 
common, and without entering into detail I have the satisfaction to state that 
the operations imder the Board of Works in that county are in a very improving 
condition, not excepting Strokestown, where matters had been going on but 
indifferently up to this time owing to the non-residence of the inspecting and 
engineer officers, and also to the very impracticable and indolent Committee 
there established. This Committee, Lord Lorton kindly gave me to understand 
that he would re-organize, if the names of gentlemen, likely to do better, were 
submitted to his Lordship ; but all my anxiety on this subject was to no purpose. 

Task-work is now generally established throughout the county, to the great 
advantage of both the labourers and the public, through the energy of the 
officers, from all of whom I experienced the most cordial and serviceable assist- 
ance during my sojourn amongst them. 

It is with very great pleasure that I also can inform you, that during my two 
days’ journey from Roscommon to Athlone, and from the latter place to Dublin, 
I remarked, on the right and left of the road, more ploughs at work in the fields 
than I had seen during all my joumeyings through Ireland for the last three 
months ; I also saw the farmers generally along that line preparing the manure 
peculiar to the country 20 miles east and west of the Shannon, namely, lime- 
stone, gravel, and bog mould, which Providence has placed abundantly at their 
very doors. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



145 



I also passed on the roads crowds of young men, and not a few young women, 
and some children journeying towards Liverpool, with the intention of pro- 
ceeding thence to America. 

What with this early and numerous emigration, and what with the deaths 
which have occurred, and must continue to increase, I do not think that Ireland 
will be deemed over-peopled next harvest. 



Mr. Walker to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public TVurks, Dublin , 
February 11, 1847. 

I am directed by the Commissioners of Public Works to request you 
will draw the attention of the Lords Commissioners of Her Majesty’s Treasury 
to the period which may intervene between the present time and the carrying 
out the new arrangements for relieving the destitute in certain districts in 
Ireland ; and to state that it is also desirable that Presentment Sessions should 
be held, to enable the Board to continue works already commenced but not 
completed. 

But it w'ould appear to be desirable that the amount of the presentments 
granted in each case should be limited to a sum barely sufficient to employ 
the destitute then on the lists, in any barony, for the period of six weeks, to 
commence from the 20th February instant. 



Treasury Minute on the above. 

February 16, 1847. 

Write to the Commissioners of Public Works that the Relief Works carried 
on under the 10th Viet, c. 107, should be discontinued as soon as the means 
of subsistence have been provided for the destitute in each neighbourhood, 
either under the temporary Relief Act which will shortly be passed, or by 
employment on any of the publice or private works of improvement which are 
in progress or may hereafter be undertaken. 

This rule may be modified in certain cases in order to prevent the inconve- 
nience which might arise from a work being brought abruptly to a close; 
and in reference to this part of the subject, their Lordships consider that it will 
be sufficient for them to repeat the instruction given by them on the occasion 
of the termination of the Relief Works carried on under the preceding Act, 
9 Viet., c. 1.* 

“In discontinuing Relief Works, care should be taken to leave them, as far 
“ as possible, in a serviceable state, as far as they have gone ; as, for instance, 
“ a section of a road actually in progress may be completed to such an extent 
“ as will render it of some use, and will admit of its being easily carried on 
“ hereafter by a loan secured by grand jury presentment ; but it must be clearly 
“ understood that the paramount object in every case in which such works are 
“not required for giving relief, is to bring the work to an early close, and that 
“ the intention of the slight modification above adverted to, is merely that this 
“ object may be carried into effect with as little sacrifice as possible of any inci- 
* dental benefit that may have been expected from the works.” 

Acting on these principles, the Commissioners of Public Works will bring 
to an immediate close any work carried on under the 10 Viet., c. 107, the con- 
tinuance of which is not required for either of the reasons above adverted to; 
and if it should be necessary to recommend for sanction a new presentment for 
the purpose of affording relief, it should be limited to a sum sufficient to employ 
the destitute until such time as the new Relief Act may be expected to come 
into effective operation, which period, as suggested by the Commissioners, 
should not in any case exceed six weeks. 

In’ all their proceedings on this subject the Commissioners will have a 
careful regard to the paramount object of preventing the Relief Works from 
interfering with the ordinary cultivation of the land ; and as the season of 



* See page 242 of the Relief Correspondence laid before Parliament in 1846.

spring labour has nearly arrived, it is desirable that some effectual steps should

Their Lordships desire that after the Commissioners shall have considered 
the several points above adverted to, and shall have communicated on the subject

with his Excellency’s sanction, they propose to adopt.

Lieut.-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, 
February 13, 1847. 

The accompanying paper, containing an extract from a report by Mr. 
Neville, county surveyor in Louth, may not be uninteresting, as showing the 
opinion of an experienced and practical man as to the system of county works 
as compared with those performed by the Board of Works. It will, I think, be 
a point of great importance to establish, that the completion of works should be 
left entirely to our discretion and judgment, charging the counties with the 
expense. 



Enclosure. 

Extract from Letter of John Neville, Esq., Surveyor, County Louth, dated 
February 7, 1847. 

In order to meet the destitution, as near home as possible, many of the presentments 
were for the repairs and remodelling of the existing roads, and in several instances these pre- 
sentments have superseded the necessity for the usual Grand Jury Presentments; indeed, 
there are only one or two on the books for the next assizes. In spite of the difficulties of the 
relief system, the result of the expenditure on these works has shown clearly that the system 
of repairs by daily labour under the Board, is better and more economical than that by con- 
tractors. The reason is evident ; constant attention to the surface is necessary, and the poor 
contractor, who is only paid once in the year, cannot afford to give his time and money without 
large profits. 

The number of persons at present is 6395, and the last week’s expenditure was 
I6C6Z. 11s. 101 d. 

The persons employed on the works are of every age, from 10 upwards, males and females; 
the weak, infirm, and some able-bodied. The loss sustained, as far as labour is to be consi- 
sidered, by the effect of the weak, the infirm, ami those not fit to work, on those who are, is 
considerable. The absolute loss would be less by paying many to remain at home ; for the 
little wrought by the weak is lost alongside the reduced work and relaxed energies of those who 
can labour. 

The people have exhibited good sentiments with a quick feeling of what is right and what 
is wrong, and, according to circumstances, may achieve much good or perpetrate much 
injury. 

It is a fact, that the system of putting the old and infirm on Relief Works is mischievous ; 
these persons ought to be supported by those who have the means, or those who can earn wages 
connected with them, or by out-door relief at home. But the young and able-bodied, the 
pith and sinew of a country, should be taught self reliance, and that a fair day’s wages must 
be the result of a fair day’s work. How does the system under which we are obliged to work 
effect this? Why badly; infirmity is a reason to recommend for employment, and physical 
power a reason to send the possessor to seek work elsewhere. A labourer in appearance, 
having perhaps a family, must get 10c?. per day, whilst a labourer in reality may get no more. 
The task system has, to some extent, remedied this anomaly. But in the present state of the 
country that system cannot be well carried out. From the numbers put to work at any parti- 
cular project, from their various degrees of physical power, and the. generosity evinced by the 
strong to the weak-bodied, it is difficult to manage. One fact is, however apparent, that if 
the system of supporting the destitute by Public Works is to be continued, the most cheap, 
the most efficient, and effectual way will be to pay in proportion to the work done, discarding 
every other consideration, and to raise the present scale of wages, if it must be, so that the 
wages earned will support all, and that the able-bodied man get 2s. 6 d. per diem if he earn 
it, giving to the weak-bodied man in proportion also what he may earn, though it be but Id. 
I am writing here of labour alone, its value, and the effect of a system on the minds of the 
.people. The weak and infirm have other claims, but these do not belong to my subject. 

It is necessary that an engineer should have a choice of hauds in carrying out any works 
entrusted to him. The present system takes away that choice, and makes very nearly physical 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



147 



infirmity the test of admission on Relief Works. This paralyzes all exertions, and those who 
can work will not. On last week 280 men employed at making common mound fences, for 
which Is. 3 d. per perch, a very fair price, was paid, earned each but 2 hd. per diem ; certainly 
47 men working fairly would have executed as much work as the 280.

Lieut. -Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, 

February 16, 1847. 

The order to furnish a nominal list of the men struck off the labour-roll 
by Captain Wynne will be very difficult to execute, and the only way in which 
it can be accomplished is to get the books prepared by the Committees, and 
presented by them to Captain Wynne. I have applied to his Excellency to 
procure them, he has given directions accordingly. Captain Wynne is fully 
prepared to make his statement, which he feels assured will be satisfactory. 

Our accounts from the country, one and all, complain of the way the Relief 
Committees are acting — many of the gentry and landed proprietors not doing 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 






148 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



anything, — and what may he considered worse, many are discharging the few 
labourers they have had employed. There are no signs of a desire on the part 
of the holders of 10 acres and under to cultivate their land. They say the 
rents are too high, and as they could barely afford to pay them in good seasons 
with potatoes, they will he utterly incapable of doing so if their land is sown 
with grain. They therefore consider it better to earn something upon the roads, 
(which all goes into their pockets,) than to incur an expenditure and liabilities 
for the benefit of others. At the same time, they have a great disinclination to 
give up their leases, preferring to hold on upon the chance of what may turn up. 

At this moment we are paying a very large body, when those most in need 
are not deriving the benefit intended for them, for all our officers state that the 
most destitute are in numerous instances excluded from the lists. The Com- 
mittees are ruled by one or two individuals, and the others comply, but after- 
wards go to the inspecting officer and tell him what they ought to have done. 

I do not see my way at all in regard to the tillage of the small holdings, nor 
do I understand how the new Act will be brought into play without food. This 
is an extraordinary country ; while the newspapers are crying out about the 
distress at Sligo, immense quantities of provisions are passing through it into the 
country, but it will all be not enough.

Captain Winne to Lieut. -Colonel Jones. 

BaTlina , February 11, 1847. 

This county appears free from any sort of outrage. In the county Galway there is a 
good deal of sheep-stealiug, and about the neighbourhood of Tuam some disposition to 
insubordination on the works, but in this county all is quiet. 

I regret to say that extreme distress prevails notwithstanding the immense amount of 
employment (about 62,000 in the county, as nearly as I can ascertain from the inspecting 
officers). 

Here, as elsewhere, the same cause has crippled the operation of the Relief Act, viz., the 
determination on the part of the Committees to take care of their friends. Thousands of the 
very poorest class are still unemployed and dying daily in vast, numbers. I have asked the four 
inspecting officers how this happened, and though all young, energetic, intelligent, and zealous, 
they have declared their utter inabilitity to correct this fatal abuse. 

1 called this day on the coroner, having previously made inquiries in every other quarter 
likely to be informed. I was accompanied by Lieut. Cox, inspecting officer. The result of 
my visit was, that there were too strong grounds for the numerous verdicts lately published in 
the local journals. I was anxious to find out the facts, as I discovered a case iu Galway where 
the man upon whom the. verdict of death from starvation was pronounced was in possession at 
his death of 60 sheep and several cows ; his name was Mullen, a tenaut of Mr. Blake, of Castle 
Grove, from whom I heard the particulars. 

Some deaths have undoubtedly occurred from actual want of food, but very many from 
insufficiency of food and exposure to the inclemency of the weather, the peculiar habit of the 
peasantry ot this county being heretofore “ to sit over the fire the entire winter rarely leaving 
their cabins.” One pay-clerk told me that five persons were buried yesterday in his district 
without coffins, a practice which I understand from the coroner is very common. 

I am glad to have his (the coroner's) opinion, that no blame is attributable to the officers 
of your B iard, of whose exertions he spoke most favourably. 

There is scarcely any attempt at the ordinary operations of agriculture in this county, 
scarcely any crops down, and no preparations being made ; it is not°a wheat country. There 
are many applications for substitution of other members of families for those at present 
employed, which looks like a movement in that direction, but the people do not care to till 
their small four or five acre farms, as they say they cannot expect any benefit from them 
after paying their rent; if tilled with grain alone, I fear it will be very difficult to induce them 
to till on any terms. There is scarcely such a thing as a large farmer in this division of the 
county. There are some stacks of oats to be seen in the haggards, but I understand that, in 
many cases, they have been threshed and made up again as security to the landlord for his rent.

I may, in the first place, mention, that the population of this town and neighbourhood is 
constantly changing, from the people going away and passing through, who are endeavouring 
to make their way out of the country, and numbers of beggars and others who have come in, 
attracted by a gratuitous distribution of soup, but from which they find themselves excluded, by 
the rule of not giving it to strangers. 

At the last. Quarter Sessions there were upwards of 5000 processes for rent. The persons 
against whom they were issued abandoned their homes and wandered through the country. 
No one had. any interest in obtaining relief or employment for them, and it was difficult for 
me to obtain any information about them. This, with the change of food, together with the 
tendency of the people to ascribe all deaths to starvation, may account for many of the verdicts 
that hat e been brought in, particularly as it was difficult to obtain any jury capable of dis- 
criminating without prejudice, they being taken in many cases from the men employed on the 
roads; indeed, when I looked over the copies of the inquests in possession of the 'coroner, it 
was a rare instance to find a juror capable of signing his name. 

With reference to the amount of employment that has been afforded, it is only within the 
last few days that I could get nearly the number of works I considered necessary to put in 
operation, though the engineers have done little since tlie last sessions but start them. 

I think that the lists of labourers (though no doubt they still contain the names of many 
who ought not to be employed) have been tolerably well purged. 1 have already had them 
revised lor the second time, and having now nearly all the works necessary in operation, I shall 
acrain be able to go through this process for the third time , which I hope will make them 
tolerably correct. 

A list of 60 persons, for a work on which there was supposed to be more independent, 
persons than on any other, I compared yesterday with the Poor Law valuation, and out of 
that number, I found only one person whose tenement exceeded 6 1. per annum. 

I may add, that nothing can equal the difficulties I have had to contend with here, the 
details of which it would be useless to trouble you with. I will mention a magistrate and 
chairman of a Relief Committee demanding from the pay-clerk the money he had, to pay some 
of his tenants who were employed on the Public Works, and abusing him for not doing so.

Mr. Mulvany to Mr. Trevelyan. 

22, Craven-street, February 25, 1847. 

Feeling the importance of obtaining correct information as to the present 
state of destitution, and the prospects for the next year as regards the crops in 
different parts of Ireland, I addressed, on the 13th instant, a note (see copy) to 
several of our engineers in different parts of Ireland; who, not being engaged 
in the administration of measures of relief, might he enabled to state, impar- 
tially, their opinions on those subjects, as strangers resident in the midst of the 
scenes they describe. I beg leave to send you the answers I have received up 
to the present time, and will forward the others as they arrive. 

In the meantime I wish to call your attention to the remarkable coincidence 
in their statements throughout : — 

, 1st. As to the increase of destitution, and decrease of the strength of the 
people to perform the ordinary works of labour. 

2nd. As to the neglect or total inability to cultivate small holdings. 

3rd. As to the deficiency of seed ; and, 

4th. As to the consequences which must result from such a state of 
things in the present and for some future years. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




150 BOARD OF WORKS, 

After very anxious consideration of these letters, and of many other commu- 
nications that I have seen, I confess that, though some increase of tillage may 
be expected on the part of large farmers and persons with capital, I am forced 
to conclude that, on the whole, there is imminent danger of a very considerable 
portion of the small holdings remaining uncultivated and unproductive. 

Considering the large extent of the tillage land of Ireland that is occupied in 
small holdings, such a result would be attended with the most disastrous con- 
sequences as regards the supply of food for next year ; every energy, therefore, 
of the proprietors of lands should be put forth without delay, to avert con- 
sequences so injurious to the country and so fatal to their own interests as 
landlords. 

I have heard of means adopted by Lord Courtown and some other proprietors 
which seem well calculated to effect this object, viz., the proprietor enters into 
a species of voluntary partnership with the distressed tenants ; he, on the one 
hand, provides the seed, employs the tenants in the cultivation of their own 
lands, and supports them while so engaged without any interference with their 
rights of tenure ; while they, on the other hand, bind themselves to allow him 
a given proportion of the next season’s crop in liquidation of the expenses 
incurred by him and of his claim for rent. 

Such a course, adopted concurrently with the introduction of the new mea- 
sures for relief by the distribution of food, seems to be quite practicable, and, 
in many respects, desirable as serving to unite both proprietor and tenant in one 
co mm on interest, for the benefit of the country. 



Private Note to District Engineers and other Officers of the Board of

22, Craven-street , Strand, London ,

I have to request that *you will let me know, from your own observa- 
tion, what is the actual state of destitution in your district, and furnish me with 
a statement of any facts, in reference to this subject, upon which you can rely, 
and with which it would be useful for me to be acquainted. 

With respect to the future, I am anxious to know what has been done, or 
what is expected will be done, for the cultivation of the soil. Is there seed 
enough in the country ? and what hopes or fears, founded on your knowledge 
of your locality, do you entertain with reference to the state of the people and 
of the country during the next autumn and winter ? 

In the course of your travelling I wish you would, as far as it is practicable, 
go into the houses yourself, and become personally acquainted with the real 
state of things ; and from time to time communicate to me the result of your 
observations. 

Pray let me have an early answer. 

(Signed) W. T. Mulvany. 



Mr. T. J. Mulvany to Mr. Mulvany. 

Richmond Harbour , near Longford, 
February 15, 1847. 

longford. I am sorry to say that the symptoms of general distress and frequent 

roscommon. destitution are becoming every day more unequivocal. I speak first with refe- 
rence to this immediate neighbourhood, which, of course, comes most under my 
own view. The number of deaths latterly has been considerable ; some of 
them old people certainly, but nearly all the results of scanty and unwholesome 
diet, and superinduced disease. I have not met with any of those shocking 
cases we hear of, people dropping dead in the street or in their cabins from 
actual starvation ; but the cases I have alluded to are no less surely the effects 
of destitution. These deaths, too, add to the number of widows and Orphans 
whose cases are frequently most miserable, and who must absolutely perish but 
for private charity. For the last week this misery has been much increased by 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



151 



the snow and frost, which put a total stop to out-door work, except that some 
of the relief workmen were kept partly employed cleaning the snow off the 
leading roads. In consequence of this weather, the canal being frozen so as to 
stop the supply of food by that means, and the roads being almost impassable, the 
market at Longford, which had been gradually falling slightly for the previous 
three weeks, rose considerably on Saturday, — oatmeal 2 7s. 6d. per cwt., or just 
3s. 6 d. a stone. The people come in from a great distance, from the county 
Roscommon and other places, in the hope of getting a cheaper market in Long- 
ford than elsewhere. They have most of them to walk the whole distance, 
carrying back the ba.g of meal on their backs in the evening ; and I am told 
that one man died on the road atTarmonbarry on last Saturday evening on his 
way home from Longford market. 

A great deal of the distress at present is beyond the reach of relief by means 
of Public Works, as in the case of a large family of young children, where the 
father is either dead or dying, or so enfeebled as to be unable to do any rea- 
sonable amount of work. 

The most serious consideration just now undoubtedly is the cropping of the 
land. Very little has yet been done towards it. There have been some patches 
of land sown with wheat, and the crop looks very promising ; but the great 
majority of the fields lie just as they were left last year, — the corn-fields with 
the stubble unploughed, and in many cases the potato fields undug. For the 
last week, of course, nothing at all was done. Now the snow is gone, and if 
the farmers exert themselves, there is time enough to put down their crops. I 
cannot, however, see my way clearly yet as to what is likely to be done to the 
land. I have no doubt there is seed enough for corn crops in this part of the 
country ; but the price is so high that it is almost impossible for those who have 
not got it of their own to buy it, and those who have it are more disposed to 
sell, or keep it for their own food. I fear that much of the land in occupation of 
small farmers will be let to lie waste if left to themselves to manage. 



Mr. Forsyth to Mr. Mulvany. 

Drainage District Office, Belturbet, 

February 16, 1847. 

It appears to me that the queries contained in your note of the 13th cavan. 
February are four. I shall answer them seriatim as well as I can from my own Fermanagh. 
observation. leitrim. 

First. — What is the actual state of destitution in your district? 

That the destitution in this district is great, I have what appears to me strong 
proof. I have observed, for some months past, a gradual falling off in the 
earnings of the workmen, and on inquiry I have found that the quantity of food 
which they are able to procure is quite inadequate to enable them to work, as 
they must do, to earn a day’s wages on our works. In a conversation I had 
lately with some of them, they said it was impossible that they could stand it, 
being unable to earn more than 8 d. or KW. per day. Two scanty meals is 
therefore all they can get per day ; one-half of the day’s wages, or 4c?. for each 
meal. One of them said to me, “ Set down a fourpenny loaf, not quite 1^ lbs., 
to a family of six to eight persons for their morning meal, and the share which 
the man could get is very inadequate to give him strength and support for the 
day’s work.” In numerous instances it is worse than this, for the family being 
larger, or the earnings smaller, one meal per day is all they can get. 

I confess this state of things has made me apprehensive that our works would 
be deserted altogether. When they found their earnings less than the wages 
given on the Relief Works, and their strength so much diminished, they have 
endeavoured to obtain tickets for the relief. 

I consider this a stronger evidence of the destitute condition of the labourers 
than many more appalling cases ; because these men were industrious, and 
inclined to support themselves as long as they could, without having recourse 
to the Relief Works, or receiving any eleemosynary assistance whatever; while 
others who were not of industrious habits, and trusted altogether to support 
without labour, sunk into destitution which might have been in part at least 
avoided. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




152 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



There is a class of the poor awfully destitute, and no charge of laziness or 
idleness can be brought against them. Many poor families have no one capable 
of working, or being employed on the Relief Works, and every other source of 
assistance is shut up. There are also many who have experienced great difficulty 
and delay in procuring employment, and when at last they obtained it, they were 
so emaciated and debilitated, they were unable, during the inclement weather, 
to work so as to keep up the natural warmth of the body, and fatal disease has 
been the consequence. 

Many in this district have been carried off by dysentery. After long absti- 
nence, from sheer want, they have used Indian meal incautiously or ignorantly, 
and, being unaccustomed to such food, they have been visited by the abuve 
disease. 

I am fully aware that it is more difficult to ascertain the real state of the 
destitution in this district than is generally believed. In confirmation of this I 
shall mention two or three facts, as a set off against what I have said above. 

I have had occasion to visit and examine a great number of mills during the 
whiter, some of them in the poorest parts of the country ; in every case they 
have been crowded to excess, and they continued day and night where the 
power wuold admit. Many of those crowding the mills and mill-yards appeared 
to be of the poorer class. 

The small quantities of oats that remain unthreshed are carefully concealed, 
generally under some straw, hay, or other fodder. A reason assigned for this 
is that they are afraid of robbery. Many robberies have been committed, but 
there is evidently much ingenuity exercised to conceal their real circumstances, 
and make their case appear as bad as possible. There is no doubt that, gene- 
rally, the grain which should have been sold to pay the rent, has been retained 
for their own use, and this has furnished them food at the expense of the land- 
lord. Many of the farmers have also sold their cows, and are now living on 
the proceeds. 

There is still, however strange it may sound, a large quantity of potatoes in 
fhedistrict, but generally so carefully concealed that it would be quite impossi- 
ble to form an estimate. They bring them for sale, carefully concealed from 
all but those who are likely to be purchasers. I could purchase them now for 
family use, but when they demanded 14 d. per stone I ceased to buy. 

Second. — What has been, or is expected will be done for the cultivation of 
the soil ? 

The present destitution is calamitous, but, in my opinion, the prospect, so far 
as the cultivation of the soil is concerned, is sufficiently portentous of evil. 
Any small exceptions found throughout the district are not of such extent as to 
make it too much to say that nothing has been done. I have conversed with 
several farmers on the subject, and they uniformly say that if they procure 
labourers from the overseer of the Relief Works, they must pay them 1C )il. to Is. 
per (lay, and receive in return only about 4 d. worth ; this they cannot afford, 
and they are expecting some better system. 

As regards the small farms and potato gardens, there is neither ability nor 
disposition to touch them, unless the tenants are paid for it, or supported during 
the time, which is the same thing. They are dependant on every day’s wages 
for existence, and therefore unable to spare any of their time to this work. It 
is true much might be done after hours when the days are a little longer, as 
they generally quit the Relief Works about 4 o’clock, and some may say no 
time is lost ; but their half-starved condition has destroyed their energies ; exer- 
tion is at an end ; and a disposition to the most pitiable helplessness, and abject 
dependance, seems to have wholly possessed them. The cases of robbery and 
murder may be adduced as instances of a contrary effect, but I believe the people 
generally have no sympathy with those who commit such crimes. 

Third. — Is there seed enough in the country ? 

What I have stated above will show that this query is difficult to answer. 
As far as I can judge, the larger and more substantial farmers will have enough, 
but those imder six or eight acres will be entirely without any. It is surprising 
with what shrewdness, and even cunning, they seize upon the sayings of certain 
persons who have endeavoured to make themselves notorious during the present 
distress. They are persuaded that it is imperative on the landlord or the 
Government to assist them in the present case, and entertain the prospect of 
being provided for at the pnblic expense ; they have imbibed the much agitated 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



153 



doctrine, that the Government are hound to provide for them. Two or three 
landlords have published reports of providing all kinds of seed for their tenants, 
but I am not aware of any having been furnished. 

Fourth. — What hopes are there in reference to the state of the people and 
country during next autumn and winter ? 

The answer to this query is necessarily hypothetic, but the hypothesis will be 
nearer or farther from the truth in the ratio in which it is based on right pre- 
mises. I have endeavoured to take a practical view of the causes or agencies 
now in operation, and to calculate the results to be expected. I confess that, in 
any view of the case, to me they are not cheering, as it regards next autumn and 
winter, or for a longer period, if the potato be extinct, or nearly so, in this 
country. 

The first fact I would mention is the backward and neglected state of the 
husbandry. This must have a very great influence on future prospects. 

The next is, if the labouring population are to be employed during the spring 
and summer months at thorough drainage, the produce of a large portion of the 
arable land must be lost, as the drainage will not be completed in time for the 
land being cropped. If it be possible to effect the drainage in time for cropping, 
there will be a lack of employment at the period when it is most required. 

In every view of the case which I have taken, I camiot see how the present 
population of the country is to be supported for years to come without the 
potatoes. According to the best information I can get among the farmers, it 
will require from three to five times as much land to produce any other kind of 
food necessary. Suppose the lowest estimate be taken, and grant for argument 
that the improvements contemplated will double the produce,— -and I am far 
from being so sanguine as to expect this to be the case for several years hence, — 
there is still minus one-third of the necessary quantity. If it be said that 
imports will supply that or more, whence then is the revenue to be raised, 

. — poor-rates and landlords’ rent ; and not, to speak of the incumbrances now 
on the land, and the sums to be laid on for the present distress, and for 
the proposed improvements. If there be truth in these remarks, and I think 
there is some, it is Utopian to think that this country can maintain its present 
populatien merely by agricultural improvements and speculations in any other 
way than heretofore ; that is on the miserable potato diet. 

The cultivation and improvement of the land can never require more than 
half the available labour, there must therefore be one-half of the chief wealth of 
the country lost — that is, the profitable employment of its inhabitants — and the 
superabundant population must press most prejudicially on the general pros- 
perity. While such an amount of the labour of the inhabitants of any country 
remains unemployed, or as a drug in the market, the population cannot rise far 
above a state bordering on pauperism. 

I make these remarks because little is said or proposed but agricultural im- 
provements. These are of the highest importance, and productive of the most 
beneficial results ; but I deny that they are sufficient to meet the case, or to main- 
tain the rapidly increasing population. Useful employment must be afforded to 
the surplus population, by which they may become producers of wealth, and not 
liable to calamitous distress like the present, when failures take place in the 
crops. It would be well, therefore, if something were done to develope some of 
the other ample resources of the country, with which you are -well acquainted. 

To confine myself, however, simply to the query, I cannot but think there is 
an awful risk, and it is difficult to see how it can be avoided. Should the next 
crop not be abundant, and there is little prospect of it at present, what will 
become of the people? The landlords are almost beggared, the rates to be levied 
under the new relief or poor-law ■will have nearly the same effect on tradesmen 
and others, and the State will have advanced an immense sum without prospect 
of repayment except by disinheriting the proprietors. What the result of all 
that will be I confess I am unable to say. 

I shall endeavour to collect as many facts bearing on the above queries as I 
can, and report them without loss of time.

Mr. Roberts to Mr. Mulvany. 

Garriclcmacross, February 20, 1847. 

There is to be a presentment sessions here on the 1st of March; the 
Rev. Edward M'Gowan, P.P., with whom you are already acquainted, has, I 
believe, urged this upon the Government. 

It is not difficult to gain information as to the amount of destitution, for it is 
now becoming very great. Hitherto the extensive employment afforded to men, 
women, and children, of all ages, secured to each family some means of sub- 
sistence ; this kept away famine and disease. There are few families in the 
barony requiring employment who did not receive from 6d. to Is. 6 d. a day for, 
labour. This euabled them to procure turnips, upon which they chiefly live; 
but upon such food they cannot work, so that at high prices for what they do 
they are barely able to live. 

Until the last snow, there was not much disease, not much more than in ordi- 
nary years ; but dysentery is now making its appearance very fast. , 

Upwards of 7000 people have received employment on the drainage works, 
though 5000 has been our greatest daily number. Our works are now drawing to 
a close, and the employment is, of course, becoming limited ; the people thrown 
out of work have no resource whatever ; hundreds spend days without food, and 
in the absence of proper subsistence have recourse to most unwholesome diet. 
Their deserted and wretched cabins, their forlorn and distressing look, with 
pain and sickness so dreadfully depicted in every countenance, is horribly painful 
to look at ; and with all this human misery, there is no person putting his 
shoulder to the burthen, — no proper efforts are being made to relieve the 
people. How it will end, God only knows. 

The large farmers are tilling their lands, but the smaller are not. In Farney 
the way the small farmers cultivate their land is — they and their children carry 
the manure to the ground in baskets — they then hire horses to plough. I think 
the proprietors ought now to supply them with means to dig or plough their 
land, and give them seed, which would ensure the land being tilled ; I see no 
other course that will. I have urged in the strongest manner I could the 
necessity of looking to these matters in time ; but nothing is yet done, and if 
works are presented for at this approaching sessions, and public employment 
given to the people in March, Farney is lost. 

I find great difficulty in closing the works, that is, making them complete 
for the exact amount to be expended. This you may conceive when I tell you 
that there are 75 lots or depots of work in the barony, averaging 120 1. each. % 



Mr. T. J. Mulvany to Mr. Mulvany. 

Richmond Harbour, February 21, 1847. 

Since I wrote last I have been a good deal through Roscommon, in the 
direction of Strokestown, Elphin, Croghan, and Boyle. The people are generally 
very badly off in that direction ; their whole dependence appears to be “ the Pub- 
lic Works,” and they pay no attention to the land, although they all admit that 
they are alive to the necessity of putting down their crops if they are to expect 
anything to live on next year, but say they cannot afford to give up the pay on 
the works, and seem generally to have a vague expectation that the Government 
will crop the land, or as they term it, “ give them some encouragement” to do it 
themselves. I find they are not much in the habit of putting down the crops 
before March, so that the present neglected state of the land is not so alarming 
yet ; but they have only six weeks before them at most, and little or no pre- 
paration made as yet. In one place near Croghan I met a small farmer who 
holds 15 acres from Lord Lorton. Of this quantity he has only about or 2 
acres cropped with wheat and rye, the rest nearly all pasture, as he had been in 
the habit of feeding cows. In reply to my query why he had not broken some 
of his fine lea land and put down oats, he said that he ought to have done so, but 
was waiting to see what encouragement they would get ; that it was now too 
late, as the lea should have been turned up during the winter, and consequently 
he has to go some miles off to pay a high rent for two acres of con-acre oats.
