The farm adjoining this man’s land consists of 38 acres of good land, nearly 
all under com crops last year, but nothing whatever done to it since the corn 
was cut. The houseis not bad, and there are five stacks of corn and three cocks 
of hay in the haggard ; and yet the two young men who rent this farm (their 
father being dead) have been and are still employed on the Relief Works, to 
the utter neglect of their farm, and probably to the exclusion of really distressed 
parties. The conduct of the Relief Committees is very much complained 
against. I have the foregoing statement from the man I alluded to above, and 
therefore suppose it to be correct ; — if so, it is certainly shameful. 

The employment on some of the roads in that part of the county has just been 
suspended, I suppose by order of the Board. This has caused great consterna- 
tion among the men employed. On Friday I met a large body of them, or 
rather two or three bodies of 10 or 12 each, going off across the country between 
Boyle and Carrick. They told me they had just been thrown out of work oil the 
Toads, and were going to Mr. Mulloy, of Oakport, to get “ some redress.” 

I hear it remarked in some places that the practice of giving out soup without 
any solid food, as they do at some of the soup kitchens, tends greatly to increase 
the dysentery which is so prevalent. Fever and other sickness have become very 
prevalent in this neighbourhood (Cloondra) within the last week. 



Mr. Fraser to Mr. Mulyany. 

Burris in Ossory , February’!!, '1847. 

My absence from head quarters prevented me from replying to your 
letter before this date. I have taken means to have correct inquiry made by my 
overseers in their various localities, and having just completed a tour of my 
districts, I have within the last two weeks seen the greater part of Kilkenny, 
Queen’s County, and Tipperary. 

From my own observation I can say that the people are in a most destitute 
condition, although in none of those counties are they actually starving, as very 
generally they are employed upon the Public Works. But I have known some 
instances in which the men (who were upon our own works and who had large 
families) had not tasted .food for an entire -day, and have existed upon much 
less than half food for nearly a week. This has occurred when, on account of 
floods, &c., we have had to suspend our operations, or when the men have come 
newly into our work. 

With respect to the cultivation of the soil, nothing almost has yet been done, 
except sowing wheat. In this country, Tipperary particularly, there will, I 
think, be little difference this year with regard to that crop, as it is a favourite 
one amongst the people, and the land suits it. But there is very little prepara- 
tion for sowing oats, or anything else, amongst any class of farmers,— none at all 
amongst those who hold farms under 9 to 12 acres. They are entirely depen- 
dent upon their daily wages for their daily bread. I think, from present appear- 
ances, that you would not be far from the truth in supposing that, at least, 
one-third of the entire quantity of land belonging to the small farmers ■will be 
left uncultivated, unless they are paid for cultivating it. If they remain at 
home to till their fields they starve, as their day’s pay is barely sufficient to 
keep them from starvation. 

Taking into account the quantity of land left available for grain crops, on 
account of the failure of the potatoes, I do not think there is seed enough in 
the country. If they had the usual quantity of potatoes to plant, there might 
be, amongst all, grain enough for seed. But even suppose there was enough 
for all, if divided, the poor farmer cannot purchase. Oats are now Is. 9d. to 
Is. 10 d. per stone in Roscrea, and every prospect of the price increasing. 

In conclusion, I would earnestly urge that for humanity’s sake you should do 
something to provide indoor work for females. It is most discreditable, to say 
the least, to have them working on the public roads exposed to every hardship. 
•I have succeeded with the Committees about here ; but elsewhere there are 
from 12 to 20 on almost every work.

Mr. Kennan to Mr. Mulvany. 

Killybegs, February 22,' 1847. 

Your favour of the 20th instant, is to hand this moment, and I hasten to 
give you a reply from my past experience. I have been a great deal amongst 
the people in their cabins, for this reason, that, having some knowledge of 
medicine, and a small private fund to distribute, I have from necessity gone 
amongst them particularly. 

In reply to your first query, I would state that the destitution is frightful ; 
two or three funerals pass by my window every morning, arising of course from 
want of food, which produces, first, diarrhoea, then prostration, low typhus 
fever, and death. I could write you a volume on this subject. 

With respect to the future, nothing has been done, except in fisheries ; nothing 
for the cultivation of the soil; the people have been hoping that the Govern- 
ment would turn them to the cultivation of their own farms, paying them, as 
they are now doing for roads that will never be finished. 

There is no seed in the country, except perhaps a small supply held by the 
gentry ; when I say there is no seed, I mean potatoes, turnips, barley, oats, and 
wheat. 

With regard to the future, my humble opinion is, that when the new crop 
comes in from the United States (I speak from my own personal knowledge of 
the United States), food will be much cheaper, but, in the meantime, what are 
the poor to do ; and what, moreover, must be the prospect, unless the lands are 
tilled ; and the lands will not be tilled, unless the people are paid in the same 
way as they are for the road work ; because they will starve, unless they have 
some immediate income to support them. 

In regard to your last inquiry, as I stated before, I attend the sick and dying, 
and see the people in their own homes ; and I assure you my heart bleeds to 
see the miserable state in which the poor, honest, and industrious man is 
placed. 



Mr. Barry to Mr. Mulvany. 

Drainage Commission , Engineers' Office, 
Ballinrobe, County Mayo, February 22, 1847- 

I am in receipt of yours of the 13th instant, and I trust the following 
particulars relating to the subject you wish me to write about will prove 
satisfactory. 

Since I have been here, actual observation fully convinces me that the 
reports printed in the newspapers on the subject have not exaggerated in the 
least the misery, famine, and disease that is at present existing in this part of 
the country. 

I will now state what the circumstances of those are who are at present 
employed on the districts under my charge. 

The generality of the labourers are either tenants or small farmers, married, 
and having families. 

The produce of their fields and con-acre, on which they relied for support, 
consisted last year, as you are aware, only of a small quantity of grain, which 
has been, with very few exceptions, since the cold weather set in, totally 
exhausted, and the men and their families are now solely dependent either on 
our works or the relief works, for the means wherewithal to get food : for 
that reason, a marked change has lately come over their appearance, which 
is most distressing. Their meals consist either of a piece of dry fadge or a 
mixture of barley-meal and turnips ■, and from the extremely bad quality of 
this food, as well as from its scarcity, dysentery has prevailed to a great extent, 
which has greatly reduced the physical strength of the men. 

On the Moyour and 0 wenabrockagh drainages, the wives and children of the 
labourers who have constant employment on our works, are begging alms from 
house to house, obliged to yield to the law of necessity ; their appearance, clean 
and decent, distinguishes them by melancholy contrast from the class of 
habitual beggars : but there is one thing greatly to the" credit of the labourers, 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS* 



157 



which I must state, and that is — all those who can spare anything help those in 
want, and each pay-day a regular subscription is collected by the gangleaders. 

With regard to the people who are not on our works, I am naturally not 
brought so much in contact with them, but their white emaciated-looking 
countenances fully testifies what they must be suffering : this applies to persons 
who were always heretofore considered to be in good circumstances ; and I have 
been given to understand, that the deaths registered from coroners’ inquests are 
a mere nothing compared to the deaths which have occurred amongst this better 
class of people. 

5 As to the cultivation of the soil little or nothing has been done as yet, and 
I see no preparation whatsoever. 

The stubble of last year’s corn crops, which in other years the most negligent 
had either dug up or ploughed in November or December, is, with few 
exceptions, exactly in the same state in which it was left by the reaper ; the 
cause has been the employment that was afforded to the people on the Relief 
Works. As for seed, I believe there is very little in the country, and what 
there is consists of barley and oats. 

The soils on the western coast along the sea-shore are, I understand, unsuited 
for wheat, and the inhabitants are totally unacquainted with green crops of any 
kind, so that barley and oats must be their sole food-crop for the coming season. 
The increased quantity of seed, viz., barley and oats, that will be required if the 
land was so to be tilled would be very considerable, there being no potatoes to 
sow, which was always the principal crop heretofore. 

As to what will be the state of the people and country during the next 
autumn and winter I can scarcely venture an opinion, since that, I think, must 
depend upon a variety of circumstances. 



Mr. Rankin to Mr. Mulvany. 

Drainage Commission Office, Killimor, 

February 23, 1847. 

I am in receipt of your letter of the 13th instant, and beg to return you galway. 
my answer to the queries contained in it as well as I am able. 

What is the actual state of destitution in the district ? — Very great (75 per 
cent.), the poor people depending for subsistence on the wages they earn from 
day to day, and invariably in advance with the shopkeepers for provisions, 
who, of course, charge them accordingly. Receiving subsistence money on our 
work has not done anything to check this, as might have been anticipated, the 
men preferring to get the whole of what money is coming to them regularly 
every fortnight. 

With respect to the future, what has been done or what is expected will be 
done for the cultivation of the soil, &c. ? — A few patches of wheat are sown 
and a little here and barley in a few gardens. The few wealthy farmers are 
preparing to turn up the soil preparatory to sowing the oat crop, and the few 
industrious poor are also doing so are under the impression that Government 
will supply them with seed. 

Is there enough of seed in the country ? — No. Unless there is some great 
change effected by the Government measures now under consideration, there 
will certainly be a very bad chance for the poor next autumn and winter. At 
present there is quite enough of employment, and if provisions were plentiful 
in the market, I have no fear but we could struggle through it.

at the request of Captain Hutchinson (Inspector), and there were facts esta-

All through the line I travelled, Tuam, Castlebar, Ballina, and to Belmullet,

paration worth mentioning for sowing and cultivation was between Bally-

general that it quite cheered me to see that some portion of the country had 
“ the will and the way ” to do it. 

The only fact of importance I can mention to you as to exertions on the part 
of proprietors to meet this, which came to my knowledge, is one communicated 
to me by an old acquaintance whom I met at Ballina. He has been specially 
engaged by the trustees to Lord Clanmorris’s estates ; he had been in the neigh- 
bourhood of Galway, and was then proceeding to the other estates of Lord 
Clanmorris, one near Foxford included. His mission was to report to and make 
arrangements, on behalf of the trustees, to crop the land. I had not an oppor- 
tunity of learning farther from him than that it was to be done amply throughout 
the whole of the estates by the trustees. 

I saw one woman die in the streets of Belmullet from the effects of previous 
starvation ; she had had some food for two days before her death, but it came 
too late. I have seen a great many there and in other places, particularly 
about Crossmolina, who, I do not think, -will live long. 

There are some who have little stores hiding. I found out from a man 
whom I had as a guide in one of my rambles through the “ Mullet,” that he 
had up to that time some potatoes concealed which he hoped would “ keep him 
and his family up” two or three weeks. Some people talk of small potatoes, 
to a certain extent, existing still in the ground, and that they may be yet 
planted out for a crop. I doubt it, for I have seen in many places the mere 
children rooting up the oft-turned earth in search of an odd one which might 
have escaped the previous searches. 



Mr. King to Mr. Mulvany. 

District Office, Cork, February 27, 1847. 

C0RK - I have just received your letter of the 25th instant, and as I am just 

returned from the remotest end of my district, I can, from my own observation, 
vouch for the following state of things : — 

From Skibbereen to Skull, or, I may say, to the sea in that direction, the 
people are literally famine-stricken. On Thursday last, at Rosscarbery, nine 
persons were consigned to the grave without coffins, three of whom were young 
women, all without coffins. I have seen but two persons actually on the verge 
of death myself ; one on the road-side, and one in a wretched cabin off the 
road ; they were both women ; they were both alone. The person in the cabin 
was between Rosscarbery and Skibbereen (Mary Lally) ; she was beyond all 
power to save her when I saw her, and she was in appearance a skeleton. The 
lands on either side of the road from Clonakilty to Skibbereen are sown with 
wheat and oats, and look well ; but westward from Skibbereen there is scarcely 
a trace of tillage of any sort. We have had only 20 men on the' Ratooragh 
district, there being no room for more ; five of those are now sick. 

On the Owenkeagh district, the men that heretofore earned Yid. per day 
cannot now make more than 10 d. per day ; such' is the effect of the high 
price of food that men are not able to work. I have advanced them \d. per 
yard (the work is in that forward state that I am able safely to do so), and 
yet there is no improvement in their wages ; the truth is, the men have lost 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



159 



their strength ; how can it he otherwise ? A little half-boiled meal and water 
is their whole support (Indian meal). They cannot wait to have it well boiled ; 
many of them have not fuel to boil it with, although turf is very plenty there ; 
but then, when creatures have to occupy all their time in procuring food, they 
cannot afford to save even as much turf as would do them for a week. 

There is no hope for the people here ; you cannot rid them of the idea that 
they must starve. No poor man has either heart or strength to sow his field, 
even if you give him seed ; so certain are they that death will take them before 
they could see it above ground. 

In fact, Sir, you can have no remote idea of the truly fearful state of things 
now passing in the west of this county. 

In the priest’s parish of Clonakilty (you are aware the priest’s parish is much 
more extensive than the regular defined parishes, sometimes embracing three or 
four of those properly defined), which comprises the parishes of KilgarrifF, 
Clonakilty, and Kilmanus, and a population of about 13,000 persons, during the 
last week alone 60 children and 30 adults have died from want of sustenance ; 
this I have from good authority ; that is, about ttt of the gross population of 
the parish for one week, and I believe the mortality is progressing. 

Immense numbers are leaving the country as they best can. There is no 
hope in any direction for the great mass of the people ; it is the Almighty only 
who can now redeem them from the truly awful fate of starvation. Every 
Drainage W ork, I am certain, must be stopped, unless you procure aid from the 
Relief Department ; it is plain that when a man cannot work from want of 
strength, and the engineer in charge of the work is bound to a certain figure, 
that he must stop the works, or else exceed his estimates, and exceed everything 
connected with it ; and this will make matters worse as far as the poor are 
concerned. 



Mr. Fitzgerald to Mr. Mulvany. 

Ferbane, February 28, 1847. 

I have yours of the 25th instant, and hasten to give you a general view king’s county. 
of the state of this part of the country ; and hope, in a short time, to be able to 
give you a detailed account. 

The people are generally very quiet ; indeed, they are not able to act other- 
wise ; and, with the exception of some few cases of sheep and cow-stealing, there 
has not been any violation of the laws. 

With respect to the future crops, from what I can learn, the quantity of wheat 
sown is less than the average of former years, in consequence of many of the small 
(five acre) farmers being unable to • sow it ; and, on a rough estimate, I should 
think that about one quarter of the district is occupied by this class of farmers, 
averaging about five acres, nearly all of whom are unable to sow their land, and 
up to this time have made no preparations for it ; indeed, they seem so paralyzed 
in mind as well as body, that they are unwilling to look beyond their present 
wants, which are extreme, and which are but very scantily supplied by means of 
the Relief Works, whereon they are nearly dll employed. Their appearance and 
the colour of their faces is sickening to behold. 

The greater part of this class of small holders, if supplied with seed, would be 
unable to prepare the ground for it; and in many cases, I think, they would be 
tempted to grind and eat it if not prevented by some authority. They would 
supply the present wants, and run -chance for the future. I am of opinion thin 
unless these people are supplied with seed and the means of sowing it, the land 
will lie waste. , . . . ■, 

Perhaps there is no part of Ireland where there was so much land under 
potato crop as here, owing to the facilities for getting bog stuff, which, when 
mixed with other manure, produced good crops on this limestone soil. This 
year they have done very little in preparing that manure, as the potatoes are next 

*° I do’not know any landlord, with the exception of Lord. Ross and another 
small proprietor, who have taken any measures to enable their poor tenants to 
sow their lands. There are other proprietors who act like the besiegers of a 
town in “ starving them out cant their cows to-day, and get the tenants on the 
relief list to-morrow. I heard that three landlords acted m that way, and 1 
mentioned it before some of them.

There are very few of the resident gentlemen about here but let the most of 
their labourers go on the Relief Works ; and the labourers like it better, as they 
are paid ready money on the Public Works, which would not be so in some of 
the other cases. 

There are scarcely any potatoes for seed, and the very few who have any are 
afraid to plant them. 

I have heard of but one case of death from destitution in this barony (Garry, 
castle). He was an old man and lived by himself, and there is great reason to 
fear that he died of hunger ; but the people are dying fast from want of food and 
clothing, and fever brought on by bad. and insufficient food. They are wasting 
and dying by inches. If some proper measures be not taken, I fear the summer 
will be awful. 



Mr. Forsyth to Mr. Mulvany. 



CAVAN. 

FERMANAGH. 

LEITRIM. 



District Office, Belturbet , 

March 9,1847. 

I have been round the greater part of this district, and I have endea- 
voured, as much as possible, to ascertain, with accuracy, the condition of the 
population. I have entered into conversation with many in different parts, and 
I find I can add but little to the statements I formerly made. I shall go* over 
the same questions as before, and give such further answers as I can. 

1st. The actual state of destitution : — The portion of the population suffering 
from destitution seems now more separated from the other portions ; there is 
a more distinct line of separation between them. This portion is divided into 
two classes, — those employed on the Public Works, and those who have no 
means of support, but are wholly dependant on eleemonysary contributions. 

The former are very nearly in the same condition as I stated before. Mr. 
Pendergast, who is in charge of the thorough drainage in Leitrim, confirms 
this opinion. The labourers are not able to earn their usual day’s wages on 
the drains, at 4 id. per perch, for lack of physical strength ; however, what 
they have done, is very creditably executed. 

The second are now chiefly collocated in the towns and neighbourhood of 
soup kitchens, and present a most melancholy picture of absolute destitution. 

2nd. It is with much pleasure I state, that considerable activity is mani- 
festing itself among the farmers in the cultivation of the fields. The stoppage 
of many of the roads has aided much in producing this sudden change, and 
the farmers, willing to take advantage of the present very favourable weather, 
have encouraged the labourers to work for them by paying them every night. 
I enclose a letter of Mr. M'Gowan’s relative to this, and there are several other 
instances ; I have given instructions to promote this object as far as possible. 
Ihe smaller farmers, however, appear to have done nothing so far, nor indeed 
will they while they are loitering on the Public Works, and it is much doubted 
if they can unaided. 

3rd. From the agricultural operations now in progress, I think what I said 
before on the subject of seed, was nearly correct, so far as the larger farmers 
are concerned; but unless the smaller ones are aided, there is little hope of 
their ability or willingness to crop their ground. I have again visited the 
mills, they are grinding night and day, and from what I could learn, much of 
the poorer population are living on what was formerly preserved for seed. 

i he rumour of seed being furnished to them by the landlords, has done much 
to induce them to part with, or use, the little they had, and the great question 
with them all at this moment is, — when, or how far they are to be supplied. 

I have not been able to -find out that seed has been given by any of the 
landlords -worth noticing. Lord Erne has made some additions, to his usual 
supply of the best kmds of seeds, some for green crops such as he recom-

4th. From what I have stated above, it will he perceived, that the prospects 
in reference to the state of the people and country, are brightening. The 
weather is most auspicious for seed time, and the farmers are making laudable 
exeitionsto take advantage of it. If the same spirit spreads generally, and 
sui a i e ai e given to the really needy, with the blessing of propitious 

weather, we may yet venture to expect an abundant harvest.

Extract from Report of W. H. Mackintosh, Esq., Engineer in Charge, 
Barony Berehaven, County Cork, dated 15th February, 1847. 

Though I informed the Relief Committee that no persons could be 
allowed on the works but such as were on the Inspecting Officer’s list, they 
continued, especially Mr. Healy, to send notes to the overseers and stewards, 
requiring them to employ labourers. 

I was compelled to make an example of one steward, whom I dismissed and 
fined for receiving men in this manner. 

I have on no occasion received any assistance from the Relief Committee in 
the performance of my arduous duties ; and up to the present time they are, 

I assert it on the evidence of an eye-witness, knowingly putting down a larger 
family than the truth, in order to entitle applicants to employment for a 
second. 

The whole duty of revision devolved on the Inspecting Officer, myself, and 
my overseers and check- clerks. 

While Captain Gordon, 59th Regiment, remained, his sound judgment and 
business-habits kept the lists in order. 

I received most valuable assistance from the Earl of Bantry, who, through 
his agent Mr. Patrick O’Sullivan, of Mill Cove, in all cases used his immense 
influence in furtherance of the wishes of the Board. 

The Rev. Richard Wright, rector of Kilgaskan, who resides at Adngoole, has 
aided me much, and the lists compiled under his direction are the most regular 
in the barony. 

The system of task-work is now universal in this barony, the prices being 
written in the overseers’ books, -where any of the stewards can see it. 

The roads are over-crowded : the work could be done for one-third less if 
there were fewer men. 

The prices I assign for the tasks are enormous, generally two-thirds more than 
I could do them for at any other time ; but the people have not strength to 
work, and I thought it better to pay proportionably high than to have the 
dreadful scenes of other places here. 

I have been much inconvenienced, and much valuable time has been lost, in 
consequence of a habit most prevalent in this barony, viz., the malcontents 
writing reports on every trivial occasion. While Captain Gordon, 59th, was in 
office, this habit had nearly died out, but it has now arisen with fresh vigour: 
this annoyance the Relief Committee could put a stop to, but instead of that 
they are urging it on. . . 

I would take the liberty of suggesting to the Board, that, from an intimate 
knowledge of the Relief Committee during five months in this barony, it is my 
decided opinion that, from their continual disunion, arising from sectarian 
difference, it would be unsafe to confide to them the distribution of relief 
under the new system.

Lieut.-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, 
February 25, 1847. 

I am just returned from the county of Down ; I was glad to see as I 
travelled that the farmers had still stacks of corn in their haggards, and were 
winnowing their oats with the intention of sowing them, for which I saw a good 
deal of land prepared. Still the small holders were leaving their land un- 
touched. In many places I observed parties engaged in digging up the potatoes 
of last season, which were sound but small. From Down I was informed that 
the men are migrating fast to Scotland, leaving their families behind ; some few 
make remittances to their friends in Ireland. From all I can learn the small 
holders will not do anything ; they are content to get as much money as they 
can ; fearing to take farm employment lest they should not get paid, but that the 
value of their labour will be set off against the rent. In one district in Cork an 
attack has been made upon the soup-kitchens, at Butterstown, the men consider- 
ing that the works will cease as soon as the soup-establishments are brought 
regularly into play. The pressure is heavy for employment.

Sir R. A. O’Donnell to Assistant Commissary-General Lister. 

Neivport House, February 22, 1847. 

Much has been said in Parliament and elsewhere condemnatory of the Irish landlords 
for not anticipating the present condition of Ireland. I therefore forward to you a few facts 
upon this subject, which prove beyond doubt that every exertion to prevent the usual quantity 
of potatoes beincr sown this year was used by the landlords of this district. I enclose a notice, 
dated the 9th March, 1846, which was circulated by me ; and to induce my tenants to give up 
planting the potatoes, I procured 70 tons of seed oats, which I gave to them upon 12 months’ 
time, at the rate of 6s. 9 cl. percwt. I enclose a second notice, of the 17th March, 1846, to 
the tenants of the Marquis of Sligo, as also my own, by which you will perceive that flax seed, 
clover, vetches, &c., and 80 tons of guano, were provided for the use of our tenants, to enable 
them to anticipate the present crisis, but what was the result; the seed oats in very many 
instances were taken upon credit from my stores, and sold to the merchant by the tenants, and 
at this moment the money is still due for the oats, flax seed, clover, vetches, and guano. 

Inis year 1 again procured seed wheat for my tenants, and having prevailed upon a few of 
them to prepare their land tor the seed, I gave them at the rate of 14*. per cwt. at 12 months’ 
time, and although the ground was prepared for the seed, they did not sow it, so that 1 had to 
stop giving out any more to them. 

I have a farm of 60 acres now out. of lease ; it was let on lease by my grandfather to one 
person ; I find 13 families at present upon this farm, 3 of which are solvent, and 10 are 
paupers ; they refuse to give up possession. I have offered to divide the farm amongst six of 
these fanuhes, and to give employment to others as labourers, or to give them land elsewhere, 
which they reject. I have offered them 100Z. to enable them to provide for themselves, as the 
60 acres are inadequate to support the 13 families, and to enable them to pay their rent; 
ported 7 afe determmed t0 hold the land ^though they will not till it, as they must be sup. 

These are simple facts of frequent occurrence, and knowing, as I do, the fixed determination 
of the vast proportion of the tenantry of this county to keep possession of the land, but not to 
famine^’ ^ CanUOt ° Ut ant,c, P ate as great a calamity the ensuing season as the present awful

Take Notice, that various trials having been made this season, the result of which prove the 
lamentable fact that the disease in the potato will be greater in the ensuing than in the past 
season, the tenants of the Newport estate are earnestly recommended by their landlord to 
plant no more than about one-half the quantity of potatoes they planted last year, and not on 
any account to trust to them for sustenance. 

Few can afford a risk in the article of food, but with you a certainty is indispensable. 

The disease in the potato is iu many instances impossible to detect, and therefore the seed 
you plant may be diseased without your knowing it. 

Oats is a much better food than potatoes, and can be relied upon. 

It is in any case a shame to plant your best land with the worst kind of food which the earth 
is capable of yielding, and under present circumstances it would be wickedness to do so when 
the danger that attends it is thus providentially discovered in time. 

Remember you and your families are deeply interested in this matter. I ask you then to 
meet this visitation with the energy and determination with which you meet other things that 
do not half as much concern you, and by your forethought and exertions turn this calamity 
into a blessing. 

The best seed oats; and every other kind of seeds necessary for the use of the tenants, to be 
had from your landlord at first cost price. And also, 80 tons of guano upon the same terms, 
and which is expected daily into Newport. 

(Signed) R. A. O’Donnell. 

Newport House , March 9, 1846. 

Notice to the Tenants on the Newport Estate. 

I recommended you last March not to plant more than half the usual quantity of potatoes 
for this year ; I now recommend you to plant, next month your small gardens with potatoes, 
deep and well manured, and if they do not succeed, you can sow oats, or something else, in the 
same ground next spring. 

I also recommend the tenants to keep a good supply of seed oats for next spring. 

(Signed) R. A. O’Donnell.

Abstract Constabulary Reports. 

February 24, 1847. 

Considerable rioting took place at Newcastle on the 18th inst, a 
number of persons having been struck off the Public Works who had been im- 
properly put on by the connivance of the check-clerk, who, being dismissed, 
led the riot and assailed Capt. Watson, the engineer. Mr. Locke, J. P., refused 
to interfere. One of the workmen arrested had 3/. 14s. 6 d. in his pocket. The 
people though so clamorous for work, are not destitute in this locality, save in 
some solitary cases.

Captain Labalmondierk to Mr. Walker. 

Killamey, February ‘27, 1847. 

I regret to have to report that a most wanton assault was yesterday committed upon 
Mr. Armstrong, engineer in charge of the Kilorglin District, by some of the labourers upon 
“ the Post road from Cahirciveen to Kilorglin, between the barony bounds at Diomar and 
Curreheen Bridge.” 

He was upon the work in company with Mr. Todd, engineer in charge of Iveragli barony, 
and having expressed some dissatisfaction at. the manner in which the work was done, and that 
it must be done over again, he supposes that the labourers thought they were to do it again 
without payment, for as he proceeded along the line, a crowd of nearly 200 came after him 
knocked down the steward, attempted to stop them, and struck Mr. Armstrong with their 
spades; and as their violence increased he took to flight, and got shelter in the priest’s house 
at Glenbigh, amid a shower of missiles. The crowd remained around ike bouse for some time 
but at length dispersed, and he, having an appointment with me iu Kilorglin, returned there 
this morning and reported the attack. 

I have directed the suspension of the work, and, if the ringleaders can be identified, that 
warrants shall be taken out against them. 

I shall proceed there next week to endeavour to establish order, and set on the work again. 

The peasantry of that locality have the reputatiou of being very wild and lawless.

Mr. Trevelyan to Lieut.-Col. Jones. 

March 2, 1847. 

■ The excessive rate at which the relief expenditure is proceeding, and 
the apparent absence of any effectual steps to bring it under control, have 
attracted the serious attention not only of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, but 
also of other members of the Government, and I have been desired to write to 
you on the subject. 

We are called upon to provide funds at the rate of 40,000/. a-day for the 
Relief W orks alone, and this is in addition to the expense of the establishment, 
to the Commissariat expenditure, and to the expenditure under the new Com- 
mission, which, if some decided measures are not taken, will soon overlap, to a 
fearful extent, the expense of the Relief Works, which it was intended to 
supersede. 

Sir Charles Wood requests that you and your colleagues in the Board wiU 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



167 



take this most critical and important subject into your early and serious con- 
sideration, and submit, in accordance with the instructions with which you have 
been already furnished, your view of the measures which ought to be taken to 
bring the Relief Works to a close; and in doing this, it is desired that you 
should act in the closest concert with Sir John Burgoyne, as well on account 
of his excellent judgment and long experience in such matters, as because the 
early closing of the works is mainly dependent upon the gradual organisation 
of the relief machinery under the new Commission. 

It is impossible for me to describe in too strong terms the degree in which 
the public credit and safety are considered to be involved in your Board acting 
with firmness and decision in this matter. 



Captain Fishbourne to Mr. Trevelyan. 

JEnnistimon, Clare , February 25, 1847. 

I delayed writing till I had seen the most part of the county. 

I am quite convinced that there is no destitution in this county that might 
not be met by half the amount of employment which is now given in the 
county were the proper objects lor employment selected, which I regret to say 
is not the case ; thus, for instance, within these few days Captain Gordon has 
removed 244 from the lists at this place, but before we could arrive at the 
information necessary to effect it, we had to sit down and do the work which 
ought to have been done by the Committee before a man had been put on the 
work. These were men in comparatively comfortable circumstances, while 
there were many starving who were not on the work. The fact that the 
generality of the Committees will neither furnish us with the information to 
enable us to revise the lists, nor do it themselves, leaves no room for any other 
conclusion than that they have some interest in continuing the abuses. Indeed 
it could hardly be otherwise, as the class of persons who are frequently found 
on them are not independent ; thus, for instance, in the Clondegad district of the 
Ennis Union two Poor Law Guardians and ex-officio members had them- 
selves placed on the Public Works in charge of gangs, and one of these was 
removed only a few days since, and a large proportion of those mentioned as 
being removed from the Ennistimon lists, had from 15 to 30 acres of land and 
stock. There are many on the lists in the barony of Burren who are valued 
under the poor-law at from 12/. to 60/. ; the most melancholy feature about 
which is, that they are kept there by the Committee to the exclusion of starving 
people, and who would have starved hut for the assistance of neighbours. The 
Bally vaughan Committee have been told, three times or more, that the works 
would be stopped if they did not send in their lists, and yet without effect 

I would suggest that the new Bill should not be tried in any parish till a 
complete census of its population had been completed, containing the state and 
circumstances of every individual as nearly as could be obtained ; then if each 
person in the parish who gave employment would testify to the Committee 
how many he would employ, all the work of the Committees might be done 
without the collection of crowds which invariably intimidate the weak, and 
occasion disaffection and idleness. 

The Committees now take upon themselves to put many upon the works 
with a large average as poor men, and thus perpetuate a pauper tenantry, 
though they make the poverty of the tenantry as an excuse for the unimproved 
state of many parts of the country. There are large tracts of this country, that 
could be vastly improved at a very small cost, in the hands of men with no 
capital, therefore practically unproductive, men who are so miserable that a 
little disco uragemeut in one way, and encouragement in another, would induce 
them to emigrate ; these, by work, and especially the task-work, in the long 
days, are enabled to cling to this miserable existence ; there are an immense 
number of these upon the property of Baron Richards. 

I may add, that the task-work system is now working very much against the 
farmers, and if continued, will have the effect of preventing much agricultural 
work from being done, for farmers dare not take a man off the works against 
his consent. 

When I came to Clare I found the Committees contemplating a meeting to 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




168 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



petition the Government to give them seed, labour, and manure, so I drew up a, 
scheme to raise 14,500/. amongst themselves, which if turned twice would 
realize 25,000/., and purchase sufficient seed for such of the farmers of Clare 
as needed any such assistance ; this had the effect of turning their thoughts to 
county exertions. Yesterday they met, and Sir Lucius O’Brien proposed that 
this collection should be made, if at all, by parishes, in order to bring home to 
each the necessity of individual exertion ; they are beginning to see the evil of 
undue interference, particularly with a people amongst whom there exists such 
an idle and mendicant spirit as amongst the lower order of Irish ; nothing can 
be wiser than in each case making them take the initiative ; Mr. Malony of 
Kiltannor, the largest proprietor in the large parish of Feakle, is of opinion that 
that part of Clare is the best off, and in this I agree with him, and he accounts 
for it by saying that they were least interfered with. Very large tracts of this, 
(that is, Feakle,) are sown with corn ; indeed there is a larger proportion of 
wheat sown in this county than usual, though there is a deficiency in some 
parts from an idea, I think, that they would have had seed given to them. 
The amount of tillage is daily increasing, and but for the Public Works much 
more would have been done ; as a proof of this I may mention that the most 
is in Ruan, barony of Inchiquin, where the works were stopped in consequence 
of auoutrage that was committed. 

There is much wheat and oats still in the county. I should say not much 
under 100,000 barrels. 

There is no indisposition to sow potatoes where seed is to be had, as I 
have seen them preparing land for them in different parts of the county. 
Turnips are becoming much more general. 

Infinite credit is due to Colonel Wyndham for his exertions to obtain a 
better mode of husbandry amongst his tenantry, and for the way in which he 
has had the market of Ennis supplied. Notwithstanding the sums lie has laid 
out, he is going on with extensive works in draining, fencing, building, &c., in 
several parts of the county. He deserves anything of his country that can be 
given him, for none can know the difficulty of effecting any improvement in 
Ireland except those who have tried it. A gentleman desirous of assisting his 
tenants, but at the same time of insuring that his plan should be carried out, 
purchased a quantity of seed wheat and steeped it in a solution of sulphate of 
iron ; they all said that they would sow it until they heard that it had been 
steeped, when scarcely one would take it. 

A judicial blindness seems to have visited the people. The people are 
refusing Is. per day, Is. and food to work with the farmers, and 7s. a-pair for 
horses to plough, also 10s. per ton to draw meal 12 miles; they have forsaken 
the fisheries, with few exceptions, though every facility is given them to go to 
fish, and to return to the Public Works when the weather is unsuitable, but no, 
every productive work is rejected for that of the Public Works. There is a 
very large capital deposited in the several banks which would be invested in 
land immediately if there was an opening. Undefined expectations now buoy 
the people here up, and prevent their emigrating, and the land from passing 
into the hands of persons who have the means of cultivating and improving it. 
It is thought that it will be sown, and I believe it will be so to a considerable 
extent, not generally by the present holders, but by being let for the crop, thus 
prolonging a little the miserable state of things and in an aggravated form. 

We are in the anomalous position of “meal going up while corn is going 
down,” owing to the great deficiency of mill power, but this lias increased with 
the demand, and several small mills have been rebuilt and enlarged ; a per- 
manent increase of mill power will be required, to meet which, Colonel Wynd- 
ham is going to build. Any undue interference of the Government or others, 
by introducing meal largely into the country, would have prevented the enter- 
prise which was called out in these mills, and which has rendered such signal 
service in keeping the price of meal down by relieving, in some measure, the 
pressure from the Limerick and other mills. 

Soon after coming to Clare I found it necessary to issue a circular, with the 
hope of inducing the Committees to do their duty, but I regret to say the 
attempt was unsuccessful; indeed, there is generally an entire want of con- 
fidence manifested by the people towards the Committees, they believing that 
it is only from the Government officer they can expect justice. 

I must be understood when speaking of distress as alluding to that which is 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



169 



recent and severe, and not meaning to underrate the amount of distress which is 
long-standing, for masses of the people have evidently been for a long time 
only one remove from destitution, so much so, that I have no hesitation in 
saying, that where the family does not exceed three, and one of these only on 
the work, they are better off than they were before the failure of the crops. 
There can be no doubt of this where they are earning high wages, as some of 
them are, for instance, 2s. 4 d. per day. 

Since I commenced this letter the weather has been more favourable for 
agricultural pursuits, and I was glad to observe a great increase of persons in 
the fields. The engineers continue in some parts of the country to employ a 
large number of horses to the great injury, I am sure, of agriculture ; thus at 
Newmarket, or Fergus, I requested the engineer not to employ more than he 
could possibly help, and yet a few days after he made a requisition to the Com- 
mittee for 28 additional horses. 



Captain Gordon to Lieut.-Colonel Jones. 

Office of Public Works, Macroom, 
February 17, 1847- 

My time has been taken up until very lately by Relief Committees per- 
sisting in calling on me, and after each and every one stating they would not 
delay a minute, all asking the same question, all requiring that employment 
should be given at one and. the same moment of time in every district, taking 
into no consideration the necessary work there to be performed in regard to the 
works already in hand, and the arrear I had placed on my shoulders, the total 
want of experience of my officers (good in every other respect) with regard to 
relief operations, task-work, &c. When works were opened, and an increase of 
employment offered (although entailing by the opening of fresh accounts more 
work on myself and assistants), you would suppose that every encouragement 
would have been given, and every facility afforded, but on the contrary, I was 
opposed in every direction. The magistrates on three different occasions only 
inflicted Id. fine for obstructing my surveyors. One case (the first) was under 
very aggravated circumstances, and a poor man in defending the surveyor had 
his head cut to pieces with stones ; this assault case was (as usual) compromised. 
The obstruction case, however, was adjudged as I above stated. The magistrates, 
Mr. Massy and Robert Waller, promised to be very severe the next time, but 
no such thing has been done, and the fine of Id. was inflicted. There is 
no doubt that all the subsequent opposition I have met with has arisen from 
the mistaken leniency of the first case. In fact, I knew persons who intended 
physically opposing a line were present at the first trial, and did so oppose 
afterwards. I wrote for the stipendiary magistrate, Mr. Little, after the first 
case ; he could not arrive in time for the second trial, and the third sessions 
he wrote to say he would come if he were well enough ; he did not appear 
however. You may conceive the great delay that was occasioned when I tell 
you that, at the first case, myself and one of the engineers had to attend ; the 
second, myself and one of the surveyors, my two valuators, the overseer, and 
two head stewards of the road. No. 101, had to attend; the case was postponed 
to the next sessions (February 3), and all had to attend again ; and at that 
sessions came on the third case, when another of my surveyors had to come 
away from his work ; this last case was on No. 50 road, Cl ondrohid parish, which 
Mr. Kyle has written so much to the Board about. How can there be other- 
wise than delay ? of course I lost a great deal of the ground I had gained after 
working night and day, and payments are in arrear three or four days. I can 
only say that I will still work as hard as I can. I have only been in bed twice 
since the 24th January, and. many a night sat up without sleeping a wink even 
on a chair. I think by to-morrow I shall have answered all the correspondence 
referred to me. 

I forgot to mention that the case I was summoned on relative to wages caused 
me no little delay. Surely parties could be prosecuted on the authority ol the 
cautionary notice of the 19th September, in such a case. I reported all to the 
Board, and answered a reference of it, with solicitor’s memorandum thereon, 
three days ago.

Extract from Report of William Hyde, Esq., Inspector of Finance, 
Dungarvari, February 22, 1847. 

I regret to find that agriculture is not more attended to, the poor people 
infinitely prefer -working on the roads to labouring with the farmers. This is 
most unfortunate, and will be productive of future evil. 

Wheat is sown more generally than is supposed : the grass corn looks well 
where the ground has been properly cleared out ; potatoes are not thought of, 
except by the gentry, and very scantily by them. A few nights since Mr. 
Walsh, an ex-pay clerk, resident at Kilmacthomas, and a large and wealthy 
farmer, had a field of potatoes rooted up, which he had sown four days’ pre- 
viously. This was done by people of the place, and for the sake of the food. 
Kilmacthomas is, however, one of the most distressed parts of this country, and 
has been always notorious for its wretchedness. 

The new arrangements will, I trust, relieve much of this misery. If it were 
possible to supply the people on the works with soup and porridge a great 
benefit would be gained, and at no increased cost ; a tally or ticket handed to 
the check clerk would be an offset to the corresponding value in pay ; without 
employment, the people, though fed, will be worse off' than before ; the transi- 
tion to comparative idleness is by all means to be avoided. There is an apathy 
to all farming operations, and the ground is neglected where potatoes were 
grown, and failed last year. In many places the blighted crop of the past season 
has neither been dug or ploughed out, and the surface presents the same black- 
ened appearance it did in September last. 



Lieut-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, February 27, 1847. 

We are not now paying for labour, but paying money to enable the 
people to feed themselves. The prostration of strength in many incapacitates 
them from earning a fair day’s pay, and the consequence is that they are only 
entitled to a small sum, or else they are paid subsistence without a return 
for it. The task-work system, or the one nominally so styled, must soon be 
exploded. 

Eight thousand of the lower class crossed from Dublin to England in the 
month of January by the city of Dublin steamers. 



Lieut.-Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public TP orks, March 2, 1 847. 

The extracts from the officer’s journals will show the state of things in 
this country. The accompanying letter from Mr. Barclay, the county surveyor, 
King’s County, gives a very correct account of the state, feeling, and conduct of 
the peoplex generally. The patience and submission of the lower classes must 
be regarded as an extraordinary and remarkable feature in the character of a 
people so easily excited to acts of violence and bloodshedding. 

There is a great outcry in regard to the small farmers not doing anything in 
the way of tilling their land. It is true to a great extent ; but the farming 
operations this year will not afford the same amount of employment, as is 
ordinarily the case. The preparation of the land for potatoes has ceased, and 
the farmer now turns up his land with a plough to save the expense of the 
labourers, which he would otherwise have had to employ; this will affect 
us throughout the summer by the lesser demand for labour. All the small 
farmers, I understand, are looking to the Government for seed.

Lieutenant Gekenwell to Mr. Walker. 

Listoml, March 1, 1847. 

In reply to the accompanying inquiry, I have to state, for the information of the Com- 
missioners, that my Report that many persons are daily being added to the hundreds who 
have perished within the last two months, in consequence of the insufficiency and change of 
food, “ especially to the west of Dingle,” was dictated by my own actual observation and con- 
versation, and was not “merely a loose expression,” as the following particulars will clearly 
show, viz. : — Mr. Adams, the engineer in charge of Public Works, barony of Corkaguiney, 
wrote to me at Listowel, stating that in the parish of Ventrv, 40 persons had died in one week, 
and 26 in Dingle. On going to Dingle shortly afterwards, I. made special inquiries concerning 
the distress, and was informed, on the best possible authority, that from 6 to 10 persons died 
daily in the parish of Ventry; and the Protestant clergyman stated, that since the month of 
October, no less than 800 persons had perished or fled the country ; the population, as given 
by the census of 1841, being under 3,000. Kilquane parish is in as bad, if not a worse con- 
dition. Dunarlin, Duneguin, and Kilmalkedar, are also very badly situated. Funerals are 
continually to be met with on the roads, and most of the labourers are so debilitated as to be 
unable to work by measurement. 

The remark, before committal to paper, was well considered, and, had it been withheld, I 
should justly have brought rebuke upon myself for neglect of duty. 

If my former reports on the barony of Corkaguiny be examined, it will be found that I have 
always given a fearful, yet, I believe, truthful account of its condition and prospects.

Lieutenant Hamilton to Mr. Walker. 

Parsonstoim, March l, 1847. 

With reference to my weekly Report of yesterday’s date, I beg to acquaint you that I 
called this morning on Hutchinson Vaughan, Esq., D. S. of Golden Grove, 23 of whose 
labourers have left his employment. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




172 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



Mr. Vaughan showed me his labour-account book, by which it appears that he has given 
employment to between 30 and 40 men daily since this time last year ; sometimes makin? 
work for them, and giving them lOd. a-day, both on wet and dry days. 

In addition to this, he has a soup kitchen for his labourers. 

Mr. Vaughan then accompanied me to the Relief Work at Coolroe, from which I selected 
the best men for him, and dismissed the father of one and brother of another man who had been 
in Mr. Vaughan’s employment ; telling them, as they had quitted it voluntarily, I could not 
look upon the family as destitute, and consequently they were not objects for the Relief Works, 
which are only intended for those who cannot procure employment elsewhere. I told the men 
that if they give the least trouble for the future, or any more people should strike for wages 
that moment the Relief Works should be stopped. 

Some of the men who left Mr. Vaughan have been employed by a Mr. Bergin at Is. a-day; 
but I think, when he has done with them, and they find it not so easy to get on the Relief 
Works, they will discover the mistake they have made in not remaining with a liberal and a 
constant, employer. 

I have not heard of any labourers having followed these men’s example. Mr. Vaughan is 
of opinion that the steps taken to-day will deter them from so doing. I hope so ; particularly 
as he has shown much determination and firmness on the occasion. 

I may take this opportunity of mentioning, that the power conferred by his Excellency the 
Lord Lieutenant’s letter of the 16th October, 1846, has been of great benefit in preventing 
insubordination on the Relief Works in this county, and to show that it has not been abused, 
only one instance has occurred of its being put in force ; and then it was had recourse to bv a 
Relief Committee, of which Sir Nicholas Fitzsimon, one of the magistrates of the Head Police 
Office, was the chairman, pending a reference to me ; and that neighbourhood (Blue Ball) has 
been quiet ever since.

The number of labourers during the month has varied from 19,939 to

labourers, and one check clerk for every 280 labourers, or on an average for

being on an aver age* for each of the 24 working days Is. per labourer. 

This average sum includes women and boys, who are paid less than men ; 
the daily wages of 8 d. are only paid when the work is not performed by task, 
which every effort is made to introduce, and they are above the ordinary wages 
of that comity, which are 8c/. in summer and only 6 d. in winter. 

The Board have received representations from their officers, as well as from 
individuals, that 8 d. is too low a sum at the present prices of provisions, but, on 
the other hand, the Board are urged to use every effort to prevent the labour of 
the country from being absorbed into the Relief Works, to the injury of agri- 
culture, and they have preferred meeting the case, by allowing additional 
members of families to be employed, rather than by making a general advance 
of daily wages, still leaving the task-work open. 

It cannot be doubted that from weakness many of the labourers are unable 
to work by task, and it is earnestly to be hoped that the new measures for relief, 
without the medium of work, may speedily be introduced.

Captain Gordon to Lieut.-Col. Jones.

I must go to Ennistimon again to-morrow, as I can really do nothing with 
that Committee, and cannot get correct lists ; in fact, as I have often stated> 
there is not one Committee in my district that has acted upon the instructions, 
and the Ennistimon Union worse than any. At this present moment, there are

Extract from the Report of John Long, Esq., Engineer, dated Athlone, 
February 26, 1847. 

In the parts I visited south of Athlone, the distress does not appear to be by 
any means so great as in the districts northwards. -The Relief Works and soup 
kitchens appear to have done all that was necessary to meet the distress, or nearly 
so. In the north of Longford, in Leitrim and Roscommon, the relief afforded is 
quite deficient 5 I attribute this a good deal to the want of soup kitchens, and 
in the Rooskey and Boyle districts, to the low pay they are receiving on the 
works, there being, as I understand, but little task-w r ork, and the wages only 
8 d. per day, which is the lowest standard in any part that I went through. 
Besides the population were always in a greater state of destitution, and there 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



175 



was, I consider, a greater destruction of the potato crop. Altogether the star- 
vation appears to lean with a very heavy hand in this part, and the deaths are 
numerous. 

In general, I think the farming operations are not so backward. Tillage is 
stealing on gradually, and ploughing is now, I would say, very brisk. I do not 
expect that there will be less field labour this year than hitherto, in the culti- 
vation of grain crops. The plough is more used than manual labour, and as a 
good deal of grain will now be sown, where potato would have been the crop, 
I fear the demand for manual labour by the farmer, will be much less than 
hitherto. As regards the potato crop, there appears to be a prevailing desire 
among the people to try them again this year, a notion that I think ought to 
be discouraged as much as possible, for it is nothing but a hazard with the 
chances greatly against its success. The landlords appear to wish to try them, 
but even with them it ought to be deprecated, for although able to bear the 
loss, if a failure should occur, yet their sowing them will encourage others less 
able to bear the loss, and besides if extensively practised, will create a general 
deficiency in the harvest produce. 

I trust I have not written with too much length, but having made a few 
observations in going through the country, I thought they might be acceptable. 



Lieut. -Col. Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public TVorks, Dublin, 
March 4, 1847. 

With reference to your letter of the 2nd instant, calling the attention 
of this Board, to the large expenditure daily incurred for the Relief Works, 
apparently without any effectual steps having been taken to bring its increase 
under control, I beg leave to state that the subject has for some time engaged 
our serious consideration, and on the 22nd ultimo, we issued a circular, No. 66, 
requiring all our officers and engineers, to use the utmost vigilance in scruti- 
nizing the lists of men sent to them by the Relief Committees. This duty, we 
believe has been sedulously attended to : but the fact is that nearly all the 
Committees have abandoned the duties which they were expected to perform, 
turning loose upon our officers, every man, woman, and child, who applies for 
relief. If the officer refuse them employment, he is then told that their deaths 
will be laid to his door ; and the deaths are rapidly increasing. Under the 
existing state of the country, and the pressure that is put upon us, we do not 
see how we can do otherwise ; circumstances have forced this upon us. Our 
officers shall again be directed to use their utmost vigilance in scrutinizing the 
lists, and enforcing work, so far as the declining strength of the people will 
admit ; but we see no chance of abating the evil, until the new system of relief 
under the new Acts shall be brought fully into play. W e have made a commu- 
nication to Sir John Burgoyne and the Commissioners, upon the subject of your 
letter, and I had an interview with his Excellency upon the subject. It is 
scarcely necessary for us to add that every post brings numerous representa- 
tions for works to be ordered, so as to afford employment for additional num- 
bers ; and we would request the special attention of their Lordships to our 
last report, which explains fully our proceedings during the past month. 



Enclosure. 

Circular, No. 66. 

[Relief Department.] 

Sir, Office of Public Works, February 22, 1847. 

The operations of Government being about to undergo a change, by which relief will 
henceforth be administered in food, instead of through the medium of labour, it is more than 
ever necessary that the lists furnished by the Relief Committees should be thoroughly scruti- 
nized, so that none may remain upon them, who either possess, or can obtain a maintenance in 
any other way. The inspecting officers are therefore requested to use every exertion for this 
purpose, not only by removing from the lists the names of every one not entitled to be placed 
upon them, but by taking every opportunity of pointing out to the magistrates and gentlemen 
with whom they may come into contact, how materially it is for their interest to employ as 
many labourers as possible, even independently of the urgent necessity for tillage with a view to 
future crops, so that they may obtain some return for their expenditure, inasmuch as all who 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




176 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



WICKLOW. 



are not employed, and therefore destitute, will be fed at their expense. The Public Works are 
drawing to a close, and it is very important that the number who are now crowded upon them, 
for the purpose of relief, should be reduced gradually, by the absorption into private employ! 
ment of as large a number as possible, because, as soon as the new measures are in operation, 
the Public Works must be executed creditably and economically, employing only the able! 
bodied, and of them only so many as are necessary, by which the remainder will be thrown 
wholly upon the proprietors themselves, either to be employed, or, as the alternative, fed at 
their expense ; and as this state of things must soon take place, it is manifestly the interest of 
all parties that it should be effected gradually, rather than by the sudden discharge from the 
works of all who are not wanted.

Mr. Boyle to Mr. Walker. 

Engineer's Office, ArJclow, 
February 25, 1847. 

I have the honour to request that you will be so good as to lay before 
the Commissioners of Public Works the following report, which I beg to say 
is founded on facts which I have observed, and information which I have 
acquired, while visiting, during the past fortnight, every district of this county. 

Within the period referred to I have attended two Extraordinary Present- 
ment Sessions, attended an influential meeting of the gentry of Upper Talbots- 
town, and met at the assizes the grand jury of the county, before whom, as a 
body, 1 laid the present condition of the county with respect to food and tillage, 
with the view, if possible, of urging on them the absolute necessity that exists 
for an immediate effort being made to provide for the food of another year. 

The results of my inquiries have in almost every department of society been 
such, as, in my humble opinion, to render it imperative on me to submit them 
for the consideration of the Commissioners of Public Works ; and I feel the less 
hesitation in doing so from the anxiety, yet absence of all intention, on the part 
of the landed gentry to combine in making the powerful effort which is now 
called for, and must within the next six weeks, if ever, be exerted in promoting 
the tillage of the land by the small farmers,” i. e., by those holding from 3 to 
12 or 15 Irish acres. 

While I state this with respect to the gentry of this county, I am bound to 
add that a high sense of honour, and of humanity and benevolence, has uniformly 
characterized their proceedings since the Relief Works w r ere first entered on, 
and that while they presented most liberally for the relief of destitution, they 
on all occasions evinced a determination to exercise a prudent restraint and 
economy, and manifested an intention to keep good faith with Government as 
to repayment of the sums advauced. So far as respects myself, they have, with 
scarcely an exception, spared no exertion in assisting me and in co-operating 
with me to an extent that I could not have expected or hoped for. 

But unfortunately for the comitry, its peculiar physical formation is such as 
to render its districts on either side of its mountains more like two counties 
than portions of one, and as many circumstances tend to vary the condition of 
the people on each side, there is but little unanimity on country matters among 
the gentry of the eastern and western sides of the county. They therefore 
rarely act in unison, and unfortunately, on the present occasion, their anxieties 
and discussions relative to a subject on which all felt alike terminated without 
any plan being contemplated. 

I fear from what I have stated that tillage by the small farmers, who of 
course constitute in this country the great majority, will be but very partially 
resorted to ; for, taking the county as a whole, there is not more than one-half 
of the usual seed, and as this county in but a few isolated spots grows wheat, 
the amount of food that so far has been, or is likely to be provided for, will 
fall far short of that which is required. 

_ Potatoes, I need scarcely remark, are almost extinct, but turnips will in some 
districts be extensively cultivated. 

The ‘ large farmers,” that is, those of from 15 to 20 Irish acres and upwards, 
are now beginning to exert themselves, and will sow probably more than usual, 
but they constitute in this county a small proportion of the community. 

They are mostly in much better circumstances than they have for some years 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



177 



been ; that is, they have money, for they took advantage of the high prices to 
thrash off and sell their grain, hut they have little food, and haggards are very 
unusual among them. They have been the least useful, least humane members 
of society during the present calamity, rather making a pretext of it for with- 
holding assistance or giving employment, than coming forward when called on 
to assist the gentry, even in affording facilities in the drainage of their lands. 

Destitution is rapidly creeping up among the less extensive farmers. To my 
knowledge there are men with six acres of land, and possessed of a miserable 
cow, and perhaps, also, a donkey, who, while they have rent and taxes to provide 
against, are at this moment as much objects for relief as any peasant on our 
works. There are many hundred such cases. How can these be expected to 
till or sow ? yet they will not give up their land ; and I feel assured that many 
of them would not permit their landlords to cultivate for them. 

An impression prevails among the small farmers that the Government will 
sow and cultivate for them, and this without any exertion on their part. Among 
the labourers the idea has already gone forth that they all are to be fed and to 
be permitted to idle. 

The feeling of dependence, so comfortable to an Irish peasant, has completely 
seized the small farmers and labourers, and nothing could at this critical period 
of seed time have proved more unfortunate, for it has tended to check and 
destroy any remaining spirit of industry and exertion. 

The conversations among the labourers employed on the works very frequently 
excite the idea that there is a purpose in their evading agriculture or agricul- 
tural employment, and that when so many even in the same work have died of 
starvation. It is strange, but true, that hunger possesses no horrors for them. 
Daily do numbers faint on every extensive work, and more than 30 men have 
died, some actually on the work, others in returning from it, yet they do not 
seem to care or to feel. 

One fact is evident, that no labourer will, if he can avoid it, accept of em- 
ployment in preparing for the food of another year. 

I very much fear that there is a systematic determination in the south of this 
county, and towards Baltinglass, not to cultivate ; there is, I know, a hope that by 
leaving the land untilled, the farmers will have it either at lower rents or at no 
rent. There has for some time been a sort of organization in progress at Wex- 
ford, and it has within three weeks extended to that portion of the barony of 
Ballinacor South which joins the comity W exford. Whether it exists elsewhere 
or not in Wicklow I cannot say, but this I can state, that so well aware are the 
large farmers that this system exists among the labourers, that they dare not, 
in most districts in the west and south of the county, take a man from the Public 
Works, “less the houses should be burned.” 

Recruiting parties have for many months been stationed in Baltinglass and 
ATklow, the two great seats of misery in Wicklow, yet scarcely a man has been 
induced to enlist. In Arklow, during eight months past, only two men have 
entered the service, yet the young men are as badly off as the old. No man 
w ill enlist, for all look forward, as they express themselves, “to better times, 
resulting from some great event which they do not seem to comprehend. 

I cannot but regard the condition of some parts of the county, especially that 
of the town of Baltinglass, as extremely critical. There are in it, and within a 
circle of half a mile around it, 500 men who are employed on Relief Works. 
For not quite 200 of these will there be agricultural employment. They are, 
generally speaking, a most dangerous and inflammable community, chiefly con- 
sisting of the rejected from other districts and counties, bound by no ties of 
connexion or character, living on a property where there is neither a resident 
landlord nor agent. 

In summer they earn some money by cutting turf, and during the hurry of 
the harvest ; during the remainder of the year they idle, steal, and beg. I 
cannot contrive two months’ work for them ; with great difficulty can I make 
out employment for even a week ; yet these men fancy they must and 'will be 
fed. Nothing could be more dangerous than to leave them to go about unem- 
ployed. I am quite convinced that to establish the proposed private depot of food 
at Kiltegan (four miles distant) without affording suitable protection, would be 
but to tempt a foray from the rabble of Baltinglass from one side, and from the 
wild and starving people of Moyne and Imale on the other. 

The countrv gentlemen are willing to subscribe most liberally for the purpose 
[b. w r . 2.] 2 B

BOARD OF WORKS. 



• 

of introducing food into the district of Kiltegan ; hut to do so without having 
provided protection would be most imprudent. 

What to do, or how to act under existing circumstances, the country gentle- 
men know not : they are as it were paralyzed. Some difficulty interposed to 
defeat every proposed plan for promoting tillage ; this remark particularly 
refers to the south and west of the country. The season of seed-time is now 
arrived ; yet it will proceed, and probably pass over, before anything be deter- 
mined on. Even in the great Fitzwilliam estate, embracing one large barony, 
two-thirds of another, as little (if not less) is being done in husbandry as in any 
part of Wicklow. In these baronies, with a population of 29,000, there are 
2903 men employed on Relief Works. The mortality is great, and rapidly 
increasing, and the labourers cannot return more than 4 d. worth of work for 
Is : see my reports for Carnew of 15th February. 

Under the circumstances which I have related, the season of seed-time having 
now arrived, our prospect is worse than our present condition. As destitution is 
increasing, and as unwillingness to till the ground on the part of some, and an 
apathy on the part of the majority of the community prevails in this county, 
I have considered it to be my duty to lay the facts before the Commissioners 
of Public Works.

Mr. M’Cloy to Mr. Boyle. 

Barony of Upper Tallotstovm, Fcbmary 20, 1847. 

Having very carefully examined every part of this barony, both as regards tillage, seed, 
food, and the condition of both farmer and labourer, I now beg to lay before you my report 
thereon for your information. 

1 . The district of Donaghmore and glen of Imaal. 

In this district the small farmers have tilled very little, nor are they able to do so ; they 
neither have seed nor food, and are not able to buy. The larger farmers have a fair quantity 
of land tilled, and a little bere sown, but very few of them have seed, and they are not able to 
buy. There is not more than one-third enough seed and one-eighth food in this district. 
Many of the small farmers and labourers are very much reduced and quite unlit for labour. 

The people of this district get food from Dublin. 

2. District from Donaghmore along the valley to Kilranalagh, lying between the coach road 
and the mountains. 

This district the small farmers have, very little tilled, nor are they able : they have neither 
food nor seed, and many of the larger farmers have very little tilled as their land is much under 
pasture. There is a small quantity of bere sown, and looks very well. The quantity of seed 
and food is very small in this district ; the average of seed would be about one-fifth and food 
about one-eighth. 

The small farmers and labourers are in a very poor condition, and their strength very much 
reduced. This district gets food from Dublin and Baltinglass. 

3. The district of Stratford, Rathsallagb, Ballymane, and Prangear. 

In this district there is a large quantity of wheat and some bere sown, and a fair quantity of 
land tilled, and many of the small farmers are well off, both for seed and food. All jhe tenants 
of Mr. Pennefeather and Mr. Saunders, and many of Mr. Carroll’s, have both seed and food ; 
and as a large portion of this district is tilled by gentlemen and gentlemen farmers, there is not 
much want of seed here: yet there are a great many who are and will be “ill off for food.” 
Many of the labourers are much reduced. There is about one-third seed and one-sixth food. 
This district is supplied from Dublin and Baltinglass. 

4. The district of Timoran, Baltinglass, Kiltegan, and Rathdangan. 

In this district there are a great, many small farmers : nearly all of them are very poor, and 
have neither seed nor food, and, of course, have tilled very little, and many of them are posi- 
tively starving. Some of the large farmers and gentlemen have sown some wheat, and here, 
and have some laud tilled for oats, but on a very small scale, and there is not one-third of the 
land tilled in this district that should be. There is about one-fifth seed and about one- tenth 
food enough in this district. 

The labourers and small farmers are in a most awful condition in this district, generally, 
having neither food nor clothes ; and many of the middle-class farmers are very badly off, and 
will have to sell their cows to buy seed and food. The greater part of this district is on the 
verge of starvation, and not able by any means to till the land. 

hood obtained from Dublin and Carlow. 

I may here remark, that there is a great want of energy even with those that have the means 
of tilling the land, and if there is not an effort made by those who are able to have their land 
tilled and sown, we may dread the consequences of next year. I may also remark, that the 
poor are very peaceable and patient under their sufferings at present, although many of them 
are starving.
