, Lieut.- Colonel Jones to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Office of Public Works, March. 3, .1847. . 

I had hoped to have sent with our report a statement showing the sums 
certified by us to the grand juries at the present assizes, but the 'certificates 
themselves not being all prepared prevents me from doing so. ,1am glad to 
be enabled to inform you that, so far as the assizes have proceeded, there have 
not been any objections, although the county surveyor was strictly examined 
with a view to discover mischarges or mistakes. 

The accompanying report from Captain O’Brien, who was sent down to make 
some inquiries in the neighbourhood of Sligo, shows a lamentable state of the 
people. Without the addition of famine, their social condition must at all 
times have been wretched in the extreme.. From Sligo to Ballyshannon it is 
like a rabbit warren. 

Mr. Kincaid lias sent me a very interesting paper, showing how very light 
the taxation to meet advances will be ; and he gives in a tabular form, attached 
to it, a schedule, based upon the valuation of the county of Longford, with which 
he is well acquainted. Such a document should be printed with our report, as 
it will show, in its true light, the burdens thrown upon proprietors. 

We are now entering the month of March, and from all I hear, and from 
all the accounts we receive from the country, the small holdings will not be 
cultivated. It is no use preaching to the people ; their minds are made up 
that Government must feed tliem, and they will therefore not exert themselves, 
as they say, for the benefit of their landlords. It is melancholy to reflect 
upon such a state of things. The assizes are passing, where the wealth of the 
counties is brought together ; and what has taken place ?— nothing as regards 
the improvement of the condition of the people, who are dying around them, 
but much in condemnation of the Government measures. 

I was told this morning, from an undoubted source, that there is not a piece 
of sea- weed to be picked up on the coast west of Skibbereen — all taken away 
for food by the people living adjacent to the coast.

I send you a return, which will show the operations of the Labour Rate Act in this LONGFORD, 
county, and which, I think, most satisfactory as tending to prove that the burden may be made

so light upon the counties by the extension of the time for repayment to 22 years, that it will

and that a moiety should be remitted, and payment of the other moiety accepted as before at

which one half would be payable by the tenant, and the other half by the landlord, or only id. 
per pound to each.

annum, with 5 per cent, interest, and that the assessment should be, say IO 5 . in the pound on 
the ordnance valuation, the tax would be on an average of the 10 years, from 6 d. to 9 d. per 
pound; and if the assessment should be 205. in the pound, the tax would be from Is. to lj.6d. 
per pound per annum for the 10 years, of which one half would be payable by the tenant, and 
the other half by the landlord. 

The Poor Law valuation being generally higher than the ordnance valuation, the tax will be 
somewhat smaller than the above rates. 

I think the publication of this would be useful, as tending to allay unnecessary alarm.

Captain O’Brien to Lieut.-Colonel Jones. 

Dublin, March 2, 1847. 

SLIGO. Having proceeded to Sligo, in compliance with the Board’s orders, dated 20th, I be- 

came aware that great destitution existed in the northern part of that county, especially in the 
barony of Carberry. I therefore acceded to the desire of Sir Robert Gore Booth, that I 
should personally satisfy myself by inspection of the exact state of affairs there. 

The first place I visited, was a wretched hamlet of three cottages, with outhouses, containing 
three families, numbering in all 32 persons, belonging to three brothers; the whole having 
lived on 12 acres of land, which they had inherited from their father, who, when a young man, 
had obtained a lease of the 12 acres for a period of lives. They lived on the potatoes, they 
drew fuel from a neighbouring bog, for which they paid little or nothing, and they paid their 
rent by raising a little corn, and by the sale of a pig. Last year, they thought themselves so 
well off, they refused to take 60/. to give up the lease and depart. N ow they are starving, I 
visited the locality on the 25th of February, in company with the Rev. Mr. J effcote, the Pro- 
testant clergyman of the parish. One of the brothers, and three others of the families, had 
died during the previous week. The widow was lying on the ground in fever, and unable to 
move. The children were bloated in their faces and bodies, their limbs were withered to bones 
and sinews, with rags on them which scarcely preserved decency, and assuredly afforded no 
protection from the weather. They had been found that day, gnawing the flesh from the bows 
of a pig which had died in an out-house. 

This was stated to me by Mr. Jeffcote. I saw the pig, I believe the fact. 

On the 27th, Sir Robert Booth took me to a place, called the tf Sands/’ situated on the north 
shore of Sligo Bay. It takes its name from the following circumstances. 

Within the last 25 or 30 years, it was thought to be the finest land in the country, but lately 
the sea sand has swept over it, as it has done on the French coast to the westward of Boulogne, 
and along the Belgian Coast, by Nieuport, Ostend, &c., rendering the soil utterly unpro- 
ductive. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



181 



The “ Sands” embraces about 450 acres, and contains 60 huts, or thereabout, scattered over 
it, with a population of five to each hut. The sand has drifted to the tops of the walls of the 
huts, and in many places has accumulated, so as to be almost even with the ridge of the roofs. 
The entrance is by the old door-way, from which a sloping passage is daily cleared to the 
surface of the surrounding sand, and it is impossible to enter without crawling on hands and 
knees. The door is kept constantly shut to exclude the drift of the fine particles. Windows 
there can be none ; hence the inhabitants are in darkness, even in noon-day, during the greater 
part of the year. Some of the families have been there since, previous to the land being ren- 
dered unproductive. Others are squatters in these burrow-holes, when deserted by the original 
inhabitants. Hitherto they have lived by fishing, by cutting turf from a neighbouring bog, and 
selling it with marine sand for manure, in the town of Sligo, by conacre on the firm ground 
within two miles of them, and not a few of them by theft. 

The ground is the property of a Mr. Gethan, whose means I was told, are totally inadequate 
to render them any assistance. 

With Sir R. Booth, I went into five of these huts indiscriminately, in fact just as they lay in 
our path. 

In the first, into which I crawled with difficulty, lay a coffin holding the owner’s wife, who 
had died three days before, of want. The owner stood near the door, having come from the 
" Public Works” (where he had been earning 8d. per day) to see to burying his wife, and he 
told us he was about to depart “ to dig a hole to put her in, and try and get a couple of men 
from the works to help him to carry her there." A skeleton of a living child was in a cradle, 
in a corner near the turf fire. A woman, a neighbour, was sitting by it, and rocking the cradle, 
and said it would be dead before morning, and added, (truly !) “ It would be better if we were 
all dead." The child ’3 cradle, and a broken table, comprised the entire furniture. 

The door of the second hut we came to, was shut. We called, and knocked. A voice an- 
swered from within. The door gradually opened, and out of this hole, appeared the head of a 
man. By degrees we saw his body, as he crawled into the light, and knelt down in the door- 
way, his head touching the upper framing, that is the eaves of the roof. His face and lips 
were colourless. His entire clothing consisted of a dirty coarse shirt, in shreds. When he 
saw us, he called out “ Send for the priest to me ; I will be gone before morning ; I am dying 
of the starvation.” In answer to our questions, he said, " he could do nothing, he could not 
go to the works ; his belly was all swelled, and he had bad pains all through it to his back. 
Sir Robert Gore Booth asked him if he had. any one to send to the meal depot, which was two 
miles distant. He called a little girl from the hut, but when Sir Robert was giving her direc- 
tions where to obtain half a stone of meal, the man cried out., “ Can you give any bread, I will 
be dead before the meal comes, give me bread now ; there is a shop not a mile off; give me a 
bit of bread now." I doubt that he is now alive. 

From the door of the third hut, which we stopped at, came a tall strongly made man, fol- 
lowed by a woman with a child in her arms, and two little girls. The child in arms was 
evidently dying. I asked the man if he had been at work. He showed me his feet, and asked 
me how any man could work with feet in that state ; they were so swelled, the skin appeared 
ready to burnt ; the soft-yielding sand permitted him to walk, where I saw him ; he could not 
have moved a step on the hard road. He had within the previous week buried his mother and 
his sister. 

Into the fourth hut we came to, we crawled backwards on our hands and knees. On a bed- 
stead with a little straw over it lay a man covered only by an old quilt; his face was so 
swollen his eyes were scarcely to be perceived ; his feet and ancles also much swelled ; his 
knees and thighs, which he showed, wasted to the bone ; “ his belly swelled up too; his wife 
was cowering over an iron pot, suspended above a turf fire, with a young child in her arms. 
Three other children were sitting about, and a young man was preparing a fishing-line. The 
father showed his limbs, and said he believed himself to be dying ; the mother held up the 
infant, bared its body, and discovered to us its little bones almost starting through the skin. 
She made the other children turn their faces to the light, which came in at the door-way, and 
made us observe how they were “ swelled with starvation." She put aside her own petticoat, 
which she told us she had that morning borrowed from a neighbour to go out with decency to 
beg or borrow a little barley, and showed us the only garment she possessed, which was the 
remains of a green stuff petticoat, but so much in shreds as not to conceal many, and consi- 
derable portions of her fleshless legs. The young man said, he was going out to fish m the 
morning, as he hoped to do no more in that way, to “ stop the starvation, than he could by 
earning 8 d. a-day on the Public Works. I asked what was in the iron pot; the woman 
answered that it was the barley she had begged in the morning. She stirred up the liquor 
with a ladle ; we could see no barley, save a grain or two ; the liquor was not more nourishing 
than so much hot water. , 

The fifth hut was on the verge of the Sands, and not buned as were the others. ^ I here 
was evidence that things here had been better at no very distant period; the dresser, and a few 
odds and ends of crockery were clean, but the effects of famine were more perceptible even 
than in the other huts. The family were eight in number. Where the father was, I do not 
remember, but, I am almost sure that, whether alive or dead, he rendered them no assistance. 
The mother was lying on the ground huddled near the fire, attenuated and moaning. 1 wo 
lads of the ages of 16 and 18 in a bed, where they had been for two days, not able to go to the 
Public Works, upou which they had been previously earning 6 d. each ; and they presented in 
their thin limbs, swelled and yellow faces, and sunken eyes, the unquestionable eflects ot 
famine. The only healthy person of the family was a daughter, probably 22 years old. bhe 
told us she had been on the Public Works earning 6 d. a-day; but as that was nothing among 
so manv, she thought it better to stay at home, and mind the sick in the house.

Beyond this district to the westward is the large and populous village of Ballyconnell ; I did 
not go there, but I was told it was scarcely better than “ the Sands.” To the north, as far as 
Cliffony, matters are scarcely better; and, I was infortned, the same sad tale was to be told of 
nearly every place in the baronies of Carbury and Rosclogher, except where provision has 
been made by Sir Robert Booth to feed the people. 

Sir Robert Booth’s estate is large, and the supplies he has procured would keep those of his 
own well enough, were he not pressed also to feed his neighbours’ tenants. At his own place, 
Lissadele, he has established two soup boilers, which make each 140 gallons of soup, and I 
calculated the cost of the soup in each boiler to be about 3'2 j. Crf. He gives, gratuitously, 
280 gallons of this soup per day, every day including Sundays. He sells, six days in tfie 
week, 150 loaves per day, each being 4 ounces larger than the 4 d. loaf sold in Sligo, and 

sold by him at. 2d. per loaf. He also sells 30 tons of Indian corn per week at a reduced price, 

and gives a portion of Indian corn to about 30 persons daily. 

In this manner he has provided for the poor, and sold through the agency of his chaplain, 
Mr. Jeffcote, since the 29th of August : —

Much good would be done if the Government could assist Sir Robert Booth* in having this 
large quantity of food transported into Sligo. What, he has done for the part of the country 
where he resides, has been so well done, that it would prove a real blessing to enable him to 
do more. 

I understand that he intends to write to Mr. Redington on the subject. 

From what I have stated, it is no exaggeration to affirm that, in the baronies I have alluded 
to, the people are dying from starvation by dozens daily ; but. for Sir Robert Booth they would 
be dying by scores — by fifties. Immediate relief is necessary to save a remnant. Many cannot 
crawl to the Public Works, much less do anything when there. 

• Food is what they require. 

In the neighbourhood of the poor-house they come in to die in order that they may receive a 
decent burial. 

Typhus fever and dysentery have added their horrors. Besides cases in the fever hospital, 
there were in the Sligo poor-house on the 24th of February, 208 cases of fever, and 145 of 
dysentery. The master of the poor-house and his tour sons, the matron and her daughter, the 
schoolmaster and his assistant were among them ; eleven had died during the previous night ; 
the matron is since dead. 

On my return Irom Sligo yesterday afternoon the driver of the mail coach told me that when 
coming in at nine o’clock that morning he was passing Hollybrook, about seven miles from 
Boyle, he saw in a field close by the road the body of a man who had fallen and died there the 
previous evening. He said that it had remained there all night, somebody having thrown an 
old cloth over it, and that we should probably see it as we passed. When we did pass, how- 
ever, and made inquiry, we were informed that it had been removed at one o'clock by some 
persons who took it away to bury it at once. The man was from Boyle, and he was known to 
be in a state of starvation. 

I do not hesitate to say that I believe such events to be of no uncommon occurrence in several 
parts of the country, I have made three tours of inspection in the south, and one in the north- 
west of Ireland since the middle of last December. It lias been my painful duty to mark the 
progress of destitution, and I have seen it. gradually going on till it has arrived at its present 
height. The faces ol the people are visibly altering for the worse; and strange as it may 
appear, it is nevertheless true that the beggars who frequent the streets of the towns do not 
show in their countenances the traces of want which are visibly depicted in those of the men, 
women, and children who are congregated on th e Public Works in the remote districts.

Gibbon Raleigh, a check clerk on the Public. Works at Gortsken, was

up his books. Their object was to force him to make false returns. The

Lieut. Inglis to Captain Larcom. 

Limerick, March 3, 1847. 

A man named John Hogan of Adare has complained that in consequence 
of the death of his daughter he was dismissed from our works. 

To show you how incorrectly, and how unjustly these statements are made, 
and how wrong it would be to believe all that is said of our mismanagement, I 
■will give you the real facts of the case. 

On the 24th October last, John Hogan was recommended by the Adare 
Committee, and almost immediately after, was returned by us for employment, 
his family at that time consisting of four persons altogether. 

On the 3rd November his daughter died. 

On the 16th November, his son was returned for employment, somewhat, I 
think, by an oversight of the Committee, as our regulations do not admit of 
more than one person being employed in a family of less than five members. 

In the beginning of January, Mr. Langley, who has the contract for the mail 
coach road, complained that he could not keep the road in proper repair, be- 
cause all the men he had upon it, had left him for the Public Works, although 
he had raised their wages from KM to Is., and he particularly begged that six 
men he named, might be ordered back to his work, and accordingly I at once 
dismissed, by an order dated 10th January, as many of these men as I could find 
upon the works, and John Hogan as one of them. 

Hence it is evident that he was not dismissed on account of his daughter’s 
death, for after his daughter’s death, an additional member of the family was 
taken upon the works, and he himself was not dismissed until more than two 
months after his daughter died, and not until he had an opportunity of getting 
employment elsewhere. 

I saw the man myself the other day, and he refused to explain his grounds 
for the assertion that “ there were instances to be found in the locality of people 
“ who had both land and corn, with money in the savings bank, working on 
“ these roads, having been sent there by their landlords.” 

He is not by any means a poor man, and I have heard, on very good autho- 
rity, that he has something of an “ independence.” 

It is a gieat pity that these statements are set forth before some inquiry is 
made as to their correctness. This memorial from John Hogan, was written by 
a schoolmaster of very questionable character, living in Adare, who went upon 
the works not long ago, offering to write a similar document for any more who 
would remunerate him to a certain amount, and the fact of its having been 
made public, has been regarded in this district as a great triumph. 

Whatever may have taken place in the division of the county of Limerick, in 
the way of mismanagement, nothing, I am sure, approaching to “ determined 
oppression,” can be imputed to us. I am extremely sorry to have troubled you 
with so long a letter, but I am anxious, at least, to remove from the minds of 
the Commissioners, any false impression that may have been made.

Captain O’Brien to Mr. Walker. 

Board of Works, March, 5, 1847. 

In compliance with the directions of the Commissioners, conveyed to 
me in your letter of the 24th of F ebruary, that I would inquire into and 
report upon the circumstances alluded to in a paragraph of the “ Dublin 
Evening Post” of the 23rd of February, taken from the “ Sligo Champion,” 
and headed “ Jobbing on Public Works f I endeavoured, while in Sligo, to 
ascertain whether or not there was any foundation for the statement re- 
ferred to. 

With the general allegations that “the Board of Works is humbugged,” 
“ the Government cheated,” “ the poor defrauded,” &c., &c., it is quite impos- 
sible to grapple. A general assertion can only be met by a general assent, or 
a general denial, neither of which can carry conviction. 

The particular allegations resolve themselves into : — 

1st. “ The sons of magistrates,” “ of grand jurors,” “ of parsons, &c., &c., 
are quartered on the public.” 

2nd. “ Two men overseeing seven labourers.” 

3rd. “ The poor are neglected, plundered, and robbed. In many instances 
" their miserable stipend of 8 d. a-day is so long "withheld that they sink down 
" exhausted by the wayside and die Government creditors, while the sons of 
“ grand jurors and of parsons are drawing their 21. or 3/. a-W’eek.” 

The first and third allegations clearly apply to the pay-clerks. With respect 
to these allegations it became my duty to inquire who the pay-clerks w r ere, 
and how their business w r as conducted. 

It is quite true that among them are to be found the sons of a clergyman, 
of a magistrate, and possibly of a grand juror ; but it must be remembered 
that a heavy pecuniary responsibility is attached to the situation of pay-clerk, 
and in every case two securities are required, each in the sum of 400/. Hence 
none but persons of approved integrity can be appointed, because they alone 
can find solvent sureties. They must also have a knowledge of accounts. 
Hence a certain extent oi education is necessary. Respectability of character 
and position are therefore absolutely essential to the successful aspirant for 
such a situation. Again, if simply “ jobbing ” were the object of the indivi- 
duals so employed, it must be presumed that they would “job” for more 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



185 



remuneration and less labour. Whereas their toil is considerable while their 
-wages are comparatively small. For example, Mr. Sherlock has to come into 
Sligo, a distance of 22 miles, every Saturday for his money; he begins to pay 
the men at the different works to which he is attached on Monday, finishes on 
Thursday, and has only Friday to make up his accounts. 

Mr. Thomas Yeates commences to make his payments on Saturday, and 
finishes early on Thursday, sometimes beginning his labours at a distance of 
seven or eight miles from home, as early as the men appear at work, and con- 
tinuing them till 9 or 10 o’clock at night, having afterwards six miles to go 
home. On Friday he makes up his accounts. 

Mr. Richard Yeates commences his payments on Monday, finishes on • 
Thursday, being out from 6 o’clock in the morning till 9 o’clock at night, 
travelling upwards of 30 miles each day, having Friday to make up his accounts, 
and Saturday to obtain his money. 

For this toil the pay is 21 . per week. 

The sons of a clergyman, to whom the paragraph in the “ Sligo Champion” 
evidently refers, are the two Mr. Yeates, whom I have mentioned. Their 
father, the late Mr. Yeates, was a clergyman of the highest respectability, who 
died, leaving a family so poor that a subscription was entered into in the 
county. The sons are respected by all classes ; and I have the testimony of 
Sir Robert Gore Booth, of Mr. Wynne of Hazlewood, and of other gentlemen 
resident there, that their character is particularly high. I must say, that I have 
seldom heard of two gentlemen who have met with more sympathy and respect 
from those who have known them from their childhood. 

Mr. Whelan is the son of a stipendiary magistrate, he is a gentleman who is 
quite respectable, and I am told not wealthy. 

Mr. Neynoe is the second son of Mr. Neynoe, of Castle Neynoe, who, I 
believe, has been on the grand jury of Sligo ; but so far from this gentleman 
“ enjoying the fat of the spoil,” as stated in the newspaper, he labours hard, 
gives high security, and is under great responsibility for a very small salary. 

Among the remainder are gentleman who hold and cultivate land, and there 
are two officers of the militia. But can the duties which these public servants 
have to perform be entrusted to individuals who are themselves mere objects 
of charity ? Assuredly not. It is a mere waste of time discussing such a 
question. * 

The appended list of pay-clerks shows the districts to which they belong, 
the dates of their appointments, and the times when they commence and finish 
their weekly payments. 

The week’s labour in the county of Sligo terminates on each Wednesday. 
The necessary returns are made to the Board of Public Works on Thursdays. 
On Fridays the money is transmitted from the Board. It is received by the 
pay-clerks on Saturdays, and on Mondays, no later, they are required to com- 
mence the payments to the respective gangs. But it frequently happens that 
some of the pay-clerks have small balances in their hands on their accounts 
current ; and when this is the case, they are enabled to pay the labourers out 
of those balances without waiting for the remittances from the Board. 

That the payments have been made at the times' stated in the return I have 
the assurance of Mr. St. Leger, the county surveyor, and of Captain Kelly, the 
inspector of finance. And I beg to draw the attention of the Commissioners 
to the testimony borne by the latter officer, in the accompanying letter, to the 
efficiency, zeal, and respectability of the entire of the pay-clerks in the county 
of Sligo. ... 

In these circumstances, therefore, I can hold but one opinion, viz., that the 
statement contained in the paragraph as regards the characters of the pay- 
clerks, and the way in which they discharge their duties, is unfounded, and it 
was said and believed by gentlemen of respectability in Sligo, though I am not 
prepared with absolute proof of the fact, that the attack made upon these 
gentlemen was the result of some individuals, certainly one individual, having 
been refused by the Board’s officers to be recommended for the situations ol 
pay-clerks in that county. 

With respect to the statement, “ We saw two men overseeing seven labourers,” 

I need only say that on Sunday last, the 28th ultimo, the editor of the 
“ Champion” told Captain Gilbert, the inspecting officer, he had made a 
mistake, inasmuch as when he happened to pass where some labourers were at

Captain Gordon to the Relief Commissioners. 

Ennis, March 5, 1847. 

Since, my arrival in Clare as inspecting officer I have used every 
endeavour to turn all farmers off the works, and I am sorry to say I have 
received no - assistance from the gentry or Committees (except in a few 
instances) to effect this object. 

The consequence is that little or no tillage is going on in West Clare, and I 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 






BOARD OF WORKS. 



187 



would therefore respectfully urge the necessity of compelling the Committees 
to turn off all parties holding land, or furnish the inspecting officer with the 
information that he may do so. 

I am borne out in this by two facts, viz., that in the parish of Ruan, where 
the works were suspended, there is far more cultivation than in other parts of 
the district, and also by seeing the land being tilled in Clondegad, near a 
work that has lately been suspended, whilst the country around is quite 
neglected. 

A strong circular would have great effect to gain this object ; and a rate of 
wages should be named in order that the farmers may be able to procure 
labourers at a fair rate of wages. 



Captain Gardiner Fishboukne to the Chairman of the Relief Committee 
of Kilmurry. 

Ennis, February 27, 1847. 

I am sorry to find that many of the persons on the lists for public work 
in the parish of Kilmurry are relatives, tenants, or tenants of employers of 
members of the Committee of that parish, and these persons have been placed 
on the lists by the Committee, while they have omitted a considerable number 
of those who should have been placed there, because they were in actual 
necessity of relief, having no other resource or means of subsistence than em- 
ployment on Public Works. (See 19th Art. of “ Instruction to Committees.”) 
In justice to the poor who have been thus set aside, I must say that the Com- 
mittee cannot but be held responsible for many of the deaths which have 
occurred in the parish, and also for much of the destitution which now pre- 
vails. Some one or more' of the Committee may be partially exculpated, but 
not wholly so, unless he protested against such gross injustice, and, if persisted 
in, represented the case. 

I would take this occasion of again urging upon the Committee the necessity 
of making collections for the relief fund, and of immediately commencing a 
soup kitchen, with the funds in hand. Strange to say that where, in the county, ’ 
most exertion is requisite, least should have been made. 

I trust the Committee will see the necessity of setting a suitable person to 
make a census of the parish (perhaps the collector of taxes or poor-rate) ; the 
census to contain the age, average state and circumstances of each individual, as 
correctly as possible. 



Mr. Teely to the Inspector-General. 

Cahirciveen, February 27, 1847. 

It has been this evening reported to me by the constable in charge at 
Glenbegh that an attack was made yesterday afternoon on Mr. Robert Arm- 
strong, the Board of Works officer superintending the Public Works in the parish 
of Glenbegh, by the men employed on the new road between Claliane and Bal- 
linakilla. On coming there he found fault with the manner in which the 
work generally was being done, and particularly the fences. After a little 
time, seeing that they were collected round him in a menacing manner, he was 
proceeding to leave the place, when one of them gave him a blow with a spade 
on the thigh ; upon which he made for the priest’s house as fast as he could, 
pursued by about 200 people, throwing stones' after him. Mr. Armstrong says 
he has the names of several of them from the stewards; but the constable states 
he does not seem inclined to take any proceedings against them.

How to expect the overseers to get value for the expenditure on the

Enclosure. 

DUBLIN. Copy of a Report from R. H. Frith, Esq., County Surveyor for the County Dublin, dated 

February 28, 1847- 

Herewith 1 beg to transmit through you to the Board my monthly report on the 
Relief Works in my district, and in pursuance of the instructions in circular No. 64, of the 
15th instant, I beg to accompany same with a few general remarks on the state of the works, 
and their effect on the labouring population. 

During the past month a considerable proportion of the people employed on the Relief 
Works have been removed to the Drainage, now going on in the district. I do not find any 
difficulty in this transfer being effected, as represented in Circular 22 of the Boqrd, a copy of 
which has recently been forwarded to me from the office in Dublin, as owing to the stringent 
system of task-work whicli I have succeeded in carrying out, the men readily go to the drainage 
or other farm-work when required. I have had the satisfaction of detailing in former reports 
the progress then being made in this respect, the difficulties to be encountered, and the effects 
of the system on the habits of the labouring classes ; and I am still glad to be able to state 
that the Relief Works in this district have not tended to demoralize the working population 
by encouraging habits of indolence, of which we hear so much in all quarters. In corrobora- 
tion of this statement, I beg to transmit, for the information of the Board, a letter which I have 
received on the subject from a clergyman in my district, the Rev. Mr. Potterton, whose testi- 
mony cannot fail to be regarded otherwise than highly satisfactory. 

I still find that the labourers employed in cutting Jarristown Hill do not make adequate 
wages at the rate which I have allowed for the work, although by proper exertion I am satis- 
fied that it is sufficient. Before making any alteration in this respect, however, I may mention 
that I intend to make a change in the allocation of the overseers, as 1 expect that by placing 
Maguire in charge of this work, he will be able to so arrange and assist the men as to enable 
them to earn competent wages, and, if 1 succeed in this, I shall consider any trouble I shall 
have had regarding it as amply repaid. In presenting my next monthly report to the Board, 
I trust that this work will not then be referred to as one in reference to which any difficulty 
exists. 

1 have further to refer with pleasure to the removal of all irregularities in the payments to 
which 1 was obliged to refer in former reports. From the short time available for making up 
the accounts, so that the whole of the people might be paid on Friday and Saturday, we ex- 
perienced considerable difficulty in the first instance in effecting it; but through the active 
co-operation of my assistant, Mr. Johnston, as well as that of the several check clerks, I have 
succeeded in removing the difficulty, and there is now no irregularity in the payments. Mr. 
Johnston and the check clerks are usually engaged during the whole of the nights of Thursday 
and Friday in making up the accounts for the pay clerks for the following days ; and it is only 
doing justice to Mr. Crawford to state, that he gets through his portion of the work so as to 
afford entire satisfaction, and thereby aid us in accomplishing this important object. 

_ Lush Glebe, February 24, 1847. 

Dear Sir, 

I am much obliged for your subscription to our Lusk Relief Committee, and in returning 
you thanks for the same, I cannot help adding, you ought to receive the thanks of the entire 
, neighbourhood here, for the public good you have accomplished in altering the habits and, I 
may add, the feelings of the day labourers. 

I have heard it remarked by members of our Relief Committee, that the system of piece- 
work which you have so efficiently carried out, notwithstanding the many difficulties you hal 
to encounter in so doing, has done more good in teaching the labourer the value of time, than 
anything that has taken place in this locality for years. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



189 



At all events, from my knowledge of tlie poor of Lusk, which is not a little (after nearly 12 
years’ residence), I can assure you, your piece work has drawn a line of demarcation between 
the indolent and industrious, that I trust will tell upon both parties, as encouragement to the 
latter, and as reproach to the former. 

I wish all Ireland could be dealt with only on the piece-work system, and I think we would 
soon see a different race of people. 

I am, &c.j 

E. H. Frith , Esq. (Signed) John Potter ton.

In regard to the first, viz., inspecting officers, there is little 
their duties with Relief Committees have continued the same. 



now to record ; 
The increasing 



destitution has, in many places, rendered impossible the rejection of any con- 
siderable number of applicants, and the only limit has been the impossibility 
of finding works adequate to the increasing numbers with the rapid falling out 
or completion of the existing works. The reports of the officers speak for 
themselves, and the country looks with the utmost anxiety for the introduction 
of the new measures. 

On our part, we have endeavoured to make such arrangements as may tend 
to facilitate the transition. We have at once transferred the greater part of 
our inspecting officers to the Relief Commissioners, who have stationed them 
as nearly as possible in the same localities in which they were before serving, 
so that they may continue to act for us as long as our connexion with Relief 
Committees continues ; but the Committees themselves are also on the point of 
being changed, and as these changes will not only be changes of persons but of 
districts, from the Poor Law Unions, which are to be the new limits, not being 
coterminous with baronies or parishes, which are the present limits, there will 
be temporary danger of confusion in the supply of labour to the works. Every 
exertion must be made to encourage private employment, but the people evince 
no readiness at present to avail themselves of it, nor will it be wholly practi- 
cable at once to convince them that the works which remain in progress are no 
longer to be considered merely as Relief Works. Even the magistrates and cess 
payers will represent that as their presentments were for the purpose of relief 
they have a claim to consider them as still available for that purpose, while it 
will be difficult even for us to judge how much of the falling short of an esti- 
mate is due to original defect in the estimate itself, and how much to the 
crowded and defective labour with which it has been executed, and hence 
claims for a continuance of the half grants, and even of free grants, will ■ 
doubtless arise. 

We do not, however, anticipate any serious troubles on these points, or indeed 
any which care and foresight may not prevent or remedy ; we only advert to 
these here as in some degree incidental to the change from a system of relief 
by labour to one without that test, the first step of which has necessarily been 
the removal of that class of officers on whom we chiefly depended for the deli- 
cate and important duty of interposing between the pressure of the Committees 
and the freedom of the works, and we cannot close our report of inspecting 
officers without a strong expression of the obligation we feel to them for their 
labours.

BOARD OF WORKS. 



191 



The employment of military officers was a bold experiment, and it has been 
perfectly successful. We were urged to appoint the gentlemen of the country 
as inspectors, and have been reproached for not doing so, and when the purely 
local nature and object of the relief was so obvious, the proposition presented 
itself most favourably. « There were numerous country gentlemen of integrity 
and ability most ready, and from the highest motives anxious to co-operate with 
us in that position. We should probably have secured local support among the 
influential classes from such appointments, and we gave the subject the fullestand 
most serious consideration. But there would have been some greater difficulties 
m the selection ; every appointment or removal would have been the subject 
of question and interest. It might have been difficult to satisfy all parties. 
The people themselves would have canvassed the appointments, and it would 
have been difficult to have produced the entire feeling of impartiality in their 
minds which they now have. We therefore considered that as the gentry and 
property of the country were represented in the Relief Committees and Pre- 
sentment Sessions, it. would be better to form the executive and administrative 
from persons looking only to the Government ; and the experiment, which 
began with a small number of officers of engineers, reporting on works and 
projects, had given such general satisfaction that we resolved to extend in that 
direction, and confine the class of inspecting officers entirely to military men. 

The prompt and perfect facilities afforded by his Grace the Commander-in- 
Chief, by the Master-General of the Ordnance, and the Commander of the 
Forces in Ireland, enabled us to bring the system into immediate operation, 
and the judicious discrimination exercised in their selection of officers, removed 
from us all further difficulty. To the known presence of military officers we 
cannot but think the comparatively orderly conduct of the immense mass of 
people employed is mainly due ; and when their numbers are considered, when 
we see more than 700,000 labourers daily drawn from their homes and fields 
and banded together upon the roads, and, with few exceptions, peaceable and 
orderly, the magnitude of the task requires no comment. 

We have found additional and increasing confirmation of the prudence of 
this course. The officers under great and constantly varying difficulties have 
been guided by one simple principle — duty. By the gentry and the people 
this w r as felt alike'. They may have been thought lax by the one, or stringent 
by the other, but no partiality or favour has ever been as much as attributed to 
any one. They have earned the good opinion and the confidence of all, and 
have added another to the many duties a British officer is liable to be called 
on to fulfil, and in which it has been said by that great authority to whom all 
look up, “ He must not only be always in the right, but always successful too, 
if he would escape blame.” 

The next great branch, the engineering, has undergone but little variation 
during the month. There can he no doubt the works will in most cases prove 
very expensive, but we have reason to believe that even this is far from univer- 
sal, and on a general review of all the roads which have been made or im- 
proved, there is no doubt many of the former class in the remote and mountain- 
ous districts, will be found very useful to the country, and of the latter, when 
the confusion into which they have been thrown, as well by the season, as by 
the work upon them, has been removed, and they are brought to completion, 
they will on the whole present a great amendment on their former state, while 
the thorough investigations to which the communications of the country have 
been subjected during the last few months, has furnished a mass of useful infor- 
mation, which cannot fail to be hereafter of general use. 

In the correspondence, attached to this report, there are as usual details of 
outrages and attacks. The works would indeed in many places appear as. it 
were to be carrying on in the presence of an enemy. At Newcastle, Major 
Watson and Captain Butler were attacked in the streets, Mr. Kearney, the county 
surveyor, again stands prominently forward, and in that turbulent county, it has 
again been necessary to suspend several of the works for a short time. This 
salutary power has alone prevented the still greater evil of withdrawing from 
some districts altogether. Our effort has in every case been to confine the pun- 
ishment as far as possible to the guilty, and the culprits have in consequence 
been occasionally given up to justice by their comrades. In West Muskerry the 
efforts made by one of our officers, Captain Gordon of the 75th regiment, to 
carry out a more regular system of employment, has not met with the support

which might have been anticipated. We have only further to state, under this 
head of engineering, that as the works may now, we trust, soon he expected to 
assume a more regular character, we are collecting returns, plans, and sections, 
as far as possible, of that has been done with the view of bringing the works to a 
creditable and economic close. On the important subjects ol payments, we have 
every reason to believe the arrangements detailed in former Reports, have become 
successful, and where they have been fully and fairly carried out, great regular- 
ity has been attained. There have been no robberies, and no defalcation hag ren- 
dered' it necessary to fall back upon securities. The system ol control in the 
pay inspectors, has been successful, and the organization and frame-work being 
complete, the number of payments, and amount paid, may be increased to any 
extent, so that greater or less promptness is now simply a question of expense, 
requiring the appointment, of more or less additional pay clerks to a district. 
Complaints of non-payment usually prove, on inquiry, to have arisen from the 
unauthorized intrusion of extra labourers on the works. 

F., p. 205. In regard to the reproductive works, under Mr. Labouchere’s letter, we 
have the pleasure to state that considerable progress has been made during the 
last month ; and that in almost every instance, the labourers have conducted 
themselves in a satisfactory manner, and the works have been executed at fair 
prices, considering the enfeebled state of the people, arising from want of suffi- 
cient food. 

The number of distinct Drainage presentments granted in 134 baronies, 
amounts to 386,607/. 19$. Ad. 

The actual number of works in operation, is 918. 

The number of labourers employed, is 16,161. 

And the sum already sanctioned in the favourable report of our Drainage 
inspectors, amounts to 152,370/. 4$. 9 d. 

The number of labourers employed is increasing, and would do so more 
rapidly, had it not been that greater exertion is required to earn good wages on 
the Drainage works, than on the roads, where, as we shall hereafter have occa- 
sion to remark, the task work is not so rigidly carried out ; in consequence none 
but able-bodied and willing men will leave the roads, unless forced to do so, by 
being struck off the labour roll, and when this occurs, the men, at least in the 
commencement, work unwillingly, and in consequence earn small wages, but 
when each man finds that a particular task is allotted to him, and that others are 
earning from 1$. to 1$. Ad., and 1$. Qd. per day, he gives his mind to the work, 
and endeavours to emulate his neighbours, and finds at the end of the week that 
his earnings are sufficient to support his family ; hence the labourers, when accus- 
tomed to draining works, are satisfied to continue.

In order to obtain the advantages to be derived from the Land Improvement 
Bill, now under the consideration of Parliament, several landed proprietors, par- 
ticularly in the counties of Down, Cavan, Wexford, and Limerick, have applied 
for loans under the Treasury Minute of the 1st of December last, and have re- 
quested permission to withdraw, or postpone their undertakings for Drainage pre- 
sentments under Mr. Labouchere’s letter, this circumstance, though acceded 
to, has caused some delay in the local employment of the people, which we hope 
will be soon remedied by the commencement of the Drainage works under the 
0 ., p. 226 . Treasury Minute. 

With reference to the particulars of the several Drainage presentment works, 
we beg to refer to the extracts given in the Appendix from the reports of our 
Drainage inspectors, but we may state generally, that the Drainage presentment 
works, in the northern counties, are being carried out in a very satisfactory 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



193 



maimer, the labourers executing their tasks willingly and successfully, and 
generally speaking, completing them at the rates usually paid for such works. 

In looking through the weekly returns for Drainage work done during the 
last month, we do not find much variation in the earnings of the labourers, 
which range from lOd.to Is. 6 d. per day, the average being Is. 2d. per day, but 
in every case where the labourers have been crowded together for the purpose 
of giving immediate relief, the work has been ill executed, and the earnings 
small ; on the contrary, where each individual has a weekly task allotted to 
him, and he is allowed to execute it, if he pleases, with the assistance of his 
children, we find good earnings and satisfactory results ; as by this arrangement, 
if the labourer completes his task in four days, he has two which he can 
devote to the cultivation of his own small tenement. This system has been 
successfully introduced in many places, and we hope to have it generally 
adopted. 

In some localities, but particularly in parts of the county of Limerick, our 
Drainage operation has been less successful than we could have wished ; too 
many feeble labourers were forced into the works during wet weather ; the men 
refused to work by task, at least at first, and in consequence the expenditure 
was considerable in proportion to the real value of the work done. Under these 
circumstances, deeming it to be unjust that private individuals who had become 
security for the repayment of the money should suffer, we thought it advisable 
to discontinue the works until order and system could be restored, and endea- 
voured to find employment for the people on the roads, but we have the pleasure 
to state, that in every such case the proprietors themselves requested that the 
works might proceed, and that they would be satisfied with the expenditure of 
the money, though the benefit they anticipated -would be lessened by the dimi- 
nution in the extent of land drained. 

But from our last returns we are glad to find that matters arc improving ; 
that task-work has been introduced, and though the prices are higher than 
usual, still a reasonable amount of work is performed when compared with the 
cost. 

On the whole, when it is considered that our establishment for carrying out 
Drainage presentments was formed without any previous arrangement, that our 
operations are scattered over 134 baronies, and that 918 works are in progress, 
giving regular employment to upwards of 16,000 men, we have reason to be 
satisfied with the result as far as it has gone, and we have no doubt that the 
record of every succeeding month will prove the benefit which the country has 
derived from the introduction of reproductive labour, under Mr. Labouchere’s 
letter, in aid of the Labour Rate Act. 

During the month, under date of the 24th instant, we have received your 
Lordships’ final sanction, and the provision of funds, for the earthworks ol the 
Waterford and Limerick Railway, for commencing which we had previously 
completed our principal arrangements, and we expect that next week the work 
will commence in at least two of the four baronies, the engineers, assistant 
engineers, and subordinate staff, being nominated and paid by the Company, 
the pay clerk and inspecting officer only being charged to the presentments, 
and the latter only so long as the necessity of employing labourers from Relief 
Committees continues; after which we propose no other restriction on the 
choice of labourers than that they shall be taken from the barony through 
which the rail passes, the funds for which are provided by the barony. 

It would be unjust to omit any opportunity of expressing to your Lordships 
the sense we entertain of the zealous and unremitting exertions of the office 
force in Dublin. ■ The ordinary duties of the numerous departments combined in 
this Board, demand the full exertions of a considerable number of persons of all 
classes, at all times, but the immense additional pressure during the last six months 
has required, and still requires great additional labour, and considerable method 
and arrangement in its organization and employment. Communications are to 
maintained through engineers and inspecting officers with the numerous Pre- 
sentment Sessions in every barony, with Relief Committees all over the country , 
with the whole of our own local officers engaged in the execution of the works, 
which cause more correspondence precisely because they are not of a regular 
and scientific nature than would be necessary if they were so, with contractors, 
tradesmen, applicants for employments, and complaints of every description, 
from every variety of motive, and finally with the Irish Government and y oui

194 



BOARD OF WORKS 



Lordships, from whom all authority in the first instance proceeds, and on whom 
all the results in the end press, are responsible to the public for the failure .or 
success of the measures adopted. Thus the correspondence alone has arisen to 
the receipt of more than 5,000 letters and returns on a single day, which have 
required five or six hours merely to open and distribute. The account branch 
has equally shared this pressure. The payments of an immense army in num- 
berless detachments, with all concomitant expenses of tools and staff, presents, 
indeed, the only analogy, but without the previous organization which a military 
body possesses. 

The banking establishments of the country have met our wants with the most 
laudable exertion and activity, the supply of specie has begun to adjust itself to 
the demand, but these would all have been insufficient without the most untiring 
and incessant toil in the accountant’s department at head quarters, and the 
work of these branches of correspondence and accounts has had to be performed 
for the greater part by untrained hands, rapidly brought together for the occa- 
sion. The examination of the schedules from Presentment Sessions, and col- 
lection and classification of facts which would enable us to approve or reject 
them, together -with the supply and distribution of maps and plans, has also 
required a considerable force. 

We have in all the numerous bearings and combinations of these different 
bodies endeavoured to anticipate difficulties by previous arrangement, and 
remove them rapidly as they arose, and we trust your Lordships will feel that 
this tribute to the labours of our Dublin officers is justly due to their exer- 
tions. 

We still witness with pain the most unfounded statements made by influen- 
tial persons, who possess the means of acquiring better information, because 
though such attacks and statements can always be met by facts and answered 
afterwards, they are eagerly echoed by the press, and create ill-will and con- 
fusion among the people whose very existence depends on their confidence in 
the immense efforts either made or in progress for their relief. That so gigantic 
an administration is wholly free from abuse, in some of its endless ramifications, 
no one can expect.

Fisheries. 

In our last Monthly Report we had occasion to record the commencement at 
least of success in those measures undertaken for the encouragement of the 
fisheries on the western shores of Ireland. These measures had been entered 
upon with the sanction of your Lordships with the double object of affording a 
present means of employment and subsistence to a numerous class of some of 
the most destitute inhabitants of the land, and of creating a permanent source 
of supply in a substantial and nutritious article of food. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



195 



We have already reported the establishment of three well-ordered curing- 
stations at Roundstone, Killybegs, and Belmullet. We have now to record a 
fourth. 

Your Lordships’ sanction having been received to the establishing a station for 
the curing of fish at Baltimore, in the county Cork, steps similar to those in the 
cases of the establishments on the western coast were immediately taken. Mr. 
James R. Barry (one of the Board’s inspectors), was directed to proceed at once 
to the spot, and from his report it will be seen that the most material preli- 
minary steps have been accomplished. An experienced curer has been engaged 
and an agent appointed. Even these steps have had their good effects already 
in giving rise to speculation of a private nature towards similar objects, but 
principally in calling forth some degree of hope and energy amongst the now 
destitute and desponding fishermen of the locality. 

By the report of our inspecting officer, Mr. Ffennell, which will be found in 
the Appendix, it will appear that the expected results from the establishment of 
these stations have been still retarded by the inclemency of the weather. There 
are, however, favourable grounds for the anticipation of success when fine and 
settled weather may set in, from the fact that at Killybegs the result of only 
four days’ fishing was the purchase by our agent of four tons weight of cod and 
ling, and in two days at Belmullet one and a half tons. 

This fish, which is purchased for about 41. per ton, can be sold when cured 
for above 6/., thus realizing a certain profit without either difficulty or exaction. 

Shannon Navigation. 

We have little more to add respecting the Shannon Works than what has 
been previously reported, during the winter months the operations being mostly 
suspended until the water in the river subsides, the only exception being the 
harbour at Foynes, the excavation for which has afforded considerable employ- 
ment, and the dredging of the shoals in the neighbourhood of Athlone, which 
are both proceeding very favourably. The new bridge at Carrick-on-Shannon 
has been opened for public use ; these, with the preparing of stone, and its con- 
veyance when dressed to the sites of the various works, complete the proceedings 
as regards the Shannon. 

Tire average number of persons employed daily during the month of February 
is 378, the total for the month being 9,067. 

Piers and Harbours. 

In the month of February operations have been commenced at the following 
places, the works being carried on by day-labour w r ith the Board’s overseers 
under the direction of the harbour engineer : — 

Carlingford, County Louth. 

Annalong, County Down. 

Arran Island, County Galway. 

Slade, County Wexford. 

We have held a meeting at Newcastle in the county of Down, and an assess- 
ment of 1,500/. on the district, for the re-construction of the pier there, has been 
assented to by the rate-payers. The final notice will be published, and contracts 
advertised for forthwith. 

The average number of persons employed daily on piers and harbours during 
the month of February is 276; the total being 6,631. 

Conclusion. 

In conclusion, we would only remark that, at the present moment, the object 
of greatest importance is, to enable the people to leave the Public Works, and 
till their own farm tenements, but, to effect this object, the labourers must be 
supplied with food, and perhaps persons holding land exceeding two acres in 
extent, should be removed from the Public Works in the first instance. As a 
preliminary, it w r ill probably be desirable to discontinue the system of task- 
work in all Poor Law Unions in which the new Temporary Relief Act, 10 Vic. 
c. 7, shall be in operation, and limit the pay of labouring men to the minimum 
rate of 8d. per day, which will have the effect of inducing them to receive food 



See Fishery Series. 



H., p. 215. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit

BOARD OF WORKS. 



instead of money wages, and also to accept employment from the farmers at U. 
per day. This is at present offered in vain, because the men employed on the 
road works, on account of their numbers, can rarely be sufficiently attended to, 
and are consequently suffered to idle ; as well as because where task-work has 
been introduced merely as a means of affording higher wages, in the first instance, 
the ordinary prices of manual work have been gradually increased, to enable the 
increasing numbers of inexperienced, ill-fed or unwilling labourers still to earn 
from Is. to Is. 6d. per day. 

This is a sad, but unfortunately a faithful picture of the system, the gradual 
introduction of which has been forced on the engineers and overseers of the 
Board, by the peculiar circumstances in which they are placed, being obliged 
to receive all persons, no matter how old, decrepid, or weak, whose names remain 
on the list after its scrutiny by the Relief Inspecting Officer, and to provide them 
with employment at prices which will enable each to earn sufficient to support 
himself, as well as the several individuals' dependent on him for sustenance. 
Such circumstances have naturally introduced a laxity in the system, and, in 
several of the most impoverished districts, task-work has, to a certain degree , 
become nominal, the labourers idle, coming late to the works, and leaving 
early, alleging that being employed by task, their time was their own, though 
on the pay-day all expect to receive, at least Is. for every day they have been on 
the works. Though fully alive to the evil effects which must follow from such 
a system, we feel that as long as the number of the destitute continue to increase 
as they have done, at the rate of about 20,000 persons per week, and as long as 
every person sent to the work must be employed, and, no matter how idle, 
cannot be dismissed, except on account of insubordination or outrage, the over- 
seers, the greater number of whom have been necessarily taken from the sur- 
rounding country, are unable, perhaps sometimes unwilling, to enforce regula- 
rity or system, in works executed by a mass of unskilful and frequently weak, 
and even dying creatures. This is matter of regret, but not reproach. We 
feel, that fully as much has been accomplished as could have been expected, 
when the condition of the people and the adverse circumstances by which our 
large and imperfect establishment is surrounded, are taken into consideration. 
No doubt, when the whole of the aged, the decrepid, and the weak have been 
removed from the roads, and provided with food under the new arrangements, 
the works will present a very different aspect, hut still we are of opinion that 
during the months of March and April, and part of May, it will be desirable to 
keep down the public wages, so as to induce the labourers to engage with the 
farmers in agricultural works, in preference to remaining with us. All our 
arrangements for these purposes will of course be made in concurrence with the 
Relief Commission. The stoppage of works, or reduction of wages, must be 
gradual and progressive, not sudden and simultaneous, and always deferred 
till other means of providing subsistence have been brought into operation. 

The injurious effect of the present system of employment on the roads, as 
already noticed, has been felt, not only by farmers, but by the officers of the 
Board employed in carrying out Drainage works under Mr. Labouchere’s letter. 
In several districts, the labourers refusing to work at fair prices by task, left the 
Drainage, and went to the roads, on which of course they were not received, and 
when returning to the Drainage, partly from weakness, but in many cases from 
unwillingness, they earned but small wages, though the prices were ample, 
more especially where several proprietors who undertook the Drainage, parti- 
cularly in the county of Limerick, of their own accord, had requested that the 
prices might be increased, and that they would be satisfied to diminish the ex- 
tent of the land to be drained, for the sum presented, the repayment of Which 
has been guaranteed by them. 

Much has been said on the cost of superintendence ; we can only again and 
again call attention to the facts, and place them prominently forward in our 
Reports. But it is worthy of remark, that while, on the one hand, we are 
assailed for a too extensive superintendence, we are on the other, in daily receipt 
of representations from the resident gentry and others, of the insufficiency of 
the number to control the people employed.

EXTRACTS FROM REPORTS OF CONDUCTING ENGINEERS, 
Province of Ulster. 

Mr. John Frazer, County Down. 

Barony of Mourne. — When the works at Dunmore Hill were stopped, there was some 
grumbling ; but when the works, by order of the Board, were resumed, the people were very 
thankful ; and now, not only here, but throughout the barony, the labourers seem pretty well 
satisfied. There is a wish to have higher wages, and many of the able-bodied labourers have 
gone to the railways in England and Scotland. What the people want is plenty of work, and 
at such a rate of wages as would give food to themselves and families. There should be em- 
ployment cut out, so as to keep the people busy with the coming harvest. 

Barony of Upper Iveagli, Lower Half. — At the commencement there was rather a mur- 
muring in respect of task-work ; however I endeavoured to point out the advantage of task- 
work over daily wages, and showed the men that they ought not to rest or be satisfied with a 
shilling per day, but to exert themselves and earn more money ; nearly in every case this has 
had the desired effect, and at the present those that formerly earned lar. per day, have lately 
earned Is. 3 d. to Is. 6r l. to Is. 9 d. per day. 

Barony ofNcwry. — No complaint worth stating ; at first, on opening quarries, some little 
confusion as to getting proper implements, but at present we are proceeding very well. 

General Report on those Baronies. — Herewith you have the monthly return of February, 
1847, for the baronies of Mourne, Newry, and Upper lveagh, lower half. Generally this 
county has not much destitution. In the neighbourhood of Belfast at. Ballymacarrelt, (a 
suburb of Belfast,) there are some persons badly off, but the gentry aud inhabitants of the 
district have been very active in affording aid. 

_ The parts of the county of Down that most require assistance for the poor, lie in two direc- 
tions, namely, in a line from Newcastle by the sea, through the barony of Mourne up to Newry ; 
then from the town of Newry up by the towns of Rathfirland and Hilltown on to Castlewellan, 
making a bend round by Diemand, Ballinalnnch, Seaforde, and joining in upon Newcastle. 

In fact, in the mountainous district of the county, the proprietors of the barony of Xinnalachy, 
Mr. Forde and Mr. Ker, are living employment to the people by drainage measures under 

the Board of Works. ° 

The Marquis of Downshire is affording extensive employment out of his own private funds, 
and the Earl of Roden is doing the same. The new pier at Newcastle will create some labour 
in that quarter. There are many other gentlemen giving employment, but still the employ- 
ment given by all these sources is not sufficient. There ought to be some large trunk work 
that would run right through these poor districts ; for instance, a new line of post road from 
Downpatrick to Newry is very much required; this would go right through the district requir- 
ing aid; then there is a coast-road wanted round from Newcastle to Kilkeel; at least the 
improvements now being made under the Relief Works should be carried out and completed. 
This road would also °ive employment where required. Then from Rathfirland to Die- 
[B.W.2.] ° 2 F 



DOWN.

DOWN. mand a road is in being, but is notoriously hilly and bad, and here is a district very badly off 
for employment. In fact, in the neighbourhood of Diemand there is considerable destitution 
The people of the county of Down are orderly, peaceable, and wish to be amenable to the laws. 
To keep them so it would be of the greatest possible importance to give them employment, and 
that at a fair rate of wages. 

What the value of the employment should be it is not for me to say ; but be this as it may 
work should be procured, so as to enable the poor to maintain themselves and families at the 
present very pressing season. 

For so far the labourers on the works have conducted themselves very well. No violence 
has been attempted. Our pay-clerks can go in all directions without any protection from the 
constabulary. 



DONEGAL. '• Mr. H. White, County Donegal. 

Barony of Tirhugh and Banagh. — No complaints from labourers in these baronies. 

Extract from General Report on the above Baronies. — The works in this district are proceed- 
ing favourably, though but little is shown for the money expended; but when I consider the 
small degree of animal strength in the labourers, the want of competent overseers, (who are, 
for the most part, but the more intelligent of the labourers themselves,) and the hurry in which 
such works are necessarily commenced, I am surprised to find things proceeding so well as 
they even do. I find great difficulty in the system of task-work, the overseers being, in most 
cases, incompetent to direct the labourers how to proceed in the easiest and cheapest manner 
for themselves, whereby men, although most anxious to work hard and earn money, would he 
losers if paid at a reasonable price for the work executed. And at the same time, with a good 
overseer, who has some knowledge of his business, the men are enabled to earn more, and the 
work is done cheaper than on other roads where the labourers have not that advantage. 

The system I have been obliged to adopt, is to have the work measured as a check, and to 
allow the gaugers, who are evidently striving to do well, something more in proportion to the 
others. 

In the barony of Tirhugh a good deal of sowing and field work is going on among the 
larger farmers, and I think there is no disinclination shown to attend to the land. 

I am happy to report that in this district no disturbance has taken place ; the men are gene- 
rally patient and obedient. I was compelled lately to remove some men from one parish to 
another, and heard reports that an ill feeling existed ; hut which I believe originated more from 
the jealousy of the gentlemen of the county than from the labourers themselves. 



Mr. Arthur Ormsby, County Donegal. 

Barony of Emishowen, West. — Occasional complaints, arising from distance necessary to be 
travelled to site of works. 

Barony of Ennishoioen, East. — When a work is suspended for want of funds to continue it, 
the complaints made by the labourers are loud and general.

they are got to task-work and see that they can earn something more, they seem to be we 
satisfied.

Province of Monster. 

Mr. William Hilliard y County Cork. CORK. 

Barony of Kinnattalloon. — The only complaint made is a general one, that not more than 
one person is allowed from one house, and this by order from the inspecting officer. I have 
heard of no complaints, except those of persons suffering from starvation. All payments were 
regularly made by pay clerks. 

Barony of Ballymore.—No complaints, but that the wages they can draw, or will draw, will 
not meet the increased price of provisions. 

There are no complaints made by labourers, except of the scarcity of food and consequent 
dearness of it. The people are living, for the greater part, on one meal in the 24 hours, and, 
consequently, we have not what would have been called last May an able-bodied man on the 
works. The pressure on their minds occasioned by gloomy prospects and the dire distress and 
misery that they know so well remains at home after them, has completely broken their spirits. 

Insufficiency of employment, not more than one person being allowed to a family at or under 
seven members. 

The highest wages they can earn does not afford them sufficient food, and, in consequence, 
the workmen and their families are in the most abject state of want of day as well as night 
covering. 

Any articles they had that were worth selling have been either sold or pawned long since. 



Mr. W. H. M‘Intoshj County Cork. 

Barony of Bear. — Dissatisfied at being obliged to work. Think they shall get lOd. per day, 
whether they work or not. 

Extract from General Report on this Barony. — The destitution in this barony is daily in- 
creasing. The employment afforded by the works has hitherto warded off and alleviated in a 
great measure the distress, but, I am now obliged to dismiss numbers (in the parish of Kilca- 
therine) from No. 3. Of the 27,000 inhabitants of this barony, 26,000 are paupers, and in this 
large number, I believe, there are but 3500 able-bodied men. 

Of this number (3500) 500 work at the copper mines ; 1000 can and will support themselves 
and their families by fishing and some additional relief; about 500 more will be employed on 
the drainage, and 800 will be required for the cultivation of the soil; leaving 700 able-bodied, 
representing a population of 5000, to be provided for by employment on the Public Works. 

The barony is and has been perfectly peaceable ; the people are, in truth, completely servile, 
with all the accompanying vices, low cunning, a disposition to cheat, and a want of common 
honesty. 

Several complaints of non-payment of labour have been made ; but, on inquiry, I found, 
without exception, that the claimants had worked unauthorised by the list of the inspecting 
officer. 

The labourers who are willing to work are earning from Is. 2d. to Is. 6 d. per day, and are 
perfectly contented. I am sorry to state that in the eastern part of the barony (parish of 
Kilcaskan) some ill-disposed persons have persuaded the labourers that they will be paid 10d. 
a-day, whether they work or not, and, in consequence, the return is most unsatisfactory. 

In conclusion, I would take the liberty of suggesting these points as worthy of consideration, 
viz., the large amount of surplus labour, the almost total want of roads, the immense utility of 
further works of this character, not only as the best means of affording relief in this peculiarly 
circumstanced locality, but as opening up the very considerable resources of the barony, now 
almost completely undeveloped. 

Sir Thomas Deane , County of the City of Cork. 

No complaint of labourers in this district. 

Extract from General Report on the Work in this District. — The total number of men em- 
ployed on all the works under me in the city of Cork, up to this date, is 1446. 

There is yet great want of employment ; yet, as relief will now be given in another shape, I 
deem it right gradually to reduce the crowded state of the works, which, with having had to 
work through the short days of winter, as well as the wretched men I was compelled to employ, 
causes all calculation of amount of expenditure to be greatly exceeded. I have endeavoured 
to get the work done creditably, and, under the trying and melancholy circumstances, have 
done the best I could for the public. 

The poor employed under me are thankful.

Mr. A. Bernard, County Cork. 

Barony of Bantry. — The only complaints made by labourers are, that they are too weak to 
work hard, and that- any that have families cannot earn as much as can support them. 

Extract from General Report on the Works in this District. — There will be no work close to 
u 1 a m a

BOARD OF WORKS. 



CORK. the town of Bantry in a few days, in consequence of a work on which the sum sanctioned will 
be expended ; and I shall be obliged to divide the destitute labourers through the works most 
convenient, though in many instances those works will be unavoidably four miles from the town 

I have thus entered into detail, as in the intended change of the system of relief it may, jn 
some measure, assist the Commissioners in deciding on road projects which may be laid before 
them hereafter. 

The labourers are generally contented and quiet, not offering any violence. Any spirit of 
insubordination that may have existed has totally disappeared, and they seem to give themselves 
completely to despair. 

The state of the country is wretched in the extreme ; there is no hope but on the Public 
Works ; and every day I hear of several being absent from cold and weakness, which is followed 
invariably by death. The spread of fever is rapid and fatal, and many are buried without coffins. 

The agriculture of the country is totally neglected ; the farmers are trying to get on the 
Public Works, and seem not at all to think of, or inclined to cultivate the ground, and are, in 
my opinion, in most instances incapable of procuring the necessary seed. 

The works in the barony (Bantry) will be executed for about twice the sum, as by con- 
tractors in ordinary years, but, considering the many disadvantages attending their construction 
it is not to be wondered at. 

1st. The numbers crowded on the works, and consequently the labour cannot be economized, 
with unwilling workmen, and, unavoidably, ignorant inefficient gaugers. 

2nd. The majority of the labourers are so feeble, they are not, even if willing, able to per- 
form near the task they would heretofore. 

3rd. The works being carried on during the shortest, and the five wettest, coldest, and most 
ill-adapted months in the year (particularly so in this locality) . However, in my opinion, the 
majority of the works being constructed in this barony (Bantry) will be of such a useful and 
certainly reproductive nature as would warrant the expenditure of a large amount.

Baronies of Cork. Barretts, Kcrricurrihy, and Imokilly. — No complaints made by the

Barony of Kinnalea. — The labourers are generally satisfied. The only cause of complaint

. Barony of Kinsale. — The rate of wages inadequate to the price of provisions.
