LIMERICK. Mr. William E. Maunsell, County Limerick. 

Barony of Upper Connell. — No complaints made by the labourers in the barony. 

Extract from General Report on this Barony. — In this barony the employment is very ex- 
tensive; 7159 to a population of 29,814, during the last week of February. The Committees 
still recklessly urge for more. No violence has been attempted on the works during the 
month ; but the engineer in charge reported to me yesterday a Whitefoot outrage of a daring 
character, in which two horses, the property of a pay clerk, were deliberately shot. The 
outrage, though committed against this officer of the Board, was not connected in any way 
with the Relief Works, but with the taking of a place or farm. 



Province of Leinster. 

Mr. F. Mahony, County Westmeath. 

Baronies of Moy ashell, Fartullagh , Moycashell, Farbill, Delvin, Rathconrath, Demifore, and 
Cocharee. — No complaints made by the labourers in those baronies. 

Barony of Moygoish. — No complaints against any officials, but. complaints made against 
the scarcity and dearness of provisions. 

Extract from General Report on those Baronies. — In forwarding my monthly report on the 
works carrying on in the nine baronies under my charge in this county, I beg, in the first 
place, to observe, that the works applied for at the Extraordinary Sessions have been generally 
of, what is usually termed, an unproductive nature : this term is, however, much misapplied. 

All works relating to roads are not necessarily unproductive; in some instances they are the 
most productive that can be undertaken ; and I can safely assert that, even in the county of 
Westmeath, the repairing of roads leading to extensive and populous districts, and leading to 
bogs, has been productive of the utmost good, and has afforded accommodation to a numerous 
class of persons, usually large holders of land, who have been paying cess for the maintenance of 
the public roads of the barony, but whose residence was so remote that they derived little or no 
advantage from them. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



209 



T J. e £ e P airin 6 of ^ve-roads in these districts has given the accommodation to the inhabitants 

to which they were always entitled, having contributed to the public burdens as much as their 
more fortunate neighbours, but which accommodation was denied them until the Labour Rate 
Act came into operation. This has made the working of the Act popular with the farmers 
generally, and will prevent the repayment of the sum expended being looked upon as a burden 
The second class of works applied for was, the lowering of hills. The impossibility of carry- 
ing on works of this description during the winter, without inconveniences to travellers, has made 
the lowering ot hills rather unpopular. But that such works were not always considered of an 
unproductive nature, I can state, from my own knowledge, that, since I came to this county in 
1834, there has been at an average 1000Z. a-year presented by the Grand Jury for lowering 
hills in this county. J n 

The works have been generally, I may say, universally carried on by task ; the. prices allowed 
had to be much higher than the usual prices in the country. The shortness of the days the 
destitution and debility of labourers, and the excessive number that had, in some instance* to 
be employed, caused the works to cost at least 75 per cent, more than if let to contractors in the 
usual way. But, the object the Legislature contemplated has been attained without the usual 
farming operations, up to this, being interfered with by those who had the means of carrying them 
on ; and the system of task being generally pursued, has prevented that demoralization so much 
complained of. 

New roads have been few, and confined to four or five baronies : those applied for and sanc- 
tioned will be found useful when completed. 

Mr . Bland Hood Galland, County Westmeath. 

Baronies of Kilkenny West, Clonlonan, and Brawncy . — No complaints made by the labourers 
in these baronies. 



Mr. H. S. Lindsay, County Meath. 

Baronies of Upper Kells, Lower Kells, Upper Slane, Lower Slane, Lower Navan, Fore, and

Mr. S. Searanke, County Meath. 

Baronies of Shreen, Batoath, Lower Moyfenrath, Upper Moyfenrath, Lune, Upper Navan , 
Upper Duleek, Lower Deece, Upper Deece, and Lower Duleeh.—No complaints made by the 
labourers in those baronies. 

Extract from General Report on those Baronies. — With reference to the manner in which the 
labourers employed on the Relief Works in this district have conducted themselves, I beg to 
inform the Board that, with one exception, I have heard no complaints. The case I allude to, 
as the exception, occurred in connexion with a turn-out against task-work, on the hill of Grange, 
in the barony of Lower Deece, during which the labourers, in large bodies, perambulated tne 
country adjoining, calling on gentry and farmers in the vicinity, on whom, by the intimidation 
of numbers, they levied what I may term “black mail.” This occurred at the beginning of 
the month ; shortly after which they returned to their work, and have remained therein, behaving 
themselves very correctly since. 

There have been several turn-outs against task-work in different baronies, but I have received 
no information of the labourers having acted otherwise disorderly in consequence.

DROGHEDA. Drogheda. 

For county of the town of Drogheda, see report on the Barony of Ferrard. 

Extract from General Report on the works in this County. — There is no small difficulty in 
distinguishing between the able-bodied and infirm on these works : the numbers are taken 
from the returns as sent in by the check clerks; but the number of the former is, in 
reality, small, and of the latter large. The amount paid for the last, week of February was 
2153Z. 9s. Id. The numbers are increasing, and the works, in some districts, are becoming a 
mere out-door relief system : the numbers also exceed those which it was originally contem- 
plated to provide employment for. The population of Louth, in 1841, was 112,000 in round 
numbers ; there is, therefore, now about one-thirteenth of that population employed, or about 
one-sixth very nearly of the male population. 



Mr. John S. Mason, King's County. 

Baronies of Clonlisk, Eglish, and Balhjbrit. — There have not been any complaints from the 
labourers in these .baronies. 

Extract from General Report on the above Baronies.— The works in my district are done by 
task, and I have no doubt but I have more work done than if the men were paid by the day; 
at the same time I have been obliged to pay very high prices for work, owing to the number 
that have been sent to me for employment, when I had no room for them ; the works have, 
therefore, not advanced in proportion to the number of men, but the prices for work have been 
advanced to enable the labourers to earn from lOd. to Is. per day when crowded together, and 
in each other’s way. I have found also great difficulty in getting confidential and qualified 
overseers ; and to the want of them, the works have not been so satisfactorily carried on as 
I should have wished, and the expenses have exceeded my estimates : however, this is a circum- 
stance over which I had no control, as I was obliged to employ more men than I required; 
and so many of the labourers are infirm and incapable of hard work, that if l did not allow high 
prices for task-work they would have earned very low wages. 

The revision of the labour lists appear to be very much neglected, and many comparatively 
comfortable persons have been returned for the works. The secretaries of the Relief Com- 
mittee are, in all cases, clergymen (excepting one) in my district, whose benevolent feelings 
are more disposed to employ every candidate than to exclude any from the work. 



Mr. J. A. Murphy , King’s County. 

Baronies of Lower Philipstown, Coolestown, Warrenstoum, Geashill, and Upper Philipstown. 
— No complaints among the labourers employed in the above barouies. 

The average number of persons employed on the Public Works amounts to 2,485. Of the 
total number of persons registered on the books of the different Relief Committees I have no 
accurate account, but I may state that in the barony of Upper Philipstown there are upwards 
of 900 persons registered ; of these, 695 are engaged on the Public Works, and assuming that 
in the other baronies in my charge the employed bears the same proportion to the unemployed, 
it is evident that, although the farmers may engage a number of persons, and that the labourers 
may turn their attention to the cultivation of their own ground, yet a sufficient number will re- 
main on the lists to supply their places, and indeed I may say that from the increase of desti- 
tution the present number is more likely to be augmented than diminished. With regard to 
the general disposition to cultivate the land, with a view to future crops, I may say that as yet 
little or no progress has been made ; and here I cannot help remarking upon the reluctance of 
the farmers to employ the men engaged on the Public Works. 

The Board is aware of the reluctance evinced by the labourers to engage with the fanners, 
while they are able to earn moderate wages on the Public Works, but when a number of men 
are dismissed from the works, and entirely at their disposal, it is the duty of the fanners to 
employ at least a portion of that number, and thus convince the men of the sincerity of their 
intention. 

I make these remarks in consequence of an application made to me a few days ago request- 
ing that a number of men, amounting to 129, might be dismissed from the Public Works, as 
tne farmers experienced a difficulty in getting men. The men were accordingly dismissed, 
and it has been reported to me that upon the men assembling the next morning not one was 
offered employment. 

The secretary of the Relief Committee, at whose request these men were dismissed, has since 
sent a letter by order of the Committee requesting that 57 of them ought to be again employed 
on the Public Works. The remaining number not being resident in the electoral division in 
which the works are situate, no order was sent respecting them. 

With regard to the manner in which the labourers have conducted themselves, I beg to say 
that no violence has been offered by them, nor any interruption caused by the progress of the 
works.

General State of the Works, 8fo. in this County. — With regard to the state of the country, I 
am happy to state that the peasantry are peaceable and well disposed. The portion on the Public 
Works have conducted themselves well, I have not heard any complaints from any of them. 

They appear to be, in a great many instances, declining in strength and appearance, notwith- 
standing, they show no ouHvard symptons of discontent ; they appear to be grateful to the Go- 
vernment for the relief afforded them. 

Until within the last week, little or no preparation was being made for putting down the 
crops ; unless seed be supplied by the Government or the landlords, the lands of the small 
farmers and cottiers must remain unproductive ; the onlys upport of this class of persons, is the 
weekly wages they get from the Public Works, one week’s suspension of which, unless em- 
employed elsewhere, would bring them to actual starvation. 



Mr. Lionel Gisborne, County Leitrim. 

Barony of Mohill. — Some labourers in this barony worked badly for a fortnight, and were 
dissatisfied with pay in consequence; others, good workmen, were very troublesome at first, 
but are now the most satisfied men in the barony. Many are very poor and distressed, but 
willing to work. , . 

Extract from General Report on this Barony .— I find the system works well, the men being 
now on most works their own measurers, that is to say, they check for their own security the 
measurements made by the district overseers ; they are generally well satisfied, but very few 
complaints being made of any description. The works are, however, in most cases overcrowded; 
and latterly the class of persons employed are old decrepit men and small boys ; the latter 
are indeed so numerous and useless, I find it difficult to allow them to earn wages sufficient 
for the support of their families. The principal work in hand is quarrying and breaking 
stones, and in some cases I have taken advantage of the present fine weather, to spread the 
metalling on the dryer portions of the upland roads. 

The country is quiet, and the people generally well satisfied ; they seem to repose great con-

The destitution is, however, on the increase, and the calls on private chanty very great. The

of the population unable to work, and having no means of support ; but it is a system which 
cannot be made pay on a small scale, and must consequently be to a limited extent. Every 
one is most anxiously looking forward to the measures for relief about being instituted by the 
Relief Commissioners.

• SLIGO. Sir, Ballinatc, County Sligo, March 5, 1847. 

I have to state for the information of the Board, that in many parts of my district 
able-bodied men are leaving the works and going to field labour, at. the same time sending 
their wives and children as substitutes to assist for their support, as they state they cannot live, 
or do labour (which I believe), unless some of their family are employed on the Relief Works. 

If all the gentry and farmers would give employment many of the able-bodied would, no 
doubt, leave ; but the landlords in this part of the country are very slow about so doing. The 
circular that was lately sent to the inspecting officers I have explained to alLtliose with whom 
I have had communication. 

There are so many women and children looking for work now, that if employed, would be 
very injurious to the finishing of the roads. I request you will be so good as t.o let me know if 
I am to continue putting them on as substitutes, in the men’s places, when they leave ?

Extract from Monthly Report of Captain Mayne, C.E., in the County of Waterford, for WATERFORD. 
February, 1847. 

Task-work, which I have been pressing on by persuasion and force, is now generally esta- 
blished where it is practicable in my district. There is great variety of feeling iu the people 
about it : all object at first ; some fearing they cannot earn better wages ; some preferring to 
idle on the works ; others thinking it hard dealing, and sulkily refusing it. I have been obliged 
to order 10 or 12 works to be stopped till they accepted task-work, but none continued so 
more than a day, hardly any so long. The great majority of these now working by task are 
delighted with it. The assistant engineers and some of the overseers have been zealous and 
successful in assisting me to effect this desirable change in the mode of working. When the 
works are freed from the infirm and women, who are an incumbrance to them, they will go on 
better as to task-work, and in every respect. During the introduction of it, I have net been 
able to reduce much the number of stewards ; before the next report I hope to have made a 
large reduction. The stone-breaking, for which there are large presentments, turns to some 
profit, besides metalling the roads. In Waterford, Clonmel, and other places, we find pur- 
chasers for the stones. 

To all appearance the return from the land will be small in the next year. The farmers of 
from 5 to 15 acres, who hold so much of it, have not money to expend on their farms, or seed 
to sow, and must probably will nearly all become labourers, as many are now, their land beincr 
given up. The people generally seem to look beyond any exertion of their own to supply food 
for the time to come. The larger farmers generally have been preparing their land, so far as 
the very w r et state it has been in from rain would permit, for wheat and oats will be the general 
crops. This kind of cultivation would leave vast numbers unemployed. In my district, people 
are not without food, but it is often insufficient in quantity and quality, the forerunner it is to 
be feared of disease and death. The destitution in many places is exaggerated. 

A fortnight ago, in the town of Waterford, when the inspecting officer and I agreed that 
about 25 only out of upwards of 100 recommended by the Relief Committee need have work 
supplied by us, the Bishop of Cashel, as chairman, announced to the remainder, that while 
without work they should have each daily a loaf of bread and a quart of good soup, never 
more than about 30 came for it. 

The people are generally in this county peaceable and well disposed ; some wild parts here 
and there are the exceptions. 

(Signed) W. Mayne. 



Extract from the Monthly Report of William Peirce, Esq., in the County Galway, GALWAY, 
dated 3rd March, 1847. 

I am happy to inform you that the general state of the country is peaceable. There is no 
appearance of combination or organization amongst the peasantry. Outrages are occasionally 
committed beyond what was heretofore known in this proverbially peaceable district, but they 
may be considered of a private nature, such as the killing of cattle and sheep, and the result of 
absolute necessity. As to the conduct of the labourers employed on the Public Works it is 
subordinate in the extreme. 

No complaints have reached me from the labourers. Those in employment generally appear 
content and peaceable. 

(Signed) William Peirce.

Killybegs, February 28, 1847. 

I reported to you from Sligo, on the 20th instant, that I was on my way from Bel- 
mullet to Killybegs, and that I had been taking measures to provide markets for the cured 
fish w hich might be obtained. I then expressed a hope that I should find, on my arrival here 
that the state of the weather would be such as to enable the fishermen to resume their labours ; 
m this I have been disappointed. The weather has continued stormy, and the fishermen’s 
exertions, consequently, nave been almost entirely suspended. 

I have teen engaged, since my arrival here, in ascertaining, so far as lay in my power, the 
capabilities which the locality possesses of realizing the objects sought to be attained, and I con- 
sider them ample. I have visited the different fishing stations adjacent, and by conversing with 
the fishermen, and ascertaining their deficiencies in system and practice, I have been enabled 
to suggest to them some hints upon improvements, quite within their present reach, which I hope 
may not have been thrown away. 

The ageut has not purchased any fish, with the exception of a very few haddocks; since the 
13th instant the weather has not permitted the fishermen to go out, except to a very partial 
extent upon one or two days, and until the weather settles down to some uniform degree of 
calmness, much cannot be expected. I find, however, that there is a general anticipation on the 
part of many of the benefit they hope to derive during the ensuing spring and summer, who 
have not yet attempted, on any occasion, to fish since me curing station commenced operations. 
They are, I have no doubt, anxious to avail themselves of the opportunity afforded, and will do 
so, I am confident, when the time arrives when they can fairly calculate upon being able to 
apply themselves with constancy to the work. At present the greater number of the fishing 
population are employed upon the Public Works, and fear to leave them until they find that 

2 G 2 



DONEGAL. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




216 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



DONEGAL. they can settle continuously to fishing, hut the produce of the occasional day upon which they 
only could calculate as likely to permit them to fish, would fall short of yielding the means of 
subsistence. This is a feeling quite justifiable, when the class of their fishing craft is taken 
into account, the nature of the coast, and the poverty of their food and raiment, which latter 
incapacitates them physically at this season of the year to a great extent. 

I find, on the part of the fishermen here, a great ignorance with respect to suitable bait. They 
are often idle for want of it, when different kinds abound in plenty ; but they have been in the 
habit of relying solely upon one or two particular descriptions, and have not had sufF cient inge- 
nuity to discover substitutes when their favourite ones cannot, be had. I have taken much pains 
to instruct them upon this head, and many have said they would avail themselves of it. 

As I before stated, the purchase of fish at this station has been suspended since the 13th 
instant ; there were up to that time about four tons’ weight of cod and ling taken in, and this 
amount was obtained during/owr days only of fine weather, which I take to be a proof that 
abundance will be had when the fine spring weather, now, I hope, near at hand, sets in. At 
Belmullet, up to the time I left it (the 17th), about one ton and a half was purchased in two 
days, and the same remarks apply ; therefore, although the amount realised up to this time at 
either of the fishing stations is small, still I think that under the circumstances which 1 have 
stated, it affords sufficient ground to calculate with confidence upon an ample quantity being 
obtained when the season arrives which will, not. only as regards weather , facilitate capture, hut 
also bring with it a greater variety of lands of fish in abundance. 

The demand for the cured fish, and the prices obtained, so far, I am glad to he able to state, 
justify very favourable anticipations on this head. By the last account. I received from the 
agent at Belmullet, I find that the greater part of the cured fish had been disposed of by retail 
in the immediate locality, at prices fully remunerative. Here (at Killybegs) a similar demand 
has commenced, and the agent has been offered a price for the tohole stock on hands by one 
person, with whom I had entered into treaty while at. Sligo, which, though refused for the present 
by my advice, would be sufficient to realise a profit quite adequate, upon a reasonably extended 
amount of business, to ensure a remunerative return after meeting all expenses. The fish pur- 
chased at each station has cost, after removing the offal (heads, &c.), at the rate of about 4 L 
per ton ; the price obtained by retail is at the rate of about 6Z. 3s. per ton, being 21. 3s. per ton 
profit ; the price offered by the person before mentioned for the whole stock on hands here was 
at the rate of bl. 8s. per ton, being 1 1. 8s. per ton profit. The weekly returns of the agents 
will show more accurately these results, which will he found to be very nearly what I state. 
Though the amount of transactions up to this time has been limited, and the prices obtained for 
the cured fish higher than can be expected to be realised for a continuance, still sufficient has 
been done to exemplify two things : 1st. That great advantage may be derived by preserving 
fish, by suitable cure, when it is taken in abundance, until the time arrives when more in a fresh 
state can be had, thereby not only supplying the very coast population themselves with food 
previously captured by themselves (and of which at Belmullet, as well as here, many of the 
immediate inhabitants, and even some fishermen, have been glad to avail themselves), but also 
furnishing food to the interior of the country, where it could not otherwise reach in an edible 
state. 2ndly. I think that sufficient has been done to prove that private parties could profitably 
embark in such an undertaking ; and I have little doubt that some with whom I have had 
communication will, when they see successful results more largely and more generally realised 
under the management of a public department, take up the matter for their own benefit, and 
establish a permanent commerce in our Irish fisheries in its own more natural and legitimate 
character. 

I am so fully convinced, by all the inquiries I have made, and all the facts which I ascertained 
since the Board in August of last year directed me to inspect and report upon the fisheries of 
this coast, and so much of the conclusions I arrived at then being confirmed by my more recent 
opportunities while here at Belmullet, that I now feel fully satisfied in offering my humble 
recommendation that some further aid may be furnished to work out this measure, and the 
addition I would propose is, that to the staff at each station a suitable fishing boat, with two 
experienced hands (the remainder of the crew being made up with hands from the local 
fishermen), should be added, to introduce by example more effective modes of fishing, as the 
people on the west coast of Ireland generally are not only deficient in their class of boats, but 
extremely igwrant with regard to their tackle, and the use of suitable baits ; those boats could 
also be used, to great advantage in bringing the fish taken by the people to the curing station. 
The principal fishing ground, both here and at Belmullet, is so far removed from the stations, 
that the labour of bringing it there is too much for men who have suffered considerable fatigue 
in taking it; in addition, the loss of time is a great drawback upon the quantity which might 
be captured. A fisherman after his night’s work would require to “turn in” and have his rest; 
pulling a bad boat, with worse oars, 10 or 12 miles to sell his fish, and returning again, is too 
great a loss of time, aud takes “ too much out of a man.” 80/. to 100Z. would furnish the boat 
with gear lor each station.. I am convinced it would pay in a money sense, besides the great 
advantage which would arise from such means being afforded of introducing improvements 
through the force of example. 

I hope to leave to-morrow for Dublin, and on my arrival shall furnish more detailed inform- 
ation if the Board desire it. 

I am, &c., 

W. J- FfENNELL, 

Jos. C. Walker, Esq., Inspector of Fisheries.

Sir, Eolhymount, March 6, 1847. MAYO. 

I have the honour to report, for the information of the Commissioners, that on Wed- 
nesday, I attended the Ballyharris Relief Committee in the above barony. No meeting had 
been held for more than three weeks, and it was the first I could be present at, siDce taking 
charge of Costello. No books or registry have been kept, at least so I judged from the fact 
of none being produced, although repeatedly called for. Their method of making lists of la- 
bourers has been to divide the district between certain members (the priests having the greatest 
proportion) who furnish names of their own choosing, for the signature of the chairman; no ex- 
amination or revision of their lists in Committee having been ever considered necessary. My 
chief object in attending this day was lo strike off about 60 persons in good circumstances 
whom I found to be employed on the Public Works. The meeting took place in the Court- 
house, which was accessible to all parties; and multitudes of the lower orders were crowded 
both in and outside the building. The appearance of the Inspecting Officer seemed the signal for 
a most violent, insulting, and abusive attack on him (by Mr. Pendergast, the Catholic curate 
for the parish of Aughamore), as the Government officer ; which tended to create the greatest 
possible excitement amongst the multitude, to whom an appeal was made, if any alleviation of 
their distress could take place when such blackguards, alluding to myself, were sent amongst 
them, taking pleasure in hastening their deaths by withholding the relief intended for them. 
Remonstrance against such language seemed vain, although the Chairman, and two other 
gentlemen of the Committee, attempted to stop the proceedings, and at my suggestion caused 
the Court to be cleared, with creat difficulty, of the peasantry, who, however, soon after forced 
the doors, and burst in, to hear the same attacks, and similar abusive language, from another 
priest, Mr. Geregt.y, C. C. 

Business was out of the question, and the Chairman dissolved the meeting ; for to attempt 
anything, in the midst of a multitude raised to the greatest excitement, would have been 
useless. 

To leave the Court-house by myself, which I attempted, was impossible, as the people had 
become most violent, and ihe only way was to force through the crowd assisted by the Com- 
mittee, and the very priests who had raised the storm, and who afterwards apologized for their 
wan l of caution, in allowing themselves to be carried away by their feelings ; as if apologies 
could hinder or would make amends for the excesses of a tumultuous and too easily excited 
mob. With the greatest difficulty I regained the house I was staying in, from the violence of 
he people. 

From what I can learn, the meetings of this Committee, few and far between, are carried 
on in the same style, although in a manner not so violent. These same priests attacking any 
gentleman who may attend it, and instead of doing good, have a contrary effect, for when one 
of them attempts to speak, he is invariably cried down. 

There are but very few gentlemen residing in the locality, and no magistrate within nine 
miles of the place. Owing to this circumstance, great difficulty would arise in reorganizing

this Committee, however advisable such a step may be for carrying into effect the new mea-

I have, &c., 

(Signed) W. W. Primrose. 

P.S. From what I have since learned, the most violent of the mob were persons notin 
destitute circumstances. Employment has been, since provided in this district for upwards of 
one-fifth of the entire population.

Extract from a Letter of Thomas Butler, Esq., addressed to R. Griffith, Esq., dated 
March 3rd, 1847. 

I have just returned from Clare and Limerick. I was at Newcastle for a day with my 
brother. Captain Butler, 59th, who is engineer in charge of five baronies. He told me the 
inspectors there could not get the people to work at, drains cm any terms, and he believed he 
would have to stop all the road works to force them to compliance. 

****** 

I was very much pleased with the appearance of my gangs that were working in Callanand 
Crannagh the last two days. Though it was only the second week that task-work had been 
established, there was scarcely a man who was not stripped to his shirt. 

With regard to our men, the Committees have generally sent me able-bodied men, but they 
were out of condition, and many of them never cut a drain in their lives. I considered it 
useless to set such men to work by task without, a little training, and I now have gangs that 
would readily earn 3s. a-day as navigators. 

I had as many as 1100 at work last week, but they dwindled down to an average of 833, 
on being obliged to work by task ; some from disliking the system and others from inability. 

I find a great difficulty in getting check clerks to do anything with regularity.

Extract from Letter of John Walter O’Gradv, dated February 25th, 1847. 

I have just finished a presentment of 50Z., obtained under Mr. Labouchere’s letter, and am 
so well pleased with the work and men, that I wish, if possible, to continue j but the subsoiling 
was very difficult, being almost as bad as a quarry, from the number of stones and the size of 
them ; but notwithstanding the work is so well done, that I have not the least doubt of it paying 
right well, at least double what the land paid before. Ten per cent., viz., 51. has been stopped 
out of the presentment for what are called contingencies, but I superintended the whole 
thing myself', having neither overseer or check clerk, and not even tools or the mending of 
them.

[Relief Department.] 

Circular, No. 61. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin, 
February 12, 1847. 

As it frequently happens that many of the "Weekly Labour Returns” are not received 
at this office until after the general return for the kingdom has been compiled and forwarded 
to the Lord Lieutenant and the Lords of the Treasury, I am directed to call your attention to 
the circumstance, and to request that steps may be taken to compel the check clerks to forward 
them, so as to arrive here without fail on the Monday succeeding each week ; and as it is feared 
that returns for many labourers are not received at all, I am to request that you will establish 
some check to insure the transmission of correct and complete returns, and in proper time. In 
cases where the check clerks forward them direct to this office, the Commissioners request they 
may be called upon to furnish, by the same post, to you, a list of the returns they have so for- 
warded, with the totals of each, &c., which if you find to be correct, you will forward to this 
office, that the Commissioners may also have the means of knowing whether complete returns 
have been received. The returns of each check clerk should be numbered inconsecutive order, 
1, 2, 3, &c., and by this means, a simple return to you, such as the following, might be the 
best to adopt, which, if correct, should be countersigned by you, and sent on by first post to this 
office.

[Relief Department.] 



Circular, No. 62. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin, 
February 12, 1847. 



I am directed by the Commissioners to call your attention to the Circulars of 16th 
October, 18th November, 1846, and Circular No. 39, and to express their surprise that although 
it is now* the middle of the month very few of the returns called for in them have been received, 
and most of those were too late to be acted on, as they were not received for several days after 
the monthly report had been prepared and forwarded to the Lords of the Treasury ; the result 
of which is, that the Commissioners are compelled either to again send forward the returns for 
the previous month, or send imperfect ones. They therefore again request that these returns 
may be all forwarded, so as to reach this office without fail, on the 1st of each succeeding month. 

Should they be delayed beyond this period in future, the Commissioners wish the late returns 
to be accompanied with the names of the clerks or assistant engineers, &c.,who have so delayed 
them : but as each engineer has a correct return in his office of all the assistant engineers, over- 
seers, &c., employed under him, with authorised rates of pay, &c., &c. ; the inspecting officers 
have in their offices correct returns 'of all the check clerks, &c., employed under them, with 
authorized' rates of pay, &c., &c., and the inspectors of drainage, &c., have correct returns of 
the persons employed under them, with authorised rates of pay, the Commissioners trust such 
delays will in future be avoided.

[Relief Department.] 

Circular, No. 63. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin, 

Memorandum. February 15, 1847. 

In reference to Circular No. 59, the Commissioners desire that, before you continue any 
work in anticipation of a Presentment Session, you will report the same to the Board, stating 
the sum which you consider necessary to complete the work; and make the matter likewise 
known to the inspecting officer, for the information of the magistrates, in order that they may 
immediately apply to the Lord Lieutenant for a session. 

By Order, 

Jos. C. Walker, Secretary. 



[Relief Department.] 

Circular No. 64. 

Office of Public Works, Dublin, 
February 15, 1847. 

I forward herewith some blank forms of monthly reports, which the Commissioners 
request you will carefully fill up and forward for each month, so as to arrive at this office on 
the 2nd of each succeeding month, in time for the monthly report to the Lords of the Treasury. 
They are to be made up to the end of each month ; but to allow you time to receive the requi- 
site information from your assistants, the Commissioners have named the 2nd for receiving them 
at this office, and they hope to receive them all punctually on the morning of that day. 

The names of the overseers and check clerks are not to be written on the same horizontal 
lines as the names of the engineers, i. e., if lines 1, 2, 3, &c., are required for them ; the names 
of the overseers should be written on lines 4, 5, 6, &c., and the names of the check clerks on 
lines 7, 8, 9, &c. 

In the letter enclosing your monthly report, you are requested to afford as much detailed 
information as possible in regard to the state of the country, the manner in which the labourers 
employed have conducted themselves, and whether any violence had been attempted, persons 
injured, &c., naming the parties so injured, with full particulars of the case. 

Stating, also, whether any complaint had reached you, or whether the labourers generally 
appear to be, and express themselves contented, &c. 

By Order, 

Jos. C. Walker, Secretary.

[Relief Department.] 

Circular, No. 66. 

Office of Public Works, 

SiR, February 22, 1847. 

TnE operations of Government being about to undergo a change, by which relief will 
henceforth be administered in food, instead of through the medium of labour, it is more than 
ever necessary that the lists furnished by the Relief Committees should be thoroughly scruti- 
nised, so that none may remain upon them who either possess, or can obtain, a maintenance in 
any other way. The inspecting officers are, therefore, requested to use every exertion for this 
purpose, not only by removing from the lists the names of every one not entitled to be placed 
upon them, but by taking every opportunity of pointing out to the magistrates and gentlemen 
with whom they may come into contact how materially it is for their interest to employ as 
many labourers as possible, even independently of the urgent necessity for tillage with a view 
to future crops, so that they may obtain some return for their expenditure, inasmuch as all who 
are not employed, and therefore destitute, will be fed at their expense. The Public Works are 
drawing to a close, and it is very important that the number who are now crowded upon them 
for the purpose of relief should be reduced gradually, by the absorption into private employ- 
ment of as large a number as possible, because, as soon as the new measures are in operation, 
the Public Works must be executed creditably and economically, employing only the able- 
bodied, and of them only so many as are necessary, by which the remainder will be thrown 
wholly upon the proprietors themselves, either to be employed, or, as the alternative, fed at 
iheir expense ; and as this state of things must soon take place, it is manifestly the interest of 
all parties that it should be effected gradually, rather than by the sudden discharge from the 
works of all who are not wanted. 



To 

The Inspecting Officers. 



I am, &c. 

Jos. C. Walker, Secretary.

[Relief Department.] 

Circular, No. 68. 

Office of Public Works, 

Sir, February 22, 1847. 

The Commissioners have great pleasure in making known to the inspecting officers, 
engineers, and others, that the Government have been pleased to express their entire satisfaction 
with the exertions of the Department, in a letter, from which an extract is annexed, which the 
Commissioners take the present opportunity of making known, as the system of relief is about, 
to be changed, but which will still require a zealous continuance of the same exertions, though 
in a different way, and nnder different direction, respecting which instructions will speedily be 
issued. 



I am, &c. 

Jos. C. Walker, Seci-etary.

Mr. Brewster to Mr. Walker. 

Kilfinane, March 7, 1847. 

I beg to report, for the information of the Board, that I was this day 
obliged to throw out of employment a large number of labourers, who were 
employed on the Relief Works in this barony. 

On the road from the village of Glenbrohone to the bridge at Ahayoona, 
where about 50 were daily employed, I found that an armed man had appeared 
on the work, and in the presence of all the labourers, did, with pistols in his 
hands, threaten, and intimidate the check clerk, and desired him to desist from 
setting task-work, or being hard on the men. 

On the new road from Ballylanders to Michelstown through Ballybrien, I 
found, that an armed party of five persons were seen on the w r orks, and that 
one of them came forward, and ordered both the check clerk and overseer to 
walk out from the men ; he then produced a pair of pistols, and desired them 
to kneel down, and after appealing to the workmen, to know if they had any 
complaint to make, and threatening them with death, he discharged the pistols 
over their heads. None of the men interfered, but, on the contrary, were 
chuckling and laughing the whole time. 

This conduct being so completely subversive of all peace and order, and 
acting on the printed circulars of the Board to that effect, I have suspended 
the w'ork for the present. The police are all on the alert, and I hope to have 
the parties arrested before very many days, but consider it, in the mean time, 
to be my duty to report the matter for the information of the Board. 



Major Ainslie to Mr. Walker. 

Office of the Inspecting Officer , Ballinasloe, 
March 8, 1847- 

I have the honour to state, for the information of the Board, that a 
large body of men assembled in this town this morning, giving out that they 
came to see the Relief Committee of the parishes from whence they chiefly 
came, in the county of Roscommon, close to the town. 

The crowd then paraded the town with clamour and noise, headed by a man 
carrying a loaf of bread on a pole, and who is in custody. Some excitement 
continues to prevail, and the troops w r ere under arms in the street, but no 
further outrage has been attempted up to the hour of post. 



Sir G. Grey to the Earl of Bessborough. 

Whitehall, March 4, 1847. 

I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Excellency s 
letter of the 27th ultimo, transmitting to me the first Report of the Relief 
Commissioners. . 

Her Majesty’s Government learnt with much satisfaction that the Com- 
missioners had taken all the measures which were practicable, prior to the 
passing of the Act under which their proceedings were to be regulated, for 
bringing into operation, as early as possible, the new system of relief with the 
superintendence of which they are charged. You will have received from me, 
subsequently to the date of your letter, copies of the Act itself, w'hich received 
the Royal Assent on the 26th ultimo. . „ 

Her Majesty’s Government are deeply impressed with the importance oi 
rendering the provisions of that Act generally available for the relief of desti- 
tution in Ireland with the least possible delay. The large increase which has 
taken place within the last few weeks in the number ol persons employed on 
Relief Works, under the Act 10 Viet, c. 107, has engaged their serious attention. 
It appears from the latest returns received from the Board of orks that, on 
the 17th ultimo, there were no less than 668,749 persons so employed, at a rate 
of expenditure not less than 40,0001. a-day. It further appears that, in addition 
to the sum of upwards of 3,000,000/. sanctioned by the Treasury, new present- 
ments have recently been provisionally authorized by your Excellency to the 
amount of 440,604/. T 

[b.w.2.] 21 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




230 



BOARD OF WORKS. 



Her Majesty’s Government feel the indispensable necessity of adopting imme- 
diate and decisive measures for bringing that system to a close. 

This conviction is not founded exclusively on considerations, however weighty, 
of the enormous expenditure which its continuance occasions : the interests of 
all classes in Ireland appear to the Government to demand that the system 
should cease. 

Efficient superintendence and adequate precautions against imposition and 
abuse have been found impracticable in dealing with works of such extent and 
with numbers of such magnitude. 

Representations, also, continue to be received by the Government, from various 
quarters, of the disposition on the part of the people to flock to the Relief 
Works to the neglect of the ordinary employment offered them in the cultiva- 
tion of the land. It is needless for me here to advert to the fearful consequences 
which must ensue from such neglect, as I am well aware that it is a subject 
which has occupied the careful and anxious attention of your Excellency ; but 
every day lost at the present season increases the danger to be apprehended from 
this 'cause. Her Majesty’s Government, therefore, feel it to lie an imperative 
duty to take those measures which are requisite for discontinuing, at the earliest 
period, a mode of relief which, though it could not be dispensed with while 
other means were wanting, must, if persevered in, be productive of the most 
injurious consequences. 

In my letter to your Excellency of the 28th January, I informed you, that 
while the plan of relief proposed by the Bill then about to be submitted to 
Parliament, and which has since received the sanction of the Legislature, was 
intended to be a substitute for the mode of relief provided by the 10 Viet., c. 107, 
Her Majesty’s Government were sensible of the difficulties which could not 
fail to attend the carrying into effect the change from the one system to the 
other, and that they did not contemplate the possibility of its being done at 
once and simultaneously throughout the country. They are also fully aware of 
the necessity which has existed of continuing the system of Relief Works, under 
the increasing pressure of distress and destitution, while the new measures of 
relief were incomplete, and were under the consideration of Parliament. Now, 
however, that Parliament lias granted the powers necessary to bring these 
measures into operation, i feel it my duty to impress upon your Excellency the 
importance of acting without delay on the views of Her Majesty’s Government, 
as expressed in my letter of the 28th January, by your causing it to be known 
that the Government will, as a general rule, decline to sanction any new pre- 
sentment under the 10 Viet., c. 107, and by your refusing your provisional 
sanction to any sucli presentment, except under the peculiar circumstances and 
for the limited object specified in that letter. 

Every new presentment, and every addition to the numbers employed on 
Relief Works, will only increase the difficulty of bringing that system to a close ; 
and I have, therefore, to express, in the strongest terms, the desire of Her 
Majesty’s Government that no extension of the system shall take place for mere 
purposes of relief, and that the gradual discharge of persons already employed 
shall be at once commenced, and shall be proceeded with as speedily as circum- 
stances will admit. 

Whenever additional relief is required, it should be afforded through the 
means of the Relief Committees to be formed under the Act which has just bear 
passed, and the relief given must be in accordance with the provisions of that 
Act, and not under the former Act of 10 Viet., c. 107. 

If in any special cases a departure from this rule should, in your Excellency’s 
opinion, be indispensable, I am to request that, before you give your sanction to 
any new presentment, or authorize the commencement of any Works, you will 
transmit to me, for the information of Her Majesty’s Government, a report of 
the peculiar circumstances which may induce you to consider such a course 
necessary, of the amount for which you think any presentment to be made 
under such circumstances is required, and of the nature of the work on which 
the money is to be expended.

The Earl of Bessborough to Sir George Grey. 

Dublin Castle , March 8, 1847. 

With reference to your letter of the 4th instant, I beg to state that 1 
am fully sensible of the importance of giving effect, with the least possible 
delay, to the provisions of the Relief Act, 10 Vic., c. 7, and of bringing to a 
close the system of relief by public employment, under the Act of last session. 
The neglect of cultivation which has been occasioned by the preference given, 
either from choice or necessity, to labour on the Public Works, has induced 
me to call the immediate attention of the different Relief Committees to tliis 
most important subject, in the hope that this fatal indifference to the wants of 
a future year may be checked, and that the occupiers of land may be compelled 
to proceed with the cultivation of their farms. With this object, I have directed 
a letter (of which a copy is herewith enclosed) to be addressed to the chairman 
of each Committee. 

While I am anxious to discountenance the mode of relief provided by the 
Poor Employment Act, I have nevertheless felt that, until the operation of the 
Act of the present session had provided other means for the relief of destitution, 
it would be impossible to stop all proceedings under the former measure. 

In many instances the works previously sanctioned for the respective baronies 
had been executed ; in others, although not completed, yet the sums voted for 
them had been expended, and it became therefore necessary to provide further 
employment by allowing new works to be presented, or further sums to be 
voted by the Presentment Sessions, for those already in progress. For this 
purpose, it was requisite to issue proclamations convening the justices and cess- 
payers in several baronies. * I have, however, only provisionally sanctioned such 
small sums in each locality as will suffice for carrying on the works for a 
limited period, and the Board of Works have been guided in their recom- 
mendations by the same view. 

I will, however, henceforward be guided by the opinions of Her Majesty s 
Government, as expressed in your letter of the 4th instant. 

The necessity of creating a perfectly new machinery for carrying out the 
arrangements proposed by the 10th Vic., c. 7, for the temporary relief of desti- 
tution has occasioned an unavoidable delay, but I will endeavour to accelerate 
its general operation by every means in my power. 



Enclosure. 

S IRj Dublin Castle , March 5, 1847. 

I am directed by the Lord Lieutenant to request your attention, and that of the Relief 
Committee over which you preside-, to the great importance of securing by all possible means 
the immediate cultivation and sowing of the land, in order that the country may be saved from 
a recurrence of famine in the ensuing year. The people should not be allowed to indulge in 
the idle hope that, the present system of relief, either by means of public employment or by 
gratuitous distribution of food* can be perpetuated. The only means by which another famiue 
can be averted is by endeavouring, during the present season of spring, to secure future produce 
from the soil. 

His Excellency has observed that the number of persons daily employed on the Public 
Works has of late rapidly increased, and be has also learned that many have been admitted to 
the relief lists who could not he considered dependent on public employment for their support. 
He trusts, therefore, that immediate steps may be taken for the revision of the lists of each 
Committee, and that all who can by any means procure subsistence for themselves and their 
families, as well as those who, holding land, have failed to take- any steps for its cultivation, 
may be immediately struck o£F those lists. . 

There are. many districts where the farmers find sl difficulty in procuring labourers to enable 
them to carry on spring work. In such localities, the Committees should refuse employment 
on the Public Works to the able-bodied labourers who have shown their unwillingness to seek 
other employment. But the larger class are those who, being themselves holders of land, 
would be enabled in many instances, while one of the family is receiving relief on the Public 
Works, to provide for the cultivation of their small holdings through the other members of 
their family. It would be proper, in this case, to refuse reliet or employment on the Public 
Works to those who neglect the cultivation of their farms. 

His Excellency feels that he cannot too strongly impress on the minds of the Rebel Com- 
mittees the vital importance of using every exertion during the present month to provide against 
that want in a succeeding year which must of necessity ensue it the land shall be left waste and 
unproductive. , 

1 have, &c. 

The Chairman of the Redef Committee T. N. Redington.

Extract from Report of Lieutenant Anderson, Inspecting Officer, County 
Wicklow, on the Proceedings at the Extraordinary Presentment Sessions 
held at Ballinglass, dated 5th March, 1847. 

I regret to have to report that the landed proprietors of this neigbour- 
liood, generally speaking, do not seem inclined to take more labourers into 
their employment. 

The small farmers have an idea that Government will till their land for 
them. The chairman told them they might give up all such ideas. 

The labourers on some of the drainage works in this neighbourhood have 
shown a great disinclination to work by task ; a body of men came into me 
evidently with a view of getting Is. a-day instead, I told them both in and out 
of Court that they might either work by task or not at all. 



Lord Glengall to Sir R. Routh. 

Cahir, March 8, 1847. 

To show you the difficulties we landlords meet with, and to give you 
an idea of what may be expected on the subject of the beans and peas the 
Government are importing : — 

I procured a large quantity of these seeds. My tenants near Clogheen pro- 
mised to plant them. This day the seeds were sent there, my steward attending, 
&c. All the tenants refused to take them, fearing that they would be stolen 
when they grew ; for even the young cabbage plants are torn out of the ground. 
Reasoning was of no use. These men hold from 20 to 40 acres of fine land. 

They all run upon turnips and carrots. 

I hope to succeed better in other districts. 

A great deal has been said about landlords ploughing up their grass lands for 
green crops ; but it is overlooked that none but stubble lands will grow beans, 
peas, or carrots, &e. 



Captain Giffard to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Donegal, March 10, 1847. 

There is not much distress about here, the worst part of this Union 
being the division of Dunkineely. I find a very general feeling prevails among 
the landlords that it will be better for them to leave the small holdings (which 
form a large portion of the arable land) uncultivated this year, if the tenants 
will not give up possession to them, rather than supply the tenants with 
seed, as they say the tenant will be unable to pay rent and feed himself on a 
small farm of three or four acres, and they "will have to pay for the seed and 
get nothing for it. In many cases they are correct in this, and I fear a great 
portion of the land will be neglected instead of more being sown than was done 
last year. 

If the wages on the Public Works were reduced, more persons could be 
employed for the same money, and the inducements to go to the land would be 
greater, for at present they prefer the roads to draining, and will not go, and the 
farmers are afraid to complain. 



Mr. Trevelyan to Sir J. Burgoyne. 



March' 10, 1847. 

shall be obliged to you to follow the same practice which the Board 
of Works and Sir R. Routh adopted with great advantage to us all, that is, to

progress of events in Ireland, everything is mooted and discussed almost as soon 
as it occurs. 

The extracts appended to this letter relate to an important point, which we 
have taken much pains to explain, as any misconception upon it might be 
attended with the unfortunate result of bringing upon the national funds the 
entire burthen of the ordinary administration of the Poor Law system in 
Ireland. We shall be obliged to you to give the subject your particular atten- 
tion, and to take care that your accomitant, and others who may be entrusted 
with the settlement of the financial details, are fully aware of the state of the 
case. 

The rejection of the offer of the Admiralty to allow volunteers from among 
their half-pay medical officers to go to the most distressed districts in Ireland, 
to assist in giving medical aid, and in the distribution of suitable food, continues 
to give pain here ; and I should be glad either that the offer should be accepted, 
subject to any conditions and precautions that may be thought proper, or that 
the reason of its rejection should be given so as to satisfy people’s minds. 

Although I have not had the pleasure of hearing from you lately, the patient 
and persevering exertions you are making to reduce the new system to order, 
and to get it into motion, have reached me through several channels, and you 
have my earnest wishes for your success. 

I hope to be able to send you to-night a copy of the Treasury Minute, making 
the gradual reduction of the number of persons employed on the works impera- 
tive. It has become absolutely necessary to grapple, in a direct and effectual 
manner, with this monstrous evil ; for, setting aside the agricultural question, 
the mere financial result of having two such sluices open at once, as the Public 
Works and the new Relief Act, would have been formidable in the extreme. 

Sir Robert Ferguson was asking to-day when copies of the new Act would 
be distributed to the Relief Committees, and I told him that you had had a 
small edition printed, ready to distribute with your instructions.

Enclosure. 

Captain Gordon to Mr. Walker. 

Ennis, March 11, 1S47- 

With reference to my last report, I beg to enclose the- returns of cheek clerks for the 
parish of Killilagh for the weeks ending the 20th and 27th February aud the 6th March, by 
which it will he seen the numbers were reduced from 1583 to 666. 

On Tuesday last I attended the Committee at Fisher-street by appointment, and received 
lists from the Committee containing the names of 1885 persons selected them in Committee, 
and took off 719, leaving still an immense proportion for work, although reduced by upwards 
of 400. I am now employed classifying these ; and by the information I hare, and bv the 
valuation, I shall attend again next week and reduce the number to 800. 

I visited Lisconnor yesterday and checked their registry of destitute in Committee: the 
numbers will be greatly reduced, and I shall duly inform the Board of the exact number. 

In Burren, however, the greatest reduction has taken place (the numbers I shall report ), 
since the greatest abuses did exist. T am acting upon every information I can get, and proceed 
to Ballyoogban early to-morrow, in order to have a further revision. 

New lists (exclusive of Carron, Aughtemana Abbey,) were sent in containing 2810 names, 
and from these I took off 940, and wrote to the chairman to say that the numbers must be 
further reduced. 

In Ennistymon the greatest confusion prevails, and there is, I may sav, no Committee, ami 
nothing can consequently be done, as some families have all employed and others none. I in- 
tend to exert myself the next week in that place, and I hope the new Committee may be at. 
once formed. 

More tillage is going on than before, but not, to the extent it should do. The turning off the 
farmers in Killilagh has had a good effect, since it has obliged them to do something to their 
land; and when I told the people there, that no personshaving land or cattle could be employed 
they weut away quietly, and, I understand, -expressed their intention of tilling their ground as 
long as their means allowed them. 

On one work, between Ennis and Ennistymon, I found 27 had left far agricultural purpose; 
out of 42.

ANTRIM. Extract from Journal of Mr. Maxwell, Inspecting Officer, County Antrim, for week 

ending 6th February, 1847. 

Mr. Lanyon, the county surveyor, informs me that the people employed on the Public 
Works (roads) have worked steadily and well, and have earned good wages. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Maxwell, Inspecting Officer, County Antrim, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

The Public Works have been stopped repeatedly this week from the extreme severity of the 
weather. The conduct of the people is reported to me as excellent ; there are no outrages 
. occurring even in the most distressed districts. The workmen on the Public Works are hard- 
working and industrious, and earn good wages. Farm operations have been going on as in 
former years in this county. 



Extract from Report of Mr. Brooke, Inspector of Drainage, County Antrim, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

From the state of the weather little could be done on the drainage works. I therefore, at 
the suggestion of Captain Maxwell, had die people called on the special relief system. Nothing 
can be better, generally speaking, than the conduct of the working people ; not so of some of 
the farmers, many of whom are throwing every obstacle in the way of the drainage works 
going on. With one or two exceptions, the Relief Committees in the four baronies under my 
charge are not working well ; indeed some of them not at all. I am happy to say that the 
field-work, so far as ploughing is concerned, is generally as far forward as usual at this time of 
year. I would beg to suggest that the roads under the Relief Acts should be stopped for a 
time, and all the hands turned to draining, in order to get the land ready for labouring. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Maxwell, Inspecting Officer, County Antrim, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

From all the information I have been able to obtain, I find that great distress is prevalent 
in the northern and sea-coast baronies, and the applications for relief are daily increasing. 
Several of the Relief Committees have only begun to meet in their districts, and are as yet 
quite unacquainted with their business. But all that I have met are most anxious to attend 
and follow the Government instructions. 

The county is perfectly quiet and well behaved. I have only heard of one instance of turnip 
stealing since my arrival. The farmers are tilling their land much as usual. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Maxwell, Inspecting Officer, County Antrim, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

The farming operations are going on much as usual; but as yet not many farm labourers 
are employed. I have considered it my duty to give the greatest publicity to the Board’s 
Circular of the 29th October, 1846, “allowing farmers to apply for labourers to the stewards 
on the Public Works.” 



MONAGHAN. Extract from Journal of Captain Flude, Inspecting Officer, County Monaghan, for week 

ending 20th February, 1847. 

The small portion of farm-work going on is entirely confined to farms above 10 acres ; those 
below that amount do not show the slightest disposition to apply their labourers to their farms. 
The poor-houses in every Union in the county are full to overflowing. 



Extracts from Journal of Major Townsend, Inspecting Officer, County Cavan, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

The state of the county generally is peaceable ; some robberies have taken place which I 
understand have not been by destitute persons, but. by them who make the general distress a 
pretence for disorder. The Committees transact their business generally with regularity ; that 
of Drumhunnion the least so. There are very few resident gentry in that district; the chair- 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




BOARD OF WORKS. 



237 



man, Mr. Dease, lives in Longford county, and does not attend regularly. The secretary too 
is inattentive. I have had to send some documents back to him, owing to the careless manner 
in which the secretary drew them up. The engineers are satisfied with the conduct of the 
overseers. The check-clerks are generally becoming attentive, but I have had to dismiss one 
or two for taking orders from Roman Catholic priests, members of Committees ; one who 
refused to obey a priest’s order was falsely accused to me by the priests, who was very angry 
at my refusing to dismiss him. 

The labourers on a few of the works have shown a disinclination to task-work, to which I 
thought it right to express a determination not to give way. In general, however, the works 
are proceeding regularly, and I have not heard any complaints except when individuals think 
themselves unfairly rejected, and an undue preference to be given to others. The Roman 
Catholic clergy are often accused of a preference to those of their parishioners who pay them 
their dues, instead of the poorer who have not the money to give. But I have not yet suc- 
ceeded in bringing home such a charge, the men being in evident dread of the authority of the 
priests. 



Extract from Journal of Major Townsend, Inspecting Officer, County Cavan, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

There were two Presentment Sessions in the past week at Bailieborough on Monday; at 
Virgenia on Friday. The former was characterised by long speeches and waste of time ; the 
latter, by a more business-like mode of acting. But at first there was much disorder ; the 
chairman. Rev. Mr. Sargent, having to call Rev. Mr. Cavaity, P. P., of Killenken, to order, 
and to threaten to compel obedience to his authority by calling in the police. Mr. Sargent’s 
firmness restored order. The Drumbanner Relief Committee continues irregular aud unsatis- 
factory ; I have had to return several documents carelessly and incorrectly drawn up. The 
severity of the weather has prevented progress in agriculture, which is very backward. 

The works have not generally beeu retarded by the frost or snow of tiie precedincr week, 
especially in these works where the labour is performed by task-work. The labourers are, 
many of them, weakened by want of sufficient nourishment. Many cases of dysentery and 
fever, also some of dropsy, have been reported to me. Soup kitchens have been established 
with very good effect. It is reported to me that the Roman Catholic clergy at Virgenia entirely 
hang back from aiding these soup kitchens. 



Extract from Journal of Major Townsend, Inspecting Officer, County Cavan, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

The same reckless spirit of voting large sums of money, by those on whom but little of the 
weight of repayment will fall, still prevails. At the late sessions at Ballynagh an attempt was 
made to check this spirit, but it was clamorously overruled. 

Much sickness prevails, and is likely to increase, owing to misery and starvation. The 
peasantry seem disinclined to labour at agriculture, and seem to trust wholly, or nearly so, to 
the measures of Government. The spirit of despondency is far from diminishing, perhaps it is 
on the increase. 

Agriculture is still much neglected, though a certain progress is making. 



Extract from the Journal of Major Townsend, Inspecting Officer, County Cavan, for 
week ending 27th February, 1847. 

The general state of distress in the country still continues, and but little effort appears to he 
making by the peasantry themselves to meet the emergency. Agriculture continues much 
neglected, though more fields are under the plough than last week. The smaller farmers say, 
and I believe with much truth, that they have not means to work their farms. From all 
quarters I hear of persons emigrating or preparing to do so, chiefly those who have some means 
of their own, the utterly destitute being left behind. 

'ILe Relief Committees, generally, exert themselves to meet the emergency ; but some of 
the members appear disposed more to throw blame on others, than to contribute their own 
efficient assistance. The works are all more or less making progress ; but the state of physical 
weakness of the labourers, occasioned by want of food in sufficient quantity, does not permit 
much active exertion. Disease also is prevalent, caused by privation and suffering.

Copy of Report from Mr. Doherty, Inspector of Drainage, County Donegal, for week ending 
13th February, 1847. 

During the preceding week the snow storm was so great that very little drainage has been 
performed ; the work, however, is being carried on steadily by the stronger class of workmen, 
who could withstand the stormy weather, while the weaker and worse clad, and perhaps badly 
fed workmen, were not able to endure it. 

The country seems in a very poor state ; many will die of starvation if they do not obtain 
constant employment. 

I cannot say that there are any Relief Committees here. No farm operations are in progress 
yet, with the exception of a very few of the wealthier class, who have commenced to plough. 

I beg to observe that I meet with great opposition by some of the farmers whose land I have 
to get drained; they are afraid of some very heavy tax (they say) being put on the land on 
account of the expenditure, and it is with much ado they will permit me to get on with the 
drainage in some instances ; they will neither improve the land nor suffer others to do so. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Vilhers, Inspecting Officer, County Donegal, for 
week ending 20th February, 1847. 

In the barony of Boylagh the land is nearly all lying waste. I did not observe the slightest 
appearance of any farming going on.

Extract from Journal of Mr. Wilson, Inspector of Drainage, County Tyrone, for week TYRONE, 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

I have to remark that the proprietors of lands on which drainage is being executed are well 
pleased with the works. A gentleman (James Scott, Esq., of Bloomhill, Dungannon) stated 
at a meeting of the Agricultural Society, on Thursday last, that the works going on on his 
estate under the Board are better executed, and more amount of labour done for the money, 
than if he were doing it himself. The amount of destitution is great in this barony. The 
money on some presentments will be expended in a fortnight, in others it will last two months. 

The usual farming operations of the season are much neglected, by small farmers particularly. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Colomb, Inspecting Officer, Tyrone County, for week ending 
6th February, 1847. 

The Inspectors of Drainage have remarked to me that in hard stony ground, or where large 
stones frequently occur in the line of a drain, it is impossible for the men to earn enough for the 
support of their families at the rate of 4 d. per perch. 

I have had complaints from the labourers on the same subject. 

The works I have visited are progressing rapidly, and are executed in a creditable manner. 
The country is quiet. 

The Relief Committees I have attended are very zealous in the discharge of their duties ; but 
those of Caledon and Aughnacloy have not as yet made out their lists of destitute for me, which, 
however, I expect early next week. The engineers are satisfied with their overseers. 

In general the usual farming operations are progressing as usual.

Barony of Omagh.

Extract from Journal of Captain Brereton, Inspecting Officer, County Down, for WPot 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

I would again beg to call the attention of the Committee to the very great distress pre 
vailing at Rathfryland, the Committee of which place have made frequent reports to me that 
the distress in their locality is rapidly increasing, with a population of 22,000 inhabitants, and 
a third of this number in a state of utter destitution. The people have no relief whatever i n 
this district from Public Works, and the funds of the Committee are utterly inadequate to 
administer relief to the wants of this fast-increasing misery. I would also mention that the 
principal landed proprietor, the Hon. General Meade, is an absentee, and his agent seems 
authorized to give but sparingly to his famishing tenantry. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Brereton, Inspecting Officer, County Down, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

From the very enormous price that oats have arrived at in this locality, it. having i n this 
week’s markets brought 3D. 6d. per barrel (seed quality), the poorer farmers find it quite 
impossible to purchase at this ruinous price, and the greater number of them have already con- 
sumed the small quantity they had reserved for seed, in order to keep themselves and families 
from starvation. I therefore greatly fear that unless they get immediate assistance to’ enable 
them to procure seed, many of them will be compelled to leave their ground untilled. I am 
sorry to have to state that a most malignant fever is now rapidly spreading among the inhabit- 
ants of Newry. The streets in die old portion of the town being narrow, filthy, and densely 
populated, add to the increase of the disease. One of the Relief Committee fell a victim to this 
malignant fever this present week, caught in the discharge of his duties while attending at the 
soup kitchen. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Brereton, Inspecting Officer, County Down, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

The farmers who hold large farms in some parts of the county, particularly in the barony of 
Seeall, are already giving employment to many of the hitherto unemployed labourers, by tilling 
their ground and getting in their seed, &c. Mr. Forde, of Seaforde, a gentleman who holds 
very extensive property in this part of. the county, has purchased 16007. worth of seed corn for 
his tenantry. Although of benefit to them, it has proved injurious to the small farmers of the 
neighbourhood, in consequence of raising the markets at Castlewellan and Rathfryland. The 
poorer farmers are now entirely precluded obtaining seed for their ground ; in most cases having 
already used the little store they had intended for that purpose. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Griffith, Inspecting Officer, Armagh County, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

In the barony of Armagh ploughing has commenced pretty generally, and tire other ordinary 
farm operations appear in the state of progress usual at this season of the year, especially in the 
neighbourhood of the principal towns. In the smaller holdings, however, (same as in other 
years,) there is, as yet, very little labour begun. 

In my letters of yesterday and the day before, I have referred to the destitute condition of 
the people in Upper Orier, and the accounts I have received from Upper Fews are no better. 
There is also as deplorable destitution in parts of the barony of Armagh, though less ex- 
tensive.

Extract from Journal of Capt. Labalmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for 
week ending 6th February, 1847. 

The farmers very generally are evincing a disposition to leave the works in a week or ten 
days’ time ; I am turning them off wherever I can find them. In the relief district of Brusna 
the greatest abuses of this kind have existed from the commencement, in consequence of a (most 
mistaken) resolution passed by the Committee, allowing farmers to be placed on the works 
through whose grounds the roads passed, on condition of their not claiming compensation for 
damage done. Now these men are in many instances not only independent but wealthy ; they 
have usurped almost all the gangmanships, and I am confident amount in numbers to nearly 
one-twelfth of the whole number of labourers employed in them. I have, of course, turned 
them off whenever I could find them, and have applied for fresh lists from the Committee, 
excluding all these persons. As yet there is little or nothing going on in the fields. 

I have made a special report of the state of affairs at Miltown. I do not think that this 
Committee transact their business in a satisfactory manner, and that of Killnylin is even more 
irregular. A very strong feeling exists of maintaining parochial boundaries in the allotment of 
labourers, and I conceive that this distinction is kept up instead of being removed by the 
influence of the Roman Catholic clergy. The consequence has been that men who have been 
sent into another parish to work, the worl£ in their own being exhausted, have been beaten back 
by their neighbours ; and it was only by the exertions of the priest in restraining their violence, 
that the presence of military was rendered unnecessary. 

I should add that many of the farmers, admitted as above, have been and will be benefited 
instead of injured by the roads.
