KERRY. Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Green-well, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for 
week ending 6th February, 1847. 

Distress appears to be on the increase, in spite of the immense sums weekly expended in the 
country. 

Dysentery and fever are every day becoming more virulent, and though in this part of Kerry 
no well-authenticated case of death by starvation has as yet been published, it is beyond question 
that, the want of food has generally reduced the strength of the people and laid them open to 
the attacks of disease. 

The country has, as usual, continued in a tranquil state, one instance of insubordination haying 
occurred, and in that the destitute labourers were not implicated. 

The Relief Committees, with the exception of those acting in Listowel, are, as I have before 
slated, composed of very objectionable persons, and it is exceedingly difficult, though using every 
exertion, to obtain proper relief lists and afford relief t.o. the really destitute. A most common 
practice is, on a requisition being made, to fill in the sheets with a number of persons in com- 
paratively comfortable circumstances, and then on forwarding the sheets to represent, and fre- 
quently with truth, that a number of really destitute have been omitted, hoping by that means 
to get work for all. 

Two or three Committees have also refused to fill in the forms as required, not possessing the 
courage to make a proper selection, alleging as an excuse that the general destitution was so 
great, that it was impossible to make any distinction. The consequence has been that several 
poor persons have been struck off when we were reducing the number to that required by the 
engineer. 

Farm operations can hardly be said to have yet commenced, and in this county never will, so 
as considerably to lighten the pressure upon the Public Works. ' 



Extract from Journal of Captain Labalmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, 
for week ending 13th February, 1847. 

Barony of Trughanacmy. 

The Killorglin Relief Committee’s method of transacting business is very unsatisfactory, their 
lists, when I can get them, (which is very seldom) very confused, and little attention ap- 
pears to have been paid to the selection. The labourers, too, are the most turbulently disposed 
of any in my district. I dismissed some from the works for abusing and assaulting a superin- 
tendent, and turned off a number of persons whose names appeared on no list. A few ploughs 
may now be seen at work, but I fear little prospect exists of diminishing, to any very great ex- 
tent for some time, the relief as afforded by the works in this part of Kerry. 



Extract from the Report of Mr. Fitzgerald, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for 
week ending 13th February, 1847. 

I regret to' state that I have been informed, that since my visiting the drainage works in the 
electoral division of Ballylongford, the labourers employed thereon have left the works,' stating 
that the rate of pay was too low. The rates for the details of the works have been fixed by me 
fully as high as the interests of the “undertakers” would permit, and at those rates, a labourer 
working fairly, might get from 15 d. to 16<f. per diem; the same practice of “turning out,” 
however, has been practised in other districts, and not being successful in obtaining extravagant 
prices, the parlies have since returned to the works. 



Extract from Report of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

The works iu Irraghticonnor are now in full operation, without however sufficiently supplying 
the wants of the people; in Clanmaurice, there is not the same regularity, nor are the works so 
equally distributed. New works in both baronies have been by me recommended for execution, 
sufficient, provided the destitute only be employed, to relieve distress during the next six or 
eight weeks. Insubordination is becoming more general; parties from Ballylongford andBally- 
bunnion having entered Listowel during the past week, and although prevented committing 
violence to persons or property, displaying a spirit and determination rarely witnessed in the 
inhabitants of this neighbourhood, near the causeway; also the labourers and populace have 
become discontented and rebellious, having on one occasion, driven the steward appointed by the 
engineers off the road, and put another man, by their own election, iii his place. 

The position of the engineer is difficult and dangerous : there are no resident gentry, no police ; 
the people have no confidence in the members of committee, with the exception of the parish 
priest, Mr. E. McCarthy, whose authority is uncontrolled, and whose exertions are all directed 
to the cramming of labourers upon the roads, irrespective of the advantages to be derived thereby. 
The Relief Committees in Clanmaurice are without exception inefficient, and sufficient proofhas 
already been given, that in the statements of several no confidence or reliance ought to be 
placed. On my making a requisition for labourers to the Inamore Relief Committee for the 
Bienny road, they declined complying with my request, stating that the distress was so great 
and pressing, that no selection could possibly be made, and that double the number ought to 
employed : frequent demands were likewise made by the Lennan Committee to put more men

Extract from Journal of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

The misery of the people appears to be at its height : in consequence of the insufficiency and 
change of food, disease is on the increase, especially to the west of Dingle, and many are daily 
being added to the hundreds who have perished within the last two months. Athough statements 
were made at the January sessions, by several influential persons, that large sums of money 
would be taken and expended under the “Treasury Minute,” and on that account an objection 
was made to Mr. Laboucbere’s letter, yet their promises still remain unfulfilled, and I cannot 
discover that any steps are being taken by the proprietors (excepting two gentlemen of small 
properties) to meet the distress and the demand for employment on the closing of the present 
works. The business of the Dingle Relief Committee is unsatisfactorily carried on, and their 
book of destitute labourers is still in a very unfinished state. Farm operations have not as yet 
commenced. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Labalmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for 
week ending 20th February, 1847 

Baronies of Magunihy and Trugkenacmy. 

I begin to see a few more signs of cultivation ; but the number of people at work in the fields 
is very limited. nn 

A very intelligent farmer told me, that whereas in ordinary years he employed iy or A) men 
for about 10 weeks in the spring, he should this year only employ four or five men for three 

The diminution in the quantity of land under potatoes, will necessarily decrease the demand 
for spade labour, and much more will be done by horse work, than has hitherto been the case. 

We may not; therefore, anticipate much relief to the roads, from the employment of the 
people in the fields. 

Extract from Report of Lieut. Greenwell, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

In the parishes to the west of Dingle, the.poor are suffering great privations. Even when 
possessing money, it is difficult to obtain a regular supply of food, depots not having been as 
yet established in the hamlets for the sale of small quantities ; and in Dingle the supply being 
hardly equal to the demand, and the arrival of vessels uncertain, the price is always consider- 
ably higher than in Listowel or Tralee. In Irraghticonor nearly all the labourers are em- 
ployed, a considerable number being at work under Mr. Labouchere s letter in the vicinities 
of Listowel and Ballylongford. Though their tasks are set so as to give remunerative wages, 
they are discontented and desirous of returning to their old employment, seeing that persons 
much their inferiors in bodily strength and skill are earning equal wages on the roads, t arm 
operations have not as yet become general ; no disturbances had occurred dunng the past week.

Extract from Report of Captain Labalmondiere, Inspecting Officer, County Kerry, for

in this parish is sufficient to have supported the destitute population for a twelvemonth. A 
few farmers are leaving the works, but little general field labour is apparent.

Extract from Journal of Mr. Poe, Inspector of Drainage, County Tipperary, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

I went to Doonane to-day, and found 1 2 men at work. They commenced on Wednesday 
to open the drains. Four men went to one drain and two to the other. I find the two men 
will nearly finish their drain in two days, which will pay them at the rate of 13rf. to I5rf. ^ 
day. The other four men by their side will not complete their drain in less than twelve days, 
which would leave their wages about 5 d. per day. Those four men came from the Public 
Works the same day, and considered they would earn lOd. per day, no matter how they worked 
for it. You will see by the pay-sheet how I dealt with them : “ I gave them but 6 d. per day.” 
This is but a sample of the way the “ roadmen ” will work. 

Farming operations are backward all through the country. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Ogle, R.E., Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, South 
Riding, for week ending 6th February, 1847.

Extract from Journal of Captain Norris, Inspecting Officer, County Tipperary, for Week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

I regret to say it is very difficult to keep improper persons off' the' works, in consequence of 
-some of the Committees not performing their duty. The leading members of many of the 
Committee's are priests, who have no landed property, and consequently no interest in keeping 
down taxation, but, on the contrary, have an interest in enabling their flocks to pay their 
tribute. Some of the resident gentry, from disgust at the proceedings, rarely attend the Com- 
mittees, and others who do are afraid to perform their duty ; for if they object to improper 
persons being put on the lists, the small farmers, who are also often members of the Committees, 
and only one degree removed from those employed on the Public Works, soon let it be known 
out of doors who are the members of the Committees who prevent their friends being returned. 
The police are the only persons from whom I can get correct information ; and I am satisfied 
that, if every list returned by a Relief Committee was given to the sergeant of the police at the 
nearest station to the work for which the men were returned, and the veracity of the return 
inquired into by him before the men were put on the work, that half the abuses inflicted on the 
country by Committees would be avoided. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Stoney, Inspector of Drainage, County Tipperary, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

The cultivation of the wheat crop has taken place to some extent ; but, generally speaking,

Extract from Report of Mr. Lane, Drainage Inspector, County Tipperary, for week ending 
6th February, 1847. 

Barony of Slievardayh. 

There being a dislike to task-work very prevalent amongst the labourers in this part of the 
country, I commenced the drainage of this barony on my own land, where I had men pre- 
viously accustomed to it. However, they grumbled at being required to work by measure- 
ment under the Board. I exercised my influence with them “ to give it a trial,” and succeeded 
in keeping them at the work (reluctantly) two days. On the third day they struck, and idled 
about, as also the day following ; but on their applying to the Relief Committee for admittance 
to the works on the roads, and being refused, they returned to the task, and do not find it a 
hard one.

BOARD OF WORKS. 249 

In several instances farmers put their servants’ boys upon the works, and made them hand 
over their wages to them. 

No tillage is going on, except immediately around Ballyvoghan and the New Quay, and 
almost all the fishermen are upon the work, although there is an abundance of fish upon the 
coast. 

Tbrickane . — About Miltown Malbay, and to the south of it, a good quality of potato-seed 
remains. 

I have been endeavouring, as far as possible, to reduce the numbers employed, which could 
easily be done if I received fair returns ; but it is quite impossible ; since I may take off 300 
names, and in another fortnight they are sent in, in a disguised form, and get upon the works 
by means of misrepresentation and concealing their families and circumstances. 

I am turning the farmers off the works who have any stock, and I cannot, except under 
peculiar circumstances, employ more than one out of a family of six ; but I cannot succeed even 
in this, since the Committees seeing it, put the father at the beginning of the sheet, a son lower 
down, and, after more names, another, and so on. 

Some families have, consequently, all employed, and others only one. 

In other places undue influence is used, and parties are paid to return men in comfortable 
circumstances; in fact, nothing can be worse : and instead of the actually destitute receiving the 
relief meant solely for them, and which would afford it in an ample manner, the Committees 
have almost invariably looked after the parties whom the Government never intended should 
have been on the works, and they have frustrated, in every way, the carrying out of a measure 
which would amply meet every real cause of destitution in the country. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Fitzgerald, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week ending 
20 th February, 1847. 

There are some localities in my district where, either from the want of residents or from a 
lack of exertion on the part of persons nominally members of the Relief Committees, the inten- 
tions of the Board of Works or Government in applying relief by Public Works to destitute 
persons, and to them only, have been in a great degree frustrated ; I refer especially to the 
district of Feakle in Upper Tulla. 

The small farmers cling with desperate tenacity to the roads. 

Extract from Report of Captain O’Brien, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week ending 
20th February, 1847. 

Ladies, and others who have been in the habit of visiting the peasants’ houses, inform me 
that various articles of comfort gradually disappear, and that poverty and destitution are making 
their way into numerous abodes for the first time. 



Extract from Report, of Major Fitzgerald, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

Baronies of Upper Tulla and Upper Bunratty. 

For the first time I have the pleasure of reporting that this week I have seen tillage in pro- 
gress in my district. Some of the workmen have left the roads to sow their wheat and oats. 
I am aiding this salutary movement in every way I can. I have struck off from the Relief 
lists this week upwards of 1200 names, and shall probably get rid of more next week; two 
of the Committees having complained to me that in consequence of the Public Works there 
is a difficulty in getting horses for farm labour, I have requested the engineers to dispense as 
much as possible with horse labour. 



Extract from Report of Captain Gordon, Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week ending 
27th February, 1847. 

On Monday I proceeded to Ennistymon, and took off 244 persons who were at work, and 
who had cattle and land. 

On Friday visited the Relief Committee at Liscannor, and pointed out the names of persons 
on the works comparatively comfortable. 



Extract from Report of Captain O’Brien, R. A., Inspecting Officer, County Clare, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847- 

Though I have seen an occasional plough at work, the usual farming operations can hardly 
be said to have vet commenced. ' . ,. 

I regret to say that I see no prospect of any considerable portion of the labourers in this 
county being taken into private employment. The farmers having to pay a high price for 
manual labour will do without it as much as possible, and, at all events, the tillage which must 
now be substituted for the culture of potatoes will employ comparatively very few hands. 

The landlords, receiving but a small portion of their rents, find it difficult to give even the 
usual amount of employment.

Extract from Journal of Captain Hubani), Inspecting Officer, County Cork, South of 
West Riding, for week ending 6th February, 1847. 

The crops which are now in the ground are looking well. 

The Relief Committees of my district are again getting troublesome, and particularly captious, 

at my scrutinizing their lists. Whatever measures Government may pass for the relief of the 
poor, if the present Relief Committees are to be continued, some very stringent regulations 
should be adopted to make them certify clearly that the persons upon their lists are actually 
destitute; and they should be restrained from returning any one likely to become destitute 
if present relief be not afforded,” as it is by this pretence that so many persons are placed upon 
the relief lists who should never have been ‘there. Committees consisting of clergy only should 
be absolutely prohibited, as they are quite unmanageable, and not being rated do not. care about 
whom they place upon their lists, or how many. The aid of the police should be required to- 
make out the lists. For the purposes of die new Act, persons receiving food or wages in the 
name of another, by personating him, should be made liable to fine or imprisonment: this, 
offence now is very extensive and difficult of detection. The purchase of rations issued for 
relief should be made punishable, otherwise a regular trade in rations will spring up. Too 
great precautions against the craft of the people cannot be taken. I have had several com- 
plaints lately from farmers that. Relief Committees had placed their farm servants- upon the 
lists without 'their consent. A farmer, tenant to Mr. Beamish, complained to me yesterday 
that two of his farm servants, who were receiving 2s. per week and their diet, had lefi. him to 
go upon the roads, and that another was about to leave him : this man was accompanied by- 
his landlord, who said it was quite true. A magistrate also told me that his ploughman and 
herdsman had been placed upon the relief lists without his knowledge, but had uot left him;, 
their brothers had gone upon the works. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Brooke, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
6th February, 1847. 

The distress in this part of the country seems to be increasing, for the farmers are making 
little or no exertions towards cultivating their land, and have discharged even the few labourers 
they had. A man cannot even get employment, for food only. 

The Committees are daily sending in supplementary lists, occasioned by the discharge of the 
men employed by the farmers; but I have to be very particular, as I find the Committees of 
the parishes, where there are only one or two resident gentlemen, are in the habit of returning 
members of a family iu different parts of the lists as living by therflselves. At the different 
public meetings 1 have attended, the Roman Catholic clergymen seem to make a point of 
accusing the Board and its officers of supineness, and thereby causing the deaths of the people 
by starvation. Deaths are very frequent here from dysentery and fever, brought on by des- 
titution. 

No. 107 : several men on this road refused to take iheir pay, and were very riotous, so much 
so that the pay clerk had to threaten to shoot the first man who attacked him. It appeal's 
that hitherto they have been working by the day and got 8d. per diem ; and on the 2nd instant, 
when the first payment was made to them by task, some of the men who only got at the rate 
t of 8d. per diem felt disappointed, and tried to break into the house where the pay clerk was : 
in consequence of the sessions at Coachford, I could not inquire into the circumstances before 
to-day, when I found the men mentioned had left the work lor fear of being punished. I ex- 
plained to the others that they were paid according to their work, and should have to suspend 
making the road if there were any more complaints of them. 



Extract from Report of Captain Brooke, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week en ing 
13th February, 1847. 

During the last week all farming operations seem to have been suspended by the severily of 
the weather. Destitution still increasing, and deaths much more numerous, in this locality. At 
Mill-street the poor are in a miserable state from disease and destitution. The Relief Com- 
mittees are still sending in fresh lists, and the Roman Catholic clergy doing all they can to get 
the farmers included. In many of the lists I find farmers, holding as much as 30 acres, returned 
as having no land, and every scheme is resorted to for the purpose of getting them and their 
families upon the works to the exclusion of those really destitute. 



Extract from Report of Mr. Longfield, Inspector of Drainage, County Cork, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

The weather being so severe is much against draining operations. In many parts of the 
barony there is very great distress. The working farmers in general have not many persons 
employed. Some of the Relief Committees are manufacturing soup in large quantities.

Extract from Journal of Mr. Parker, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
13th February, 1847. 

The demand for employment does not diminish. The mortality has been very great indeed 
lately, and there is a great deal of fever, dysentery, dropsy, & c. The agricultural operations 
are very limited. Notwithstanding there are upwards of 80 works going on in the East and 
West Divisions of West Carberry, and about 14,000 persons employed, the demands for employ- 
ment are not satisfied. 



Extr act from Report of Captain Huband, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
13th February, 1847. 

There is little or nothing doing upon the farms throughout my district generally. The people 
are very unwilling to go to the farmers, and will not accept 2s. and 2s. 6rf. per week and their 
diet to support their families : this might be true where there is only one man in a large famiiy 
able to work, but when there are several able-bodied men in a family there must be some more 
cogent reasons for refusing their diet and the cash wages. The Public "Works are so popular 
that I fear that they are considered as a refuge for idleness, with high wages as ils reward. 

The fishermen all along the coast should be forced to resume their occupation when once they 
can get bread (under the new regulations) to eat with their fish. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Burke, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
20th February, 1847. 

The Committees still continue sending in lists, and some inform me that they fear work 
cannot be found for all the applicants, they are increasing so. 

On comparing the Dumballogue relief lists, I find they are filled with farmers holding as 
high as 30 and 40 acres, and, in one case, 74 acres, returned as having ho land. 

In the parish of Kilcorney, where no gentlemen reside, and no works were opened till very 
lately, there appears to be more land cultivated and sown than any part of the country I have 
been in. 

Extract from Journal of Captain Huband, Inspecting Officer, County Cork, for week ending 
20th February, 1847. 

Barony of Kinalmenky . 

I have been a good deal over the country since it was told to me that the farm operations of 
this part of the county usually show symptoms of activity, but I cannot see much doing any- 
where; nothing on the small holdings. 

Having learned from Mr. Little, the resident magistrate of this district, that he was going 
to Tinioleague, by the request of the local magistrates, to consult on the peace of that locality, 
I accompanied him there, and learned that a large assemblage of persons (many of them by 
no means destitute, and a good many intoxicated) had gone to the soup kitchens at Butler’s 
Town, and pulled them down, and that they had afterwards gone to the parish priests, from 
whom they got money or provision; from thence they went to the residence of Mr. Jonas 
Travers, J. P., and endeavoured to drive away some of his cattle, but were stopped from doing 
so by his remonstrance. 

The reason which they alleged for destroying the soup kitchens was, that it was the intention 
of the Government, to take them oft’ the roads, and just keep them alive on soup, in order to 
save the money of the baronies. If this notion spreads we shall have some trouble. 

The soup kitchens should be placed near the police stations for security, and there should be 
some power given to stop the issue of soup in places where the people are unruly or commit 
outrages. 

I went to see a man who was taken up with a sheep in his possession, and lodged in the 
Bridewell ; he had 6s. 4 d. in his pocket, was a labourer on the railroad, and does not appear 
to be anyway in want ; a fine able-looking man. 

On passing through Ballinasloe, east of East Carberry, on Tuesday last, I found a Com- 
mittee who were sitting at the police station there, for the first time, having been formed by the 
Lieutenant of the county a day or two before. 

I think that au order is peremptorily called for from head qnarters, to prevent any one 
receiving pay (other than Inspecting Officer) from being a member of a Relief Committee : the 
greatest abuses can be perpetrated if this be allowed ; it is the case in many places. 

When I am present, I do not allow parties so circumstanced to vote, but I am sure that it is 
done behind my back ; and if there be not some order on the subject issued, under the new 
system the abuse will be more frequent, from the number of small commitees.

UMERICK. Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Inglis, Inspecting Officer, County Limerick, for week 

ending 6th February, 1847. 

The dismissal of a check -clerk, found to have returned measurements with great errors and 
generally inclined to deception, has caused a great feeling in the district towards Mr. Kelly, 
die engineer, and much dissatisfaction has been expressed on the subject. A system of com- 
bination appears to be springing up, which I fear will prove of a serious nature if steps be not 
taken to punish severely the first, attempt at violence or insubordination; these steps, however, 
can be taken, and the proceeding of these people during the next few days will be closely 
watched. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Watson, Inspecting Officer, County Limerick, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

The works carried on by the Board in these baronies continue to proceed with regularity. 
Farming is only carried on to a very small extent through labourers not wishing to leave the 
Public Works, the farmers not being either able or willing to give them the same rate of wages 
they can obtain by task-work on the roads. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Telfer, Inspecting Officer, County Limerick, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

At the earnest representation of the Bruff Relief Committee, arrangements were made a 
fortnight since for the employment of about 60 women in and about the town of Bruff ; last 
Monday they were paid, when it was found their earnings did not average above 1 \d. per day. 
They accordingly gave up, and have not gone on the works since. 



Extract from Report of Mr. Pratt, Inspector of Drainage, County Limerick, for week 
ending 10th February, 1847. 

I observe that few of the small farmers have commenced to till their ground for the spring 
crops, and there remains a quantity of stubble land yet unturned. There is, however, a fair 
average quantity of wheat sown, which appears very healthy and luxuriant. 

I beg to remark that the works in this presentment have been carried on to my satisfaction, 
and are being executed in the very best manner, and will be finished a good deal under the 
amount presented for. It is of paramount importance that other proprietors should undertake 
similar works in this locality along the rivers Shannon and the Maigue. 



Extract from Report of Mr. Pratt, Inspector of Drainage, County Limerick, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

Thursday, the 4th of February, was the last day that these men worked in the drains, 
having deserted their task and went to work on the roads in defiance of the engineer in charge. 
They have been all through most troublesome and difficult to get to work honestly, although 
they received good wages; they will not be paid for working on the roads for the last week.

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Anderson, R.H.A., Inspecting Officer, County

Understanding a depot is about to be established at Arklow, I feel it to be my duty to re-

Extract from Journal of Mr. Bayley, Inspector of Drainage, County Wicklow, for week

Farm operations in the barony of Arklow proceed as usual on large farms. On small farms 
work is not proceeding as it usually does at this time of year, when the working day becomes 
longer. I fear the bad condition of the horses will tell against both large and small fanners. 

The men seem satisfied with the rate of wages at which I have set the opening of the drains 
to them, namely, 4 d. and 4 \d. for sub-mains, and from 2 \d. to 2>\d. (per perch of 7 yards) for 
the frequent drains. 

Extract from Report of Mr. Wright, Inspector of Drainage, County Wicklow, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

Owing to the severity of the weather, I have but little to report upon except the great desti- 
tution which exists amongst the labouring and poorer classes in this district. Only a soup 
kitchen has been got up within the last 10 days at Kilbride, in this electoral division, those 
classes would have been much worse off. It has been the means of great relief, particularly to 
those in the immediate neighbourhood of it. 

The progress of agriculture, which has been carried on with a good deal of animation, has 
of course been stopped for a period by the fall of snow, which has nearly disappeared within 
the last 48 hours. This is the first week that the drainage has been put on, with the exception 
of a few meij the latter part of last week. The weather has been so very severe that the men 
could not get on with the work ; and the previous week they were under the impression that they 
would be paid at the rate of 1 s. per day (as on the roads), work or play. However, I feel 
satisfied they think otherwise now, and I hope I shall be able to report favourably hereafter.

WICKLOW'. Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Anderson, Inspecting Officer, County Wicklow for 
week ending 20th February, 1847. 

At Moyne, on Thursday, and at Sheanna, yesterday, I saw many men and women, who one 
and all assured me that for days they bad lived on gruel. Their appearance certainly verified 
their statements. For some districts, I am happy to be able to report that the farmers are 
beginning to attend to their land. I have been told that many farmers are afraid to apply for 
men to be taken off the Public Works. Where I know men can get employment, 1 dismiss 
them off the works; then they seek the farmer. 

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Anderson, R.A , H.B., Inspecting Officer, County 
Wicklow, for week ending 27th February, 1847. 

I have urged upon the different Committees the necessity of revising again and again their 
lists, and have further impressed upon them the propriety of inducing the labourers to seek the 
farmers, instead of the fanners having to seek labourers, as now the farmers must employ men. 
During the past week, the large farmers have been busy ploughing and sowing oats, while the 
so-called farms having from 3 to 10 acres of land are doing nothing, the generality of them 
having nothing to sow. I feel convinced there is plenty of seed in this county, if the large pro- 
prietors will give it to their tenants. I am sure Circular No. 55 will be the means of doing 
much good.

ending 6th February, 1847. 

Farming operations are commencing among the higher and middling farmers. At the 
small holdings, no signs of activity. 

Extract from Journal of Mr. Hamilton, Inspecting Officer, King's County, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

In many of my weekly reports and letters I have been forced to make sudden and unexpected 
demands on the Board, and were it not for the manner in which those demands have been 
met, the consequences might have been very deplorable. I am of opinion that although some 
deaths may have been hastened by want of the comforts of life, none have as yet occurred in 
this county from actual starvation 

I have before mentioned how indebted I am to Lord Rosse for his valuable advice and assist- 
ance ; and every day confirms me in the opinion that to his Lordship’s exertions and judicious 
selection of Relief Committees may be attributed the comparatively speaking prosperous state 
of this county. 

Extract from Journal of Mr. Sadlier, Inspecting Officer, King’s County, for week ending 
6th February, 1846. 

I am sorry to say all farmers holding under 10 acres seem to be neglecting their ground. 
From all I can hear, they have not the means of supporting themselves whilst tilling it, or of 
providing seed. In this barony there is not seed for the land (still unthrashed). 

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Hamilton, Inspecting Officer, King’s County, for 
weekending 13th February, 1847. 

The Relief Committees have all expressed their wishes to see the labourers more profitably 
• employed ; but, notwithstanding, the Relief Works are crowded, and applications are continually 
pouring in for employment, not only for labourers, but from some Committees for farmers and 
their horses. 

Extract from Report of Mr. Benn, Inspector of Drainage, King’s County, for week ending 
13th February, 1847. 

Farm operations going on as usual. People quiet and inclined to work. Weather very 
severe all the week. Little work doing.

Extract from Journal of Captain Adams, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, for week WESTMEATH, 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

The Relief Committees at Tyrrell’s Pass have, besides their soup kitchen, established a store 
for the sale to the people of meal, vice, peas, &c., at a fair market price. This measure has 
proved very beneficial, in checking the exorbitant prices charged in many of the retail shops. 

Too much praise cannot be bestowed upon the Rev. William Eames, the secretary of the 
Committee, for his unwearied exertions in behalf of the suffering poor of his neighbourhood. 

The people are generally very quiet ; and, although evidently suffering severely, I have not 
learned that any deaths have been caused by want of food. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Telford, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, N. D., 
for week ending 6th February, 1847. 

All parts of my district are as peaceable as possible, and since I entered on the duties, of 
my office I never met with the slightest, obstruction or annoyance on the part of the poor 
people, even when most clamorous for employment, who often expressed themselves bitterly 
enough at the negligence and inefficiency of Relief Committees, and sometimes of their clergy 
in their behalf. It strikes me that since the fall in the price of provisions, and the resumption 
of farm operations, that matters are not quite so bad with the working classes as they were 
heretofore. Out of 40 persons whose names were returned me for work by the Mullingar 
Relief Committee last Thursday, only three came forward on Friday morning, when the over- 
seer of drainage was prepared to give them employment. The railway here will absorb a good 
deal of the labour at present expended on Public Works, which, together with the Brusna 
drainage, will take all the able-bodied hands. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Smyth, Inspector of Drainage, County Westmeath, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

Baronies of Moycashel and Magheradernon. 

There is not more than half of the ploughing done in any part of the country where I have 
travelled. It is supposed that the oat-sowing will be late, this year. The wheat crop appears 
pretty good. The white-thorn are quite bare of haws, which will cause the quick to be dear. 



Extract from Refort of Captain Adams, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, for week 
ending Saturday, 13th February, 1847- 

Every assistance has been cheerfully afforded 1 to me by the gentlemen of the Glasson Com- 
mittee, who perform their duty most admirably. 

The severity of the season has caused a great increase of destitution, particularly in the 
neighbourhood of Kilbeggan, where there are already a vast number of persons without employ- 
ment, and a great many more will soon be unless the Board sanction the opening of some new 
works. I have great regret in reporting that three deaths, from starvation and. inclemency of 
the weather, occurred during the week in the barony of Moycashel. The sufferers were a 
woman and her two illegitimate children. The people are at present perfectly quiet. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Duffus, Inspector of Drainage, County Westmeath, for 
week ending 13th February, 1847. 

Barony of Demifore. 

The men in each of the east divisions being, from want of food, unable to work at first, and 
being entirely unacquainted with draining, they were notable to earn what would support them; 
but now, seeing they are to be paid by task, and from what they have already been paid' being 
fed better, I find that by next week’s report some of their pays will be as high as 1 j. 4 d. per 
day. I find a great improvement in their work during the present week, notwithstanding the 
inclemency of the weather.

Extract from Journal of Captain Telford, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

As yet, the substantial landholder is more inclined to reduce his establishment of labourers 
than take in additional hands; indeed, the disinclination to give employment extends to even 
those with abundant means, the ordinary wages given heretofore being so inadequate to meet the 
pressure of these calamitous times, and an increased rate being very distasteful to the most of 
them. However, when the weather breaks up, the Public Works must be relieved of a great 
number of hands, if the land is to be cultivated at all. The plough, I observe, is in general 
requisition wherever I go, and it is only about this time of the year that a movement takes 
place in most parts of Westmeath towards cropping the land. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Adams, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

The Relief Committees are generally doing much good by their judicious distribution of 
food, but the funds at their disposal are too limited to do ns much as required. 

During the last week I have noticed a considerable increase of the numbers employed in 
farming operations, but I have not been able to ascertain that any persons have been withdrawn 
from the Public Works to be employed by the farmers. 

There are very few resident proprietors ia the district of Ballymoe, and the absentee land- 
lords have in almost every instance evinced a strange insensibility to the urgent demands made 
upon them by the Relief Committees for assistance. No soup kitchen is established, but a dis- 
tribution of rice and meal takes place. 

The appearance of the people plainly shows that their sufferings are great. In the midst of 
much destitution, it is satisfactory to find that the conduct of the poor creatures has been 
uniformly good, and that no thefts nor acts of violence have occurred amongst them. At Moate, 
in the barony of Clonlonan, much distress exists, but not to the same extent as in Kilkenny 
West. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Telford, Inspecting Officer, County Westmeath, N. D.. 
for week ending 27th February, 1847. 

I find the plough in full operation throughout my district, but as yet no increased demand 
for labourers has taken place. The disinclination to give employment on the part of pro- 
prietors and landholders is very great at present. 



MEATH. Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for week 
1 ending 6th February, 1847. 

The relief lists are daily increasing fully 100 per day for the last fortnight. The dismissals 
on scrutiny have been about. 35 per day. Great abuses existed under the old check clerks. 

I see no inclination on the part of farmers or landowners to employ a sufficient number of 
men. In this part of the country, I see little prospect of any great decrease in the numbers at 
present at relief labour. I have left no means untried to make farmers and landholders take 
some of them off the work but without success. Tillage is unusually backward. The small 
holders, on several extensive properties, are utterly neglected and unaided, and I fear can or 
will do nothing. I cannot see how the Public Works can be stopped or even decreased unless 
a very different spirit prevails among landowners and landholders. 

The people must be employed or fed. They are barely existing from hand to mouth. 
There have been some trifling disturbances arising from a disinclination to undertake task- 
work. 

Many Relief Committees have become worse than useless, one individual (or two) obtaining 
such ascendancy that the others from indolence or intimidation absent themselves. 

The works are much retarded owing to bad weather ; works overcrowded by men half fed. 
Great opposition is offered to task-work, but where undertaken they earn fairly. I am putting 
them to it in detail to prevent any outbreak, and anticipate the best results from it. Dis- 
couraging idlers and getting some value for the money. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

The small farmers are doing little or nothing : want of means and sullen listles3ness cha- 
racterise the whole class ; but a very few of the landlords or proprietors are bestirring them- 
selves ; and some, I could name, of large property, are turning away the few labourers they 
have, and forcing them on the Public Works.

Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for week MEATH, 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

I see no prospect of any decrease in numbers ; they are pouring in daily; disease and desti- 
tution rapidly on the increase. Many who could live in the early part of the season have 
exhausted their means, and now resort to relief labour. Farmers are discharging those whom' 
they only fed (without wages), owing to the price of provisions. 

I anticipate a large number of acres being left totally untilled and uncropped in this county. 

Office work till 12 o’clock p. m., almost every night. 

Most of the works progressing favourably, and task-work being more generally introduced. 

I am striking off about 200 men weekly upon scrutiny, but the increase is above 1 50 per day. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Kennedy, Inspecting Officer, County Meath, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

The county is quiet ; the labouring poor patient and indolent beyond credence. The small 
fanners are doing nothing, all living in a state of expectancy. The labourers employed on the 
works at wages show a marked disinclination to work for farmers. I have dismissed many for 
refusing to do so. The very low wages heretofore given has excited a strong feeling against 
employers. There are very few of the landed proprietors helping their tenantry to crop their 
land. A lamentable want of energy and self-reliance pervades all classes. The works are 
progressing as well as can be reasonably expected with half fed labourers. They earn well at 
task, but are still very averse to its being adopted. I have been obliged to disemploy the 
ringleaders on several works where they refused to work at task and broke up the portions set 
for them. I carried my point in every instance. Task-work should be universally adopted 
for the able-bodied.

ending 6th February, 1847. 

All corn sown in autumn looking very sickly. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Coleman, Inspecting Officer, County Wexford, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

But from all that I can learn the people are very badly off. Farmers holding 30 acres of 
land, Irish, being obliged to seek employment on the Public Works, and, consequently, suspend 
all operations on their own farms. Farmers holding from 50 to 70 Irish acres, generally 
speaking, are tolerably well off, yet not employing the number of hands required for the proper 
or profitable management of their farms. Men holding two to five acres, Irish, are in almost 
utter destitution ; those who hold no land at all, and who are able to obtain employment, are 
best off. On my way to and from my work, I visited as many of that class as my time would 
allow ; they seemed to feel as if in the greatest poverty. But on questioning them a little, I 
found the family to be receiving from 14s. to 17s- per week, so that their destitution was more 
imaginary than real. The people very peaceable. Weather tolerably fine ; rather wet yes- 
terday, and some rain this morning too, which retarded our work a little as we could not use 
the mops. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Coleman, Inspecting Officer, County Wexford, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

On account of the quantity of snow lying on the ground, was not able to do anything except 
make some inquiry about the state of the small farmers and the labouring class in the neigh- 
bourhood. No works going on with small farmers. No manure heaps collected. They 
seem to have lost spirit, and hardly think of doing anything on their own land. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Dalton, Inspector of Drainage, County Wexford, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

Barony of Shelburne. 

The people are quiet, though suffering great privation, few of them being able to obtain two 
meals in the day. The spring work has not yet commenced. 

I wrote to Mr. Houghton and Captain Richards, Lord Templemore’s agent, relative to the 
drainage on their estates, and received an answer from Captain Richards ; but, in consequence of 
the heavy fall of snow and severe frost, it was useless to inspect the ground during this week. 

The snow is now rapidly disappearing, and on Monday I will proceed with my inspection 
of the lands. 

No Drainage Works have yet commenced in the barony of Shelburne.

Extract from Journal of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Longford, for week 
ending 7th February, 1847. 

Baronies Granard and Longford , and part of Ardagh and Moydore. 

I have been employed nearly the whole week, as last, receiving lists and scrutinising them 
with Relief Committees, preparing lists for engineers and inspecting officers of drainage, which, 
with the endless applications from Relief Committees for transfers and exchange of labourers, 
the necessity for which is produced by the inaccuracy of their own original lists, has so occupied

now writing this report in the most hurried manner for the post. 

On Monday and Tuesday I was entirely occupied in the parish of Kilcashan, where the 
Relief Committee have acted in such a manner as will oblige me, as soon as I have gone 
through a thorough investigation of all their late proceedings, to make a special report to the 
Board on it.

Extract from Journal of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Longford, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

Friday, presenting sessions for barony of Ardagh, in Longford. The remainder of this day, 
as a great portion of every day, devoted to correcting the innumerable errors fallen into by the 
several committees in filling their lists, especially the Killashin, Newtown Forbes, and Upper 
Killoe. If I were to attend to the hourly applications from the chairmen, secretaries, and 
individual members of these committees, I could not satisfy their demands, and they will not 
furnish me with the lists, their instructions and mine require, in consequence. I have now 
positively refused all applications from the Committees until they do so. 

A comparatively active disposition begins to be evinced towards farming operations since 
the snow disappeared; but the small farmers and cottier-tenants cannot go upon their own lands 
to work, except in cases where they have so many grown-up children that a sufficient number 
can be employed on the Public Works to support the family, and leave one or more to attend 
to the lands ; the numbers of families so circumstanced, of course, are few ; the neglect of the 
land great. The same description of outrages as usual. Oatmeal sold this day from 3s. ?d. 
to 3s. 7 d. per stone, the only quantity, or less, in which the labourer can buy it at this price. 
A man’s wages will barely keep himself, wife, and one child, and in my district, there are many 
hundreds of families, varying from four to seven, and some more, depending on the wages of 
one.

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Hotham, Inspecting Officer, County Carlow, for 
week ending 20th February, 1847. 

On Thursday last I had an interview with Mr. Doyne and the Rev. Mr. Magennis, both 
Chairmen of Committees in barony Rathvilly. We all agreed that too many labourers were 
employed in the barony, that is r that many of them if turned off could get private employment; 
and they then asked me for a positive order to turn them off ; I replied, I had no fear about 
the responsibility of giving an order, but preferred that it was done by them on my recom- 
mendation. They replied, that. Relief Committees were so constituted that they never could 
gel that recommendation acted up to, and the only chance was my giving an absolute order, 
which I did. The numbers will be reduced 140 this week, and 100 the next. I mention 
this to show the working of the Relief Committee system. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Hotham, Inspecting Officer, County Carlow, for 
week ending 27th February, 1847. 

The important feature in this week’s proceedings is the commencement of a reduction of the 
numbers employed. The season of the year is very favourable to it, yet it will be impossible, 
with the utmost exertions of the landlords (and they are exerting themselves), to give employ- 
ment to anything like the number of able-bodied who require it; I do not apprehend any diffi- 
culty in making the necessary reduction throughout.

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Baillie, R. E., Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, 
for week ending 13th February, 1847. 

The extreme severity of the weather during the past week rendered progress with any of the 
works extremely difficult, and with some impossible. 

The Ballickraoyler Relief Committee having raised upwards of 6007. by private subscription, 
and obtained an equal sum from the Government, have commenced affording relief by distri- 
buting provisions to a large number of destitute persons in Sleivemargy barony, even including 
families of men on the works. Mr. Cooper informed me that he gaVe soup out of his own 
house to about 200 persons daily. I found other pevsons giving relief in a similar manner. 
In fact, persons resident on the spot, and exposed to solicitations of famishing people, which 
their humanity will not permit them to refuse, while some non-residents merely send small 
subscriptions, or perhaps none at all, are very heavily burthened, and are besides exposed to 
the pain of witnessing scenes of misery.

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant, Baillie, R. E., Inspecting Officer, Queen’s County, 
for week ending 20th February, 1847. 

The road works in the electoral division of Abbeyleix, barony Cullenagh, are drawing to 
a close, and it is not without difficuliy that employment can be found for all of those hitherto 
at work on them on the drainage works. However, it is anticipated that if the weather would 
become dry, a considerable number would be absorbed by the spring agricultural work, and 
the cutting of turf; at the latter work they are stated to earn in ordinary years 1$. 6 d. per 
diem. 

Mr. Trench on Wednesday inspected the drainage presented for at sessions of the 2nd of 
January ; but Lord De Vesci had previously commenced it, to prevent the people from starving, 
with the hope that he will be repaid the money he has then expended. 

At Ballylinan the sessions proceeded under the Act, and confined themselves to voting sums 
to complete the road works in progress. Mr. Trench stated that he had been prevented by 
the tenants from proceeding with the drainage on the townland of Boley. However, a Mr. 
Budds, a coroner, stated that he had obtained a sum of 4007., to be expended in seed and 
tilling the land, with which he undertook to employ all those who might want work in that 
neighbourhood. 

The feeling against feeding the able-bodied labourer, under the new Act, without exacting 
work, appears to be as general and as strong as was formerly the feeling against the Poor 
Employment Act ; in fact there appears now to he rather a wish to continue the operations 
under that Act, if the labour in the fields be not substituted for it.

The men in general very well disposed, but weak with hunger ; they are gradually giving in 
to task-work ; Is. a day sounds like high wages, but it is quite insufficient to keep a man in 
working condition, and support his family besides. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Gallwey, R. E., Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, 
for week ending 6th February, 1847. 

1 would suggest to the Commissioners that great attention be paid to the re-construction of 
Relief Committees (which I understand is to take place). There is a great influx of farmers, 
whose evidence would always be useful, but still they are not capable of acting as members of 
a Relief Committee, without bias of any kind. I would also suggest that the rules respecting 
the clergy, viz., “ that the head of each church only should be members,” be strictly adhered 
to, as I have seen Committees composed only of Roman Catholic curates and farmers. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

All the small farmers are neglecting their land. In going through the Borberin distrinct on 
Thursday/I did not see more than three ploughs at work. The fact is, these small farmers 
have no seed to put in the ground, and often no means of support but the Public Works. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

The ground being covered with snow has prevented any farm operations. Many of the 
labourers have been discharged from the railroad, and now come to the Public W orks. 

I attended the relief meeting at Newmarket, Harvey de Montmorency, Esq., in the Chair; 
nearly all the farmers on the Committee attended, and there was such an unwillingness to give 
information, together with their being afraid to remove any one from the works, that I could not 
get above 5 out of 200 names we went through removed, and they made so much delay about 
these, that the meeting had to break up. The chairman and secretary, the Rev. J . McCheane, 
are the only gentlemen on the Committee, and though they have every wish to do their duty, 
but from being at the extremity of the district do not know all the people, and have to depend 
upon the farmers, who are so completely influenced by intimidation, and the desire of popularitj , 
that they will not do their duty. This is a poor district. There are now about 800 upon the 
works, and 200 applicants; no bread fund established, or any public charity. Mr. de Mont- 
morency gives away a great deal of food, but that cannot equal the benefit of a meal fund. 
There is constant sheep-stealing going on whenever the opportunity offers.

Extract from Report of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny for w PP t 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

There have been armed parties going about near Hagginstown, barony Knocktopher, this 
week, searching for arms ; but in other places the people are quiet. The discharged railway 
labourers in Thomastown were inclined to be troublesome, but have been supported from the 
bread fund there, until put upon the Public Works, that is, the most destitute of them. 

I still receive a great many applications for employment on the Public Works, and the lists 
required scrutinising very much, but it is very difficult to get the Committees to do it. The 
liberal presentments that have been made seem to lead the Committees to think that they may 
crowd a proportional number on the works. In re-organising the Committees, I hope the 
necessity is seen of excluding many of the farmers, and in other places the shopkeepers, who 
bring forward the persons in whom they are interested. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Walker, Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

The country seems quiet, but there is not much doiug to the land except by large farmers. 

I am urging upon the farmers the necessity of employing as many as they can, to reduce the 
number on the Public Works; but there is a great unwillingness to take them till they are 
obliged, and the landlords seem very slow in offering assistance to the small farmer. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Galwey, R. E., Inspecting Officer, County Kilkenny, 
for week ending 27th February, 1847. 

There seems but little effort making by the gentry to employ the people. Soup shops are 
becoming more general, which seems to me to satisfy the people much, as the hucksters were 
.in the habit of extorting very high prices. 



KILDARE. Extract from Journal of Lieut. Brandling, Inspecting Officer, County Kildare, for week 

ending 6th February, 1847. 

I have the honour to report that, during the past week, I have visited all the Drainage Works 
under the superintendence of Mr. Hamilton, in this county. The labourers were working well, 
and the proprietors appear to be satisfied with the manner in which the works are executed. 
I found that many of the labourers, either from the want of sufficient food or old age, quite 
unable to support themselves at this employment, so I was obliged to make an exchange of 
mien between the Public Works and the Drainage. 

Foiir of the labourers employed on the Public Works in the barony of North Naas were 
'■committed last week for stealing corn out of a canal boat. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Brandling, Inspecting Officer, County Kildare, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

Some of the labourers that could not pursue their usual occupations, were employed in clear- 
ing the snow from the roads and footpaths, and on account of the high price of provisions, they 
were returned for lj.per diem. A great part of my time during the past week has been taken 
up in investigating a most wilful act of incendiarism, which took place in the barony of Connell. 

A stable belonging to an overseer, named Fitzpatrick, was set on fire, about 12 o’clock on 
last Monday night : providentially the people of the house were all out of bed at the time, and 
able to extinguish the flames, before much damage was done. 

Three bad characters, employed under Fitzpatrick, are strongly suspected, so I have removed 
them from the work. 



Extract from Journal of Lieut. Brandling, Inspecting Officer, County Kildare, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

I have the honour to report, that the Public Works in the county of Kildare are going on 
well, but the farmers are not showing the slightest disposition to relieve us from any of the des- 
titute poor. The Drainage Works, under Mr. Labouchere’s letter, are giving great satisfaction 
to the proprietors ; and the overseer informs me that they will be completed at a very reason- 
able cost. J r

Extract from Journal of Lieut. Brandling, Inspecting Officer, County Kildare, for week KILDARE, 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

From the information I have received from some of the leading gentlemen in the county of 
Kildare, there is reason to suppose that the small farmers, holding under six acres of land, are 
not preparing for sowing their grounds. These men all say, that they have not money to buy 
the seed, and that if the landlords, or the Goverument, will not come forward to assist them, 
they must then either fall back on the Public Works, or starve. 

Thursday, I attended a meeting of the Relief Committee for the barony of Kilkeen and 
Moone, and arranged to have about 100 men removed from the Public Works. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hart, Inspecting Officer, County Louth, for weekending LOUTH. 
6th February, 1847. 

Farming operations have been carrying on very extensively throughout the county during 
the past week. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hart, Inspecting Officer, County Louth, for week ending 
13th February, 1847. 

The destitution in every part of this county has been rapidly increasing for several weeks 
past, nevertheless there is no deficiency of corn in the county ; indeed, I should conceive that 
there remains unthrashed sufficient to sow the land of several counties, but it is in the hands of 
a few large farmers. The small farmers are, I regret to state, in some instances, parting with 
their seed-corn, under the impression that Government will supply seed, and that they may as 
well have their share of it. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hart, Inspecting Officer, County Louth, for week ending 
20th February, 1847. 

The state of the county is perfectly quiet, and I am credibly informed that farming opera- 
tions are in quite as advanced a state as in former years at this season ; still many of the small 
holdings of a few acres are being quite neglected, the owners of which having no means of 
living except that afforded by employment on the Relief Works. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Gilbert, Inspecting Officer, County Sligo, for week SLIGO, 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

There is no appearance whatever of agricultural employment in any part of the county I 
have been in this last week, and distress is rapidly increasing. In the upper half barony of 
Leyny, the population of which is 27.000, 20,000 are destitute ; and it is absolutely necessary 
that 2000 men, now out of employment, should be relieved to keep them from starvation. In 
the parishes of Curry and Kilmaiitige, several deaths have occurred from want. 

The different roads are progressing as well as can be expected. The distress increases 
rapidly. Employment for at least two thousand people is required for the upper half barony 
of Leyny. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Halliday, Inspecting Officer, County Sligo, for weekending” 
6th February, 1847. 

The people are quiet, suffering, but most apathetic; it is computed that 700 passed towards 
Sligo town from Mayo, on their way to America, this week ; one lot contained 10 carts, 109 
souls ; the estimate is vague, but I believe under the truth. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Gilbert, Inspecting Officer, County Sligo, for week

Deaths have considerably increased this week by the severe state of the weather ; the labourers 
have had great difficulty in remaining on the works. 

Provisions are still exceedingly high, and the prices rather inclined to get higher than lower; 
scarcely any corn now remaining in the country. 

In consequence of the very severe weather this week, the works have progressed slowly. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Gilbert, Inspecting Officer, County Sligo, for week

No appearance whatsoever of any work going on by private individuals on tillage. The 
members of the Relief Committees in general have reported that there are still many hundred 
labourers in want of employment on the Puolic Works, and I feel convinced that whilst relief 
is given by Government, none of the landholders will work on their own property.

Extract from Journal of Captain Carey, Inspecting: Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 1 3th February, 1847. 

The weather has lately prevented land being broken up ; and from the conversation of the 
peasantry I can discover no immediate intention on their part of doing anything whatever for 
themselves. 

Selfishness is now so predominant a feeling, that I am satisfied earnings are not divided 
amongst a family, but that the old and sickly are left half fed, whilst others of the family have 
an ample sufficiency. 

Extract from Report of Lieutenant Primrose, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

Nearly everything is deserted for employment on the Public Works. Even the clergy and 
gentlemen of the country are pressing for an increase of labour, and although in some districts 
nearly one-fourth of the population is employed, still the cry is, the officers of the Board are 
starving the people. 

Generally speaking, the conduct of the people is peaceable and quiet ; but during the week 
I was obliged to stop two gangs : one on a road in Kilmaine, for threatening a check clerk, and 
the other for a like offence in Costello towards an overseer, and preventing his measurements. 
These two are the only instances which have come to my knowledge. 

Why the sessions were called at all appeal’s to me inexplicable, as scarcely any of the works, 
or at least a very small number, have been put into operation of those presented for at the second 
sessions for the barony ; but an infatuation has taken possession of the entire country, and the 
great object appears to be the desire of squandering masses of money and employing multitudes 
of people ; and although the season is fast approaching when it will be imperative' on the farmers 
to crop their lands, little is doing except in some small localities. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Cox, Inspecting Officer, County' Mayo, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

Baronies of Tyrawley and Erris. 

Destitution is on the increase. All the people' who are able to do so are leaving the country, 
and many more will go when the spring commences. Many of the deaths from starvation 
reported are amongst those employed on the Public Works, — feeble and infirm persons making 
exertions they are unaccustomed to, weakened from previous want of food; but there is much 
exaggeration in the reports brought forward. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Carey, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week ending 
20th February, 1847. 

Robberies are common, but unaccompanied by violence. There have been some few parties 
out at night, especially in the parish of Tolaneady, searching for arms, but with little success. 
The accounts of these meetings are always much exaggerated. The disinclination to till their 
own ground is still strong among small tenants. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Fatiren, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
enditi 20th February, 1847. 

Baronies of Carrigallen and Clanmorris. 

The district is peaceable. In some localities attention is directed in a small degree to the 
preparation of the land for crops; but great apathy still exists, and the impression that the 
people will be employed thereon by the Government has not yet been removed. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Cox, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week ending 
27th February, 1847. 

Baronies of Tyrawley and Erris. 

A great deal of fever and disease in this localifv, and many of the weak and infirm labourers 
have fallen victims to the late inclemency of the weather, working in wet ground, with perhaps 
a want of nourishing food ; but I think few of the deaths occur from actual starvation. 

I could bring forward an instance of a man paid his wages on Friday, dead on Sunday, and 
a verdict of starvation brought in by an inquest. The fine weather and increase of length in the 
(lays has been most favourable to the progress of the works this week, and will enable the men 
to earn good wages.

ROSCOMMON. Extract from Journal of Mr. Ikwin, Inspector of Drainage, County Roscommon, for week 

ending 6th February, 1847. 

In Castlerea district lists were supplied ; but comparatively few of those who were called 
answered their names, a great many ot them having to England, Scotland, or elsewhere, some 
(as I was informed) being dead, others sick, and some in the workhouse. All the Relief 
Committees of the barony (Castlerea) are now engaged in revising their registries, and in pre- 
paring correct lists, and forwarding them to Captain Burmester ; it is, therefore, probable that 
on Monday the Drainage Works will be.very generally in progress. 

The distress of the labouring classes is very severe, and has been for some time becoming 
progressively worse, particularly wherever there were no Public Works (or not much of them 
in operation). I am confident that the Drainage Works will give great relief, particularly as 
I have every reason to hope and expect that there will not be any combination or other mis- 
conduct among the labourers. 

In this barony (Castlerea) generally tillage is always late, arid very few farm operations are 
ever in progress at this time of the year ; but there is no doubt whatever that all who can com- 
mand soil and seed will sow as much com as they possibly can, and that various green crops, 
particularly turnips, will be extensively cultivated as substitutes for the potato. 



Extract from the Journal of Captain Burmester, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, 
for week ending 6th February, 1847. 

On some of the works, the Currasellagh road in Frenchpark, and Carrowmove in Castlereagh, 
some violence and threatening language has been used towards the overseers ; in both cases 
the offenders have been held to bail. In other respects the works have been going on well 
The state of the country is quiet. I have heard of no outrages by armed parties of late; but 
the stealing of sheep and occasional robberies ou the high roads continue. 



Extract from the Journal of Major Stuart, Inspecting Officer, Roscommon County, for 
week ending 13th February, 1847. 

The works go on slowly in proportion to the numbers employed : want of tools and fraudulent 
measurement, add considerably to the expense of them. The country here is tranquil, aud the 
conduct, of the people good. The Relief Committees generally, under great pressure and 
difficulties, appear anxious to carry out the regulations. Independent of the obstruction of the 
weather, tillage is neglected for the Relief Works, ami there appears but little prospect of a 
change while the works last. Men with small holdings have no seed; and their landlords 
cannot afford half a year’s rent, which it would cost, to provide seed for them. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Wethkrell, Inspecting Officer, Roscommon County, 
for week ending 13th February, 1847. 

Distress has greatly increased during the past week, occasioned by the severity of the 
weather. Numerous deaths have occurred. Dysentery and fever are prevalent. I have 
heard (from good authority) of cases where three and four members of a family have been 
lying dead at the same time, without the means to bury them. When I was at Kilglass on 
Thursday last a corpse was carried to the grave in a sheet, the surviving relatives not having 
the means of procuring a coffin. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Burmester, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for 
week ending 20th February, 1847. 

But few of the principal persons are making efforts to get their tenants to cultivate the land 
or bringing in seed for them. In the neighbourhood of Roscommon, however, I observed con- 
siderable numbers of ploughs at the various forges to be repaired and rendered serviceable. 
There are some complaints of the men refusing to work except on Public Works ; and I would 
recommend that no more new works be sanctioned for the present. 



Extract from the Journal of Major Stuart, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for 
week ending 20th February, 1847. 

Although several of the works must soon cease, there appears to be but little inclination or 
preparation for tillage, and the distress will be more severe, if possible, ou their cessation.

Extract from Journal of Mr. Wetherell, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for ROSCOMMON, 
week ending ‘20th February, 1847. 

The Committees, generally speaking, transact their business very indifferently, and especially 
the Strokestown Committee. I cannot obtain from them anything correct. The present 
Chairman, Mr. Knox, has tendered his resignation, having been appointed resident magistrate 
in county Sligo. The principal persons constituting this Committee are the Roman Catholic 
clergy. 

I have no doubt that the various trifling outrages that take place originate principally with 
the friends of discharged stewards and check clerks, the people in this locality having such 
large faction parties. The few residents are in great fear of these persons. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Burmester, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for 
week ending 27th February, 1847. 

During the last week the conduct of the men has, with one exception in the barony of 
Castlereagh, been regular. 

The suffering of the people in some districts, more particularly the neighbourhood of Castle 
Plunket, is very great. 

The lists furnished by the Relief Committees are extremely irregular; this may be partially 
accounted for by ihe number of persons being engaged at the assizes. 

As yet the farm operations occupy but few persons, although the weather has been most 
favourable. 

Many persons are leaving the country. 



Extract from Report of Major Stewart, Inspecting Officer, County Roscommon, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

In the barony of Athlone, more particularly, many works have been stopped, and the rest 
must soon be closed from the exhaustion of the funds. Should another Presentment Sessions 
be ordered, I would strongly recommend that as little Public Work as possible be undertaken, 
because tillage is and will be neglected for it, and the money expended exceeds in an enormous 
proportion the work done ; even yet it goes to many persons who ought uot to share it. 

Extract from Journal of Major Clarke, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847- 

There appears to me the same suspension of farming operations, through the county, amongst 
the middle and lower class of farmers. 

I was happy to find in yesterday's market, an excellent supply of grain, and for the first 
time, a reduction in price, but the bakers will not give the benefit of the reduction to the 
people. 

Extract from Journal of Captain Hutchinson, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for 
week ending 6th February, 1847. 

I have, through the last week, visited the most, distressed parts of the district under my 
charge, particularly in Connemara, where there is at present much sickness, principally dysentery. 
The dpaths, from all I hear, are principally among old. or aged people, and young children; 
there have been cases stated to me, on pretty good authority, of some on the roads in the barony 
of Ross, within the district of the Clonbree Relief Committee, where labourers were carried off 
the road, having fainted; though there is every attention paid at some of the Relief Com- 
mittees, in giving aid in the way of soup and meal. I find great difficulty in obtaining lists 
of persons to put on the Public Works, and I have been obliged to sanction the employment 
of many who would otherwise have starved had I waited for lists from the Relief Committees. 
I observe along the sea-coast, line, the collection of sea-weed goes on. The country is quiet, and 
I have not heard of any disturbance. 

Extract from Journal of Captain Carey, Inspecting Officer, County Mayo, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

Preparation for seed is not yet going on actively ; the greater number of fields are, in feet, 
still untouched. I do not, however, think this attributable so much to the actual employment 
of the occupiers on the Public Works, as to the hope that they will ultimately be paid for 
doing their own work, to their idleness, and to the intention many have of leaving the country : 
many that have seed, are not preparing their land. Robberies are more frequent than usual, 
but have rarely been accompanied by violence; and the accounts given of outrages of every sort, 
I generally find much exaggerated, though nothing could be more general than the inclination 
to dishonesty prevalent in every direction. 

There still exists, in one or two remote places, an idea that tickets give a right to wages, 
and that they need not take any tasks.- It is still impossible for the assistant engineers to set 
and measure every task themselves, and in fact day wages are really more common than 
measurement, but an extra 2 d. or 3d. is reserved to constitute the balance.
