Extract from Journal of Major Ainslie, Inspecting Officer, County Galway for wp i. 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

I wish to bring to the special notice of the Commissioners the enormous supply of grai n j 
witnessed in proceeding to Newtown Bellew, on the 2nd instant, at a market held at a cou tr, 
village called Mount Bellew, with a capacious market place. I have no hesitation in renort' 
that there are concealed stores of grain in the country, which are held back with some ulterio’ 
object : the slight fall in the markets brought, these supplies out. 

The task-work system is now generally understood, but there is no satisfying the never-endincr 
demands of the Committees, and their want of firmness generally, their constant wish to over° 
whelm thi works, and the extraordinary views they entertain, in some instances, are addi- 
tions to the duties I have to perform of no ordinary kind. 



Extract from Journal of Major Burns. Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for wee 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

During my journey through the baronies of Leitrim and Loughrea, I observed a good deal 
of corn in stacks. On Thursday, Loughrea market was well supplied with that article, and the 
price fell considerably. Farming operations by extensive farmers are unusually errear, and 
even small holders are preparing their ground lor seed. The country is tranquil ; robberies 
of sheep, &c., continue. 

Extract from Journal of Major Ainslie, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 1 3th February, 1847. 

The condition of the labourers of the parish of Buoyanagh is insubordinate. The assist ant en- 
gineer, Mr. W. Halpin, having proceeded to the line where overseer James Waldron was 
brutally assailed, together with his assistant, viz., Cashell to Cappauagh, the workmen declared 
they would carry on ihe works as they please, and would not suffer Waldron over them, who is 
an intelligent, aetive, and determined servant of the Board. This feeling has spread to two other 
adjacent lines, and threats made use of to check-clerks and overseers. This parish has received 
1220 tickets and names for employment, and in the fairness or impartiality of this exclusive Com- 
mittee, I have no confidence : it is termed the Committee of Glanamadda, and is conducted by 
the parish priest and an attorney', and vet they press for more, and have, I am sure, more im- 
proper objects on the works than any other; to which I have had time to pay only partial atteu- 
tion, hut have discharged some of them, yet many remain. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Hutchinson, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for 
week ending 13th February, 1847. 

The Vvorks in a grep.t measure have decreased from the funds being exhausted, and many 
destitute persons thrown out of employment; those in operation are going on as well as the 
heavy fall of snow, and subsequent hard frost, will admit of. The county is quiet, and no 
people have shown more patient endurance, under their severe privations from famine and 
much sickness, which latter is very prevalent in this district. The Relief Committees do not 
generally work well, so far as supplying lists of people for Public Works, though in the distri- 
bution of meal and soup to the destitute, much is done ; and in many instances, gratuitous relief 
of this kind is given by the resident landlord, and their families assisted by the clergy of all 
persuasions, a mode of relief absolutely necessary to the most destitute part of the population. 
While travelling through the countiy, I have observed that, preparation for farming operations 
is not so general as it ought to he. and in the mountain lands no operations of this nature are in 
progress, the usual seed (potatoes) not to be had, and the bog lands in their present slate not 
being fit for any other kind. There is a feeling of apathy among the farming class prevailing 
to a great extent ; the occupiers of small holdiugs are unable to till their laud, they cannot 
feed or pay the labourers; and in the whole of Connemara, with little exception, the dismal pro- 
spect of an entire country lying waste and unproductive is too apparent. This drove many, who 
never did apply before, to seek employment in Public Works; and the expenditure for the sup- 
port of the people will be immense, as it will be some time before the land I allude to can pro- 
duce, however good the cultivation may be. 



Extract from Journal of Major Burns, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

Sir John Burke, Chairman of the Woodford Committee, closely scrutinized the labour list, 
and struck off many names. His exertions and arrangements to relieve the destitute of these 
two parishes, by providing an abundant supply of food'at a cheap rate, and the establishment 
of soup kitchens are most praiseworthy. 



Extract from Report of Major Ainslie, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

I perceive no abatement in the accounts of distress ; and if the Relief Committees had but

Much apprehension exists amongst tile landholders as to the weighty effects of the auxiliary

I regret to say the market exhibits a rise here. 

Mv district is generally tranquil, excepting the parish of Killian, barony of Killian, where 
the assistant engineer reports to me that a. growing disposition to turbulence is evident; the pea- 
santry have come to his house and threatened to “smash his bones,” and I am apprehensive 
that it will be difficult to check this spirit, and keep them in order. 

In my travels through the remote parts of my district, poor lands and a pauper population. 

I saw but very few ploughs at work; if the next fortnight does not produce more agricultural 
activity, the neglect will be a serious affair. 

The works are generally conducted in a satisfactory manner, but the labourers building on 
the subsistence of lOd. daily, take advantage, and come late to work, and quit too early, but 
which it is most difficult, to check, over such extended operations. 

The new liue of road, Cashell to Cappanagh, barony of Ballymoe, has been this week sus- 
pended ; I have got the names of five ringleaders, and will refer them to the resident magis- 
trate ; but there is a system of intimidation in and around Glanamadda, parish of Boroyanagh, 
which prevents the check-clerks and overseers doing their duty fearlessly. I have no opinion 
of the impartiality of this Committee ; it is a troublesome one, ever since I knew it. I have 
always found more disposition to interfere improperly, aud oppose any regulations adapted to 
guide such materials, than in any other. 



Extract from Journal of Major Clarkk, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

No further appearance of the usual preparatory farming operations of the season ; I do not 
see a plough, or an individual employed in top dressing. 

I think that the possessors of small holdings of land look forward with pleasure to expected 
assistance, with food and seed corn, in private tillage, but the mere labourers and squatters 
would prefer public employment. 

In my exertions to further the extension of soup establishments in my district, I have had to 
struggle against the passive obstacles of non-resident landlords, and the very active although 
private opposition of corn and meal dealers, who frequently succeed in frustrating our exertions, 
notwithstanding the liberal contributions of Government. 

I have not seen a single soup establishment succeed, unless the precaution recommended by 
me was adopted, namely, of allowing the people, as far as practicable, frequently to see the 
soup in process of cookery, to prevent their credulity being imposed on by the monstrous re- 
ports put in circulation, as to the ingredients and materials, by interested persons. 



Extract from Journal of Major A ins me, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week 
ending 27th February, 1847. 

My district continues tranquil, but in the barony of Athemy, cattle and fowl stealing prevails, 
and fever has made its appearance. The Committee ol Killyan parish do not co-operate 
heartily with the assistant engineer. They press hard and unceasingly, and forbearance is 
unknown. They lean with all their weight on us. I never hear ot a Committee referred to 
when asking for i resh men on the works, or exhibit a tender regard of, or show any signs ol a pro- 
vidential care of, the funds ; I never yet knew a Committee as a body, frmly stand between 
the Board of Works, and the unceasing, increasing, and importunate demands ot the entire com- 
munity, who look to be both fed and clothed at the public expense. 



Extract from Report of Major Burns, Inspecting Officer, County Galway, for week ending 
27th February, 1847- 

Baronies of Ki'tartan, Lougkrea, and Leitrim. 

I have had hut little time during the past week to visit any of the Public Works, except on 
my progress through the above baronies to attend Relief Committees Many of these, I am 
happy to report, are making every effort to introduce a plentiful supply of food into their re- 
spective localities, and in some, soup kitchens are in full operation, by which a vast amount of 
destitute people are relieved. The state of the country is tranquil; robberies of sheep, &c., 
less frequent than heretofore. Many deaths have taken place in the above baronies, all attributed 
to starvation ; llie change of food, not ihe actual want of it, with exposure to inclement weather, 
and insufficient clothing, are principally the cause. A man was found dead on the road, near 
Woodford last week, aud ever} body had it that he died of want, but it was found that he had 
drank loo much, lay down on the road and perished ; in his pocket 5s. or 6s. were found. 

The Committees at length admit the error they committed in not scutinizing their labour 
lists; already many improper objects of relief have been removed from the books. The demand 
for employment of fresh hands upon the works continues unabated. 

Throughout the different baronies, the better order of farmers are preparing the ground for

Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Godisy, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 6th February, 1S47. 

In conjunction with Captain Dent, I attended the Drumsbambo Relief Committee, and also 
that of Carrick. There are soup kitchens established in both these places. 

There is very little agriculture going on in this barony. The people are quiet on the whole • 
but the night, before last an outrage was committed. A short distance from the town a farmer 
was robbed of 18/. and then placed at the back of the fire, and he is expected to die. 

Overseer Patrick White was struck down on Wednesday night by a stone thrown at him by 
one of the men belonging to some of the roads, that had been to Carrick-on-Shannon for pay- 
ment that day. 

Extract from Journal of Captain Layard, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

The land is certainly showing more signs of cultivation. But I am satisfied some not only 
inducement hut positive benefit must be held out at once to the tenant farmer to enable him to 
till and crop the land for next year’s harvest. 1 would suggest that seed might be furnished 
by Government to the landlords as a loan in the first instance, to be recovered when the crops 
arrive at maturity The drainage will, I trust, provide ample employment for six weeks, but 
not beyond the middle of April. 

One of the head overseers under Mr. Gisborne received a threatening communication this 
week. 

On travelling through the barony (Mohill), I perceived a greater number of men employed 
in the fields than heretofore. 

The assistant-engineer reported to me that two men had fallen down dead from exhaustion 
on Monday last, as they went home from their work. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Bull, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 6th February, 1847. 

The want of food and support is strikingly visible ill the features and deportment of the 
labouring class, producing indolence and lethargy. The people in these districts are generally 
poor, depending entirely upon their potato crops, the nature of their small tenements being such 
that com will not grow upon them ; hence their disinclination to attempt to dig their land. 
The almost total absence of resident gentry to give them assistance and encouragement, causes 
them to be almost entirely dependent upon the Public Works for support. 

Sickness prevails to a great extent, and many deaths, but not attributable to actual starvation. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Godby, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week ending 
13th February, 1847. 

The people are patient, but in great distress in this barony (Mohill) ; 30 people died in the 
poor-house during the past week ; 43 people have died in the vicinity of Drumod since the 
oth of January. Two cart-loads of children, whose parents died from starvation I suppose, 
were sent to the poor-house, but could not be taken in, the fever prevailing to such a dreadful 
extent there. A man was found dead in the snow just outside the town of Mohill, on Thursday 
1 1 th instant. These facts will prove the necessity lor the establishment of a provision depot 
at this town. 



Extract from the Journal of Captain Layard, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for 
week ending 13th February, 1847. 

The severity of the weather has of course prevented the possibility of the land being tilled. 
I therefore consider it advisable that steps be adopted by the Government to induce and 
encourage the small farmers to get the crops put down without delay. 



Extract from Journal of Mr. Godby, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week ending 
13th Febiuary, 1847. 

In consequence of the severity of the weather, very few of the works have been carried on 
during this week ; some labourers have been employed in clearing the snow from the mail - 
coach roads.

Extract from Journal of Captain Bruce, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week LEITRIM, 
ending 13th February, 1847. 

The distress of the people is greatly on the increase ; and the poor-house being full, their 
whole dependence is upon the Public Works. The greatest disinclination is shown to receive 
any other employment; and indeed the backwardness of the season, and the nature of this part 
of the country, afford at present few means of giving support in the way of agricultural em- 
ployment. 



Extract from Report of Lieutenant Godby, R.A., Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for 
week ending 27th February, 1S47. 

The Ballinamore Relief Committees are most unbusiness-like, and very irregular in the time 
of meeting and attendance of members. 

J visited the soup kitchen at Carrigallen ; it appeared to be very well managed and kept ; 
the meal store was empty, the demand being so great that it is found almost impossible to 
keep a sufficient stock in hand. 



Extract from Report of Captain Bull, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week ending 
20th February, 1847. 

I beg to state that I have used every exertion to induce the Committees to strike persons off 
the lists who have means of supporting themselves, or who ought to be employed in the fields, 
but I have failed; and the only ones who have been struck off are those I have ascertained to 
be improper persons to receive relief. On the other hand, the demand for employment increases 
daily. At one Committee application was made for upwards of 600 people to be received on 
the lists ; and on my representing the total impracticability of such being done, I was told by 
one of the Committee, "that he should seud the. starving and dead bodies in carts to my 
house.” I consider it right to mention this, in order that the Board may see the difficulties 
and annoyances that the Inspecting Officers are exposed to by the admission of improper 
persons upon Committees. 



Extract from Journal of Lieutenant Godby, R.A., Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for 
week ending 20th February, 1847. 

The country is quiet and the people are patient; disease and destitution is on the increase; 
no less than 15 deaths have taken place since 13th instant in the Union poorhouse. The price 
of food is so great, that even the wages that the people get on the Public Works is not sufficient 
to feed themselves and family. 

There has been more work going on in the fields this week than I have remarked heretofore, 
though still not so much as I conceive ought to be the case. 

I have also remarked a great number of people who appeared to he quitting the country 
during the past week. 



Extract from Journal of Captain Lugard, Inspecting Officer, County Leitrim, for week 
ending 20th February, 1847. 

The greatest credit is due to the admirable way the meal fund and soup kitchens are con- 
ducted under the superintendence and personal inspection daily of the Rev. Mr. H. O'Brien, 
and Rev. W. M. Lawler. This remark is also applicable to ihe Carrigallen Relief Committee 
district. An effort is being made to till the lands, but not to the extent which is carried on in 
the neighbouring county, Cavan. * ‘ 

I observed a larger portion of ground dug for cultivation as I travelled along the roads this 
week.

As far as my own observation goes, and from all I can learn from 
constant inquiries, the farming operations in this county are in a

These observations apply to this county, as compared with others,

Limerick . . . 


Upper Conuelloe 


D. D. Poner 


In my travelling through the country. I find no disposition on the 
pare of the lower order of small farmers to till their own grounds, 
and unless something is done to induce them to do so, and speedily, 
the country will be in a ruinous state of want and waste the ensu- 
ing year. 

I look upon the agricultural interest being ruined for want of 
labourers to aid iu the usual husbandry or tilling; as the farmers 
now cannot afford to pav the labourers the hire they now draw on 
the Public Works. 


Limerick . 


Keury 


John Kelly . 


The labour in this barony seems to be very backward, the wheat crop 
excepted. 

Those holding large farms only are preparing their lands for the 
ensuing crop of oats. The small farmers are doing nothing at 
present ; I have not seen three men doing any spade labour in their 
little farms during the time I have been travelling to and from the 
roads I have been engaged in valuing in the different parts of this 
barony. 

I made inquiry of some of the small farmers why they were not 
preparing for the ensuing crop ; some said thev were not able to 
spare time from the Public Works, as they had no means of sup- 
port ; whilst others, perhaps with more truth, said they did not 
usually sow their oats until about the 25th March. 

Many of the larger farmers say they will plant from one to four 
or five acres of potatoes this season. 

The wheat crops are looking well, in my opinion, though some 
farmers have been telling me there is a great failuie in the wheat iu 
several places, but such has not come under my observations. 

1 do not see here, ns in the north of Ireland, manure heaps in the 
fields in every direction ready for scattering on the lands. The 
farmers here seem to do nothing during the winter months, and 
only begin late in the spring to prepare for the sowing of oats.

F. Blood » 



F. Thornley . 



• Although the weather has been remarkably fine for all agricultural 
purposes, I am very soriy to say I find in these baronies, and 
indeed generally in this district (Ballinasloe), the greatest indif- 
ference and inactivity among the small farmers, up to 10 or 15 
acres, with only few exceptions ; and having now for the last six 
weeks walked on foot through a good deal of this district in retired 
and remote parts, through which new lines of road are being made, 
I find, upon examination, a great want of seed oats and barley, and 
a positive certainty, unless it be supplied from some quarter imme- 
diately, of hundreds and hundreds acres of valuable soil remaining 
uncultivated. 

. The town land ofTobermakee is of very good quality, but held in 
small parcels not exceeding two acres and two roods' to each tenant 
and several not so much, and again the small holdings are subdi- 
vided into three, four, and five divisions each in rundale, or that a 
tenant may have his three or four ridges in different and remote 
parts of. the townland ; and until the new road was made, thev 
were obliged to cross over each other’s land to get at their own. 

The townland of Rockeshard is tolerably well divided into five- 
acre faras, and the consequence is that there are better farms, and 
a better system of farming is pursued. 

The townland of Ballybride is a good sheep farm in old lea • 
the other townlands of Sheevanogue, Autoher, and Ardballaghboy’ 
are convenient to the town of Roscommon, and generally held by- 
townspeople, or persons connected with them. 

The management of this ground is better, both manured, and 
more in accordance with the approved rule of farming. 

In my journey to Tobermakee and Rockeshard, “and the other 
places, during the week, I was pleased to observe a good many 
ploughs stretched, and numbers of people digging, especially in the 
gardens, and yet all is lamentably dull and deficient in preparin'* 
for and putting down the usual spring crops. 

A great many, indeed, of the poor landholders would not be able 
to subsist, independent of the Public Works, during the time neces- 
sary for cropping the ground, and others could not procure seed 
even if the ground was prepared for it. 

These are the difficulties to provide for — first, the support of the 
people while preparing the land; and, second, the providing of 
seed, and seeing that it is really put down in the ground after it is 
prepared for it.
